Position Paper: Aging
Room: Workshop 0
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper
Duration: 90 Minutes
Towards an inclusive healthy ageing agenda that accommodates the healthcare needs and limitations in older migrants
Prof. Dr. Adrian Stanciu | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Adrian Stanciu | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Modern society is changing with increasing international migration in contexts of demographic ageing. Technological advancement facilitates timely diagnosis, treatment and prevention promoting a longer life in many people. However, socioeconomic inequalities disproportionately impact individuals in processes of growing old while maintaining high levels of health throughout the lifespan. People growing old in a foreign country—the older migrant population—are especially vulnerable due to systemic discrimination and a pervasive under-representation in research and policy. I argue that national and global healthy ageing agendas must accommodate the specific healthcare needs and limitations in older migrants and thus create inclusive personalized healthcare and sustainable future societies.

I will draw in my presentation on an initiative to long-term assessment, evaluation, and intervention that is tailored to specifics in older migrants. International interdisciplinary experts convened in Luxembourg with representatives of public and private institutions for three days in March 2025 to co-create an action plan. First, I will provide an overview of the risk factors and health inequalities that are unique to migrants. Second, I will highlight the advantages and limitations of digital technology solutions in this population. Finally, I will discuss at length the four foci of the proposed action plan structured after challenges, goals, and solutions: a) sustainable and ethical sampling and recruitment, b) theoretical, methodological, and practical relevance, c) integration of self-reported and digital data, and d) data-related, ethical, and legal aspects.

Can we simulate the effect of aging experimentally? Recent findings from studies with age simulation suits
Prof. Dr. Sabine Schaefer | Saarland University | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Sabine Schaefer | Saarland University | Germany

Age simulation suits have received increased research attention in the last years (for a review, see Gerhardy et al., 2022). The suits aim to mimick sensory declines via blurred googles, ear protections, and gloves, and reductions in whole-body physical strength and flexibility via bandages around the joints, additional weights, and “wobbly” overshoes. Note, however, that the constraints are only peripheral, since the neural integrity of the brain is not affected when wearing the suit. I argue that age simulation suits enable researchers to assess the link between perceptual and cognitive decline in aging (Roberts & Allen, 2016). Recent studies have shown that the suit reduces gross- and fine-motor performances of young adults to the level of older adults, and wearing the suit also affects mood and physical state (Vieweg & Schaefer, 2020). Performance in a motor sequence learning task while sitting on a chair did not suffer in young adults when wearing the suit (Vieweg et al., 2023). However, we found age- and suit-related differences in a whole-body motor sequence learning task (Heggenberger et al., 2025), including suit-induced reductions in explicit sequence recall following the learning the phase. Wearing the suit also made task-difficulty choices of young adults more conservative, and more similar to the choices of older adults, when stepping over a crossbar (Schaefer et al., 2025). The discussion will focus on possibilities and limitations of using age simulation suits in future research.

Room: Workshop +1
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper

08:30 am
The Art of Getting Things Done
Prof. Dr. Nicola Baumann | Universität Trier | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Nicola Baumann | Universität Trier | Germany
Dr. Katja Friederichs | Denmark

“I have never tried that before, so I should definitely be able to do it.” This quote from Astrid Lindgren’s character Pippi Longstocking illustrates a unique self-regulatory ability: the ability to shift from low positive affect (e.g. recognizing the difficulty of a new task) to high positive affect (e.g. developing the confidence to master that difficulty). The ability for affective shifting is a vital key for intention enactment (Baumann & Scheffer, 2010). Studies have shown that interventions designed to practice affective shifting lead to more effective intention enactment in both the Stroop task and the personal goal domain (Friederichs et al., 2020, 2022). In my talk, I will derive the principle of affective shifting from the theory of Personality Systems Interactions (PSI; Kuhl, 2000, 2001; Kuhl et al., 2021). As a primer: intention enactment requires the collaboration of two antagonistically related cognitive systems (intention memory and intuitive behavior control), which are activated by opposite affective states. Affective shifting opens a short "window of opportunity" during which both cognitive systems are equally activated and able to exchange information effectively, enabling intentions to be smoothly translated into action (Kuhl, 2018). In my talk, I will (a) introduce several easy-to-apply exercises that train affective shifting, (b) show the beneficial effects of these exercises on multiple indicators of self-regulation, and (c) compare the PSI-driven approach with other theories and interventions aimed at closing the intention-behavior gap.

09:15 am
Positive psychology: An overview and debate regarding its position in academic psychology in Germany
Samuel Tomczyk | Universitätsmedizin Rostock | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Samuel Tomczyk | Universitätsmedizin Rostock | Germany
Dr. Christina Ewert | Institute of Psychology, University of Potsdam | Germany

Positive psychology, which deals with the question of what makes people happy and satisfied, is a relatively young subdiscipline of psychology, but as a cross-cutting topic in psychology, it represents an important perspective on human experience and behaviour. It examines positive subjective experiences, strengths, and resources in individuals and groups, as well as organizational and institutional conditions that promote them. Research has shown that this perspective is particularly valuable in times of crisis to foster resiliency and well-being. It has become increasingly popular since the early 2000s and is academically established internationally through specific research and development tracks, training and continuing education programs, as well as academic chairs and institutes. However, this is not the case in Germany and the discipline itself is not without flaws (e.g., issues of unclear terminology, replication, or differentiation). Nevertheless, due to its potential and its wide-spread popularity, it is important to invite scholarly debate on the role of positive psychology in Germany and the DGPs. This position paper provides an overview of key developments, milestones, and the current state of positive psychology. By highlighting the achievements and added value of positive psychology as an independent discipline, it aims to advocate for giving this line of work more visibility in German-speaking academic psychology (including in the DGPs), investigating the contributions to other fields of psychology, and stimulating discussions about possible means and opportunities for its institutionalization and position as an academic field of inquiry.

Advances towards a better understanding of psychiatric diseases using meta-analytical approaches
Chair(s) Veronika Müller (Research Centre Jülich)
Room: FR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Numerous neuroimaging studies have investigated the neural underpinnings of psychiatric diseases in the last two decades. Over the past few years, different directions towards utilization of the results of these studies for drawing meta-analytical conclusions have evolved. In four different talks the symposium will give a comprehensive overview of recent results from established as well as new meta-analytical approaches to highlight how their use can accelerate the understanding of psychiatric diseases.

Neuroimaging meta-analyses: Background, concepts and their use in clinical research
Edna Cieslik-Köchling | Heinrich-Heine-University
Show details
Authors:
Edna Cieslik-Köchling | Heinrich-Heine-University
Veronika Müller | Research Centre Jülich

In the last 25 years functional magnetic resonance imaging has evolved as a standard method to investigate the relationship between structure and function of the human brain in healthy participants but also to identify brain regions that show disturbances in psychiatric disorders. However, single functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies suffer from certain limitations that reduce the generalizability of the resulting effects. Neuroimaging meta-analyses allow to overcome some of these problems, by identifying regions consistently involved or altered across many studies. The talk will provide a conceptual overview on the method as well as applicability of coordinate-based meta-analysis and how this can be translated into clinical research to foster our understanding of aberrant neural responses in psychiatric disorders. Results of a recent transdiagnostic meta-analysis will be presented exemplary that investigated deficits in emotion processing across schizophrenic, bipolar as well as depressed patients to identify shared features of these disorders that may contribute to their overlapping symptoms. The transdiagnostic approach revealed that all three groups shared consistent disturbed activity within emotion-specific regions. This is particularly interesting as the general task-effects elicited in the healthy control groups showed partly different brain regions involved. These results challenge the common view of specific and separable diagnostic groups within the standard classification system but point towards shared deficits across disorders.

The effects of childhood adversity: Two specific neural patterns
Nils Kohn | Radboud University Medical Center | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:
Linlin Yan | Radboud University Medical Center
Eline Kraaijenvanger | Heidelberg University
Ricardo Wennekers | Radboud University Medical Center
Veronika Müller | Research Centre Jülich
Simon Eickhoff | Research Centre Jülich
Guillén Fernández | Radboud University Medical Center
Natalie Holz | Heidelberg University
Nils Kohn | Radboud University Medical Center | Netherlands

Childhood adversity (CA) is associated with increased lifetime risk for psychopathology, potentially mediated by altered brain function. Prior work suggests that CA affects emotion processing, reward processing, and cognitive control, but consistent neural substrates across these domains remain unclear. We conducted Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) meta-analyses of neuroimaging studies across three task domains: emotion processing, cognitive control, and reward processing. ALE revealed significant CA-related convergence in the left amygdala and insula. To characterize the functional roles of these clusters, Meta-Analytic Connectivity Modeling (MACM) and functional decoding were applied. Results identified two dissociable networks: an amygdala-centered emotion processing network and an insula-centered somatomotor processing network. These findings indicate that CA is associated with distinct alterations across multiple neural systems, providing insight into the neurobiological embedding of early adversity.

Mapping the Structural Brain Network of Psychopathy: Convergent Evidence from Humans and Chimpanzees
Jules Dugré | University of Michigan | United States
Show details
Authors:
Jules Dugré | University of Michigan | United States
Sam Vickery | Bochum University of Applied Sciences
Robert Latzman | Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization
William Hopkins | The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center
Felix Hoffstaedter | Research Centre Jülich
Stéphane De Brito | University of Birmingham

Psychopathy is a condition marked by profound emotional and interpersonal deficits that has long been hypothesized to arise from structural brain abnormalities. Yet neuroimaging findings have pointed to widely disparate locations, yielding inconsistent conclusions. Here, we sought to resolve these discrepancies by introducing a novel meta-analytic framework. We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, and SCOPUS. Using structural covariance analyses, we tested whether the divergent locations reported across studies might reflect a shared neuroanatomical network. To validate this network, we first assessed its correspondence to 17 focal brain lesions known to be temporally causal for antisocial behaviors. Cross-species analyses were further conducted to test whether psychopathic traits predicted variation in this brain network across chimpanzees and humans.
Our systematic search identified 20 samples with spatially heterogeneous foci. We observed that these locations converged onto a common network encompassing the insular and prefrontal cortices. Remarkably, this network strongly overlapped with brain regions damaged in patients who developed antisocial behavior following lesions (r = .93). Moreover, psychopathic traits significantly predicted variation within this network in humans (16% explained variance) and chimpanzees (21%), highlighting that the neural architecture underlying psychopathy is evolutionarily conserved. Our findings demonstrate that structural brain alterations observed in individuals with psychopathy span a distributed neural system rather than isolated regions. This framework provides a unifying account for decades of inconsistent results and advances our understanding of the clinical, biological, and evolutionary bases of psychopathy.

Category- and data-driven meta-analyses: Comparison of different approaches for identification of consistent aberrant brain activation in psychiatric disorders
Changyi Kuang | Research Centre Jülich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Changyi Kuang | Research Centre Jülich | Germany
Lennart Frahm | Research Centre Jülich
Masoud Tahmasian | Research Centre Jülich
Carmen Morawetz | University of Innsbruck
Jules Dugré | University of Michigan
Leonhard Schilbach | LVR-Klinikum Düsseldorf
Simon Eickhoff | Research Centre Jülich

Neuroimaging meta-analyses are widely used to identify convergent aberrant brain activation in patients. Among clinical features, emotional dysfunction is one of prominent symptoms in several psychiatric diseases. Transdiagnostic investigation of emotion processing deficits may thus provide valuable insights into potential general psychiatric biomarkers. However, classic transdiagnostic meta-analyses might miss relevant effects that are shared across specific subgroups (e.g. shared symptoms) of studies different to known categorization systems. To address this issue, we used in addition to classical meta-analyses, a data-driven approach that combines neuroimaging meta-analyses with hierarchical clustering. We compared data- and category-driven meta-analyses, investigating if the results of these approaches differ or complement each other. In total, 302 studies reporting 510 experiments were included. Across all diagnostic groups consistent aberrant activity during emotional processing were found in bilateral amygdala, anterior and posterior cingulate cortex and left precentral gyrus. Classic category driven analyses per disease category revealed only few regions of convergence. Data-driven analyses pointed to clustering of experiments into several distinct groups, with one large group consisting of multiple disease categories sharing convergent aberrant activation in a similar but more extensive network than the overall ungrouped analysis. The remaining clusters were more specific but still consisted of multiple disease categories sharing convergent aberrant activation in visual-parietal areas. In summary, results point to shared aberrant activation during emotion processing across several disorders found in both types of meta-analytical approaches and indicate that data-driven clustering of experiments may reveal additional insights that are not captured by the classical category driven approach.

Topic:
Form of presentation: Research Talk
Duration: 90 Minutes
Wenn die Saison Spuren hinterlässt – Ausmaß und Stabilität von Angst- und Depressionssymptomen bei Elite- und Amateurfußballspielerinnen
Leslie Carleton-Schweitzer | TSG ResearchLab / Universität Heidelberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leslie Carleton-Schweitzer | TSG ResearchLab / Universität Heidelberg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jan Keller | Universität Heidelberg
Dr. Philipp Röthlin | Universität Bern / Eidgenössische Hochschule für Sport Magglingen
Dr. Lena Steindorf | TSG ResearchLab / Universität Heidelberg

Im Bereich der psychischen Gesundheit stehen Fußballspielerinnen durch einerseits zunehmende öffentliche Sichtbarkeit und steigende Leistungserwartungen und andererseits begrenzte Unterstützungsstrukturen vor besonderen Herausforderungen. Gleichzeitig mangelt es in der Forschung an großangelegten Längsschnittstudien, die die Entwicklung und Veränderung von Symptomen psychischer Erkrankungen abbilden und so ein tieferes Verständnis für zeitliche Zusammenhänge und Risikophasen ermöglichen. In dieser Studie untersuchten wir daher Angst- und Depressionssymptome bei N = 406 Fußballspielerinnen unterschiedlicher Altersgruppen (Alter: 12-17, n = 206; 18-24, n = 134; 25 oder älter, n = 66) aus sechs deutschen Amateur- und fünf Bundesligavereinen. Zu vier Messzeitpunkten innerhalb der Saison 2024/25 erfassten wir Symptome über etablierte Screening-Fragebögen (Allgemeine Depressionsskala; Generalized Anxiety Disorder Screener). Neben Punkt- und 10-Monats-Prävalenzen wurden mithilfe von latenten Wachstumsmodellen die Stabilität und Veränderung der Symptome im Saisonverlauf untersucht. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass 20–30 % der Spielerinnen Angstsymptome und 15–25 % Depressionssymptome oberhalb der empirischen Schwellenwerte berichteten. Die 10-Monats-Prävalenz lag bei 46,3% für Angstsymptome und 35,5% für Depressionssymptome. Latente Wachstumsmodelle belegten größtenteils stabile Symptomausprägungen mit signifikanten interindividuellen Unterschieden. Zusätzlich konnten wir signifikante lineare und quadratische Verläufe der Angst- und Depressionssymptome über den Saisonverlauf feststellen. Die vorliegende Studie zeigt, dass Fußballspielerinnen ähnlich hohe Prävalenzen von Angst- und Depressionssymptomen aufwiesen wie junge Frauen in der deutschen Allgemeinbevölkerung. Die Symptome blieben dabei im Saisonverlauf recht stabil, wobei manche Spielerinnen konstant belasteter waren als andere. Dennoch waren Symptome in der Saisonmitte erhöht. Insgesamt liefert die Studie wichtige Einblicke und unterstreicht die Relevanz regelmäßiger Screenings, um psychische Belastungen frühzeitig zu erkennen und gezielte Interventionen für Spielerinnen anzubieten.

Heat perceptions, behaviors, and barriers of homeless individuals in Germany
Philipp Sprengholz | University of Bamberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Philipp Sprengholz | University of Bamberg | Germany
Robert Bruckmann | University of Bamberg

The increasing frequency, duration, and severity of heatwaves raises critical public health concerns, particularly for marginalized populations such as the homeless. Employing a mixed-methods approach, we investigated homeless individuals' heat perceptions, coping behaviors, and barriers via semi-structured interviews (N = 9) to inform the design of a follow-up quantitative survey administered across 13 German cities (N = 252). Results revealed that many homeless people experience fatigue, nausea, or faintness on hot days while underestimating health risks related to severe heat. They face various challenges in coping with heat (including inadequate access to hydration and cooling spaces), take medication that exacerbates heat risks (while dosage and storage practices are rarely adapted to high temperatures), and often neglect adequate sun protection. Overall, the results warrant urgent policy interventions such as establishing dedicated cooling shelters and improving access to hydration resources. Furthermore, information-based interventions should raise awareness regarding heat-related health risks and protective actions amongst homeless populations, stakeholders working with them, and the general public.

Emerging and Context-Dependent Attentional Avoidance in Childhood Social Anxiety Disorder: A Naturalistic Eye-Tracking Study
Nadine Vietmeier | Humboldt Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nadine Vietmeier | Humboldt Universität Berlin | Germany
Dr. Nik Dietze | Bielefeld University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Brunna Tuschen-Caffier | University of Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julia Asbrand | University of Jena | Germany

Social anxiety disorder (SAD) in childhood has been linked to biased attention toward social threat, often conceptualized as a vigilance–avoidance pattern. However, empirical findings in child and adolescent samples remain inconsistent, particularly in naturalistic and stressful contexts. We hypothesized increased early gaze to audience faces followed by attentional avoidance over time.
Using mobile eye-tracking, we examined second-by-second gaze behavior in children aged 9–14 years with SAD (n = 37) and healthy controls (HC; n = 41) during two peer-evaluative speech tasks. Between tasks, participants were randomly assigned to parental support or self-instruction.
In the first speech task, both groups showed a comparable decline in gaze to audience faces over time, providing no evidence for the predicted vigilance–avoidance pattern. In the second speech task, children with SAD exhibited lower fixation probability than HC in frequentist analyses, whereas Bayesian analyses were inconclusive. Fixation durations did not differ between groups. Exploratory analyses indicated a group × condition interaction: self-instruction increased fixation probability in children with SAD but decreased it in HC, while parental support showed the opposite pattern. Age moderated gaze trajectories, with older children with SAD showing a stronger decline in fixation probability across time compared to HC.
Overall, attentional avoidance in childhood SAD appears subtle and context-dependent, emerging more clearly under repeated social stress and shaped by developmental factors and support strategies. These findings suggest that vigilance–avoidance models may require refinement in developmental and ecologically valid contexts. Mobile eye-tracking offers insights into attentional dynamics in naturalistic tasks, while highlighting methodological challenges.

Job and home crafting on Mars – and how it affects astronauts’ well-being and performance
Prof. Dr. Vera Hagemann | Universität Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Vera Hagemann | Universität Bremen | Germany
Florian Schönig | University of Bremen
Dr. Katharina Klug | University of Bremen | Germany
Dr. Christiane Heinicke | Universität Bremen

On long-duration space missions, the separation of work and personal life is a significant social stressor that can result in memory and concentration impairments, social withdrawal and slower reaction times. A great challenge is managing the stressors of the two life domains of work and home to ensure the safe execution of a mission. One way of dealing with these challenges is to adapt work and home to the individual preferences of the crew members.
Due to the increased autonomy of crews on long-term voyages, they should have opportunities to engage in job and home-crafting behaviours. No findings are available on this subject at present. This study examines the daily use of these behaviours and their relationship to the mental health and performance of astronauts.
During the World’s Biggest Analog with seven participating habitats worldwide, analog astronauts (N = 28) in isolation were assessed daily for two weeks on job (JC) and home-crafting (HC), well-being, cognitive irritation, psychosomatic symptoms, work engagement, and job performance. Data was analysed with multilevel analyses.
Perceived autonomy was associated with both JC and HC behaviours on both levels. JC and HC were significantly related to job performance, work engagement, cognitive irritation and psychosomatic symptoms on both within-person and between-person levels. Well-being was significant primarily at the between-person level with JC and HC.
Experienced autonomy in future long-term space travel enables new approaches to promoting mental health and the performance of astronauts. Preparatory training and strategies for promoting JC and HC need to be developed.

Developmental Perspectives on Social Motivation and Relationships
Chair(s) Dr. Iris V. Wahring (University of Vienna)
Co-chair(s) Dr. Tita Gonzalez Avilés (Otto Friedrich University Bamberg)
Room: NL
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium examines the development of social motivation, perception, and interpersonal relationships across the adult lifespan, moving from broad generational patterns to the nuances of daily life in old age. The session opens with Katja Witte’s study on intergenerational similarities, which investigates how social approach and avoidance motivations differ across three generations within families. Zooming into younger age groups specifically, Amina Aissaoui explores the plasticity of social perception during young adulthood, investigating how the high density of life events in this life phase shapes the stability of perceiver positivity. The focus then shifts to the stability of close bonds in Iris Wahring’s research, which identifies predictors of relationship dissolution and examines whether these predictors differ between young and middle adulthood. Moving from individual relationships to broader relational trends, Lisa Klasen analyzes historical changes in loneliness trajectories, investigating whether macro-level developments have altered the experience of emotional and social loneliness in the second half of life. Finally, Tita Gonzalez Avilés offers a detailed examination of the daily lives of older adults, utilizing experience sampling and physiological markers to elucidate how living arrangements and daily social interactions influence the well-being of the oldest old. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate that social functioning is a dynamic developmental process, shaped by life-stage-specific challenges and the broader context in which individuals age.

Across Generations: Social Approach and Avoidance Motivation Within Families
Dr. Katja Witte | Humboldt University of Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katja Witte | Humboldt University of Berlin | Germany
Prof. Jana Nikitin | University of Vienna | Austria

Social approach and avoidance motivation are central drivers of interpersonal behavior, yet little is known about whether these motivational orientations are shared within families. The present study examines intergenerational similarities and differences in social approach and avoidance motivation within families comprising three generations. Data were collected via online self-report questionnaires from N = 159 families, each including one child, one parent, and one grandparent. Measurement invariance across generations was tested. Results supported partial scalar invariance for approach motivation (with one freely estimated intercept) and scalar invariance for avoidance motivation, indicating that the construct structure remains largely stable across generations. Mean-level analyses showed that parents and grandparents reported higher approach motivation than children, while grandparents reported higher avoidance motivation than children and parents. To examine family-level clustering, intraclass correlations (ICCs) were calculated for approach and avoidance motivation. Results revealed that between-family variance exceeded within-family variance. In addition, associations with psychosocial outcomes, like well-being and loneliness, were examined. Further results and implications will be discussed. The study highlights the importance of adopting a developmental perspective when investigating social motivation and its implications for potential outcomes.

Seeing Others in a Positive Light: Stability and Predictors of Change in Perceiver Positivity
Amina Aissaoui | HMU Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Amina Aissaoui | HMU Potsdam | Germany
Prof. Richard Rau | HMU Potsdam | Germany
Prof. Johannes Zimmermann | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Michael Dufner | Witten/Herdecke University | Germany
Christoph Heine | Witten/Herdecke University | Germany

People consistently differ in how positively versus negatively they evaluate others’ personalities across traits and situations. This perceiver positivity is a core aspect of social perception and psychosocial functioning, influencing how individuals navigate their social environments and maintain interpersonal relationships. Although perceiver positivity has been found to be quite stable over a period of approximately two weeks, it has also been shown to change in response to social experiences during that time. Yet, it has remained unclear (1) if there is also stability over several months and (2) if social experiences and other life events exhibit lasting changes in positivity during these periods. To address these issues, we administered the Online Tool for Assessing Perceiver Effects (O-TAPE) in a sample of 454 individuals at four measurement occasions, each spaced 2 months apart. Focusing on young adults, the study captures a life phase characterized by frequent interpersonal and role transitions, providing a relevant context for examining longer-term change in perceiver positivity. The study employs a longitudinal structural equation modeling (SEM) approach to explore changes in positivity over time. We first evaluate the reliability and stability of generalized perceiver positivity. Then, we explore various predictors of changes in positivity, including individual differences in personality traits, indicators of psychological well-being, and life events. Together, these analyses will clarify how stable individual differences and dynamic life experiences influence perceiver positivity.

Predicting Relationship Dissolution in Young and Middle Adulthood
Dr. Iris V. Wahring | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Iris V. Wahring | Austria
Prof. Janina Larissa Bühler | University of Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Denis Gerstorf | Humboldt University of Berlin | Germany
Prof. Jana Nikitin | University of Vienna | Austria

Today, most romantic relationships in Western societies eventually end in a break-up. While prior research indicates that relationship factors are stronger predictors of dissolution than individual characteristics, a comprehensive analysis that simultaneously considers a broad range of demographic and psychosocial variables at both the individual and relationship level is still missing. Age-related motivational shifts—such as an increasing preference for emotionally meaningful goals—also raise the question of whether predictors like conflict frequency differ in their relevance between young and middle adulthood. Furthermore, although some studies have incorporated partner data, it remains unclear to what extent including information from both partners adds predictive value. In preregistered analyses based on the German Family Panel and 5,249 documented dissolutions, we assessed the extent to which 35 variables, including the Big Five, well-being, autonomy, and conflict frequency, predict relationship dissolution. We compared the predictive value of autonomy and emotion-related variables between younger and middle-aged adults. Additionally, for the subsample with available partner data, we examined whether incorporating information from both partners enhances prediction accuracy. We outline emerging patterns in individual and relationship predictors of dissolution and clarify the role of age, as well as the value of considering partner data in predicting dissolution.

Historical Changes in Emotional and Social Loneliness Trajectories in the Second Half of Life
Lisa Joanne Klasen | SHARE BERLIN Institute | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lisa Joanne Klasen | SHARE BERLIN Institute | Germany
Dr. Oliver Huxhold | The German Centre of Gerontology | Germany

Even before the onset of the pandemic, public discourse had framed loneliness as an increasingly prevalent issue, suggesting that more people than ever before experience loneliness. However, macro-level developments such as the expansion of education, improved healthcare access, and changes in social norms would suggest a decrease in loneliness levels over historical time. Empirical evidence regarding historical changes in loneliness is mixed. Discrepancies may arise because many studies have examined loneliness as a global construct. This approach overlooks potential differences between emotional loneliness, which reflects the perceived absence of close connections, and social loneliness, which reflects the perceived absence of a wider social network. Previous research that examined only changes in overall loneliness levels may have overlooked important divergent trends in these two types of loneliness, potentially leading to biased conclusions. This study addresses this research gap and investigates whether aging trajectories of emotional and social loneliness have changed over the course of historical time. Further, we test whether potential changes can be explained by historical differences in health, education, and perceptions of aging. For longitudinal analyses, cohort-sequential data from the German Ageing Survey, collected between 1996 and 2017 from people aged 40 to 85 years (N = 19,654), were used. Cohort centering was applied to investigate historical differences in individual age trajectories of emotional and social loneliness. This method accounts for cohort effects and historical change.

Living Alone and Daily Social Interactions in Later Life: Implications for Affect and Salivary Cortisol
Dr. Tita Gonzalez Avilés | Otto Friedrich University Bamberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tita Gonzalez Avilés | Otto Friedrich University Bamberg | Germany
Dr. Minxia Luo | University of Zurich | Switzerland
Ass. Prof. Theresa Pauly | Simon Fraser University | Canada
Prof. Christiane A. Hoppmann | University of British Columbia | Canada
Prof. Dr. Gizem Hülür | Otto Friedrich University Bamberg | Germany

A growing number of older adults in Western societies live alone. Since living arrangements influence opportunities for daily social contact and access to support, they may significantly impact how older adults experience and benefit from social interactions. This study examines whether older adults living alone are more sensitive to the emotional and physiological consequences of daily social encounters. Specifically, we test whether naturally occurring face-to-face social interactions predict daily well-being and cortisol levels and whether these associations differ between individuals living alone and those living with others. We analyzed event-contingent experience-sampling data from 118 older adults (ages 65–94 years; approximately 40% living alone) in German-speaking Switzerland. Over 21 days, participants reported all social interactions and their perceived quality (N = 11,171 valid records), completed daily evening assessments of well-being (i.e., positive and negative affect, loneliness) and provided saliva samples six times per day across three days. We estimated the associations between constructs both between and within individuals using multilevel modeling. The findings will clarify how everyday social experiences shape emotional and physiological functioning in later life and highlight living arrangements as a key context.

Bridging Psychometrics and Psychology in AI-Enhanced Education
Chair(s) Dr. Rudolf Debelak (University of Zurich/EPFL)
Room: FI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) into educational settings offers transformative potential for assessment, personalization, and feedback. However, utilizing these technologies necessitates a rigorous synthesis of advanced machine learning capabilities with established psychometric theory and psychological principles to ensure validity, fairness, and effectiveness. This symposium brings together four contributions that address the broad topic of AI in Education.
The first two contributions focus on enhancing the psychometric validity of AI applications. Liu and Fink address the challenge of defining relationships between items and latent attributes (Q-matrices) in Cognitive Diagnostic Models. They propose a hierarchical Bayesian Dawid-Skene framework that aggregates predictions from multiple zero-shot LLMs to statistically estimate "true" Q-matrix entries and quantify uncertainty. Debelak, Vignoud, and Tomasik subsequently present a hybrid framework for Automated Essay Scoring (AES). They demonstrate that using Item Response Theory (IRT) to generate psychometrically adjusted "ground truth" scores before fine-tuning transformer-based models reduces measurement bias and improves predictive accuracy.
Moving from assessment to adaptive support, Krishna and Tomasik introduce a personalized recommendation framework that integrates curriculum knowledge graphs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to support progressive and self-driven learning.
Finally, Qin and Schneider examine how learners perceive AI as a social cue. This experimental study investigates how the source of feedback - framed as AI, human, or human-supervised AI - impacts learning outcomes through the mediating variables of trust, motivation, emotion, and cognitive load.

Integrating Multiple Zero-Shot LLMs for Q-Matrix Construction: A Hierarchical Bayesian Dawid–Skene Framework
Dr. Tuo Liu | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tuo Liu | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany
Dr. Aron Fink | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany

Accurate specification of the Q-matrix is fundamental to cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs), as it defines the relationships between items and the latent attributes they measure. However, Q-matrix construction typically relies on expert judgment and iterative refinement based on data-model fit indices, making it time-consuming and subjective, particularly for complex or multidimensional assessments. Recent advances in zero-shot large language models (LLMs) enable automated inference of item–attribute relationships without domain-specific training, yielding a promising alternative. Yet, LLM predictions vary across models and prompts, introducing substantial uncertainty that necessitates statistically grounded aggregation.

We propose a hierarchical Bayesian extension of the Dawid–Skene model to integrate probabilistic Q-matrix predictions from multiple zero-shot LLMs. Treating each LLM as a noisy annotator or rater, the model estimates latent “true” Q-entries while explicitly modeling annotator reliability and uncertainty. Two complementary approaches are introduced: (1) an independent-entry hierarchical model that aggregates LLM outputs for each item–attribute pair, and (2) a dependent-entry extension that incorporates item-specific latent characteristics to capture dependencies among attributes within items. Both approaches yield posterior probabilities for Q-matrix entries that can be directly aggregated into Bayesian CDMs.

Performance will be evaluated using simulation studies varying test design, annotator reliability, and attribute dependencies, and through a real-data application to PISA reading items with expert-validated Q-matrices. These analyses are currently underway, and findings will be presented at the conference. The proposed framework aims to provide a statistically grounded way for automated Q-matrix construction using multiple LLMs.

Combining Classic Psychometrics and Machine Learning for Automated Essay Scoring
Dr. Rudolf Debelak | University of Zurich / EPFL | Switzerland

Authors:

Julien Vignoud | EPFL | Switzerland

The design of valid and fair automated essay scoring (AES) systems remains a persistent challenge in educational assessment, particularly regarding the reliability of training data. While large language models (LLMs) offer powerful generative capabilities, their integration with rigorous measurement theory remains an area of active research. In this presentation, we evaluate a novel hybrid framework that synthesizes latent variable modeling with modern natural language processing.

In our first step, we utilize psychometric models (specifically Item Response Theory) to disentangle rater effects and measurement error from student performance, thereby generating robust, high-quality "ground truth" scores. Subsequently, we fine-tune pre-trained transformer-based models to predict these psychometrically adjusted targets rather than raw score aggregates.

We illustrate this approach using a dataset of over 30,000 essays from a large-scale assessment in five German-speaking cantons of Switzerland, benchmarking performance against a standard approach that directly predicts raw human ratings. Results indicate that training on psychometrically refined data significantly improves predictive accuracy and reduces measurement bias compared to conventional training pipelines. We conclude by discussing how this synergy between psychometrics and AI can facilitate more scalable, valid, and fair educational outcomes.

Knowledge Graph-Enhanced GNN for Structured Personalized Learning Recommendation
Dr. Vaibhav Krishna, | University of Zurich | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Vaibhav Krishna, | University of Zurich | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Martin J. Tomasik | University of Zurich | Switzerland

Recent advances in computer-assisted learning systems have enabled increasingly personalized and interactive educational experiences. However, constructing adaptive learning pathways remains challenging due to the inherent overlap and interdependence among curriculum concepts. Existing knowledge tracing and recommendation approaches often treat learning resources or skills as independent units, limiting their ability to model structured knowledge progression and heterogeneous student preferences.
This ongoing research proposes a personalized recommendation framework that integrates curriculum knowledge graphs with graph neural networks (GNNs) to support progressive and self-driven learning. We represent conceptual dependencies as a knowledge graph and incorporate this relational structure into the recommendation process as an inductive bias. In parallel, student–resource interactions are modeled as a bipartite graph, enabling the joint learning of student and content representations. To capture heterogeneity in learning preferences and resource characteristics, we introduce a dual clustering mechanism that identifies latent groups of learners and educational materials. By learning correspondences between these clusters, the framework generates recommendations that align conceptual progression with individualized learning tendencies.
The proposed model aims to improve both predictive accuracy and pedagogical coherence in recommendation sequences. We plan to evaluate the model on data collected from a computer-based formative assessment system implemented in schools from Northwestern Switzerland, from grade 3 to grade 9. This research contributes toward more structured, adaptive, and sustainable learning experiences in digital education environments.

The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) in education has intensified interest in AI-generated feedback as a scalable alternative to human feedback. While feedback is a central mechanism of learning, its effectiveness depends not only on informational quality but also on learners’ perceptions of the feedback source. From a psychological perspective, feedback sources function as social and contextual cues that can trigger motivational, emotional, and cognitive processes during learning. However, it remains unclear whether learners trust AI as a feedback provider and how such trust shapes learning outcomes.
This study examines how the perceived source of feedback—AI, human, or human-supervised AI—affects learning outcomes through motivation, emotion, and cognitive load, and whether trust in AI moderates these relationships. Using a between-subject experimental design, university students complete an essay-writing task and receive AI-generated feedback guided by a standardized rubric, which is framed as originating from different sources. This approach controls the feedback criteria and structure while allowing the examination of psychological effects of feedback source perception.
Trust and emotional valence are assessed before and after feedback, while motivation and cognitive load are measured after feedback, followed by a revision task to assess learning outcomes. By conceptualizing feedback source as a social cue, this study contributes to psychological theories of learning with digital technologies and informs the responsible design of AI-supported feedback systems in higher education.

Mental Health of Students: Status, Prevention, Intervention
Chair(s) Dr. Monique Landberg (Pädagogische Hochschule Weingarten)
Room: GR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Studying at university offers many opportunities (Arnett, 2015); however, as the first paper in our symposium by Steinkühler et al. outlines, some groups like female students, students with children and students with health impairments are especially vulnerable. According to a health insurance report, German students’ mental health declined profoundly between 2015 and 2023 (Techniker Krankenkasse, 2023). Data from the US confirm that the situation in the US is similar for young people and students respectively (American College Health Association, 2024). The second paper in our symposium by Kählke et al. investigates preferences for delivery modes of mental health services among German first-year university students. Their findings highlight the need for tailoring interventions to increase treatment rates among students. As it is well known that learning is most effective and sustainable when learners are not stressed and feel safe (Porges, 2017), the last two papers look into interventions for students. Götz and Landberg compare a control with an intervention group who received a training incorporating various relaxation techniques throughout the semester. The goal is to test if, for example, if stress levels during the exam period are lower in the intervention group. The last paper by Landberg and Park, tests if being in different learner identity status interacted with being in the control or the intervention group regarding physiological measures in a mock exam situation. All papers try to shed light on the situation of students and how to improve treatment rates and well-being.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought students’ health and well-being into focus among researchers and university stakeholders alike. A growing body of literature highlights that the number of students experiencing health-related issues has risen across Europe in recent years (Hauschildt et al., 2024). Students are primarily affected by mental health problems like burnout, anxiety, and stress. Evidence from Germany shows that most students with health-related issues report mental health problems (Steinkühler et al., 2023). However, some groups like women, students with children and students with health impairments are more vulnerable. They experienced significantly higher stress levels during the COVID-19 pandemic than non-vulnerable student groups (Zimmer et al., 2021).
Using data from “The student survey in Germany” (2021), a nationwide student survey covering students’ health, we first show that women, students with care responsibilities and financial difficulties report higher levels of mental stress. Second, we investigate the mediating power of academic and social integration on differences in self-reported stress. We find that academic integration, especially satisfaction with academic performance and perceived fit with the academic system, along with support from teaching staff, significantly lowers students’ stress levels. Our results emphasize that there are clear differences in the stress levels of different student groups – even after the COVID-19 pandemic. Academic integration seems to be a crucial factor for explaining differences in students’ mental health. However, many questions regarding causal relationships remain unanswered yet, even though clarifying them is essential for evidence-based policy advice and institutional interventions.

Most university students with mental disorders remain untreated, creating a critical need to understand how mental health services can be tailored to improve utilization and outcomes. Using data from 1,376 students participating in the German arm of the World Mental Health International College Student Survey (WMH-ICS, 2017–2018), we assessed preferences across a range of intervention targets (disorder-specific, study-related, and general well-being areas) and delivery modes such as in-person, group, internet- and mobile-based interventions (IMIs), and blended formats.
Results indicated that in-person delivery modes were most frequently accepted (71–76% of students), followed by moderate acceptance of IMIs (45–55%), and lower acceptance of group formats (31–36%). In multivariate analyses, having a self-reported mental disorder, believing in the effectiveness of digital treatments, and lower intention to use services were each associated with greater preference for IMIs over in-person modalities. Prior treatment experience, conversely, predicted a stronger preference for in-person services. Across intervention targets, acceptance tended to be higher among female students and those with mental health conditions, although acceptance varied substantially between targets (e.g., high for study-related issues like procrastination, lower for substance-use concerns).
These findings suggest that diverse delivery modes and combinations of intervention targets may better align with student preferences and potentially enhance service engagement. Tailoring mental health service offerings to reflect these preferences could support broader utilization and more effective allocation of resources in university settings.

Whilst studying at university, many students experience high levels of stress (Weiss et al., 2022; Andrews & Wilding, 2004; Vaez & Laflamme, 2008), which is not conducive to learning. In the first week of the semester, we recorded stressors that students in the intervention group reported as being perceived as particularly stressful whilst studying. Throughout the semester, this group also received a weekly email newsletter containing instructions for short relaxation exercises and one booster session halfway through the semester, when they reflected their stress levels so far and received further stress management training. Throughout the semester, students documented their exercises (frequency, subjective effect etc.), well-being and stress level daily in a workbook. The intervention and a control group (students who did not receive any training) completed the same sets of questionnaires (e.g., well-being, mindfulness, stress) at three times during the semester (start, middle (when the intervention group received the booster session) and end of semester). It is hypothesized that students in the intervention group will benefit from the continuous mental training, thus showing reduced stress levels, higher well-being and satisfaction with their exam performance.

BIS+: Findings from the Development and Standardization of the New Berlin Structure-of-Intelligence Test
Chair(s) Dr. Vsevolod Scherrer
Co-chair(s) Dr. Moritz Breit
Room: SI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The Berlin Structure-of-Intelligence Test Plus (BIS+) is the latest entry in the BIS test series, marking the first fully computer-based BIS test. The test was developed, computerized and standardized between 2023 and 2026. The BIS+ comprises 22 tasks and was standardized for the ages 15 to 40. The tasks are classified according to the Berlin Model of Intelligence that posits two orthogonal dimensions: Operations (reasoning, processing speed, creativity, memory) and contents (verbal, numerical, figural). In addition to the established task formats of the BIS series, the BIS+ introduces two new components: A module for self-estimation of one's own cognitive profile and a working memory module including verbal, numerical, and figural tasks.
The contributions to this symposium address various research questions in the areas of test development, modeling of cognitive abilities, and variables influencing test performance based on the extensive data collected as part of this project. At the time of this submission, data collection is complete (N = 2465); the analyses for all contributions will be carried out in the coming weeks and months. The first contribution tests an innovative trifactor confirmatory model to describe the faceted structure of the BIS+ in comparison with more traditional models. The second examines changes in motivation, effort and fatigue across a testing session and the impact on test performance. The third presents the continuous norming strategy applied to the BIS+ data. The fourth examines the relationship between self-estimated and test-assessed cognitive profiles, as well as moderators of this relationship. The final contribution applies response-time IRT models to the nine reasoning tasks of the BIS+.

Testing the Construct Validity of the BIS+: A Trifactor Confirmatory Factor Analysis
Dr. Vsevolod Scherrer | University of Trier | Germany
Show details

Dr. Moritz Breit | University of Trier | Germany
Prof. Dr. Heinz Holling | University of Münster | Germany
Prof. Dr. Franzis Preckel | University of Trier

A distinctive feature of the Berlin Model of Intelligence Structure (BIS) is its assumption that intellectual performance on any given task is simultaneously explained by two orthogonal dimensions as well as the superordinate g-factor. The first dimension captures the cognitive operation involved in task performance: reasoning, processing speed, creativity, or memory. The second dimension captures the content domain on which the operation is applied: verbal, numerical, or figural. Accordingly, any given task involves a specific operation applied to a specific content domain. The BIS+ operationalizes the BIS model with 22 distinct tasks spanning all four operations (reasoning: 9 tasks; memory: 6 tasks; creativity: 4 tasks; processing speed: 3 tasks) and all three content domains (verbal: 8 tasks; numerical: 8 tasks; figural: 6 tasks).
This contribution tests the construct validity of the BIS+ by specifying a trifactor confirmatory analysis model. The trifactor model explains performance on each individual task through three uncorrelated factors representing g, one of the operation factors, and one of the content factors. Moreover, an additional, extended model tests whether the working memory module (operationalized with three additional tasks referring to either verbal, numerical, or figural content) could be integrated into the BIS trifactor model. In this model, working memory represents an additional operation factor, while the content factors follow the established BIS logic.

Changes in Intrinsic Motivation, Perceived Probability of Success, Fatigue and Effort Across a 90 Minute Testing Session

Intelligence testing typically assumes that participants perform to the best of their ability throughout the session. However, test takers differ in non-cognitive variables such as intrinsic motivation, perceived probability of success, fatigue, and effort investment. Because these factors influence performance, they can compromise the validity of intelligence test scores. Although between-person differences in these variables and their associations with performance are relatively well understood, less is known about within-person change during extended testing and about whether individuals differ systematically in these change trajectories. This gap is particularly relevant for longer sessions, where non-cognitive states may change in different directions and at different rates across test takers, potentially producing different time-on-task effects on performance.
In this study, we examine between-person differences, within-person change, and between-person differences in within-person change trajectories in intrinsic motivation, perceived probability of success, fatigue, and effort across a 90-minute computerized test session using the large, heterogeneous BIS+ standardization sample. We test whether these trajectories predict performance over time throughout the session. All non-cognitive variables were assessed at four time points: once before the test and at three equally spaced points during the session. Using multilevel modeling with random intercepts and random slopes, we examine change trajectories in these constructs over time and test whether intraindividual change in motivation (i.e., deviations from one's own average motivation level) is related to intraindividual change in test performance (i.e., deviations from one's own average performance level). This design allows us to test whether individuals whose motivation decreases over time also show corresponding decreases in performance.

Continuous Norming of the BIS+
Julian Urban | University of Trier / University of Potsdam | Germany

As cognitive abilities develop across the lifespan, the raw scores of intelligence tests are strongly associated with age. To interpret these raw scores accurately, they must be compared with an appropriate reference population, such as individuals of the same age – a process known as norming. Conventional norming, which estimates norm scores within discretized age groups, may, however, result in biased norms and requires large samples to achieve precise norms. Continuous norming addresses these limitations by using nonlinear regression to model the relationship between raw scores and age continuously based on the entire normative sample.
A growing body of research has shown that continuous norming outperforms conventional norming in terms of bias and precision, if the underlying distribution of raw scores (e.g., normal or beta-binomial) is taken into account. While guidance exists for handling score distributions in unidimensional tests, considerably less guidance is available for multidimensional tests, such as the BIS+: Several BIS+ tasks form the basis for operation and content scores, while all tasks contribute to the general cognitive ability indicator. Consequently, norming the BIS+ requires aggregating subscales while considering the distinct distribution of each subscale. This study therefore provides guidance on how to implement continuous norming for a multidimensional intelligence test.

From a practical perspective, substantial over- or underestimation of one's abilities may have diagnostic relevance. For instance, an individual who substantially underestimates their reasoning ability may prematurely rule out career paths that would in fact be well within their reach. Although substantial research on self-assessed intelligence exists, its practical application alongside standardized intelligence testing remains rare. To facilitate such integration, the BIS+ test will include a self-assessment module designed to capture the four operations (reasoning, processing speed, creativity, memory) and three content domains (verbal, numerical, figural) of the BIS model. To the best of our knowledge, no questionnaire has been specifically developed to assess self-perceptions in accordance with the BIS framework.
In this contribution, we introduce this new self-assessment module and examine individual correlations between each of the seven self-assessed facets and corresponding measured performance on the BIS+, as well as profile correlations between self-assessed and measured ability profiles based on the BIS+ standardization sample. "When you're a star, they let you do it" – Associations between narcissism, toxic masculinity, and sexual transgressions
Chair(s) Dr. Sabrina Schneider (FernUniversität in Hagen)
Prof. Dr. Andreas Mokros (FernUniversität in Hagen)
Room: CZ
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Sexual discrimination and sexual aggression cause serious harm for individuals, organizations, and societies at large. Affected individuals often experience a wide range of psychological problems, including anxiety and depression, accompanied by impaired physical and social well-being. On a societal level, sexual transgressions reinforce inequality, normalize violence, and strain justice and healthcare systems. Despite increasing efforts to stem gender-based discrimination and aggression, both remain highly prevalent. Given the high stakes, understanding psychological factors that predispose to the endorsement of sexist beliefs and behavior is crucial for any society that aspires to equality and inclusion. It has been argued that gender-based discrimination and violence – being directed at a social group rather than toward a single individual – are unlikely to be motivated by individual predispositions. Contradicting this claim, in this symposium we present empirical findings from current, multi-methods research showing that: (1) a broad theoretical foundation exists linking individual and personality differences with sexual violence (presentation 1), (2) recidivism of sexual violence can be predicted by person characteristics assessed with psychometric risk assessment tools (presentation 2); and (3) narcissistic traits are critically linked with sexual aggression (presentation 3) and the endorsement of gender-based discrimination toward both women and men (presentation 4). Moreover, the symposium will provide a broader perspective on (toxic) masculinity, which has been proposed as one factor predicting individual level sexist attitudes and behavior (presentation 5). In order to foster a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between sexual transgressions, narcissism, and masculinity, the symposium will approach the topic from different angles, combining primary empirical research (presentations 4 and 5) with meta-analytic data (presentations 2 and 3) and a spanning theoretical framework (presentation 1).

Theoretical accounts of socially aversive traits and sexual transgressions: An overview
Dr. Jonas Schemmel | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Andreas Mokros | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Dr. Jonas Schemmel | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany

Various accounts from different fields of psychology have attempted to explain sexual transgressions: Types of conduct that are intrusive, without consent, and potentially include physical aggression. The confluence model by Neil Malamuth (1986) was instrumental in broadening the view from focusing on offender samples toward men from the community – a forward-looking approach that pre-empted current insights on the apparent ubiquity of sexual transgressions. More specifically, the confluence model includes both proximate (situational, state-dependent) and distal causes for sexual transgressions. The latter comprise personality traits. In this sense, the confluence model allows incorporating other influential explanations for socially aversive behavior, such as psychopathy, antisocial personality disorder, or narcissism. Other recent theories were derived from sexual offender samples and highlight the role of motivational causes, such as the incentive theory of sexual motivation (Smid & Wever, 2016) or the motivation-facilitation model of sexual offending (Seto, 2019). Nevertheless, these motivational theories also incorporate personality traits as an explanation for deviant proclivities. Moreover, some concepts that are presumably identical turn up in various theories under different names (i.e., jangle fallacy). Although it seems highly unlikely that a unitary theory will allow explaining all variants of sexual transgressions due to equifinality, the apparent similarities in extant theoretical accounts merit further scrutiny. During the talk an attempt will be made to highlight the most salient (and plausible) components of the theories aforementioned, thereby mapping the terrain for the following talks in the symposium.

Common sexual offenses include sexually aggressive behavior such as rape, sexual assault, and child sexual abuse. To inform decision-making in such cases, risk assessment instruments are used to predict the likelihood of reoffending. This meta-analysis synthesizes evidence on the predictive validity of ten instruments used to assess sexual recidivism risk: MnSOST-R, RM2000/S, RRASOR, SORAG, Static-2002, Static-2002R, Static-99, Static-99R, SVR-20, and VRS-SO. It includes 162 studies involving 155,442 individuals published between 1997 and 2024. Results suggested moderate to high predictive validity for most instruments in predicting sexual recidivism and other outcomes, including violent, sexual-violent, general, and any recidivism. The VRS-SO showed the highest predictive value for sexual recidivism but did not differ significantly from other tools. The SORAG demonstrated the highest predictive value for sexual-violent, general, and any recidivism, significantly outperforming the Static-99. The RRASOR showed moderate predictive validity for sexual recidivism but had the lowest effect sizes for all other outcomes. A moderator analysis revealed that inter-rater reliability and the mean age of offenders significantly affected predictive validity.
This work represents the largest synthesis of risk assessment instruments for sexual recidivism to date. The findings support the viability of all instruments examined in forensic practice, although their predictive validity overlapped considerably, with more substantial effects for the VRS-SO and SORAG and weaker effects for the RRASOR. Given the overall moderate predictive validity, these instruments should be used alongside other information to guide decision-making within the criminal justice system.

Experiences of sexual aggression often have extensive physical, psychological, and social consequences for those affected, motivating research to elucidate dispositional and risk factors for sexual assault. Various theories on sexual aggression suggest that narcissism could be a relevant dispositional risk factor. In addition, recent meta-analyses indicate a moderate relationship between narcissism and aggression in general. Despite these findings and the theoretical connection, prior research examining the link between narcissism and sexual aggression has produced mixed results. This may, at least in part, be due to differences in the conceptualization and measurement of narcissistic traits across different studies. While earlier research conceptualized narcissism predominantly as a unidimensional construct, recent studies increasingly rely on multidimensional narcissism scales, which allow for a more nuanced assessment of different narcissistic traits (e.g., entitlement, exploitativeness, or lack of empathy). Current models of narcissism emphasize this multidimensionality and provide the theoretical framework to organize a heterogenous set of narcissistic traits — as well as their potential associations with sexually aggressive behavior. The present meta-analytic review (screened research articles: k = 1,927) examines extant empirical findings on the relationships between sexual aggression and narcissistic traits as defined within the Trifurcated Model of Narcissism. In addition, the relevance of sexual narcissism, a pattern of egocentric sexual behavior characterized by narcissistic traits, in predicting sexually aggressive behavior is being explored.

Who should be pretty, who should be strong? Narcissistic predictors of sexism toward women and men
Sandy Sue Spormann | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sandy Sue Spormann | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Sabrina Vanessa Gordt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Andreas Mokros | Germany
Dr. Sabrina Schneider | Germany

Sexism is defined as conscious or unconscious prejudicial attitudes and discriminatory behavior toward individuals based on their gender. Although women are disproportionately affected, men and individuals with other gender identities also report experiences of sexism, when they act against or “fail” traditional male gender roles. Sexist attitudes can produce wide-ranging individual, organizational, and societal harm, including reduced well-being, economic losses, and increased tolerance of gender-based violence. Identifying relevant antecedents of sexist attitudes may therefore enhance our understanding of, and efforts to prevent, sexual violence. In the present study, using a sample of 1,169 participants (nwomen = 864; nmen = 305), we will examine associations between various forms of anti-female and anti-male sexism and narcissistic personality traits assessed with the Five-Factor Narcissism Inventory Short Form. Thereby, the study’s objective is to test the relationships between the three dimensions of narcissism according to the Trifurcated Model of Narcissism (i.e., Agentic Extraversion, Antagonistic Narcissism, and Narcissistic Neuroticism) and sexism toward women and men using latent regression models, that will be estimated separately by participants’ gender and the target of sexist beliefs. By clarifying how specific narcissistic traits relate to distinct forms of sexism, the study may inform more targeted prevention and intervention efforts aimed at reducing gender-based prejudice and its associated harms.

Are alpha men just closed-minded, dominant right-wing authoritarianists? On potential jingle-jangle fallacies within masculinity research
Dr. Christian Blötner | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christian Blötner | Germany
Sören Michallek | Germany

Research on men’s endorsement of masculinity norms employs a multitude of labels (e.g., traditional masculinity ideology, masculine norm adherence, toxic masculinity, hegemonic masculinity beliefs) and measurement instruments. Because these labels are anchored in heterogeneous definitions of “masculinity,” they may not reference a single, coherent construct. At the same time, what is termed “masculinity” may overlap substantially with broader, better-established constructs that capture similar affective, cognitive, and behavioral domains, obscuring the uniqueness of “masculinity”. This study will examine available measures of the endorsement of masculinity norms in terms of suspected jingle (i.e., the same label, different constructs) and jangle fallacies (i.e., different labels, same construct). Building on a demographically diverse sample of men (ntarget ≥ 1,000) and contemporary guidelines for evaluating jingle and jangle fallacies, we will compare the nomological networks of masculinity measures both to one another and to those of theoretically adjacent constructs—specifically, openness to experience, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism. Therein, we will evaluate whether the ostensible masculinity construct(s) differ(s) sufficiently from the aforementioned constructs to warrant recognition of “masculinity” as a distinct research area within social personality psychology.

Development, Validity, and Utility of College Admission Tests for German Universities
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm (Universität Ulm, Institut für Psychologie und Pädagogik)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Birgit Spinath (Heidelberg University)
Room: DK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

In meritocratic admission with nationally restricted access to highly demanded degree programs, decontextualized reasoning abilities and relevant prior competencies are key predictors of educational outcomes and provide incremental validity beyond high school grade point average. Accordingly, widely used German college admission tests emphasize the importance of reasoning and knowledge in their construction, thereby meeting the presuppositions for meritocratic admission. In this symposium, we report and discuss several recent and intriguing findings concerning development, validity, and utility of admission procedures for degree programs with a high demand and limited supply such as medicine and psychology. Weppert and Jaehn study SES as an important background variable using local structural equation modeling. Knorr et al. present stav-data results concerning fairness and validity of HAM-tests. Jaehn et al. highlight psychometric results from the new TMSnat. Wilhelm et al. summarize multivariate findings from the BaPsy. Spinath concludes the symposium with an integrative discussion of all contributions.

Fairness in Medical School Admissions: The Role of Socioeconomic Status in the Test for Medical Studies
Daniel Weppert | ITB Consulting | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Daniel Weppert | ITB Consulting | Germany
Malvin Jaehn | University of Heidelberg | Germany

Empirical research shows that performance on university admissions tests is associated with socioeconomic status (SES). These findings repeatedly raise concerns about the fairness and validity of admissions tests, particularly given the substantial impact such tests can have on applicants’ career paths. To test for potential SES-related bias, we investigated SES-related measurement invariance of the Test for Medical Studies (TMS) across two test administrations. Following the TMS test periods in spring 2024 and fall 2024, an online survey was conducted among TMS participants, resulting in samples of n = 677 in each period. SES was operationalized using parental occupational status, parental educational attainment, and equivalized net income. These indicators were combined into a single SES index using principal component analysis. SES-related invariance was examined using local structural equation modeling, which allows testing along a continuous SES moderator. In both cohorts, the TMS demonstrated scalar measurement invariance across the SES continuum (i.e., stable factor loadings and item intercepts), supporting the comparability of latent means. The findings suggest that SES-related performance differences reflect actual differences in the underlying competencies (i.e., study aptitude), with no evidence of SES-related measurement bias. The results are discussed in terms of their implications for fairness, admissions testing practice, and future research.

Authors:

Dr. Johanna Hissbach | Universitätsklinikum Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany

Dr. Ina Mielke | Universitätsklinikum Hamburg-Eppendorf | Germany

Die Abiturnote ist seit Jahrzehnten ein hoch gewichtetes Kriterium bei der Auswahl zukünftiger (Zahn-)Medizinstudierender. Aktuelle Publikationen zeigen jedoch, dass die Abiturnote möglicherweise weniger prädiktiv valide für den Studienerfolg ist als vor einigen Jahrzehnten und dass sie Bewerber:innen mit privilegierter sozialer Herkunft bevorzugt. Für die Auswahl der (Zahn-)Medizinstudierenden an der Universität Hamburg werden daher zusätzlich zur Abiturnote Tests für kognitive Fähigkeiten (HAM-Nat), soziale Kompetenz (HAM-SJT) und manuelle Fertigkeiten (HAM-Man) eingesetzt. In diesem Vortrag stellen wir für die Auswahltests Ergebnisse zu a) der Validität bei der Vorhersage des Studienerfolgs zu b) der Fairness vor. Die Datenbasis für die Analysen bildet die Datenbank des Studierendenauswahlverbunds (stav), die Informationen von über 30.000 Auswahltestteilnehmenden enthält. Für Teilstichproben sind soziodemographische Daten und Studienerfolgsparameter zu Studienleistungen wie beispielsweise schriftlichen Prüfungen, interpersonellen Simulationsprüfungen, manuellen Fertigkeitsprüfungen sowie Einschätzungen von Lehrärzt:innen im Rahmen von Praktika verfügbar. Alle drei Auswahltests zeigen größere Zusammenhänge mit konstruktpassenden Studienerfolgsparametern als die Abiturnote, zu der sie zusätzlich auch inkrementelle Validität zeigen. Zudem gibt es Hinweise, dass die Tests weniger selektiv für Personen unterschiedlicher Herkunft (sozioökonomischer Status, Migrationshintergrund) sind als die Abiturnote. Unsere Ergebnisse zeigen das Potential von spezifischen Auswahltests bei der Vorhersage von Studienerfolg und bei der Reduktion von unerwünschten Selektionseffekten. Wir empfehlen daher, entsprechende Tests bei der Studierendenauswahl höher zu gewichten als die Abiturnote.

Admission into Psychology Programs in Germany: Development and Validation of the BaPsy
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Ulm University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Ulm University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Schroeders | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Matthias Ziegler | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany

Due to legal requirements, psychology degree programs across Germany decided to opt into an admission model that psychometrically capitalizes on established human cognitive abilities. More than 90% of universities offering a BSc in psychology now combine high school grade point average with performance in a nation-wide admission test – the BaPsy. The BaPsy was developed in line with overarching principles and established evidence from research on college admission and comprises a mixture of decontextualized reasoning tests and a number of measures targeting relevant expertise for successfully completing a psychology degree (e.g., math, text comprehension). The subtests are combined into an overarching score that is subsequently combined by colleges with high school grade point average and additional local criteria. Current administrations use a paper-and-pencil test format with linked parallel test forms. We report on test design, item construction, confirmatory measurement models for subtests and the complete BaPsy test, linking results, and preliminary validity evidence. We conclude by discussing psychometric challenges of admission tests, desiderata for validation, and obstacles for optimizing societal utility.
