Sahura Ertugrul | University of Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sahura Ertugrul | University of Bremen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Louisa Kulke | University of Bremen | Germany

In daily life, social events are common and often emotionally salient. It is essential to control attention in these situations, for example, shifting focus back to work after witnessing a car accident, which may be challenging most of the time. Therefore, the current set of studies examined how emotional valence (positive, negative, neutral) and social content (social, nonsocial) influence attention shifts, co-registering eye-tracking and EEG. In Study 1 (OSF DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/DX9YT), adults (N=40) were instructed to shift their attention from a central emotional image to a peripheral neutral target. The stimuli were presented in two conditions: either the central and peripheral targets appeared simultaneously (competition), or only the peripheral target was shown (non-competition). Participants were significantly slower to disengage from social compared to nonsocial images, whereas valence did not affect saccade latency. No significant effects were observed for P1 latency, although EPN was significantly modulated by valence. Study 2 (N=40) (OSF DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/MWGEQ) examined voluntary attention shifts using the same paradigm. Again, neither valence nor social content affected saccade or P1 latencies; however, both significantly influenced saccade frequency. Across all studies, the competition condition overrode social and emotional effects, resulting in significantly slower disengagement compared to the non-competition condition. In conclusion, emotional and social content appear to influence the decision to disengage attention, but not the speed of shifting, while task demand may suppress the effect of valence and social content on attention. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the social attention process from multiple angles using multimethod measures.

The Visual System Plays a Significant Role in Establishing Physiological Synchronisation
Nina Volkmer | University of Konstanz | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Stella Wienhold | University of Konstanz | Germany
Bernadette F. Denk | University of Konstanz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jens C. Pruessner | University of Konstanz | Germany

Background: Physiological synchrony has been reported to occur in many interpersonal relationships, e.g. romantic couples, mother-child dyads, close friends, etc. However, the role of the different sensory systems in conveying the information necessary to establish synchronisation during social encounters has not been systematically investigated. Methods: Here, we investigated the role of the visual system on heart rate variability (HRV) synchrony. Participants (N = 35) were randomly allocated to two dyadic settings. In both, they completed two assessment tasks in which they could either see each other (VISION condition), or were separated by an opaque barrier (NO VISION condition). Heart rate was continously recorded by a two channel ECG. Synchrony was computed as cross-wavelet power across four different frequency ranges (0.50–0.25 Hz, 0.25–0.125 Hz, 0.125–0.063 Hz, 0.063–0.042 Hz). Results: Synchrony was higher in the VISION than in the NO VISION condition in all but the lowest frequency range. Discussion: These findings suggest that the visual system plays an important role in HRV synchronisation. Its impact seems to vary depending on the specific frequency range investigated, suggesting that physiological synchrony is not a uniform process but involves different autonomic sources across different sensory systems.

The Physiology of Interpersonal Synchrony, Trust, and Reciprocity
Stella Wienhold | University of Konstanz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Stella Wienhold | University of Konstanz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jens C. Pruessner | University of Konstanz | Germany

This study examines interpersonal synchrony (IS) in heart rate variability (HRV) between strangers during an economic exchange and asks how autonomic coordination relates to trust and reciprocity. Pairs completed a modified investment game in which an investor and a trustee made decisions consecutively, allowing to distinguish between (a) simultaneous associations between HRV synchrony and trust behavior during the interaction, (b) whether synchrony during mere co-presence predicted subsequent trust decisions, and (c) whether trust decisions influenced subsequent synchrony once feedback was available. HRV was recorded continuously using two channel ECG sensors, and interpersonal HRV synchrony was quantified using cross-wavelet power (CWP) across multiple frequency bands.
In 50 dyads (N = 100), we observed phase- and frequency-specific correlations of IS in relation to specific experimental phases. During the first round of interaction, higher investor transfers were associated with greater synchrony in lower frequency HRV bands, while higher trustee return transfers were associated with reduced synchrony. These simultaneous correlations were no longer apparent after the role reversal in the second round. The synchrony of joint presence before the interaction showed limited prospective value in lower bands, but synchrony in a medium (lower HF) band predicted higher initial investments. Conversely, trustee reciprocity most consistently predicted increased synchrony after interaction in slower bands, while investor transfers showed little to no evidence of influencing later synchrony.
Taken together, the results suggest that CWP of HRV mirrors the detailed temporal social dynamics of the trust exchange.

Syncing Feelings: The Interplay of Arousal and Valence with Inter-Brain Neural Coupling in Conversation
Vanessa Nöring | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Vanessa Nöring | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Dr. Marcel Franz | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ilona Croy | Friedrich Schiller University Jena | Germany

Social interactions are a fundamental part of human life, yet they require continuous processes of mutual adjustment. It has been hypothesized that the neural manifestation of these adjustments lies in interpersonal synchrony of brain activity; however, this has rarely been observed in ecologically valid, everyday conversational settings. This study investigates how the disclosure of emotions influences brain-to-brain synchrony among friends during naturalistic conversations.
Sixty-nine dyads of friends participated in a structured conversation paradigm while their brain activity was recorded using functional near-infrared (fNIRS) hyperscanning. Over 18 trials, dyads took turns discussing both negative and neutral topics. Following each interaction, participants reported their experienced arousal, valence, social connectedness, and perceived dominance. Neural synchrony was quantified using Wavelet Transform Coherence (WTC) between homologous fNIRS channels in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and the right temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Comparisons with pseudo-dyads served as an experimental control.
The results revealed significantly higher neural synchrony in real dyads compared to pseudo-dyads. Within real conversations, high levels of arousal were associated with lower synchrony. Furthermore, greater similarity in arousal levels between the interacting partners was associated with increased synchrony.
These findings indicate that naturalistic conversational situations are characterized by neural synchrony. This synchronization reflects the experience of shared emotional intensity and is disrupted when interaction partners experience high levels of physiological arousal.

Attachment theory suggests that parents' emotion regulation abilities and responsiveness to their children's needs may be associated with individual differences in parental attachment. When parents effectively co-regulate one another within the parental relationship by mutually adapting their behaviours, emotions, physiological states and goals and intentions, they can create a more stable caregiving environment for their children.
While research has examined interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) during parent-child interaction, much less is known about INS between parents during joint caregiving. Grounded in attachment theory, this study therefore explores the link between parent-parent INS, parental attachment styles, and caregiving behaviours during a triadic play task involving mothers, fathers and children.
Fifty families with young children (4-8 years old) participate in a naturalistic cooperative game (Jenga) during which functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning data is collected from both parents (current N=20). INS is analysed using Wavelet Transform Coherence (WTC) over 10 minutes of cooperative gameplay from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and the temporo-parietal junction (TPJ). Self-report questionnaires assess parental attachment and caregiving, and behavioural interaction quality (e.g., turn-taking, gaze coordination) is coded from video recordings.
We posit that the quality of co-regulation between parents will be reflected in their INS patterns and associated with differences in their attachment and caregiving styles. By examining the neural mechanisms underlying co-parenting, this study aims to inform how individual differences in parental attachment and caregiving may shape everyday family interactions, using an interdisciplinary, multi-method approach. More data will be available until the conference date.

Introduction: Psychosocial stress is omnipresent in modern western societies and associated with detrimental health effects. In addition to personal stress experiences, individuals can also be influenced by the stress of others through bio-behavioral synchrony. This study investigated the link between attachment and bio-behavioral synchrony within an empathic stress paradigm in romantic couples. Methods: In 79 healthy romantic couples, we induced psychosocial stress using the Trier Social Stress Test in one partner ("target") while the other observed. We assessed psycho-physiological stress reactivity in both partners through salivary cortisol, heart rate, heart rate variability and self-report questionnaires. We measured interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) with functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning in bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and temporo-parietal junction (TPJ). Observers’ attachment was classified using the Adult Attachment Interview. Results: Couples with secure observers showed significant cortisol synchrony. They also demonstrated a greater increase in INS within bilateral dlPFC, whereas couples with insecure-dismissive observers showed a greater increase in INS in the left TPJ. Discussion: Our results suggest that couples with securely attached observers were physiologically more attuned during a stressful situation, which may facilitate mutual understanding. However, elevated cortisol levels may also yield a risk for adverse health outcomes. Our INS data tentatively support beneficial effects of attunement in secure observer couples because they demonstrated stronger INS in regulatory brain areas (bilateral dlPFC). Conversely, couples with an insecure-dismissive observer showed stronger INS in the left TPJ, a brain area involved in mentalizing, potentially signaling evaluation of the stressful situation without regulatory influence.

Therapist Effects in Offender Treatment: The Role of Gender and Professional Self-Concept
Ronja Timm | Germany
Show details
Author:
Ronja Timm | Germany

Definitions of offender treatment vary considerably. How forensic therapists define their professional self-concept and treatment focus can oscillate between a psychotherapeutic and a criminogenic stance (treating the disorder vs. treating criminal behaviour). So far, it is unclear whether one emphasis is superior to the other and results in better treatment outcomes. Additionally, despite their irrelevance in clinical contexts, it is conceivable that objective therapist characteristics such as gender may play a larger role in forensic treatment settings, where the population is predominantly male. Within clinical studies, an oversampling of female clients often limits the conclusions that can be drawn for male clients working with male or female therapists.

The present study analysed whether differences in client-rated working alliance could be explained by therapists' professional self-concept and gender. In a sample of n = 128 offenders and n = 26 therapists, a therapist effect was estimated at 20.1 %. In a multilevel model, gender and professional self-concept were predictive of clients’ alliance ratings. Specifically, male therapists with a criminogenic focus achieved better alliance ratings than their colleagues. Possible explanations for these findings may lie in matching processes, attitudes towards clients, and definition of what a 'criminogenic' treatment focus may entail.

Jessica Söder | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany
Show details

Jessica Söder | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Friederike Funk | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany

Prior research on punishment motive attributions has largely emphasized procedural justice but has rarely considered distributive justice, punishment severity, personality traits, or offender populations. This research addresses these gaps by examining how personality characteristics and experiences within the legal system shape punishment motive attributions and offender’s reactions to punishment. Study 1 (N = 703 laypeople) showed that distributive and procedural justice increased perceived fairness and acceptance of punishment, while procedural justice also enhanced motivation to change. These effects were mediated by prosocial and individualistic, and for motivation to change, competitive motive attributions. Study 2 (N = 502 laypeople) replicated the effects of procedural justice on perceived fairness and acceptance and confirmed its indirect influence on motivation to change through motive attributions. Personality traits such as grandiose narcissism, antisociality, and psychoticism increased competitive and individualistic attributions, whereas honesty-humility reduced them. Study 3 (N = 244 forensic inpatients) demonstrated that perceived procedural justice in court and forensic psychiatry increased perceived fairness, acceptance, and motivation to change via prosocial attributions. Distributive justice enhanced perceived fairness and acceptance of the punishment, whereas punishment severity reduced fairness perceptions indirectly through diminished prosocial attributions. Again, personality traits were shown to influence punishment motive attributions. Across studies, punishment motive attributions emerged as key mechanisms linking fair treatment to adaptive offender responses overall.

The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly impacted prison life. While protective measures limited viral spread, they also exacerbated existing pains of imprisonment. This study investigated whether pandemic-related stressors impacted the social climate in prisons and whether changes in social climate were associated with inmates’ psychological well-being. Data was collected from 26 German prisons (n=743) as part of the Corona Behind Bars project. Comparing dual ratings (pre- vs. during pandemic) of the Essen Climate Evaluation Schema revealed significant declines in inmates’ perceptions of therapeutic hold and experienced safety, whereas inmate cohesion did not change significantly. This research examines the incongruity between the German press code’s guidelines and media practices regarding the disclosure of offender nationality, systematically investigating the pronounced emphasis on non-German identities in crime reporting.

Across three experimental studies (combined N = 850), we analyzed the impact of offender nationality disclosure on public punitiveness. In Studies 1 and 2, participants read a real-life newspaper article about aggravated assault in which offender nationality was varied (none, German, Syrian). Significantly higher punitive attitudes and longer proposed sentence lengths emerged when the offender was described as Syrian, particularly among participants without a migration background, highlighting the complex interplay between media portrayals and public sentiment.

In Study 3, we used a 2 × 2 design, changing both offender nationality (German or Syrian) and offense motive (hate crime or non-hate crime). Unlike earlier studies, we saw no significant effects on punitive attitudes. These null results suggest that the impact of nationality disclosure depends on context and narrative framing, rather than being a uniform bias across situations.

In essence, this research provides empirical insights into the discourse on media influence, revealing the complex relationship between media practices, offender nationality disclosure, and public attitudes toward criminality. Beyond implications for responsible media reporting, our findings are significant for discussions on the stigmatization and resocialization of criminal offenders. Understanding how media portrayals shape public attitudes is crucial for informed conversations on criminal justice, rehabilitation, and a fair and unbiased societal perspective on those who have committed offenses.

The stated aim of correctional imprisonment is the reintegration into society and profession, in order to enable former prisoners to live independently and to prevent them from reoffending (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, n.d.). Professional reintegration is particularly important due to the negative correlation between employment and the probability of reoffending (Schüttler et al., 2023). However, former prisoners face stereotypes, particularly in the professional context, that question their professional and interpersonal skills and significantly reduce the likelihood of being hired (Nnam et al., 2023).
At the present time, little to no research has fully examined the professional reintegration of former prisoners. The majority of existing literature, largely centered on the US, is of questionable relevance in the German context due to legal and cultural differences. The presented project is primarily concerned with the question of the extent to which former prisoners are confronted with stereotypes and discrimination in the German labour market, compared to the general population. The research talk outlines the initial results of qualitative interviews with employers regarding the perceptions of ex-convicts and their willingness to hire them. The qualitative findings are supplemented by quantitative data from a questionnaire study involving 300 employers in Germany in order to examine further factors influencing stereotyping and discrimination. The project aims to uncover potential obstacles to the professional reintegration of former prisoners in Germany and, on this basis, to develop recommendations for its improvement.

The role of anticipation in social settings
Chair(s) Oliver Genschow (Leuphana University Lüneburg)
Room: LT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Previous research as repeatedly demonstrated that individuals are able to predict other people’s actions and its outcomes above chance level. Thus, not surprising, numerous theoretical frameworks from various areas of psychology highlight anticipation processes as a central building block of the human cognitive architecture. For example, anticipation processes have been proposed to play a key role in areas as diverse as motor cognition, cognitive control, psychological disorders, and learning—to name just a few examples. However, existing theories on anticipation are mainly shaped in cognitive (neuro)science, thereby neglecting taking into account whether and how anticipative mechanisms play a role in more complex social settings. To fill this gap, this symposium aims to show the central role of anticipative processes in different social settings.
The first talk investigates how penalty takers in football can anticipate goalkeepers’ dive direction and why experienced athletes are better in such anticipation. The second talk shows that people do not only anticipate other people’s future actions, but also engage in the anticipated action—mainly because they infer others’ desire to act. The third talk argues that synchrony detected within interaction partners is often a statistical artefact that emerges from averaging across trials and shows that anticipative processes best explain synchronous behavior. The fourth talk indicates that children and adults use speaker-specific common ground to anticipate upcoming utterances during social conversations. Finally, the fifth talk shows in the work context that merely anticipating being available for work in the evening impairs employees’ recovery and well-being.

Anticipating the movement of football (soccer) goalkeepers
Dr. Danna Oomen
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Danna Oomen
Lennard Fochler
Sebastian Wallot
Oliver Genschow

The outcome of a penalty kick can pivot the fate of a football match. While previous research has mainly examined how goalkeepers anticipate shot direction, little is known about how penalty takers anticipate goalkeeper movements when using a keeper-dependent strategy. The current study examined how temporal constraints shape the penalty takers’ ability to anticipate the movement direction of the keeper, and whether expertise plays a role in such anticipation. Participants (N = 253; 130 experts; 123 novices) completed a temporal occlusion task in which they viewed 64 penalty kicks filmed from the taker’s perspective. On each trial, participants indicated whether the goalkeeper would dive left or right. Videos began 4 s before ball–foot contact and were occluded at four time points (0, 200, 400, 600 ms before contact). Overall performance remained above chance across occlusion times (ranging from ~94% at 0 ms to ~52% at 600 ms). There was a strong main effect of occlusion time: anticipation accuracy decreased as occlusion occurred earlier, with significant differences between adjacent occlusion levels. Furthermore, experts outperformed novices across occlusion times. While years of playing experience predicted performance uniformly across occlusion times, the amount of football watched interacted with occlusion. That is, passive exposure was associated with better anticipation at less constrained occlusion levels, but not under the most restrictive viewing condition. Together, these findings quantify perceptual constraints on anticipating goalkeeper movements and suggest that passive and active forms of experience contribute differently to anticipatory performance.

The role of attention in anticipated social action effects
Oliver Genschow
Show details
Author:
Oliver Genschow

Past research has shown that merely anticipating a certain action in someone else leads observers to engage in the anticipated action—a phenomenon called anticipated action. In a standard experiment on anticipated action, participants watch video clips of a model engaging in triggering events such as nose wrinkling or hair falling. A typical finding is that participants engage in more nose actions while watching the nose wrinkling video than while watching the hair falling video and vice versa for the engagement in hair actions. Whereas past research has suggested that this effect is due to inferring a desire in others to act, an alternative explanation is that observing a triggering event in someone else guides attention toward respective body parts, facilitating any action toward this body part. In two experiments (total N = 386) we set this explanation to a critical test by applying a standard anticipated action effect design. The results speak against attention as driving process and in favor of inferring a desire in others to act, because merely guiding attention to the location of the triggering event with color cues did not result in anticipated action effects whereas observing triggering events in the other person did. These results have important implications for research on anticipative processes and imitative behavior.

Anticipatory behavior as a driver of synchrony during joint action?
Sebastian Wallot
Show details
Author:
Sebastian Wallot

Synchrony has emerged as an ubiquitous property of human social interaction. Synchrony – i.e., the tendency that two measures behave similarly in time at or close to lag0 – has been shown in behavioral as well as physiological measures when two or more people interact. While synchrony sometimes emerges spontaneously and subconsciously, most interactions in the real world, as well as in laboratory settings, are intentional and goal oriented: Participants deliberately coordinate to pursue a (common) goal. While synchrony is present in many interactions, its exact role as a driver (or consequence) of joint actions remains a matter of debate. In this presentation, we offer a perspective on interpersonal coordination that has been neglected thus far, but might serve as a key to understand the observation of synchrony better: (Mutual) anticipation between the interacting partners in a joint task. Specifically, we put forward the speculative proposal that observations of synchrony in joint action might be driven by mutually anticipating and reacting to one another during joint action. Such kind of anticipatory coordination might produce instances of synchrony as a consequence. To that end, we re-analyzed published data about heart rate synchrony during a firewalking ritual. Indeed, the analysis suggests that when preceding behavior of the participants is taken into account, the strength of the synchrony effect is reduced, implying that such behavior is one of the drivers of synchrony. Moreover, we discuss the implications of these findings for other characteristics of joint action data, such leader-follower relations, or fluctuations in synchronous behavior.

Turn-taking is a universal feature of human conversation and is characterized by its speed: gaps between turns are often around 200 ms. This suggests that listeners begin planning their responses based on what they predict their partner will say before the partner has finished speaking. What is the cognitive basis for generating such predictions? Besides low-level syntactic and intonation cues, common ground may act as a central source of information to guide anticipation. Common ground refers to the shared knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions established between interlocutors and continuously updated during interaction. Topics anchored in common ground constrain what is likely to be said next and thereby support prediction. We ask whether, when, and how common ground drives anticipatory processes during communication. To address this question, we developed a new experimental paradigm implemented as an interactive, tablet-based picture book. A speaker consistently refers to objects from the same semantic category without explicitly naming the category. Listeners must infer the topic and anchor it in common ground. In a first study, we showed that children use common ground to resolve ambiguous utterances. Importantly, this inference is modulated by the identity of the speaker. Ongoing work with adults combines this paradigm with eye-tracking. Preliminary results suggest that adults use common ground to anticipate upcoming utterances before they are completed. We will discuss these findings in light of our research questions and outline directions for future work on anticipation, common ground, and conversational turn-taking.

Show details

Research indicates that availability demands, the expectation of being contacted and needing to be available for work matters outside regular hours, are detrimental for employee
recovery and well-being. However, this research largely applied a between-person lens while employee recovery is a within-person process happening on a day-to-day basis. The few existing within-person studies on availability focus on actual availability, not on anticipation. Thus, the role of day-specific anticipated availability—as a future-oriented cognition—remains unexplored. Integrating the cognitive activation theory of stress with the extended stressor-detachment model, we examine the anticipation of evening availability as a cognitive mechanism underlying the stressor-recovery relationship with two complementary diary studies.
Study 1 (232 employees, 1,540 days) examines daily work characteristics (workload, work from home) as antecedents of anticipated and actual availability as, in turn, antecedents of evening psychological detachment, a crucial recovery experience, and next-morning exhaustion. Study 2 (137 employees, 791 days) zooms into the negative relationship between anticipated availability and detachment as identified in Study 1, and tests leisure absorption, the focused and enjoyable immersion in leisure activities, as both a mediator and moderator of this relationship.
Results of multilevel analyses indicate the unique detrimental role of mere anticipated availability for recovery and well-being (via impaired leisure absorption) beyond actual availability. As such, our research makes important contributions to the work-stress recovery literature by clarifying the unique role of anticipation in the recovery process.

Adaptive Resonanz in Teams: Physiologische Synchronie als Indikator adaptiver Teamprozesse
Prof. Dr. Simone Kubowitsch | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Simone Kubowitsch | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg | Germany
Natalie Hogh | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg | Germany
Lara Watermann | Technical University of Applied Sciences Augsburg
Florian Klonek | Deakin University | Australia
Joshua Braun | Germany

Ziel dieser Studie war es, zu prüfen, inwiefern physiologische Synchronie (PS) als objektiver Indikator für Teamfähigkeiten in einer komplexen, hoch interdependenten Virtual-Reality-(VR)-Aufgabe dienen kann. Gerade in virtuellen Umgebungen ist die Wahrnehmung emotionaler und kognitiver Zustände von Teammitgliedern erschwert, was die Etablierung förderlicher Interaktions- und Koordinationsprozesse beeinträchtigen kann. Ein indikatorbasiertes Maß, das unabhängig von Selbstberichten oder Beobachterurteilen ist, könnte daher wertvolle Einblicke in die Qualität von Teamprozessen liefern und perspektivisch für automatisiertes Teammonitoring oder innovative Diagnostikansätze genutzt werden.
Physiologische Daten, die Aktivität des sympathischen und parasympathischen Nervensystems abbilden, sowie Leistungsmaße der Teamaufgabe wurden bei 75 Versuchspersonen erhoben. Die speziell entwickelte VR-Aufgabe erforderte sowohl Übergangsprozesse (z. B. Strategieentwicklung) als auch Handlungsprozesse (z. B. Koordination und wechselseitige Anpassung). Mehrere etablierte PS-Metriken, darunter Kreuzkorrelationsanalysen und Multidimensionale Rekurrenzquantifizierungsanalysen (MdRQA), wurden miteinander verglichen und in Beziehung zur Teamleistung gesetzt. Ergänzend wurde untersucht, inwiefern sprachliche Angleichungsprozesse im Sinne des Language-Style-Matchings mit physiologischer Synchronie und Leistung kovariieren.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen signifikante Zusammenhänge zwischen PS und Teamperformance. Im Gegensatz zu vielen bisherigen Befunden war jedoch geringere physiologische Synchronie mit besseren Leistungsergebnissen assoziiert. Dies deutet darauf hin, dass eine flexible, differenzierte Regulation statt starker Kopplung in dynamischen, komplexen Aufgaben von Vorteil sein könnte. Insgesamt legen die Befunde nahe, dass PS ein vielversprechender Indikator für Teamfähigkeiten ist, dessen Interpretation jedoch stark von Aufgabencharakteristika, Berechnungsmethoden und den zugrunde liegenden physiologischen Parametern abhängt.

Sind Veränderungen in organisationaler Altersfreundlichkeit relevant? Zusammenhänge mit der Kündigungsabsicht von Mitarbeitenden einer Pflegeeinrichtung
Mattea Wehage | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Mattea Wehage | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Dr. Julia Finsel | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Anne Wöhrmann | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jürgen Deller | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Laura Venz | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg | Germany

Der demographische Wandel und der damit zunehmende Arbeitskräftemangel erhöhen den Stellenwert langfristiger Bindung von Mitarbeitenden – insbesondere im Gesundheitswesen. Gemäß Lebensspannentheorien verändern sich Motive und Bedürfnisse mit dem Alter. Altersfreundliche Organisationen berücksichtigen diese Veränderungen durch gezielte Praktiken und Kulturen, die helfen, persönliche und berufliche Ressourcen zu bewahren. Bisherige Studien brachten organisationale Altersfreundlichkeit in Zusammenhang mit Gesundheit und Produktivität älterer Arbeitnehmender, basierten allerdings meist auf Querschnittsdaten. Zudem wurde organisationale Altersfreundlichkeit in diesen Studien als stabiles Strukturmerkmal behandelt, jedoch anhand der Wahrnehmung der Mitarbeitenden gemessen – die sich ändern kann. Wir untersuchen natürliche Veränderungen in der wahrgenommenen Altersfreundlichkeit im Zusammenhang mit Veränderungen in der Kündigungsabsicht und prüfen, ob diese Zusammenhänge altersabhängig sind. Wir befragten 101 Mitarbeitende einer Pflegeeinrichtung in zwei Online-Befragungen im Abstand von neun Monaten. Veränderungen ermittelten wir mit Differenzwerten zwischen den Messzeitpunkten. Mittels multipler Regressionsanalysen analysierten wir die Zusammenhänge zwischen den Differenzwerten in wahrgenommener organisationaler Altersfreundlichkeit (gemessen mit dem Later Life Workplace Index; LLWI) und Kündigungsabsicht und testeten Alter als Moderator. Verbesserungen in der wahrgenommenen Altersfreundlichkeit standen in einem signifikanten Zusammenhang mit reduzierter Kündigungsabsicht; Alter moderierte diesen Zusammenhang nicht. Explorative Analysen auf Domänenlevel des LLWI zeigten mit Haupt- und Moderationseffekten bezüglich Veränderungen in altersfreundlicher Führung und organisationalem Wissensmanagement ein differenziertes Bild der Relevanz organisationaler Altersfreundlichkeit für die Kündigungsabsicht jüngerer und älterer Mitarbeitenden. Die Ergebnisse deuten auf relevante Veränderungen in der Wahrnehmung organisationaler Altersfreundlichkeit sowie auf deren Potenzial zur Verringerung von Kündigungsabsichten hin. Insgesamt tragen die Ergebnisse zu einem differenzierten Verständnis bei, wie altersfreundliche Organisationen eine nachhaltige Beschäftigung aller Altersgruppen unterstützen.

Die Kosten der Zielverfehlung: Wie das Verfehlen von Zielen Anspannung und die darauffolgende Leistung beeinflusst
Michelle Kalbfleisch | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Michelle Kalbfleisch | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Nina Keith | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany

Das Setzen hoher und spezifischer Ziele gilt als motivations- und leistungssteigernd, birgt jedoch das Risiko einer Zielverfehlung. Wie wirken sich Zielverfehlungen auf emotionale Befindlichkeit und Verhalten bei nachfolgenden Zielsetzungen aus? Theorien der Selbstregulation gehen davon aus, dass die Bewertung von Zielerreichung und Zielverfehlung emotionale Reaktionen auslöst, die wiederum die Motivation und Leistung in anschließenden Zielsetzungszyklen beeinflussen können—sei dies in günstiger oder ungünstiger Weise. Diesen Mechanismus zu überprüfen, war das Ziel der vorliegenden Arbeit. In einer experimentellen Studie (N = 104) durchliefen die Teilnehmenden fünf Runden einer arbeitsnahen Aufgabe und erhielten nach jeder Runde in ausbalancierter Reihenfolge fingiertes Leistungsfeedback (Zielerreichung vs. -verfehlung). Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die subjektiv erlebte Anspannung ansteigt, sobald ein Ziel verfehlt wird, während sie nach Zielerreichung abnimmt. Zudem sagt die gesteigerte Anspannung nach Zielverfehlung eine niedrigere Leistung in der nachfolgenden Runde vorher. Die Studie trägt zu einem besseren Verständnis von Selbstregulationsprozessen bei, die auf Zielsetzungsergebnisse (Zielerreichung vs. Zielverfehlung) folgen. Sie zeigt, dass eine Zielverfehlung und damit das Setzen hoher Ziele an sich nicht nur emotionale, sondern auch ungünstige leistungsbezogene Konsequenzen haben kann. Die Ergebnisse sind für Organisationen vor allem deshalb von praktischer Bedeutung, weil Zielsetzungen selten ein einmaliges Ereignis darstellen. Vielmehr wird in Organisationen oft ein neues Ziel festgelegt, sobald ein Zielsetzungszyklus abgeschlossen ist (z.B. jährliche Zielvereinbarungen). Zielsetzungsprozesse sollten entsprechend nicht isoliert betrachtet werden, sondern stets im Kontext vorheriger und nachfolgender Zielsetzungszyklen, um auch längerfristig motivationsfördernde Wirkung zu entfalten.

Science under threat: Understanding and rebutting misinformation
Chair(s) Dr. Philipp Schmid
Room: SK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

According to the Royal Society, we have entered an era characterised by anti-science politics where ideological agendas are employed to inhibit research, jeopardise academic freedom, and reduce funding. In addition, a number of political leaders around the globe publicly spread misinformation that contradict scientific evidence on topics such as climate change, vaccination and gender equality. These developments have negative impacts for individual decision makers. According to meta-analyses, people who are exposed to misinformation are more likely to believe it, which ultimately prevents them from making educated decisions regarding the environment, health and social equity. In this symposium we will present recent developments in psychological research on 1) how misinformation impacts key beliefs 2) what sender, receiver and contextual characteristics increase the persuasive power of misinformation and 3) which psychological interventions might help to overcome misinformation. The talks cover experimental research and systematic reviews on a variety of different topics (e.g., climate change, vaccination, gender neutral language), different target groups (e.g., general public, conspiracy believers, voters with varying political identities) and communication settings (e.g., social media, chat bot conversations). Discussions will focus on research gaps in understanding susceptibility to misinformation and pitfalls of different psychological interventions.

Hannah Logemann
Show details
Authors:
Hannah Logemann
Jacob Rode
Rakoen Maertens
Sander van der Linden

Climate change is one of the greatest threats to humanity, necessitating immediate action to combat its consequences. Although there is a nearly unanimous scientific consensus that climate change is human-caused, misinformation doubting its causes continues to circulate widely. In this study, we test the Gateway (mis)Belief Model (GmBM) which assumes that misinformation affects perceived scientific consensus negatively, which then cascades down to lower support for public action to mitigate climate change via changes in key beliefs about the issue. We present a reanalysis of data from two online studies in which U.S. participants (N1 = 207, N2 = 755) were exposed to misinformation using a pre-post mixed design manipulating assessments of the scientific consensus on climate change. Structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed causal pathways of the GmBM, and results were further synthesized using an internal meta-analysis. Results showed that misinformation indeed leads to lower estimations of scientific consensus, which cascade down to lower support for public action via corresponding beliefs. However, the pattern of significance of direct effects did not exactly replicate those in the original GBM, though misinformation still had negative direct (Experiments 1–2) and indirect effects (Experiment 2) on several downstream climate outcomes. These findings are further affirmed by the internal meta-analysis. Overall, this study highlights the negative impact of misinformation on climate attitudes and policy support and provides empirical support for perceived scientific consensus as a critical psychological gateway through which misinformation undermines public engagement with climate action.

Christopher Jones
Show details
Authors:
Christopher Jones
Maria Becker
Raenhha Dhami
Lara Guse
Vera Araújo-Soares

Health mis- and disinformation are increasingly conveyed through narratives on social media. While such narratives may differ in complexity, they often specifically target identity, social norms, or emotions of users groups, and, in turn, exert a far greater influence than isolated claims. Understanding the underlying mechanisms and social components is critical for explaining impact as well as improving detection and rebuttal.
In two systematic reviews 1) examining how narratives influence beliefs and sharing behavior (N = 57 included studies), and 2) investigating computational methods for detecting misinformation narratives (N = 25 studies), we synthesize experimental, observational, network-analytic, and machine-learning approaches.
Across studies, misinformation narratives increase belief in misleading content and are shared more widely. Specifically, narratives are thought to operate through narrative transportation, emotional arousal, and identity-based motivation, while echo chambers and social norms reinforce their effects at the social network level. Despite the strengths of binary misinformation classification, the accuracy of detecting emerging narratives is still lacking. Here, approaches integrating psycholinguistic signals (e.g., moral language, emotional framing, group identity) and community-level features outperform those purely focused on stylistic features or content.
Evidence synthesis suggests that misinformation narratives should be understood as psychologically active and socially embedded processes – not only as text units. Mechanisms that explain narratives´ persuasive power might provide future avenues to improve detection through patterns at linguistic and network levels. Integrating psychological theory into detection frameworks may therefore improve not only accuracy but also enhance subsequent interpretability and generalizability to - most crucially - improve counter measures.

Show details
Authors:

A common explanation of why people fall for misinformation is motivated reasoning. Motivated reasoning is often studied as a function of characteristics of receivers, such as cognitive reflection abilities, but it is rarely studied as a function of message features. This is a shortcoming because the subtype of misleading information, compared to false information, might support individuals to maintain a so-called illusion of objectivity – a key prerequisite of motivated reasoning.
In this preregistered study (N = 674), we test whether motivated reasoning in identifying misinformation about climate change is a function of the type of misinformation (i.e., misleading vs. false). That is, we test experimentally whether conservatives judge climate change misinformation (congruent) as more accurate and are more willing to share it compared to liberal participants (i.e., motivated reasoning). We test whether this motivated reasoning effect depends on the message type–is larger for misleading compared to false information.
Results show that there is indeed a partisan bias, causing conservatives to rate conservative congruent misinformation about climate change to be more accurate than liberals (η2 = 0.288, p < 0.001). In addition, we find that independent of identity, misleading information is perceived as more accurate (η2 = 0.078, p < 0.001), and more likely shared (η2 = 0.037, p < 0.001). We did not find any significant interaction effects on the accuracy ratings, but a moderation effect for sharing intention (η2 = 0.011, p = 0.001). These findings suggest that people might not be motivated reasoners, but motivated sharers.

A major finding in misinformation research is that politically congruent news headlines (i.e. aligning with one’s political beliefs) are more likely to be judged as true compared to incongruent headlines. However, previous studies have used equal numbers of congruent and incongruent headlines, which does not accurately reflect news environments on social media. Participants indicated for each headline if they believed it to be true, and whether they were familiar with it. We additionally measured partisan attitudes before and after the headlines were rated.
Results replicated previous research, showing that participants were generally accurate about the veracity of the headlines, and that congruence of the headlines influenced the likelihood that participants judged them to be true. No difference on these effects was found between the different news environments, indicating stability across environments of varying congruence. We also found no difference in partisan attitudes between environments. These findings suggest that congruence effects exist at the headline rather than the environmental level and inform the use of this experimental paradigm for studying behaviour on social media.

Once established, conspiracy beliefs are notoriously difficult to correct with most interventions yielding small effects only. Specifically, we hypothesize that the reduction in conspiracy beliefs might be driven by the artificial nature of the source. Participants in two treatment conditions then debated their belief with a chatbot instructed to argue against it. Results showed that the intervention effectively reduced conspiracy beliefs. Relative to the control condition, participants who knowingly debated an LLM reported a substantial reduction in conspiracy belief (−7.88 percentage points; d = −0.63, p < .001). However, this drop was even larger for those believing to debate another human, showing an additional −5.88 percentage point decrease compared to the AI-label (d = −0.3, p < .001). Gender conspiracy theories claim that gender neutral language, gender studies and gender-equality activists represent an ideology secretly designed to harm traditional values and social arrangements. More specifically, gender conspiracy theories might be more persuasive when shared by a sender who denigrates her ingroup (i.e., female sender) or when received by an individual who benefits from gender-inequality (i.e., male receiver). Moreover, gender conspiracy theories might be more persuasive when it seems justified by the context (e.g., ban of gender neutral language in schools as a status quo). There is no evidence that this impact is a function of the sender, receiver or context: all p-values > .05. Thus, exposure to conspiracy theories provides a general threat to positive attitudes towards gender neutral language. However, rebutting conspiracy theories neutralizes their persuasive impact in all experiments: d = 0.2–0.5, p < .05. Effects of additional exploratory moderators (sexism, conspiracy mentality) will be discussed. Moreover, results of a fourth experiment on whether the rebuttal effects can be scaled up using AI will be discussed.

Affektive Prozesse spielen eine zentrale Rolle für das Verständnis von Gesundheitsverhalten und insbesondere körperlicher Aktivität. Während kognitive Planungsansätze, wie Implementierungsintentionen, gut erforscht sind, zeigen sie häufig nur moderate und kurzfristige Effekte. Das Affect and Health Behavior Framework (AHBF) betont die Bedeutung affektiver Mechanismen für nachhaltige Verhaltensänderung. Aufbauend darauf verglich die vorliegende Studie eine klassische kognitive Planung mit einer kognitiv-affektiven Planungsintervention, die affektive Erwartungen und positive Vorstellungsbilder (z.B. Freude) einbezog. Zudem wurden der tägliche Affekt und deren Regulation im Verlauf der Zielverfolgung untersucht, um Einblicke in dynamische, innerhalb-personale Prozesse zu gewinnen.
In einer randomisiert-kontrollierten Intervention wurden drei Gruppen untersucht: kognitive Planung (n = 37), kognitiv-affektive Planung (n = 37) und eine Wartekontrollgruppe (n = 39). Beide Interventionsgruppen entwickelten strukturierte „Wenn-Dann“-Pläne zur körperlichen Aktivität; die affektive Gruppe wurde dabei angeleitet sich auf positive affektive Aspekte zu fokussieren. Während der Interventionswoche berichteten die Teilnehmenden täglich über Zielverfolgung, positiven und negativen Affekt sowie eingesetzte Affektregulationsstrategien.
Es zeigten sich keine Gruppenunterschiede in körperlicher Aktivität, Affekt oder affektiven Einstellungen nach einer Woche. In den Tagebuchdaten zeigte sich jedoch, dass erfolgreiche Zielverfolgung mit höherem positivem und niedrigerem negativem Affekt einherging. Explorative Multilevel-Analysen bei Zielerreichung ergaben, dass Savoring und unkontrollierter Ausdruck positiven Affekt förderten, während Unterdrückung und Ablenkung von positiven Erfahrungen negativ mit täglichem Affekt zusammenhingen.
Allerdings war die Stichprobe relativ klein, jung und aktiv, sowie die Interventionsdauer kurz, was die Aussagekraft hinsichtlich langfristiger Effekte einschränkt. Künftige Interventionen sollten kontinuierliche affektive Komponenten integrieren, um positive Bewegungserlebnisse und nachhaltige Verhaltensänderung zu fördern.

Insbesondere zu sekundären, nicht unmittelbar suchtbezogenen Outcomes (z.B. Gesundheit, Berufstätigkeit, Legalbewährung) wurden postulierte positive Effekte bislang kaum wissenschaftlich überprüft.
Zielsetzung: Das vom Bayerischen Staatsministerium der Justiz geförderte Forschungsprojekt „Haft bei Opioidabhängigkeit – eine Evaluationsstudie (HOpE)“ verfolgt das Ziel, zu untersuchen, ob eine Substitutionsbehandlung oder eine abstinenzorientierte Therapie bei opioidabhängigen Gefangenen zu günstigeren Entwicklungen nach der Haftentlassung führt – bezogen auf primäre, suchtbezogene Outcomes (z.B. illegaler Drogenkonsum, Konsumdrang, Überdosen) und sekundäre Outcomes (z.B. soziale Reintegration, Gesundheitszustand, Legalbewährung).
Methode: N = 247 opioidabhängige Strafgefangene (davon n = 139 substitutionsorientiert und n = 108 abstinenzorientiert behandelt) wurden kurz vor Haftentlassung und im Zeitraum von bis zu drei Jahren nach Haftentlassung mehrmals mit einer modifizierten Version des European Addiction Severity Index interviewt. Zusätzlich lagen Informationen aus den Krankenabteilungen, den Haftakten, Drogenscreenings und BZR-Auszüge vor.
Ergebnisse und Diskussion: Substituierte Personen hatten insbesondere während der Haft und in den ersten Monaten nach Haftentlassung günstigere Outcomes in Bezug auf illegalen Opioidkonsum und illegalen Konsum von Substitutionsmedikamenten. In Bezug auf sekundäre Outcomes wie Legalbewährung, Gesundheitszustand und Integration auf dem Arbeitsmarkt lassen sich jedoch keine Vorteile einer Substitutionsbehandlung gegenüber der abstinenzorientierten Behandlung finden. Implikationen für die Suchtbehandlung und das Übergangsmanagement werden aufgezeigt.

Methoden: Die Untersuchung analysierte Schmerzintensität und mit chronischem Schmerz assoziierte Variablen, um (1) deren Beeinflussung durch die AR-Intervention und (2) Überlegenheit gegenüber dem konventionellen Ansatz zu überprüfen. Wir führten eine ANOVA mit gemischtem Design und Bonferroni-Korrektur durch, wobei der within-subject Faktor die Zeit (Prä vs. Post) und der between-subject Faktor die Gruppe (Interventionsgruppe (IG) vs. Kontrollgruppe (KG)) war. Die AR-Interventionsgruppe nutzte eine HoloLens 2 für Psychoedukation und MBSR-Body-Scan in einer simulierten Waldumgebung und dabei die reale Welt überlagerte; die Kontrollgruppe las denselben psychoedukativen Text und hörte eine MBSR-Body-Scan-Audioaufnahme. Das primäre Ergebnis war Schmerzintensität, sekundäre Ergebnisse waren Katastrophisieren, Selbstwirksamkeit, Stress und Depressionssymptome durch Fragebögen. In der präklinischen Studie wurden 44 Teilnehmer mit Schmerzintensitätswert von unter 4 (Skala 1-10) rekrutiert. Diese wurden in die IG (n=22, M=39.63 Jahre, Range=20-67 Jahre) und KG (n=22, M=41.81 Jahre, Range=21-70 Jahre) aufgeteilt.

Ergebnisse: Ein Haupteffekt wurde über beide Gruppen hinsichtlich der Schmerzintensität (F(1,42)=29.78, p=.001), Schmerzkatastrophisierung (F(1,42)=27.95, p=.001) und Stressniveaus (F(1,42)=20.66, p=.001) festgestellt, während die Selbstwirksamkeit unverändert blieb.

Diskussion: Die Resultate zeigten (1) eine Abnahme der Schmerzintensität, Schmerzkatastrophisierung und des Stresslevels in beiden Gruppen, (2) ohne Unterschiede zwischen den Gruppen. Unser AR-Prototyp beeinflusst schmerzbezogene Variablen bei CLBP ähnlich wie herkömmliche Ansätze und bildet eine Grundlage für AR-Interventionsstudien.

Psychotherapie im höheren Lebensalter: Umgang mit Grenzen und Endlichkeit als Kern der Entwicklung
Eva Irene Fechau | MSB Medical School Berlin, Hochschule für Gesundheit und Medizin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Eva Irene Fechau | MSB Medical School Berlin, Hochschule für Gesundheit und Medizin | Germany
Prof. Dr. habil. Eva-Marie Kessler | MSB Medical School Berlin, Hochschule für Gesundheit und Medizin

Trotz steigender Inanspruchnahme psychotherapeutischer Angebote durch ältere Menschen existieren bislang kaum empirische Erkenntnisse darüber, wie Psychotherapie im höheren Lebensalter subjektiv erlebt wird. Das Projekt „PANAMA – Psychotherapie aus der Innensicht älterer Menschen“ verfolgt das Ziel, anhand der Patient:innen-Perspektive Ansatzpunkte für eine bedarfsgerechte ambulante Psychotherapie zu formulieren.

Es wurden 21 leitfadengestützte Interviews mit Personen im Alter zwischen 68 und 86 Jahren geführt, die innerhalb der letzten fünf Jahre aufgrund klinischer Depression eine ambulante Psychotherapie in einem Richtlinienverfahren aufgesucht hatten. Die Auswertung des Materials erfolgte anhand kritisch-konstruktivistischer Grounded Theory, um Kontexte und Dynamiken des berichteten Therapieerlebens sichtbar zu machen.

Für die Teilnehmenden stellte der Umgang mit Begrenztheit eine zentrale Erfahrung des therapeutischen Prozesses dar. Die erlebten Grenzen bezogen sich dabei auf unterschiedliche Ebenen, die sich in vier Clustern widerspiegeln: (1) Umgang mit den Grenzen des therapeutischen Settings, (2) Umgang mit Begrenztheit der eigenen Ressourcen, (3) Grenzen der eigenen Veränderungsfähigkeit im Kontext der Biografie, und (4) Konfrontation mit existenzieller Begrenztheit. Für die Teilnehmenden ging es in der Therapie um ein ständiges Aushandeln dessen, welche Grenzen akzeptiert werden mussten und welche überwunden oder erweitert werden konnten.
Die Ergebnisse legen nahe, dass Psychotherapie im höheren Lebensalter helfen kann, innere und äußere Grenzen in ihrem Zusammenspiel zu verstehen und einen adaptiven Umgang damit zu entwickeln. Die aktive Thematisierung von Begrenztheit, die Förderung von Selbstakzeptanz und biografischer Integration sowie die Balance zwischen Akzeptanz und Veränderung erscheinen zentral. Dies kann Autonomie, Sinnorientierung, Handlungssicherheit und subjektiv erlebte Freiheit im höheren Lebensalter stärken.

Psychodynamische Merkmale bei Adoleszenten mit und ohne depressive Symptomatik: die EPA-Studie
Prof. Dr. Annette M. Klein | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Annette M. Klein | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany
Dr. Johanna Lilian Klinge | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany


Gemäß psychodynamischen Theorien prägen Beziehungserfahrungen mit primären Bezugspersonen in der frühen Kindheit die Entwicklung grundlegender psychischer Fähigkeiten (z.B. Selbst- und Beziehungsregulation), zusammengefasst unter dem Begriff der psychischen Struktur. Unzureichende Beziehungserfahrungen können zu Beeinträchtigungen dieser Struktur und darüber hinaus zu intrapsychischen Konflikten, maladaptiven Abwehrstilen und Einschränkungen der Mentalisierungsfähigkeit führen, was wiederum mit einem erhöhten Risiko für depressive Symptome assoziiert ist. Ziel dieser Studie ist es daher zu untersuchen, ob sich zwischen 16-21-jährigen Adoleszenten mit vs. ohne depressive Symptomatik Gruppenunterschiede zeigen hinsichtlich psychischer Struktur, intrapsychischer Konflikte, Abwehrstile und Mentalisierungsfähigkeit.
Im Rahmen einer querschnittlichen Online-Befragung wurden die Daten von N = 606 Adoleszenten (Alter: M=18,49, SD=1,70; 69,1% weiblich, 22,6% männlich, 8,3% divers; 76,2% durchschnittlicher SÖS) erfasst. Depressive Symptome wurden mittels Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) erfasst (Gruppenbildung anhand Cut-off von 10). Psychische Struktur wurde mit dem OPD-KJ2-Strukturfragebogen erhoben, intrapsychische Konflikte mit dem OPD-KJ2-Konfliktfragebogen, Abwehrstile mit dem Defense Style Questionnaire for Adolescents (DSQ-22-A) und Mentalisierungsfähigkeit mit dem Reflective Functioning Questionnaire (RFQ-6).
Eine MANCOVA unter Kontrolle von Alter, Geschlecht und SÖS ergab einen signifikanten Haupteffekt des Gruppenfaktors Depressive Symptomatik vorhanden/nicht vorhanden, F(8, 591)=16,48, p < .001, η²p=.182. Nachfolgende univariate Analysen ergaben signifikante Gruppenunterschiede für alle vier Strukturdimensionen, intrapsychische Konflikte, Abwehrstile sowie Mentalisierungsfähigkeit: Adoleszente mit depressiver Symptomatik berichteten höhere Beeinträchtigungen hinsichtlich Struktur, Konflikten und Mentalisierung, sowie geringere adaptive und höhere maladaptive Abwehrstile (alle ps < .01) als die Vergleichsgruppe.
Die Befunde stützen die Annahmen psychodynamischer Theorien und bieten Ansatzpunkte für Prävention und Intervention in der Adoleszenz, die als vulnerables Zeitfenster für die Entstehung psychischer Störungen gilt.

Die Gestaltung und Rolle der familiären Lernumwelt für die die Entwicklung und Bildung von Kindergarten- und Grundschulkindern
Chair(s) PD Dr. Valérie-D. Berner (Catholic University Eichstaett-Ingolstadt)
Prof. Dr. Heike Buhl (Universität Paderborn)
Room: AT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Die familiäre Lernumwelt hat für die Entwicklung und Bildung von Kindern im Kindergarten- und Grundschulalter eine zentrale Bedeutung, indem sie Kinder stimuliert und intellektuell unterstützt. Im Symposium werden Prozessmerkmale der familiären Lernumwelt in den Blick genommen, z.B. die Häufigkeit elterlicher Aktivitäten, Eltern-Kind-Gespräche, elterliche schulische Unterstützung und die Nutzung analoger und digitaler Medien (vgl. Niklas & Lehrl, 2025). Dazu werden vier aktuelle Studien dargestellt, die unterschiedliche Konzeptionen der familiären Lernumwelt im Kindes- und Schulalter fokussieren. Das Symposium kombiniert qualitative und quantitative Zugänge sowie Testergebnisse. Zudem werden neben quer- auch längsschnittliche Analysen berichtet. Einige der auch hier herausgestellten Prozessmerkmale wurden zur Entwicklung eines Förderprogramms heranzogen, dessen Evaluation abschließend vorgestellt wird.
Im ersten Beitrag wird die Bedeutung der analogen und digitalen häuslichen Lernumwelt für die frühe Selbstkontrolle und Selbstregulationsstrategien für einen erfolgreichen Belohnungsaufschub in einer longitudinalen Studie bei 2 bis 4-jährigen Kindern betrachtet.
Der zweite Beitrag analysiert Elterndaten zur Häufigkeit von Eltern-Kind-Konversation über sozial-emotionale Themen zwischen verschiedenen Medien (z.B. Film, Hörbuch und Buch ) und der Art der Nutzung.
Im dritten Beitrag steht die Analyse familiärer Lernumwelt und die Bildungsaspiration als Prädiktoren für elterliches Schulengagement und schulische Leistungen bei Kindern am Ende der ersten Klasse im Vordergrund.
Der vierte Beitrag stellt die Evaluation eines intergenerationalen Family-Digital-Programms zur Förderung kindlicher Internetrecherchekompetenzen sowie elterlicher Unterstützungskompetenzen von Kindern am Ende der Grundschulzeit vor.
Die dargestellten Studien und deren Ergebnisse werden abschließend von Burkhard Gniewosz diskutiert und Implikationen für Forschung und Praxis abgeleitet.

Die Bedeutung der analogen und digitalen häuslichen Lernumwelt für die frühe Selbstregulation: Eine longitudinale Studie von 2 bis 4 Jahren
Dr. Marina Kammermeier
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Marina Kammermeier
Prof. Dr. Simone Lehrl
Dr. Dorothea Dornheim
Nadine Besser
Julia Zuber
Anja Linberg
Prof. Dr. Sabine Weinert
Prof. Dr. Hans-Günther Roßbach

Die Entwicklung selbstregulativer Fähigkeiten gilt als zentrale Entwicklungsaufgabe im Kindesalter. Die Bedeutung von Selbstkontrolle und Regulationsstrategien für einen erfolgreichen Belohnungsaufschub ist empirisch belegt, die Rolle der analogen und digitalen häuslichen Lernumwelt (HLE) für die Entwicklung dieser Fähigkeiten wurde jedoch kaum systematisch untersucht. Die Studie untersuchte den Einfluss der analogen und digitalen HLE auf die kindliche Selbstkontrolle und Regulationsstrategien im Längsschnitt von 2 bis 4 Jahren (n = 431). Zu drei Zeitpunkten wurden mittels einer Geschenke-Aufgabe die kindliche Fähigkeit zum Belohnungsaufschub und die während des Wartens gezeigten Verhaltensstrategien (Fokus, Kontrolle, Ablenkung) erfasst. Zum ersten Zeitpunkt wurden zudem Aspekte der analogen und digitalen HLE mittels eines Fragebogens erhoben. Generalisierte lineare gemischte Modelle zeigten einen positiven Zusammenhang zw. vorhandenen analogen Spielmitteln und der Wahrscheinlichkeit eines erfolgreichen Belohnungsaufschubs. Die Bildschirmzeit hingegen war negativ assoziiert mit diesem. Zudem zeigten lineare Regressionsanalysen, dass die analoge HLE (z.B. gemeinsames Lesen, Spielen v. Brettspielen) positiv mit der Nutzung von Ablenkungsstrategien assoziiert war, während die digitale HLE (Nutzung digitaler Bilderbücher, Anzahl installierter Apps) positiv mit fokussierenden Strategien und negativ mit Ablenkungsstrategien zusammenhing. Die digitale HLE zeigte zudem moderierende Effekte auf den Zusammenhang zw. der Ausprägung bestimmter Regulationsstrategien und des erfolgreichen Belohnungsaufschubs. Diese Befunde deuten darauf hin, dass die analoge und digitale HLE die Entwicklung selbstregulativer Fähigkeiten unterschiedlich beeinflussen und insbesondere auf die Anwendung von Ablenkungsstrategien wirken. Dies liefert Hinweise für die Gestaltung häuslicher Lernumwelten zur Förderung von Selbstkontrolle und unterstützenden Regulationsstrategien im Kindergartenalter.

Wie fühlt sich Winnie Puuh? Eltern-Kind-Konversationen über sozial-emotionalen Themen bei unterschiedlichen Medien und Arten der Mediennutzung
Prof. Dr. Jan Lenhart
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Jan Lenhart
Katharina Deckert

Gespräche zwischen Eltern und Kindern sind ein wichtiger Mechanismus für die Entwicklung kindlicher Kompetenzen und sie erhöhen üblicherweise den Lernerfolg in verschiedenen Settings der häuslichen Lernumwelt wie zum Beispiel beim Vorlesen von Kinderbüchern. In der vorliegenden Studie wurde untersucht, inwiefern sich die Häufigkeit von Eltern-Kind-Konversationen über sozial-emotionale Themen zwischen verschiedenen Medien und unterschiedlichen Arten der Nutzung unterscheidet.
Hierzu wurden die Eltern von 71 Kindergartenkindern (M = 60 Monate; SD = 11 Monate) hinsichtlich der Dauer der täglichen Mediennutzung ihrer Kinder (Kinderfilme, Kinderserien, Kinderbücher, Hörbücher) befragt. Differenziert wurde zwischen selbstständiger bzw. alleiniger Nutzung durch das Kind und gemeinsamer Nutzung mit den Eltern. Zudem wurden die Eltern nach der Häufigkeit von Konversationen mit den Kindern über die Gefühle, Kognitionen oder Verhaltensweisen der Charaktere während oder nach der Mediennutzung befragt.
Es zeigte sich, dass Kinderserien und Kinderbücher sowohl häufig alleine als auch gemeinsam mit den Eltern konsumiert wurden. Während Kinderfilme vor allem gemeinsam angesehen wurden, hörten die meisten Kinder Hörbücher ohne ihre Eltern. Eltern-Kind-Gespräche über die Gefühle, Kognitionen oder Verhaltensweisen der Charaktere fanden häufiger bei der gemeinsamen Mediennutzung als bei der alleinigen Nutzung statt (d = 0.71 bis 1.07), wobei sich das gemeinsame Buchlesen als besonders reich an entsprechenden Eltern-Kind-Konversationen erwies (d = 0.39 bis 0.58 im Vergleich zu anderen Formen der gemeinsamen Mediennutzung).

Familiäre Lernumwelt und Bildungsaspiration im Kindergarten als Prädiktoren für elterliches Schulengagement und schulische Leistungen am Ende der 1. Klasse
Tina Schiele
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Frank Niklas
Öykü Camligüney
Tina Schiele
Jana Schuster
María Valcárcel Jiménez

Die familiäre Lernumwelt ist zentral für die kindliche Kompetenzentwicklung. Aber während im Kindergartenalter förderliche Aktivitäten und Eltern-Kind-Interaktionen wie Vorlesen, Wortspiele, alltägliches Zählen oder mathematische Spiele im Vordergrund stehen, nimmt mit zunehmendem Schulalter elterliches Schulengagement eine wichtigere Rolle ein (Niklas & Lehrl, 2025). Die Studie untersucht anhand N = 368 Kindern (M = 78.20 Monate [SD = 4.11], 52,7 % Mädchen, 40,9 % Migrationshintergrund) den Übergang zwischen Kindergarten und Grundschule. Es wird analysiert, inwieweit die frühe familiäre Lernumwelt und elterliche Bildungsaspiration mit kindlichen Schulleistungen am Ende der ersten Klasse, mit der von den Eltern berichteten, Schulfreude der Kinder sowie mit elterlichem Schulengagement und elterlicher Schulunterstützung der Kinder durch die Eltern zusammenhängen.
Auch unter Kontrolle von Alter, Geschlecht, Migrationshintergrund und elterlichem Berufsprestige erwies sich die familiäre Lernumwelt im Kindergarten als signifikanter Prädiktor für bessere Leistungen in standardisierten Lese-, Rechtschreib- und Mathematiktests. Zudem sagte die familiäre Lernumwelt signifikant größeres elterliches Schulengagement und von Eltern berichtete kindliche Freude am Schulbesuch vorher. Elterliche Bildungsaspiration im Kindergarten war der einzige signifikante Prädiktor für elterliche schulische Unterstützung am Ende der ersten Klasse. Querschnittlich korrelierte nur die kindliche Freude am Schulbesuch, nicht aber elterliches Schulengagement und elterliche Unterstützung der Kinder im Schulkontext signifikant mit den Leistungstests.
Die Ergebnisse betonen die wichtige Rolle der frühen familiären Lernumwelt für schulische Leistungen (vgl. auch Niklas & Schneider, 2017) und die berichtete Freude der Kinder am Schulbesuch. Die Bedeutung von Bildungsaspiration, elterlichem Schulengagement und elterlicher Schulunterstützung für die weitere Leistungsentwicklung wird im Beitrag diskutiert.

Elterliche Unterstützungskompetenzen stärken: Konzeption, Implementation und Evaluation eines Family-Digital-Literacy-Programms
Lisa Jungkeim
Show details
Authors:
Lisa Jungkeim
Dr. Nicole Kuhn
Prof. Dr. Heike Buhl

Digitale Kompetenzen sind Schlüsselqualifikationen für gesellschaftliche Teilhabe und lebenslanges Lernen (Al-Masri, 2023). Familien gelten hierfür als bedeutsame Lern- und Vermittlungsorte (Buhl et al., 2021). In Anlehnung an das Modell der digitalen häuslichen Lernumwelt (Bonanati et al., 2022) ist elterliche Unterstützung zentral für den digitalen Kompetenzerwerb von Kindern und wird durch elterliche Rollenwahrnehmung und Selbstwirksamkeitserwartung beeinflusst (Gruchel et al., 2022). Diese Unterstützung wird im ORIM-Modell (Hannon et al., 2020) entlang der Dimensionen Opportunities, Recognition, Interaction und Modeling konkretisiert.
Hier setzt das transdisziplinäre Family-Digital-Literacy-Projekt „Gemeinsam Online (GO)“ an, das kindliche Internetrecherchekompetenzen direkt sowie indirekt durch Stärkung relevanter elterlicher Unterstützungskompetenzen fördert. Inhalte wie KI-basierte Internetrecherchen werden ressourcenorientiert in Kinder-, Eltern- und Familienzeiten vermittelt. Zielgruppe sind Familien mit Kindern zum Ende der Grundschulzeit. Zur Konzeption und Implementation wird das Programm formativ und summativ evaluiert.
Nach der qualitativen Evaluation eines ersten Zyklus‘ mit acht Familien im Herbst 2025 folgt im Frühjahr 2026 ein Weiterer: Im Prä-Post-Kontrollgruppen-Design wird die Wirkung von GO auf die Stärkung elterlicher Selbstwirksamkeitserwartung, Rollenwahrnehmungen und das Unterstützungsverhalten (Gruchel et al., 2021) untersucht. Geplant ist die Befragung von Eltern-Kind-Dyaden, wobei nur Elterndaten in der Studie berücksichtigt werden (N = 38 Eltern in der Interventionsgruppe). Eine Präregistrierung liegt vor.
Die Evaluationsergebnisse werden im Hinblick auf die Weiterentwicklung von GO sowie auf elterliches Engagement in der Förderung digitaler Kompetenzen diskutiert und lieferen Impulse für Bildungsforschung und -praxis zur Förderung digitaler (Unterstützung-)Kompetenzen sowie innerfamiliale Selbstwirksamkeits- und Rollenerwartungen.

The composition and effects of parental involvement
Chair(s) Marie-Claire Schelmat (Technical University of Munich)
Room: BG
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Family background is an important factor in educational outcomes, with parental involvement representing one possible mechanism underlying educational differences. Parental involvement refers to parents’ activities aimed at supporting their children’s education and is commonly conceptualised in three dimensions: school-based, home-based, and academic socialization (Hill & Tyson, 2009). Evidence from a comprehensive second-order review indicates that parental involvement is generally positively associated with educational outcomes, although the strength of these associations varies across dimensions (Täschner et al., 2021). Differences in these association have been observed across child and family characteristics, such as age and socioeconomic status; for example, Holzberger et al. (2023) report weaker associations for students from lower socioeconomic status families. Despite evidence for the importance of parental involvement, the mechanisms linking it to educational outcomes remain insufficiently understood, longitudinal evidence is scarce, and the role of family characteristics such as migration background is unclear. Guided by the research question, “How do different dimensions of parental involvement and their structure shape the students cognitive, emotional and academic development across divers family backgrounds?”, this symposium brings together four complimentary examining multiple dimensions of parental involvement, their underlying mechanisms, and variation across family backgrounds. The first contribution uses a video study to investigate how cognitive activation—a potential mechanism— varies between parents while they help their children with mathematics homework (i.e., home-based parental involvement). The second presentation examines how parents' expectations and aspirations (i.e., academic socialization) relate to students' achievement emotions in mathematic in a longitudinal study. The third contribution assesses differences in the absolute levels of parental involvement across all three dimensions depending on migration background, and whether migration background moderates the relationship between parental involvement and students' mathematical achievement. The fourth contribution clarifies the interplay between a migration background, parental involvement and performance by examining how the literary environment at home, together with parental expectations, influences the relationship between migration background and reading and writing skills.
This symposium advances the field by integrating multiple dimensions of parental involvement with family background variables, offering new perspectives on how parental support contributes to students’ educational outcomes. By addressing these questions, it provides both theoretical insights and practical implications that can inform interventions and strategies to support students more effectively.

Cognitive Activation as a Dimension of Parental Homework Involvement
Prof. Dr. Hanna Dumont | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Esther Brunner | PH Thurgau | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Sandra Moroni | PH NMS Bern | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Hanna Dumont | Universität Potsdam | Germany

Parental homework involvement is the most common way in which parents engage in their children’s schooling. Importantly, it is not the quantity but the quality of parental help with homework that matters for students’ academic success. Previous research has mainly conceptualized the quality of parental homework involvement on the basis of self-determination theory, demonstrating that children benefit from parental autonomy support, emotional support, and the provision of structure. Notably, no differences in these dimensions have been found between parents from different social backgrounds.

In the present paper, we argue that prior research may have overlooked an important dimension of parental homework involvement: cognitive activation, understood as parents’ ability to provide explanations, instructional support, and thinking prompts during homework. In a video study with 27 parent–child dyads, we investigated whether empirically measurable differences exist in the degree of cognitive activation parents offer when helping with homework. Sixth-grade students were invited to their school outside regular school hours to solve standardized mathematics tasks on fractions with the assistance of the parent who most frequently helps them with homework at home. The video data were analyzed using a newly developed high-inference rating instrument of cognitive activation, adapted from research on teaching quality.

The results show that parents differed in the extent to which they were able to provide cognitively activating instructional support during the task. These findings indicate that conceptualizations of the quality of parental homework involvement should be expanded to include parents’ capacity to cognitively activate their children during homework.

Parents’ academic expectations and aspirations for children: how they predict children’s emotions
Prof. Dr. Michiko Sakaki | University of Tübingen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Michiko Sakaki | University of Tübingen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Kou Murayama | University of Tübingen | Germany
Anne C. Frenzel | Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich
Prof. Dr. Thomas Götzel | University of Vienna | Austria
Prof. Herbert W. Marsh | Australian Catholic University | Australia
Prof. Dr. Stephanie Lichtenfeld | University of Münster | Germany
Miriam Wünsch | Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Reinhard Pekrun | University of Essex

Parents often envision a future of their children, holding expectations (i.e., predictions) and aspirations (i.e., wishes and desires) for their children’s academic attainment. While the impacts of such parental beliefs have been well documented for children’s academic success, less is known about their influences on children’s emotions. To address this issue, we applied contemporaneous- and lagged- predictive effects models to five annual waves of data from secondary school students in Germany on achievement emotions in mathematics. Results indicated that when parents have higher expectations, students experience more positive emotions and less negative emotions (except for boredom) during the same year. In contrast, higher parents’ expectations predicted higher levels of negative emotions, particularly anxiety, in the subsequent year. We also found that parents’ aspirations are only weakly linked to achievement emotions, once parents’ expectations are controlled for. However, when parents’ aspirations exceeded their own expectations, this over-aspiration was predictive of greater anxiety and lower levels of pride in the same year. These findings highlight the complex relations between parental expectations and achievement emotions that differently manifest over time.

Parental involvement and its correlation with mathematic achievement depending on migration background
Marie-Claire Schelmat | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marie-Claire Schelmat | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Dr. Anna Hartl | Technical University of Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Doris Holzberger | Technical University of Munich | Germany

Students with a migrant background and those from low socioeconomic status families are at heightened risk of educational disadvantage. Previous research has shown that parental involvement (PI) is positively associated with educational outcomes (Täschner et al., 2021); however, this association is weaker for students from low socioeconomic status families (Holzberger et al., 2023). Consequently, these students may experience a double educational disadvantage. In the present study, we examine parental involvement as a potential underlying mechanism and investigate differences in parental involvement as a function of migration background.
Using NEPS data, we examine whether a migration background is associated with differences in the three dimensions of parental involvement (home-based, school-based, and academic socialisation) (RQ1) and whether it moderates the association between the three dimensions and mathematical competence (RQ2[AH3.1]). Group differences in parental involvement are analysed using MANOVA, and moderation effects are tested via moderated multiple linear regression.
The following items are used to represent the dimensions: support homework; frequency of support with practising for school (home based). Contact with school - parents' evenings, discussions with teachers, counselling, school events (school based). Parental monitoring questions about school, getting along with teachers and children, homework (academic socialization). Plausible values were used for mathematical competence.
Differences are expected in both the extent and correlation of parental involvement and achievement. The results broaden our understanding of parental involvement in relation to family background characteristics and help parents and teachers adapt their behaviour to optimise parental involvement and potentially reduce educational inequalities.

The Role of Parental Attitudes, the Home Literacy Environment, and Migration Background in Preschool Children’s Emergent Literacy Skills
María Valcárcel Jiménez | Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Tina Schiele | Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich | Germany
Anna Mues | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
