Developing proficient literacy skills is important for school success. Although international literacy studies indicate that children with migration background often show less proficient literacy skills in the language of instruction compared to their peers, less is known about differences between families with and without a migration background in parental attitudes toward reading, the home literacy environment (HLE) they provide, and the associations of these factors with German literacy development (vocabulary, phonological awareness, and letter knowledge). This study examined these associations, focusing on children with and without a migration background, and investigated whether the HLE mediated the relations between migration background and literacy outcomes, while controlling for child age, sex, cognitive skills, and family socioeconomic status. The study involved N = 500 children (Mage = 60.97 months, 51% girls, 38% migration background [i.e., family language is not German only]). The results of the structural equation model show that parents with migration background expressed less positive attitudes towards reading and provided a lower quality informal[DH4.1] HLE, but a higher quality formal HLE. Children with a migration background had lower German literacy skills compared to their peers. Migration background had an indirect effect on children’s literacy skills, with the HLE mediating [DH5.1]its impact on literacy development. These findings highlight the critical role of the HLE in fostering literacy skills, offer a plausible explanation for individual differences in German emergent literacy skills among children with and without a migration background, and suggest that interventions targeting parental attitudes and HLE may effectively support literacy development.

Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christoph Abels | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stephan Lewandowsky | University of Bristol

Across the globe, democratic systems are under increasing strain. Liberal democracies, increasingly becoming an endangered species, are facing sustained pressures from authoritarian and anti-democratic forces. While these dynamics are particularly visible in the United States - where the Trump administration has engaged in practices that undermine democratic norms, including targeted discrimination against researchers and journalists and open threats toward political opponents - similar developments are evident across Europe. In Germany, far-right, anti-democratic parties have gained substantial political traction and are expected to expand their representation in several state parliaments. For many citizens, these developments constitute a growing psychological burden. Anti-democratic actors frequently display a blatant disregard for facts and shared standards of truth, openly contradicting observable realities and reframing events in ways that erode epistemic trust. Beyond concerns about democratic institutions themselves, discussions with German citizens in the context of our research on democratic backsliding reveal profound emotional responses, including fear, helplessness, anger, and resignation. Although anecdotally, individuals report a perceived loss of agency and growing uncertainty about the future stability of democratic systems. Yet, the mental health implications of democratic erosion have received comparatively little attention in psychological science. Yet prolonged exposure to political uncertainty, norm violations, and perceived loss of control is associated with elevated stress, reduced well-being, and strains on social cohesion. Psychological science must therefore prepare to systematically investigate, theorise, and address the mental health consequences of democratic backsliding - both to understand individual suffering and to contribute evidence-based insights to societal resilience.

The Psychology of Right-Wing Populism: Causes and Countermeasures
Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer | TU Chemnitz | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer | TU Chemnitz | Germany

This position paper advances an integrative psychological account of contemporary right‐wing populism and culture wars. I argue that populist mobilization is best understood as an identity‐regulatory offer that restores threatened needs for autonomy, relatedness, and competence under conditions of uncertainty and status anxiety. Drawing on social identity and self-categorization theory, I outline how political entrepreneurs manufacture a broad, morally valorized superordinate identity (e.g., “ordinary people with common sense”), render it salient via availability, normative and comparative fit, and juxtapose it against negatively stereotyped outgroups. The Stereotype Content Model (warmth × competence) explains the emotional economy of this framing—pity, envy, disgust, and anger—mapping onto helping/ignoring/harming tendencies and, ultimately, affective polarization. Symbolic threat and zero-sum beliefs translate macro stressors (economic insecurity, rapid cultural change) into micro-level need thwarting, while algorithmic amplification through social media stabilizes antagonistic norms.

I contend that psychology should move from diagnosing these dynamics to designing countermeasures. I propose testable, multi-level interventions: (1) Identity leadership that expands common ingroup boundaries without erasing difference; (2) Norm engineering toward “controversy with civility” and psychological safety, so dissent does not entail identity loss; (3) Procedural justice and transparent rules that deliver both material and symbolic security; and (4) Contact under optimal conditions (equal status, cooperative goals) targeting stereotype change.

The framework reframes anti-DEI backlash as a predictable outcome of identity and need dynamics, yielding clear hypotheses about salience manipulations, security cues, and norm interventions. I discuss implications for research, organizational and societal practice, and public communication.

Die Psychologie hat in den vergangenen Jahrzehnten enorme Fortschritte in Methodik, Theoriebildung und empirischer Präzision erzielt. Doch welche Verantwortung trägt die empirische Wissenschaft vom menschlichen Erleben und Verhalten für die Gesellschaft, in der dieses Erleben und Verhalten stattfindet?
Zur Diskussion steht ein grundlegendes Spannungsverhältnis zwischen einer Psychologie, die ihre epistemische Integrität durch politische Zurückhaltung sichert, und einer Psychologie, die den Anspruch erhebt, mit ihrer Expertise aktiv in gesellschaftliche und politische Diskurse einzugreifen.
In dieser Fishbowl Veranstaltung wollen wir dieses Spannungsverhältnis kontrovers diskutieren. Auf dem Podium diskutierten mit den Teilnehmenden: Andreas Beelmann, Eva-Lotta Brakemeier, Stefanie Hechler, Karl-Heinz Renner und Stefan-Schulz-Hardt. Moderation: Eva Walther und Tobias Rothmund.
Drei Problemfelder strukturieren die Debatte: die normative Frage nach der gesellschaftspolitischen Verantwortung des Fachs und der DGPs als Fachgesellschaft; die strukturelle Frage nach der systematischen Unterrepräsentation psychologischer Expertise in politikberatenden Gremien und die Notwendigkeit belastbarer Transferstrukturen; sowie die bildungspolitische Frage, ob eine Psychologie, die gesellschaftliche Wirksamkeit anstrebt, ihre Studierenden nicht auch in politischem Urteilsvermögen und diskursiver Praxis ausbilden müsste.
In Zeiten, die durch multiple Krisen, Wissenschaftsfeindlichkeit und die Erosion demokratischer Selbstverständlichkeiten geprägt sind, ist dies auch eine Debatte über die Zukunft des Fachs.
Dabei versteht sich die Veranstaltung als Fortsetzung von Diskussionen, die während einer Tagung im März zur Rolle der Psychologie in gesellschaftlichen und politischen Diskursen in Berlin stattfanden.

Dr. Marie Luise Schreiter | Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Marie Luise Schreiter | Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics | Germany
Prof. Dr. Manuel Spitschan | Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics / TU München | Germany

Psychology faces two interrelated challenges: pervasive sampling biases that limit the generalizability of findings and declining public trust in empirical evidence. Many studies rely on student-based samples, constraining inferences about lifelong developmental trajectories in health-relevant behaviour across neuroscientific and psychological domains. This produces exclusion-bias, as entire populations are systematically left out; sampling-bias, because convenience-samples are not generally representative; and attribution-bias, when results from narrow cohorts are generalized to broader populations, often compounded by small sample sizes that further weaken inferential strength.
Using the nationwide deployment of a mobile laboratory focused on circadian rhythms and light as a methodological case study, we present a field-based research model that reframes how psychological data can be generated. A total of 822 participants (60.8% female; M = 42 years, SD = 15.7) were tested across multiple sites in Germany, spanning a wide range of chronotypes, demographics, and ages. Experimental measures included validated self-reports of chronotype, time-of-day data on cognition, and pupillometry measures to quantify baseline pupil size, constriction dynamics, and dilation responses to spectrally defined light stimuli.
Beyond the substantive findings, the project produced a large, heterogeneous psychobiological dataset that tests methodological assumptions about timing, representativeness, and data-validity. Natural variation in setting and time-of-day enables quasi-randomization, while intrinsic curiosity rather than formal recruitment or incentives motivates participation. Standardized paradigms and preregistered analyses allow contextual complexity to be modelled rather than controlled. We position research-in-public infrastructures as a methodological extension of laboratory psychology that expands the field’s capacity to generate robust, and socially embedded evidence.

Salome Li Keintzel | University of Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Salome Li Keintzel | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Florian Scharf | University of Kassel | Germany

In experimental (cognitive) psychology and psycholinguistics, outcomes (e.g., response times) are often measured repeatedly across many trials within participants, but experimental effects are typically reduced to differences between experimental conditions averaged across trials. In this talk, we advocate a shift toward trial-level analyses that explicitly leverage temporal information by understanding experimental data as (intensive) longitudinal data.
In recent years, an increasing number of models for longitudinal data analysis have been proposed, made available in software, and adopted by substantive researchers across diverse areas of psychology. We argue that these models should also become standard tools for researchers in experimental psychology and demonstrate that re-analyses of existing data with these models can provide new insights into cognitive processes. Specifically, we show how longitudinal phenomena, including temporal trends (systematic changes over time) and autoregressive effects (outcomes depending on previous outcomes), translate into novel substantive research questions in experimental psychology. We outline corresponding modeling strategies using mixed-effects (multilevel) models and structural equation models and illustrate these approaches with empirical data examples and results from simulation studies.
We argue that explicitly investigating temporal trends and autoregressive dynamics can substantially advance theory development and provide new perspectives to investigate the mechanisms underlying experimental effects in experimental psychology.

Understanding Prior Knowledge Effects on Conceptual Learning – The Probabilistic Adjustment of Multiple Beliefs (PrAM) Theory
Prof. Dr. Garvin Brod | Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (IWM), Tübingen | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Garvin Brod | Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (IWM), Tübingen | Germany

Prior knowledge has been shown to help learning, hinder learning, or have no effect at all. These divergent findings have been difficult to reconcile within a single theory, which I will illustrate in the first part of the talk. In the second part of the talk, I will introduce the Probabilistic Adjustment of Multiple Beliefs (PrAM) theory, a unified and computationally grounded account of how prior knowledge shapes conceptual learning. PrAM represents prior knowledge as a probability distribution over multiple beliefs and models conceptual learning as Bayesian belief updating. It suggests that whether prior knowledge helps or hinders learning depends jointly on the learner’s prior beliefs and the structure of the evidence they encounter. PrAM generates precise and falsifiable predictions about how an individual’s prior knowledge will affect conceptual learning in a specific context. To facilitate the use of this approach, a Python package is provided that enables researchers to implement PrAM in their own work.

Ganzheitliche Perspektiven auf Glück und Wohlbefinden: Eine interdisziplinäre Synthese von Konzepten, Messungen und Einflussfaktoren in einem integrativen Rahmenmodell
Ricarda Kochems | University of Bremen | Germany
Show details
Author:
Ricarda Kochems | University of Bremen | Germany

Einleitung: Obwohl die Forschung zu Glück und Wohlbefinden in zahlreichen Disziplinen an Relevanz gewonnen hat, bleibt sie hinsichtlich Terminologie, Konzeptualisierung und Operationalisierung stark fragmentiert. Dieses Literaturreview verfolgt das Ziel, ein integratives Rahmenmodell zu entwickeln, das zentrale Erkenntnisse disziplinübergreifend systematisiert: Wie werden Glück und Wohlbefinden konzeptualisiert und gemessen – und welche Einflussfaktoren und Wirkungen lassen sich identifizieren?

Methoden: Ein integratives Literaturreview wurde unter Einbezug multidisziplinärer Datenbanken durchgeführt. Auf Grundlage eines Indexes aus absoluten und relativen Zitationsmetriken wurden die 230 einflussreichsten Publikationen des Forschungsfeldes ausgewählt. Mithilfe der konzeptuellen Rahmenanalyse nach Jabareen (2009) wurden zentrale Konzepte, Messansätze, Einflussfaktoren und Wirkungen systematisch synthetisiert.

Ergebnisse: Das resultierende Rahmenmodell strukturiert sich entlang der Mikro-, Meso- und Makroebene sowie über Disziplinen wie (Organisations-)Psychologie, Neurowissenschaften, Soziologie, Ökonomie und Politikwissenschaft. Die untersuchten Konzepte lassen sich als subjektivistisch oder objektivistisch einordnen; Einflussfaktoren als extern, dispositionell, interaktionistisch oder intentional. Zentrale Konstrukte sind subjektives Wohlbefinden (hedonisch) sowie psychologisches Wohlbefinden (eudaimonisch), integriert in Modellen wie Flourishing (PERMA) oder Thriving. Die Organisationspsychologie trägt arbeitsbezogene Konzepte wie Arbeitszufriedenheit oder Arbeitsengagement bei. Während subjektive Erhebungen auf Selbstberichten basieren, untersuchen Ökonomie und Soziologie verstärkt objektive Faktoren wie Einkommen, kulturelle Kontexte oder Nachhaltigkeit. Begriffliche Unschärfen – etwa im Fall von „organisationalem Glück“ – sowie die häufige Vernachlässigung eudaimonischer Aspekte verdeutlichen den Bedarf an konzeptioneller Präzisierung und ganzheitlicheren Messansätzen.

Fazit: Das integrative Rahmenmodell für Glück und Wohlbefinden unterstützt zukünftige Forschung durch konzeptionelle und methodische Klarheit sowie interdisziplinären Austausch. Darüber hinaus bietet es praxisrelevante Impulse für Gesellschaft und Bildung, indem es Glück als persönliche und soziale Kompetenz begreift und fördert.

Show details
Author:
Jens Mazei | TU Dortmund | Germany

People regularly negotiate their pay at work, so that gender differences in negotiation contribute to the gender pay gap. Unfortunately, the World Economic Forum estimates that more than a century will need to pass for the gender pay gap to be vanished. Hence, I pursue the following goals with the current position paper: To start, I will document known gender differences in negotiation. By presenting two own meta-analyses, I seek to make people aware of the existence of gender inequality in negotiations. On this basis, I will delve into the mechanisms underlying gender differences, which are at the heart of my position paper. The past literature suggests that gender differences are explained by anticipated backlash: Women are expected to be communal (e.g., accommodating), and they incur backlash (i.e., interpersonal penalties) when they violate this expectation by asserting themselves. Hence, women anticipate backlash and show less assertiveness than men to avoid it. As the evidence for this mechanism is thin, however, I extended the knowledge in two key ways: First, in two studies, I closely replicated the original research proposing the mechanism of anticipated backlash. Second, in four studies, I advanced the idea that experienced authenticity represents a complementary mechanism. In fact, my collected evidence suggests that gender differences in negotiations are multiply determined. These insights help to delineate suitable interventions for gender differences in negotiation. This is important, because organizational and political leaders will need to do more for the gender pay gap to vanish sooner than in a century.

Auch nach über 40 Jahren Theorie und Forschung zu Organisationskultur besteht keine integrierende Theorie zu Inhalt, Struktur und Dynamik von Organisationskulturen.
Theoretischer Rahmen: Dieser Beitrag präsentiert die Theorie der organisationalen Trinität, eine sozialkonstruktivistische Meta-Theorie, die Organisationskultur und (Arbeits-)Motivation verknüpft und Veränderungsdynamiken erklärt. Ausgangspunkt sind Befunde aus der Sicherheitskulturforschung, wonach sich Kulturfacetten in ihrem Reifegrad beeinflussen.
Kernposition: Die Theorie postuliert eine realitätskonstituierende semantische Dreieinigkeit von Entität, Prozess und Struktur. Kategoriale Einordnungen dieses charakteristischen Triplets finden sich in anderen Konstrukten, u. a. in Semiotik, Politiktheorie und Motivmodellen (Leistung, Anschluss, Macht). Als Kulturfacette äußern sich Entität/Prozess/Struktur in Organisationen als Qualitäts-, Kommunikations- und Gerechtigkeitskultur: Qualitätskultur beschreibt, was als „gute Arbeit“ gilt (Entität), Kommunikationskultur, wie Koordination und Beziehungen gelingen (Entität + Prozess), und Gerechtigkeitskultur, nach welchen Regeln Ressourcen und Abläufe gestaltet werden (Entität + Prozess + Struktur). Aus empirischen Befunden wird ein Ablaufmodell abgeleitet, das qualitative Abhängigkeiten zwischen den Kulturfacetten beschreibt.
Implikation: Der theoretische Rahmen ermöglicht eine Operationalisierung der Kulturfacetten und damit ihrer experimentellen Prüfung unter Laborbedingungen. Für eine geplante Veränderung in der Organisationskultur bietet die Theorie einen einheitlichen Orientierungsrahmen, um unter Berücksichtigung motivationaler Dispositionen der Organisationsmitglieder konkrete Veränderungsmaßnahmen gestalten zu können. Ein weiterer Vorteil der Theorie sind deduktive und damit vergleichbare Kulturanalysen als Notwendigkeit für die Weiterentwicklung der praxisorientierten Kulturforschung.
Diskussion: Diskutiert werden die Theorie und dessen Prüfung, Implikationen für Theorien zu Motivation und Bedürfnis sowie praktische Implikationen für Transformationsprojekte und mentale Gesundheit.

Evidence accumulation is an incremental process in scientific research. Replicability plays a pivotal role in this process by enhancing the credibility and trustworthiness of psychological science. The replication crisis led to methodology, infrastructural, and editorial changes, to make replications easier to design, find, and publish. This symposium presents recent enhancements aimed at strengthening replication research in the field of psychology.
It provides researchers with practical tools for planning, conducting, and publishing replication studies. First, we present an approach to efficiently design replication studies using sequential methods. This approach allows researchers to maintain statistical power while avoiding unnecessary resource expenditure, particularly when the effect size is uncertain (Kondzic). Second, we will present a comprehensive replication database that will facilitate the faster identification of existing replication attempts (Schüller). We will also discuss community-based publishing for replication studies that aligns incentive structures with scientific ideals (Kolber). Lastly, we introduce the Replication Research (R2) Journal as a Diamond Open Access Standard (DOAS) journal that can be used by journals with minimal resources to simultaneously improve research quality (Müller).
Together, these contributions outline a coordinated framework for advancing replication research, from efficient study design to sustainable dissemination.

Show details

Replication studies are essential for establishing the robustness and generalizability of psychological research findings. However, planning replication studies can be challenging. In particular, determining an appropriate sample size is often difficult because reliable estimates of effect sizes are rarely available in advance for specific study designs. Consequently, replication studies are often underpowered or unnecessarily resource intensive.
Group Sequential Designs (GSD), a well-established approach especially in clinical and pharmaceutical research, offers a promising yet underutilized solution to design replication studies. These designs allow researchers to evaluate accumulating data at interim stages and make informed decisions about early stopping for efficacy (e.g., unexpectedly large effect size) or futility (e.g., unexpectedly small effect size). This reduces the expected sample size and addresses uncertainty in sample size planning.
We present accessible and easy-to-implement GSD that are specifically adapted for replication studies. We illustrate how these designs can be applied to both one-to-one replications (comparison between the original study and one replication study), as well as one-to-many replications (comparison between the original study and multiple replication studies).
To demonstrate and illustrate the practical value of GSD, we apply them to data from the Open Science Collaboration (2015) replication project. These examples demonstrate how GSD can substantially reduce the expected sample size while maintaining familywise error control. We conclude with practical recommendations and provide an easy-to-use R code to facilitate the adoption of GSD for replication research.

Due to predatory publishers, intransparent and low-quality peer review, AI generated articles articles, and questionable research practices, the publication status of a research article or the prestige of the journal it has appeared is rarely an indicator of quality. We present the R2 Initial Editorial Assessment, which is in line with the Diamond Open Access Standards (DOAS) for journals and can be employed by any academic journal even with minimal resources and improve research quality.

Science's (Broken) Feedback Loop: How Failed Replications (Fail to) Reduce Citations of Original Claims
Lukas Wallrich | University of London
Show details
Author:
Lukas Wallrich | University of London

Replication is a cornerstone of cumulative science, yet failed replications often do not appear to reduce belief in or use of original claims. If replications are fundamental to scientific self-correction, why do their results so often fail to shape the trajectory of knowledge?

We used the FORRT Library of Replication Attempts (FLoRA), which includes over 1,000 replications from across the social and behavioural sciences, to estimate the causal effect of failed replications on subsequent citations of their target studies. We fit a Fixed Effects Counterfactual (FECT) model to citation data for studies with a failed replication alongside matched control studies, and then used meta-analytic regression to test whether the citation impact is moderated by characteristics such as open-access status, journal rank, author overlap, or research field. We present the estimated causal effect on citation rates, the extent of heterogeneity across studies, and the moderators that distinguish more from less impactful replications — shedding light on what it would take to make science's self-corrective mechanism more effective.

Developing and testing theories is an integral part of science. Despite the significance of this type of work, however, links between theory and empirical work in psychology continue to be rather weak. Part of this is attributable to the fact that many psychological theories are expressed only in verbal form. Critics thus claim that psychology is in a state of “theory crisis”. To help alleviate this problem, a new task force was formed as part of the larger RESQUE project for improving research assessment. The task force was asked to devise a set of quality indicators for theory work specifically. In this symposium, we report on the process and the results that the task force has achieved thus far. We begin with the establishment of a (preliminary) consensus on basic terminology (Leising et al.) and reporting standards (Musfeld et al.) for developing and testing theories. We then showcase how such standards can be used to evaluate the theoretical rigor of existing pieces of research (Wiedenroth et al.), or to guide a process of theory specification (Lange & Küppers). The symposium ends with a discussion of how integrating explicit quality criteria in hiring, promotion, and publication decisions may help establish incentives for engaging in more productive theory work in psychology.

Identity Leadership, ein Führungsansatz, der auf dem sozialen Identitätsansatz basiert und auf die Förderung einer starken geteilten sozialen Identität abzielt, gewinnt zunehmend an Bedeutung in Wissenschaft und Praxis. Trotz wachsender theoretischer Fundierung bestehen weiterhin offene Fragen zu den zugrundeliegenden Mechanismen, Kontextabhängigkeiten und Grenzen des Ansatzes.
Das Symposium präsentiert sechs Beiträge, die diese Fragen in unterschiedlichen Kontexten (z. B. Organisationen, Sport, Gesellschaft) und mit unterschiedlichen methodischen Ansätzen (z. B. Feldstudien, Experimente, Theoriearbeit) adressieren. Die Vortragenden bilden eine Mischung aus Nachwuchswissenschaftler*innen und Professor*innen von Universitäten in Deutschland und darüber hinaus.
Kratzer et al. untersuchen mithilfe von drei methodischen Phasen aus Querschnitts-, halb-längsschnittlichen und experimentellen Studien, wie Identity Leadership Teamidentifikation stärkt und dadurch psychologische Sicherheit in Organisationen fördert. Lupina-Wegener et al. analysieren in einer longitudinalen Fallstudie einer länderübergreifenden Fusion, wie kollektives Identity Leadership die Herausbildung gemeinsamer Unternehmensidentitäten unterstützt und Übernahmeerfolge begünstigt. Braun et al. untersuchen, ob und wie die Prototypikalität einzelner Teammitglieder die Auswirkungen von Identity Leadership auf individuelle arbeitsbezogene Konzepte, beispielsweise Arbeitszufriedenheit und Kündigungsabsichten, beeinflusst. Blechta et al. analysieren, wie Identity Leadership und autokratisches Führungsverhalten in Sportteams auf Selbstwirksamkeit, Motivation sowie Resilienz auf Teamebene wirken und prüfen, ob Identifikationsprozesse die Effekte dieser Führungsansätze vermitteln. Zentgraf und Piening konzeptualisieren Identity Leadership als relationalen Prozess und argumentieren, wie vertikale und horizontale Austauschbeziehungen die Wirkung von Identitätssignalen prägen. Gleibs schließlich überträgt Identity Leadership auf die Förderung kollektiven Handelns für Nachhaltigkeit und illustriert dies in einer konzeptuellen Studie. Abgerundet wird das Symposium durch die Einordnung der Beiträge durch Rolf van Dick.

Ziel der vorliegenden Forschung war es, mithilfe von drei Phasen zu prüfen, ob der Mechanismus Identity Leadership über Teamidentifikation resultierend in psychologischer Sicherheit auch auf organisationale Kontexte übertragbar ist. Forschung dazu hat gezeigt, dass IL das Team, wie auch die einzelnen Teammitglieder, positiv beeinflusst. Ein zentraler Faktor für erfolgreiches IL ist das Ausmaß, in dem die Führungskraft den Prototyp des Teams verkörpert. Bislang ist jedoch unklar, ob und in welchem Umfang auch die Team-Prototypikalität einzelner Teammitglieder eine Rolle für die (positiven) Effekte von IL auf diese Teammitglieder spielt. In diesem Forschungsprojekt untersuchten wir die Fragestellung, ob die Team-Prototypikalität des einzelnen Teammitglieds die positiven Effekte von IL auf dieses Teammitglied moderiert, wobei eine hohe Prototypikalität diese Effekte signifikant verstärkt und eine niedrige Prototypikalität sie abschwächt. Zur Untersuchung dieser Annahme wurden zwei Studien durchgeführt. In Studie 1, einer Online-Befragung mit 132 Beschäftigten, wurden das wahrgenommene Identity Leadership der direkten Führungskraft als unabhängige Variable, die Team-Prototypikalität der Teilnehmer*innen als Moderator und soziale Identität der Mitarbeitenden, Arbeitszufriedenheit, Arbeitsengagement und Kündigungsabsichten als abhängige Variablen erfasst. Studie 2 war eine Szenariostudie mit 284 Teilnehmenden, in der IL sowie die Geschlechterprotoypikalität des Teammitglieds manipuliert und ähnliche AVs wie in Studie 1 erhoben wurden. In keiner der beiden Studien zeigten die Ergebnisse einen moderierenden Effekt der Team-Prototypikalität auf den Zusammenhang zwischen IL und den Outcomes. Allerdings zeigten sich in explorativen Analysen Hinweise für andere aufschlussreiche Zusammenhänge der erhobenen Konstrukte. Der Identity-Leadership-Ansatz beschreibt diese Wirkung als Fähigkeit von Führungskräften, organisationale Identität zu repräsentieren, zu fördern und zu verankern. Diese Perspektive bleibt jedoch weitgehend führungszentriert und hierarchisch, da sie Identitätsprozesse primär als Ergebnis von Führungsverhalten konzeptualisiert. In diesem Beitrag wird daher argumentiert, dass Identity Leadership ebenso als relationaler Prozess zu verstehen ist, in dem Führungskräfte und Mitarbeitende organisationale Identität wechselseitig und beziehungsabhängig ko-konstruieren. Durch die Integration von Identity Leadership und der LMX-Theorie wird deutlich, dass der Einfluss von Führung auf Identifikationsprozesse davon abhängt, wie die Beziehung zwischen Führungskraft und Mitarbeitenden ausgestaltet ist. So wird gezeigt, dass hochwertige LMX-Beziehungen die Übertragung von Identitätsangeboten erleichtern, während relationale Vergleichsprozesse (Relative LMX) und LMX-Differenzierung innerhalb von Teams Identitätssignale verstärken, verzerren oder gar fragmentieren können. Darüber hinaus verdeutlicht die Berücksichtigung von Team-Member-Exchange-(TMX)-Beziehungen, dass horizontale Beziehungen zwischen Teammitgliedern zur Ausbildung geteilter Identität beitragen können – teils komplementär zur Führung, teils unabhängig von oder abschwächend gegenüber deren Einfluss. Insgesamt wird ein relationales Verständnis von Identity Leadership entwickelt, das Führung nicht als individuelle Eigenschaft, sondern als Geflecht vertikaler und horizontaler Austauschbeziehungen begreift und damit einen differenzierteren Zugang zu Identitätsprozessen.

Can People Change Their Personality? Evidence from a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Intervention
Fabian Gander | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Fabian Gander | Switzerland
Dr. Lisa Wagner | Switzerland
Dr. Valentina Vylobkova | Switzerland
Dr. Sonja Heintz
Dr. Jessie Sun

The idea that adults can intentionally change their personality is widely appealing, yet empirical evidence remains limited and methodologically contested. In a preregistered randomized study (N = 3,434), we examined whether an eight-week online intervention targeting a self-selected character strength produces changes in character strengths states and traits, and Big Five personality traits. Participants were assigned to an intervention, placebo, or waitlist control condition and assessed at short- and long-term follow-ups using self- and informant reports.
Participants in the intervention condition showed greater increases in targeted strength states compared to both control groups. Changes in targeted strength traits, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism outperformed the waitlist control, but did not differ from the placebo condition. Informant reports revealed no between-condition differences in trait change.
These findings suggest that observed trait-level changes may be driven by non-specific factors associated with structured, goal-directed activities rather than by the targeted content of the intervention itself. The results highlight the necessity of rigorous placebo controls and multi-informant designs when evaluating claims about volitional personality change.

Integration des „Warum“ und „Wie“ menschlichen Verhaltens: Selbstbestimmung, Verhaltensaktivierung und Verhaltenshemmung innerhalb und zwischen Personen
Dr. Axel Grund | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Axel Grund | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Philipp Sischka | University of Luxembourg

Der Beitrag widmet sich der wenig beachteten Frage, wie zwei grundlegende Motivationsansätze miteinander in Verbindung gebracht werden können. Wir nehmen dabei an, dass unterschiedliche Gründe menschlichen Verhaltens, also das „Warum“ (Deci & Ryan, 2000), differenzierte auslösende Bedingungen von Verhaltensaktivierung und -hemmung bzw. Annäherung und Vermeidung, also dem „Wie“ des Verhaltens (Elliot & Thrash, 2002; Gray, 1990), darstellen. Der zugrundeliegende Datensatz integriert drei strukturell ähnliche Experience-Sampling-Studien (insgesamt 279 Personen mit 10,723 Messpunkten), in denen jeweils Studierende (mittleres Alter = 22.9 Jahre, 82.3% weiblich) über etwa eine Woche in Echtzeit Auskunft über den Grad der Selbstbestimmung (externale, introjizierte, identifizierte und intrinsische Regulation) ihrer alltäglichen Aktivitäten sowie über ihre aktuelle positive Aktivierung (PA), negative Aktivierung (NA) und Valenz (VA) gaben. Mehrebenen-Korrelationsanalysen bestätigen zunächst die vermutete Simplexstruktur der Handlungsgründe innerhalb und zwischen Personen: Regulationsformen, die jeweils näher auf dem Selbstbestimmungskontinuum lokalisiert werden, zeigen jeweils engere positive Zusammenhänge. Darüber hinaus bestätigen Mehrebenen-Regressionsanalysen die Vermutung, dass PA überwiegend durch autonome Gründe (d.h., identifizierte und intrinsische Regulation) ausgelöst wird. NA hingegen scheint sowohl von kontrollierten Handlungsgründen (d.h., externale und introjizierte Regulation) als auch der Abwesenheit intrinsischer Motivation bestimmt. Die Befunde für VA, als übergeordneter Verhaltensdimension, bestätigen dieses Regressionsmuster, welches über alle Variablen prononcierter ausfällt, wenn Unterschiede zwischen versus innerhalb von Personen betrachtet werden. Insgesamt sprechen die Befunde für die zentrale Bedeutung intrinsischer Motivation für Erleben und Verhalten. Methodische Einschränkungen und weiterführende längsschnittliche Auswertungsmethoden der Arbeit werden diskutiert.

Auf Grundlage einer kritischen Analyse dieser Annahme (Grund et al., in press) legen wir Experience-Sampling-Daten vor, die zeigen, dass der Zusammenhang zwischen Herausforderung und Aversion vom Ausmaß der erlebten Selbstbestimmung moderiert wird. Einhundertvierzehn Studierende (Durchschnittsalter = 23.2 Jahre; 81% weiblich, 19% männlich) berichteten über eine Woche hinweg mehrmals täglich in Echtzeit über die Gründe, die ihren alltäglichen Aktivtäten (N = 4,481) zugrunde lagen (Selbstbestimmung), den Grad der mit den Aktivitäten verbundenen Herausforderung und ihren aktuellen Affekt (Aversion). Mehrebenenanalysen zeigen, dass Herausforderung und Aversion tatsächlich positiv miteinander zusammenhingen, wenn Alltagsaktivitäten als niedrig-selbstbestimmt erlebt wurden. Der Effekt drehte sich allerdings bei hoher Selbstbestimmung um. Tatsächlich wurden hoch-selbstbestimmte Aktivitäten sogar umso mehr genossen, je herausfordernder sie waren, und dass unabhängig davon, ob es sich um Studiums- oder Freizeitaktivitäten handelte. Die Analysen zeigen auch, dass der Grad der Selbstbestimmung – nicht aber derjenige der Herausforderung – erklären kann, warum Studieren typischerweise als aversiver erlebt wird als Freizeit. Dies spricht insgesamt dafür, dass die Frustration des Autonomiebedürfnisses, nicht aber hohe Herausforderungen an sich, Aversion hervorruft. Zur Förderung anspruchsvoller (kognitiver) Tätigkeiten sollte also eher mehr als weniger Handlungsspielraum gewährt werden.

Florian Scholten | Eberhard Karls Universität Tübingen | Germany

Authors:

Pairing a neutral conditioned stimuli (CSs) with valenced unconditioned stimuli (USs) or outcomes (valenced experiences with CSs) elicits behavioral responses of liking toward them. This evaluative conditioning effect is typically examined in contingent environments where a CS is paired only with positive or negative USs. However, real-world conditioning of stimuli is rarely univalent, and CSs may be probabilistically paired with combinations of positive, negative, or mixed USs. Pairings are also not always indicative of a stimulus’ actual valence: a likable person might live in a crime-ridden area and be consistently paired with negative stimuli without that meaning the person himself should be evaluated negatively. In three experiments (total N = 343), we examined the acquisition of attitudes and its underlying uncertainty in probabilistic environments. In 300 trials, participants predicted whether experiences with four companies would be positive or negative based on CS-US pairings of company logos and valenced images. We manipulated the liking and predictability of each company by (mis)matching the valence of CS-US pairings and associated outcomes. Both CS-US pairings and CS-outcome pairings successfully elicited positive or negative evaluation for each CS, Unpredictability led to a decrease in CS valence scores. To illustrate the dynamic development of uncertainty in attitudes depending on the predictability of company experiences, a cognitive process model was developed by analyzing more than 102,000 response time and choice data. The parameters of our dynamic diffusion decision model and their trajectories reflect varying pathways of uncertainty reduction in the process of liking and disliking over time.

Prof. Guido H.E. Gendolla | University of Geneva | Switzerland
Show details
Author:
Prof. Guido H.E. Gendolla | University of Geneva | Switzerland

Reconciling different theoretical perspectives on self-regulation, this talk highlights a critical yet understudied effect of personal control: action shielding against affective biases. Building on an integrative action-shielding model (Gendolla et al., 2021), a series of experiments examined how personal action choice and action-related mindsets influence task persistence—the duration of engagement before disengagement. Across studies, personal task choice reliably increased persistence and protected performance from affective influences such as happy versus sad background music. In contrast, when the same task was externally assigned—as is typical in psychological research—participants exposed to happy music disengaged earlier than those exposed to sad music. Extending these findings to experimentally induced mindsets (Gollwitzer, 2012), similar effects emerged. Under a deliberative mindset, participants in a sad mood persisted longer than those in a happy mood, whereas the reverse pattern occurred when participants were instructed to stop once the task was no longer enjoyable. Crucially, activating an implementation mindset consistently produced high persistence and eliminated mood-related differences. Integrating multiple perspectives on self-regulation, this research underscores the importance of personal control. It demonstrates that agency—instantiated through personal task choice or an implementation mindset—not only enhances engagement but also shields action execution from affective biases. Implications for designing evidence-based psychological interventions in different fields are discussed.

Introduction: Children affected by war and mass violence face a high risk of psychological distress, yet little is known about differential burdens in genocide-surviving versus war-affected populations. This study examined traumatic exposure, PTSD symptoms, psychological strain, and physical complaints in Syrian war-affected children and Ezidi children who survived the 2014 genocide in Northern Iraq. Methods: Between June and September 2017, participants completed the Arabic version of the Essen Trauma-Inventory for Children and Adolescents (ETI-KJ). Results: The sample comprised 37 Syrian children and 30 Ezidi genocide survivors (N = 67). All participants reported at least one traumatic event, with comparable exposure frequencies across groups. Overall, 31.3% met criteria for probable PTSD. Ezidi children, however, showed significantly higher PTSD prevalence and symptom severity, as well as greater psychological strain. Physical complaints were reported by 59.7% of the sample but did not differ between groups. Regression analyses identified the number of traumatic events, physical complaints, and group membership (war vs. genocide exposure) as significant predictors of PTSD severity, explaining 43.7% of the variance. Discussion: Findings highlight substantial psychological burden in both groups, with Ezidi children exhibiting particularly elevated symptoms. These differences likely reflect not only the extreme brutality of the 2014 genocide but also longstanding, transgenerational experiences of persecution embedded in Ezidi collective memory. The results underscore the need for trauma-informed, culturally sensitive interventions that integrate historical and identity-related dimensions of suffering to foster long-term recovery and resilience.

Strategien zur Verbesserung von KI-gestützter Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse
Ida Schulze Tast | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ida Schulze Tast | Germany
Sarah Humberg

Im Forschungsalltag spielt künstliche Intelligenz (KI) eine zunehmend wichtige Rolle. Ein Anwendungsbereich ist hierbei die Nutzung von KI zur Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse. Erste Studienergebnisse zeigen, dass gängige Large Language Modelle (LLMs) wie GPT-5.1 bei der Interpretation komplexer Analysen häufig typische Fehler aus der Forschungsliteratur reproduzieren. Die Verwendung von LLMs zur Interpretation von statistischen Ergebnissen kann somit zur Weiterverbreitung falscher Schlussfolgerungen führen und ein Risiko für die Validität von Forschungsergebnissen darstellen.

In meinem Vortrag beleuchte ich mögliche Strategien, um die Fehler von LLMs im Kontext der Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse zu reduzieren. Dazu arbeite ich die Vorgehensweisen für mehrere Strategien heraus, die in zwei Hauptkategorien eingeteilt werden können. Die erste Kategorie umfasst Ansätze, bei denen die internen Parameter des LLMs modifiziert werden. Ein Beispiel dafür ist das Fine Tuning, bei dem LLMs mit Daten zu gewünschten Input-Output Paaren gezielt für eine bestimmte Aufgabe nachtrainiert werden. Die zweite Kategorie umfasst Ansätze, die das LLM ohne interne Modellanpassungen nutzen, sondern die Output-Qualität über geschickte Verbesserungen des Promptings erhöhen. Dies umfasst zum Beispiel die Ergänzung des Prompts um ein oder mehrere (korrekte) Beispiele der gleichen Aufgabenart (Multi-Shot Prompting) oder die Einbindung von Wissensinhalten über ein RAG. In meinem Vortrag werde ich die Ergebnisse eines empirischen Experiments präsentieren, in dem ich diverse Strategien hinsichtlich der Korrektheit der Outputs in mehreren Interpretationsaufgaben gegeneinander vergleiche. Insgesamt beleuchtet der Beitrag verschiedene Möglichkeiten zur Verbesserung der Ergebnisse von LLMs bei der Interpretation statistischer Analysen und diskutiert damit Möglichkeiten für einen verantwortungsvollen Einsatz von KI im Bereich der psychologischen Datenanalyse.

KI-gestützte Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse: eine Warnung
Sarah Humberg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Sarah Humberg | Germany

Neuere Entwicklungen bei Large Language Modellen (LLMs) eröffnen neue Möglichkeiten für eine KI-basierte methodische Unterstützung bei der Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse. Forschende können erstaunlich leicht Hilfe bei der Auswertung komplexer Analysen erhalten, etwa indem sie einen Chatbot bitten, aus den Ergebnissen eine Schlussfolgerung zu formulieren oder Feedback zur eigenen Interpretation zu geben.

In meinem Vortrag werde ich argumentieren, dass dieses Vorgehen ein erhebliches Risiko für Fehlinterpretationen bergen kann, insbesondere bei statistischen Analyseverfahren, die in der Fachliteratur häufig missverstanden werden. Wenn Fehlkonzeptionen zur Interpretation statistischer Analysen im Trainingsmaterial der LLMs enthalten sind, könnten die Modelle dazu neigen, sie zu reproduzieren. Forschende, die sich bspw. aufgrund eigener statistischer Wissenslücken auf KI-Unterstützung verlassen, liefen dann Gefahr, zu falschen Schlussfolgerungen zu kommen. Um einzuschätzen, inwiefern die niedrigschwellige Nutzung von LLMs die korrekte Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse fördert oder gefährdet, werde ich die Ergebnisse einer experimentellen Studie präsentieren. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass selbst aktuelle Spitzenmodelle (z. B. GPT-5.1) systematisch fehlerhafte Schlussfolgerungen für bestimmte analytische Verfahren vorschlagen. Die Nutzung dieser Modelle bei der Interpretation statistischer Verfahren kann damit die Validität der empirischen Schlussfolgerungen erheblich bedrohen. Ich werde aus diesen Ergebnissen praktische Empfehlungen ableiten und die Notwendigkeit betonen, in entsprechender methodischer Forschung KI-gestützte Werkzeuge zu entwickeln, die die Risiken der KI-Nutzung bei der Interpretation statistischer Ergebnisse mindern.

In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in both everyday life and scientific research. These novel and potentially powerful tools facilitate the fast and automated extraction of text features as well as the generation of stimulus materials. At the same time, these models allow for a high degree of flexibility, as variations in prompt design, model family, complexity, and configuration may result in divergent results and conclusions. To navigate the multiverse of possible choices available to researchers, the present study proposes a structured workflow for simulating different LLM options to assess the quality of features extracted from verbal stimulus material. We also propose a template that guides researchers step by step through the process of planning and reporting a simulation study for LLM feature extraction, emphasizing critical design choices and relevant information that should be reported in a scientific paper. In a pre-registered case study, we examine the influence of model choice, response format, and details of prompt design (e.g., example type) on the quality of valence and arousal ratings. Furthermore, we assess the efficacy of various methods for aggregating repeated LLM ratings.

Dr. Verena Johann | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Verena Johann | Germany

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools among university students raises important questions about its psychological determinants and consequences. Grounded in the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, this longitudinal diary study examined whether perceived academic stress predicts AI use, whether academic self-efficacy moderates this association, and how AI use affects the development of self-efficacy over a short time period. A sample of 256 university students, aged 18–30, completed questionnaires assessing academic self-efficacy, followed by a 10-day daily diary assessing AI use and academic stress, and a follow-up assessment of self-efficacy. Multilevel logistic models showed that stress significantly predicted AI use. However, self-efficacy did not moderate this relationship indicating that AI tools were not used primarily as a compensatory resource by students with low self-efficacy, but rather served as a resource across different levels of self-efficacy. Moreover, multiple regression analyses showed that both academic stress and AI use significantly predicted changes in self-efficacy when controlling for baseline levels. Academic stress negatively affected self-efficacy development, whereas AI use showed a small positive effect. Contrary to expectations, AI use did not buffer the negative impact of stress on self-efficacy. These findings suggest that AI tools function as broadly accessible coping and learning resources rather than purely compensatory tools for students with low self-efficacy. While AI use may provide small benefits for self-efficacy development, it does not protect against the negative effects of academic stress.

Prokrastination, das problematische Aufschieben von Aufgaben, ist unter Studierenden weit verbreitet und oftmals mit starkem Leidensdruck und akademischen Leistungseinbußen verknüpft. Professionelle psychosoziale Beratungsangebote werden nur von einem Bruchteil der Betroffenen in Anspruch genommen. Peer-Beratung als eine semi-professionelle Form von Beratung „unter Gleichen“ (Egloff, 2020) kann eine aussichtsreiche, niedrigschwellige Erweiterung des psychosozialen Versorgungsangebots darstellen. An der Hochschule Düsseldorf wurde deshalb für 24 Monate ein entsprechendes Pilot-Projekt ins Leben gerufen, in dem Studierende eine kurze Schulung in der Prokrastinationsberatung erhalten und dann für ihre Mitstudierenden als Peer-Berater*innen zur Verfügung stehen. Quantitative Daten zur Evaluation von über 100 Beratungsprozessen aus der Perspektive der Peer-Berater*innen und der studentischen Ratsuchenden sollen auf dem Kongress vorgestellt und ihr potentieller Nutzen - über dieses Pilotprojekt hinaus - beleuchtet werden.

Background: Mental health problems among pre-service teachers have received increasing attention, with numerous studies reporting elevated levels of stress, burnout and psychological strain during teacher training (Aldrup et al., 2017; Gustems-Carnicer et al., 2019; Zito et al., 2024). These challenges are relevant due to their immediate impact on students’ well-being as well as their potential long-term consequences for professional development and retention in the teaching profession (Arnold & Rahimi, 2025). Despite the growing literature, research remains conceptually and theoretically fragmented, limiting cumulative knowledge building and development of theory-informed prevention and intervention approaches.
Objectives: This scoping review is the first to systematically map the literature on mental health problems among pre-service teachers by identifying (a) examined mental health constructs, (b) how these constructs are defined and operationalized, (c) applied theoretical frameworks, and (d) studied outcomes and predictors across stages of teacher education.
Methods: The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PsycINFO, ERIC, PubMed, and Web of Science, supplemented by preprint servers and targeted handsearching. A total of 44,397 records were retrieved. At abstract submission, the review was in title and abstract screening stage, conducted by two independent reviewers using a hybrid human–machine learning approach implemented in ASReview. The review will be completed by September 2026.
Contributions: By systematically mapping mental health constructs, their definitions, theoretical perspectives, and research gaps, this review establishes a conceptual foundation for future research and for theory-informed prevention and mental health support in teacher education.

In a cross-sectional survey (N = 393 students; 72% female), participants completed the German SFES and the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; Janke & Glöckner-Rist, 2012). EFA examined the factor structure, and linear regressions analyzed associations with life satisfaction.

No main effects on life satisfaction emerged in the total sample. Due to the uneven gender distribution and unexpected findings, exploratory moderation analyses included gender. A significant interaction was found for positive experiences (β=-.49, p=.03). Among women, positive fantasy experiencing predicted higher life satisfaction, whereas among men, a negative association emerged.
The German SFES validly captures two dimensions—positive and negative experiencing of sexual fantasies. Findings indicate gender-specific links between fantasy processing and life satisfaction. Men's counterintuitive pattern may reflect gender norms, alexithymia, or unique behavioral correlates of fantasizing, warranting replication and further research.

The objective function combined fit indices (RMSEA, SRMR), composite reliability, and criteria targeting both cross-informant and informant-specific factor structure. Preliminary results indicate that no subscale solution met all a priori conceptually grounded cutoffs across criteria in either sample. These findings are discussed in terms of methodological and substantive explanations, including sample characteristics and challenges in modelling the clinical subscales as latent factors in CFA.

Background: Stress is an omnipresent phenomenon, and while various coping mechanisms exist, the use of humor—specifically black humor—remains under-researched. This study addresses this research gap by developing and validating a scale to measure how individuals use black humor as a strategy to manage stress.

Methodology: The research followed a quantitative approach. Initially, items were theoretically generated and evaluated for content validity by five psychology students using Lawshe’s Content Validity Index. In the next step, an online survey was conducted with a sample of N=116. To assess construct and criterion validity, the scale was correlated with established instruments measuring the Big Five personality traits, resilience, social desirability, and general stress-coping mechanisms.

Results: Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses confirmed that black humor as a coping strategy constitutes an independent psychological construct. The final scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency with a Cronbach’s alpha of .939. Statistical testing revealed a significant positive correlation with neuroticism and a significant negative correlation with social desirability. No significant correlations were found regarding resilience, general coping strategies, extraversion, and openness.

Conclusion: The results highlight that black humor is a relevant psychological mechanism for processing stressful traumatic experiences. This newly developed scale provides a reliable foundation for future research in stress management and potential therapeutic applications.

Qualitative findings indicated that participants consistently reported early environments characterised by emotional unpredictability, relational disruptions, peer rejection or bullying, and heightened sensitivity to others’ reactions, from which avoidant coping strategies emerged and were subsequently consolidated into stable identity narratives.

CU traits, marked by lack of remorse, guilt, and empathy are robust predictors of delinquency, whereas SC represents a key protective factor. Sensitivity analyses indicated that these effects were generally robust. However, SC effects attenuated under stricter quality criteria and became non-significant for some, but not all, quality thresholds. In total, data from 3227 participants were analysed. Overall, CU- and SC-focused interventions yielded small to moderate effects, suggesting that these programs can produce measurable changes in youth and hold promise for crime-related prevention intervention efforts during adolescence.

317. Disentangling Memory and Guessing Biases in Source Monitoring Across Schizotypy Dimensions
Isabel Porstein | University of Mannheim | Germany

Authors:

Prof. Thomas R. Kwapil | University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign | United States
Prof. Dr. Beatrice G. Kuhlmann | University of Mannheim | Germany

Cognitive models of psychosis increasingly emphasize impairments in episodic memory, particularly recollection-based processes supporting source memory. Findings in sub-clinical schizotypy are inconsistent, often due to limited source types, neglecting schizotypy’s multidimensionality, and measures that confound memory with guessing. As a result, it remains unclear whether observed source monitoring deficits reflect impairments in memory or systematic guessing biases like externalization of internally generated information. Addressing this, we developed a four-source memory paradigm assessing external source monitoring, internal source monitoring, and reality monitoring. Participants viewed everyday objects presented with two external (female vs. male voice) and two internal (imagine self vs. other) sources. We extended the Two High Threshold Model of Source Monitoring (2HTSM; Bayen et al., 1996) to four sources enabling the separation of item memory, source memory, and guessing. A pilot study with N = 40 participants confirmed the fit of empirical data with the model. N = 400 participants aged 18-30 years were pre-screened with the Multidimensional Schizotypy Scale (Kwapil et al., 2018) assessing the positive, negative, and disorganized dimension separately, of which N = 150 participants took part in the experiment. Participants’ z-standardized schizotypy scores widely spanned across all dimensions. The three schizotypy dimensions and their interactions, were entered as simultaneous predictors, showing that higher positive schizotypy tended to be associated with an increased externalization bias and subtle shifts in the likelihood of guessing the internal-self source. This was accompanied by reduced source memory for internal sources, particularly when positive schizotypy interacted with disorganized traits.

318. Daily Affect Dynamics in Very Old Age Across Time: The Role of Vulnerabilities But Also Strengths
Anton Lachmann | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Petra Zöllner | Heidelberg University | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Prof. Dr. Oliver Schilling | Heidelberg University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Hans-Werner Wahl | Heidelberg University | Germany
Dr. Markus Wettstein | University Medicine Greifswald

Very old age, often referred to as the "fourth age", is commonly framed as a life phase of increased vulnerability. Developmental theories, however, postulate that vulnerabilities and strengths co-occur across the entire lifespan but compared to other life phases, strengths in very old age have been studied less extensively. Population aging and the associated individual and societal changes underscore the need to move beyond a vulnerability-oriented portrayal of very old age and foster a more nuanced understanding of the co-occurrence of strengths and vulnerabilities. The aim of the present project is thus to investigate strengths and vulnerabilities in very old age, and examine how they are linked to affective experience, stress reactivity, and stress regulation in everyday life and over time, based on a multi-site measurement burst design covering 12 months. A stratified sample (N = 360) of individuals 80 years and older is recruited in Berlin, Heidelberg, and Luxembourg. Participants complete assessments of personal resources, risk factors, health, and well-being at three measurement waves conducted at six-month intervals. At each assessment wave, participants also complete a seven-day, six-times-a-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA). These reports capture “real-time” affective experiences, strengths and vulnerabilities in daily life. Our multi-method, multi-wave design enables a comprehensive examination linking strengths and vulnerabilities with affective dynamics in daily life and their change over time. The study will yield insights regarding the interplay of strengths and vulnerabilities in very old age and thereby provide theoretical and practical implications for supporting well-being and healthy aging in the oldest-old.

319. Employees’ search for meaning: Development and validation of a value-oriented job crafting scale
Ramona Effting | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ramona Effting | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Klaus Moser | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany
PD Dr. Katharina Ebner | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany

In recent decades, there has been a significant increase in research on job crafting, defined as the proactive physical and cognitive changes individuals make at work. To date, job crafting has been considered an activity in which employees choose to change aspects of their work primarily if they see benefits for themselves. Borrowing from the theoretical foundations of logotherapy, we propose a different conceptualization of job crafting that is based on self-transcendence and where the individual’s goal is to find meaning at work by focusing outwards. We started with the assumption that there are three main ways to discover meaning: Through the realization of creational, experiential or attitudinal values. Based on these pathways, we introduce four strategies of value-oriented job crafting (VOJC): (1) Creational Crafting, relating to personal contribution at work targeting values such as responsibility, (2) Experiential Crafting, relating to openness to genuine encounters targeting values such as community and (3+4) Attitudinal Crafting, relating to (3) adopting a positive stance in face of negative work aspects, targeting values such as acceptance, and (4) adopting an appreciating attitude towards positive work aspects, targeting values such as gratitude. Integrating expert opinions, we developed and tested items for each strategy. Both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses (sample of n=731 employees) supported a 4-dimensional VOJC-model. The new scale (24 items) is correlated with work meaningfulness but is only weakly related to type of job. In sum, it provides a solid foundation for its use in future VOJC-interventions focusing on value and meaning.

320. Strategien der Glücksspielwerbung aus Sicht von Spielsüchtigen
Prof. Dr. Georg Felser | Hochschule Harz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Georg Felser | Hochschule Harz | Germany
Maja Lüdtke

Die Werbung für Glücksspiele bedient sich einer Vielzahl von werbepsychologischen Strategien, und etliche dieser Strategien verfangen bei ihren Adressaten. Glücksspiel kann zur Sucht werden, und wo dies geschieht, stellt sich die Frage, welche Rolle dabei die Werbung gespielt hat. In einer Befragung unter abstinenten Süchtigen zeichnet sich ab, dass die Werbung in unterschiedlichen Phasen der Sucht unterschiedliche Rollen einnimmt. Rückblickend stellen die Befragten nahezu übereinstimmend fest, dass die Werbung in den Anfangsphasen der Sucht noch nicht als „triggernd“ oder ursächlich für die Sucht erlebt wird. Die Funktion der Werbung scheint eher im Bereitstellen der Information über Gelegenheiten zum Spiel zu bestehen. Der Entschluss zur Abstinenz stellt dagegen einen Wendepunkt in der Wahrnehmung der Werbung dar. In der hierauf folgenden Übergangsphase sind Spielsüchtige besonders vulnerabel, und Werbung kann durchaus als „triggernd“ erlebt werden. Bei stabiler Abstinenz wird die Werbung kritisch und mit stark negativen Emotionen betrachtet. Hierbei heben die Betroffenen als besonders gefährlich hervor, wenn die Werbung reale Glücksspielgeräusche enthält oder wenn mit Boni geworben wird.
Die Aussagen aus den Interviews sind gerade aus dieser distanzierten Perspektive eine wertvolle Quelle. Die Betroffenen analysieren die Wirkmechanismen aus ihrer „Innenperspektive“ auf hohem Niveau und geben wertvolle Hinweise, worin aus ihrer Sicht genau die Faktoren bestehen, die eine Glücksspielsucht befördern.

321. More than Fresh Air: Forest Therapy at the Intersection of Mental and One Health – Feasibility, Differential Fit, and Regional Implementation
Sophie Hauck | University of Greifswald, Institute for Psychology | Germany
Ann-Kristin Reinhard | University Medicine Greifswald, Institute for Community Medicine | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sophie Hauck | University of Greifswald, Institute for Psychology | Germany
Ann-Kristin Reinhard | University Medicine Greifswald, Institute for Community Medicine | Germany
Prof. Dr. Eva-Lotta Brakemeier | University of Greifswald, Institute for Psychology | Germany
Prof. Dr. Susanne Wurm | University Medicine Greifswald, Institute for Community Medicine | Germany
Dr. Kristin Lehnert | University Medicine Greifswald, Clinic for Internal Medicine B | Germany

As psychological strain rises alongside ecological and societal challenges, the question is no longer only what improves mental health, but what can be implemented responsibly, for whom, and under real-world conditions.
Within a One Health-framework, forests represent critical resources for human health while addressing climate-related challenges. Although nature-based interventions show promising physiological and psychosocial effects, European evidence on forest therapy remains limited, particularly regarding feasibility and target-group differences.
Embedded in the BMFTR-funded T!Raum initiative, the Forest|Health project evaluates a four-week forest-therapy-program in structurally disadvantaged Western Pomerania, a predominantly rural region with growing health care demands and limited access, alongside rich natural environments. The study targets three groups: individuals with depressive symptoms recruited from psychotherapy waiting lists, individuals with hypertension, and adults 65+. Participants are quasi-randomly assigned to structurally equivalent modules focusing on mindfulness, physical activity, or creative engagement in nature.
This research talk presents implementation-oriented findings, including feasibility under regional care conditions, acceptability, perceived burden, and differential fit across heterogeneous populations. Analyses examine within-group changes in perceived stress and exploratory variation by target group, module type, perceived fit, and nature connectedness. Data collection has been completed; findings will be presented by September 2026, while follow-up assessments continue.
By moving beyond efficacy toward feasibility, context, and differential indication, the project contributes to responsible, diversity-sensitive, future-oriented development of nature-based mental health care. It illustrates how prevention and care can be strategically bridged in underserved regions and advances systematic integration of forest therapy into German-speaking health systems in alignment with One Health principles.

322. Das Reflexive Einsatztraining (RET) – Wirksamkeitsevaluation eines Trainings zur Stärkung der psychischen Gesundheit von Einsatzkräften
Prof. Dr. Renate Eisentraut | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Renate Eisentraut | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg | Germany
Maya Bräuer | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg
Prof. Dr. Birgitt Erdwien | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg
Jessica Riske-Oeffen | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg
Kyra Kirsch | Europäische Fernhochschule Hamburg

Einsatzkräfte aus Polizei, Feuerwehr und Rettungsdienst sind in ihrer täglichen Arbeit vielen Situationen ausgesetzt, die sie psychisch und physisch herausfordern und die zu erheblichen Beeinträchtigungen ihrer psychischen Gesundheit führen können. Um diesen individuellen und kollektiven Belastungsfolgen entgegenzuwirken, wurde vom Arbeiter-Samariter-Bund Landesverband Bremen e.V. das interaktive Trainingsprogramm Reflexives Einsatztraining (RET) entwickelt. Es wird davon ausgegangen, dass das RET durch die Förderung von Selbstreflexion und Ressourcenaktivierung zur psychischen Stabilisierung beiträgt, aber auch dysfunktionalen antidemokratischen Einstellungen im Dienst entgegenwirkt. Aufbauend auf theoretischen Modellen zu Stressbewältigung und Resilienz untersucht die vorliegende Studie, inwiefern das RET die Fähigkeit stärkt, kritische Ereignisse adaptiv zu verarbeiten und die psychische Stabilität der Einsatzkräfte aufrechtzuerhalten. Zur systematischen Wirksamkeitsevaluation haben wir ein Mixed-Methods Design mit Experimental- und Kontrollgruppen entwickelt. In einer quantitativen Längsschnittuntersuchung (vor und nach der Trainingsteilnahme, sechs Wochen nach der Teilnahme, vor und nach einer zweiten Teilnahme) werden kurz-, mittel- und langfristige Trainingseffekte auf Resilienz, Ressourcen, Bewältigungsstrategien und demokratische Einstellungen erfasst. Um mögliche Vor-Test-Effekte zu kontrollieren, kommt in den Erhebungen vor und nach der ersten Teilnahme zudem ein Solomon-Vier-Gruppen-Design mit zwei Experimental- und zwei Kontrollgruppen zum Einsatz. Qualitative Tiefeninterviews im Abstand von sechs Monaten zur Teilnahme und eine projektabschließende Expert:innenkonferenz liefern darüber hinaus vertiefende Einsichten in Veränderungsprozesse auf individueller und organisationaler Ebene. Bisherige Ergebnisse deuten auf eine hohe Akzeptanz und positive Wahrnehmung des Trainings hin, was die Umsetzbarkeit und Relevanz des Konzepts unterstreicht. Damit liefert die Studie einen empirisch fundierten Beitrag zur Entwicklung evidenzbasierter Präventions- und Interventionsprogramme zur Stärkung der psychischen Gesundheit in Hochrisikoberufen.

323. Need for Cognition and Burnout in Healthcare Professionals: The role of regulatory strategies
Prof. Dr. Anja Strobel | Technische Universität Chemnitz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Anja Strobel | Technische Universität Chemnitz | Germany
Kea Rüter | Technische Universität Chemnitz
Prof. Dr. Alexander Strobel | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden)

Burnout has become a global health concern, particularly among healthcare professionals. Several studies suggest a protective role of Need for Cognition (NFC)—the intrinsic motivation to engage in effortful cognitive activities—against burnout. In a total sample of N = 642 healthcare professionals from two preregistered studies, we replicated and extended previous findings on the relationship between NFC and burnout. We examined bivariate associations and multiple mediation models including self-control, emotion regulation strategies (reappraisal and suppression), as well as adaptive and maladaptive coping as mediators. The burnout dimensions reduced personal efficacy, emotional exhaustion, and depersonalization were analysed separately. Regarding direct associations, higher NFC was strongly positively associated with self-control, modestly positively related to adaptive coping, and strongly negatively related to maladaptive coping. Contrary to expectations, NFC was unrelated to reappraisal and suppression. With respect to burnout, mediation analyses indicated that adaptive coping significantly mediated the relationship between NFC and all three burnout dimensions. Maladaptive coping mediated only the relationship between NFC and emotional exhaustion. Reappraisal showed a small mediation effect solely for reduced personal efficacy, whereas suppression showed no mediation effects. Self-control did not mediate any associations between NFC and burnout. Overall, the findings suggest that individuals with higher NFC may experience a protective effect against burnout, particularly through the adoption of adaptive coping strategies. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions, the results contribute to a better understanding of the psychological factors influencing burnout and offer valuable implications for interventions aimed at enhancing well-being in healthcare settings.

324. Therapists' emotional skills impact their job satisfaction and burnout symptoms
Dr. Michaela Rohr | Saarland University | Germany
Show details

Dr. Michaela Rohr | Saarland University | Germany
Prof. Tanja Michael | Saarland University | Germany
Dr. Elisabeth Hahn

The role of a psychotherapist requires several emotional competencies, including the ability to regulate emotions in various areas (e.g. acceptance, understanding and body awareness; see Berking et al., 2010), as well as empathy and the ability to take the patient's perspective (Paulus, 2009; Davis, 1983). Although these skills are generally considered relevant in literature and psychotherapist training, there is little empirical evidence on their specific impact. Existing studies have often used clinical assessment questionnaires and thus only addressed the skills from a specific perspective. In a large, cross-sectional, online questionnaire study, we assessed the affective competencies (i.e. emotion regulation skills and empathy) of a German-speaking sample of psychotherapists (N = 1,021) using commonly employed questionnaires for assessing affective competencies (i.e. the SEK-27 [Berking et al., 2010] and the SPF/IRI [Paulus, 2009]). We examined how these skills were related to self-reported burnout symptoms and job satisfaction. Furthermore, through structural equation modelling, we established a relationship between these skills and the assessed outcome variables and the global construct of therapists' work involvement (Orlinsky & Rønnestad, 2005).In the model, lower affective skills were associated with more stressful work involvement, resulting in lower job satisfaction and more burnout symptoms. This study therefore highlights the importance of affective processing skills for both patients and therapists, and provides a basis for assessing competencies in psychotherapy training across different approaches.

325. The Impact of Sensory Processing Sensitivity on Psychological and Physiological Stress Responses in Dyadic Interactions
Annalena Knautz | Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annalena Knautz | Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Dr. Regina Schmid | Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt
Prof. Dr. Katrin Rentzsch | Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt

Over the past few years, media attention surrounding sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) has grown consistently. Described as a biologically based temperament trait, SPS is characterized by deeper cognitive processing of stimuli, greater attention to subtleties, heightened emotional reactivity, and ease of overstimulation. Previous research has shown that higher individual levels of SPS are associated with increased perceived stress and negative health outcomes. However, these studies have predominantly focused on subjective, self-reported perceptions of stress. Studies involving objective physiological measures are scarce. Furthermore, there is a lack of knowledge on how stress manifests in highly sensitive individuals within interpersonal contexts. To address these gaps, we will test how SPS is associated with psychological and physiological stress reactivity in a pre-registered study that employs a novel dyadic version of the Trier Social Stress Test. In this study, dyad members are actively and alternately involved in stress induction tasks while being able to witness each other’s performances and behavior. We will assess 100 dyads (N = 200) at zero acquaintance and collect self-report and physiological measures of stress at three time points (baseline, stress induction, recovery) from both interaction partners. We will test the hypothesis that individuals with higher sensitivity exhibit more pronounced psychological (i.e., increased negative affect) and physiological (increased heart rate and electrodermal activity, decreased heart rate variability) stress responses from baseline to stress induction. Results will be discussed with respect to their contribution to the environmental sensitivity framework and their relevance for intervention strategies for highly sensitive individuals.

326. The Role of Mental Health Literacy in the Help-Seeking-Process of Psychologically Burdened Children and Adolescents – Insights into the School Project BEWARE
Sophia Jansen | Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz (JGU) | Germany

Jennifer Piloth | Leibniz-Institut für Resilienzforschung (LIR) gGmbH | Leibniz-Institut for Resilience Research (LIR)
