Prof. Dr. Michèle Wessa | Deutsches Krebsforschungszentrum (DKFZ) Heidelberg

Background
Mental disorders in childhood and adolescence are highly prevalent yet under-treated. Besides a gap in psychotherapeutic care, barriers for help-seeking include shame and inability to recognize signs of mental illness. Mental Health Literacy (MHL) – defined as knowledge enabling symptom recognition and management, help seeking and prevention – is considered to be a facilitator of help-seeking. To date it remains unclear how MHL translate into help-seeking behavior in young people with high psychological burden.

Objective
The study examines whether students systematically differ in MHL depending on the extent of their psychological burden. Additionally, we investigate whether MHL influences help-seeking intentions and behavior among students with subclinical and high psychological burden, using the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) as a theoretical framework.

Methods
The baseline data from the BEWARE effectiveness study (see: 10.17605/OSFIO/J2SWT) are analyzed - surveying a sample of n=2468 students from grade 5 to 10 visiting secondary schools in Rhineland-Palatinate. Valid instruments measuring psychological burden (SDQ), MHL (MHLq_yp), help-seeking intentions (GHSQ), and actual help-seeking behavior (AMHSS) will be used. Pre-registered analyses (10.17605/OSF.IO/H3M8S) include: (1) group comparisons (ANCOVA), (2) structural equation modeling to test effects of MHL on help-seeking intentions, and (3) a mediation model to investigate the influence of MHL on help-seeking behavior mediated by intentions.

Expected Results & Conclusion
While data collection is complete, data cleaning and preparation is still in progress. Final results will be shared at the conference. The findings will provide hypothesis-driven insights into the role of MHL in students' help-seeking behavior.

327. Privacy Transparency and Data-Sharing Behavior in Online Self-Help Applications
Michael Felix Vogt | University of Bern | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Michael Felix Vogt | University of Bern | Switzerland
Stefanie Arnold | University of Bern
Prof. Dr. Thomas Berger | University of Bern
Prof. Dr. Malte Elson | University of Bern

Digital self-help applications have demonstrated efficacy for common mental health conditions, yet concerns about data privacy and limited transparency remain major barriers to acceptance and sustained engagement. Users often consent to complex privacy policies without fully understanding or reading them, posing challenges for informed self-determination. The present study investigates whether transparent privacy communication, guided access to privacy settings, and varying levels of anonymity influence privacy concerns, data-sharing behavior, and user engagement within an online self-help application.
Participants (N=452) with elevated symptoms of social anxiety were recruited across German-speaking countries and used an online self-help program over eight weeks. The study employs a mixed within-between-subject design comparing three program versions: an anonymous version without personal data collection, a standard personalized version with conventional consent options, and a guided personalized version requiring active interaction with privacy settings. Participants in the personalized conditions received repeated profiling disclosures, informing them about potential data collection and inferences based on their privacy settings.
Data collection has been completed, and results will be presented and discussed at the conference. Planned analyses involve mixed-effects models examining changes in privacy attitudes and behavior following disclosure interventions, alongside exploratory analyses of user clusters and adherence patterns. The findings are intended to advance transparent and autonomy-supportive approaches to digital self-help by exploring how greater control over personal data and fully anonymous program options shape user preferences, engagement, and privacy-related behavior.

328. More Complex Than Thought: An Experimental Study on Affective Habituation and Cognitive Processing
Mira Flohr-Devaud | Trier University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Mira Flohr-Devaud | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Roland Neumann | Trier University | Germany

In previous studies, we demonstrated that paramedics rate disgust- and sadness-inducing stimuli as less unpleasant and show stronger habituation to these stimuli than individuals who are not regularly exposed to emergency situations. However, it cannot be assumed that paramedics are generally habituated to all disgust- and sadness-related stimuli; rather, a more pronounced habituation emerges when they are confronted with job-related, similar stimuli. In more recent studies, we were able to replicate these findings in independent samples of both paramedics and police officers. Responses to repeatedly presented emotion-inducing pictures (disgust, sadness, fear) with conceptual similarity to real occupational situations were compared to responses to previously non-presented pictures. The findings indicate that experience plays a decisive role in habituation and that conceptual processes are of central importance for the strength of habituation. Overall, our results suggest that habituation is a more complex process than previously assumed and this has important implications for the understanding of emotional processing.

Dr. Angelika Becker | Helmut Schmidt University Hamburg; IDeA Research Center for Individual Development and Adaptive Education of Children at Risk

Children with specific learning disorder (SLD) are more likely to show externalizing problems such as ADHD symptoms and conduct problems than children without SLD. Research indicates that ADHD symptoms and conduct problems increased and exacerbated in children during the COVID-19 pandemic. As this period of time was probably especially challenging for children with SLD due to factors associated with school closure, our main research question focuses on clarifying whether SLD, among other sociodemographic factors, might have significantly contributed to the change in ADHD symptoms and conduct problems in children before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.
To answer this question, we use data of the population-based German National Educational Panel Study (NEPS) of the Starting Cohort Newborns. Data of children aged 6, 8, and 10 years will be analyzed at three measurement points before (2018) and during (2020 and 2022) the COVID-19 pandemic. N = 2217 children participated at least at one of the measurement points. SLD was assessed by parent-reported diagnosis and ADHD symptoms and conduct problems were assessed using two scales (hyperactivity/inattention and conduct problems) of the parent version of the Strength and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). As structural equation modelling allows for the examination of change over time, a bivariate dual latent change score model analysis will be conducted. Gender, parental education, and SLD will be included in the model as predictors and ADHD symptoms and conduct problems as latent change score variables.
Results of the currently ongoing analyses will be presented and discussed at the conference.

330. A Window or a Wall? Menopause, Career Outcomes, and Psychological Strain Among Employed Women
Julia Loos | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft und Recht gGmbH | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia Loos | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft und Recht gGmbH | Germany
Prof. Dr. Myriam Bechtoldt | EBS Universität für Wirtschaft und Recht gGmbH | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christian Dormann | Johannes Gutenberg - Universität Mainz | Germany

Can menopause serve as a window—or a wall—for women’s careers? Building on labor market signaling theory and research on gendered ageism, we examine whether the transition into menopause shifts employers’ inferences about women’s future availability and career continuity, and whether such changes coincide with altered psychological strain. We test these ideas using longitudinal panel data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79), focusing on employed respondents aged 45 to 55 and leveraging repeated observations before and after the survey’s menopause measure becomes available. To estimate associations with objective and subjective outcomes, we implement a difference-in-differences framework that contrasts within-person changes among women across the menopause transition with contemporaneous trends among men as a counterfactual benchmark. Outcomes include earnings (salary), promotion-related indicators of career advancement, and depressive symptoms. By integrating a life-course health transition into mainstream career research and using longitudinal data, this study contributes evidence on whether postmenopause is linked to late-career opportunity, continued disadvantage, or a trade-off between career gains and elevated psychological strain.

Keywords: Menopause; Career advancement; Earnings; Depression; Gendered ageism; Labor market signaling; NLSY79

331. Zusammenhänge zwischen internalisierenden Symptomen und Selbstregulationsfacetten in der späten Adoleszenz: Eine Netzwerkanalyse
Prof. Dr. Annette M. Klein | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Johanna Lilian Klinge | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Annette M. Klein | Internationale Psychoanalytische Universität Berlin | Germany

Internalisierende Symptome umfassen Depressions-, Angst-, somatische Symptome und Rückzug, gehören zu den häufigsten psychischen Symptomen im Kindes- und Jugendalter und können zu schweren Beeinträchtigungen führen. In quer- und längsschnittlichen Studien hängen sie überwiegend konsistent mit geringeren Fähigkeiten der Selbstregulation zusammen. Eine mögliche Erklärung dafür bietet das Spektrummodell, welches annimmt, dass internalisierende Symptome und Selbstregulation auf einem Kontinuum liegen, sich konzeptuell überlappen und potenziell auf gemeinsame Ursachen zurückgehen. Um dieses Modell empirisch zu überprüfen, untersucht diese Studie mithilfe einer explorativen Netzwerkanalyse die Zusammenhänge von einzelnen Depressions- und Angstsymptomen mit drei Facetten der Selbstregulation: emotionale Reaktivität, Planungsverhalten und Emotionsregulation (verschiedene Strategien). Die Stichprobe umfasst 570 Adoleszente (54.4% weiblich) im Alter von 16-21 Jahren, wobei alle Maße fragebogenbasiert im Selbstbericht erfasst wurden. Die eingesetzten Instrumente umfassen das Patient Health Questionnaire 8 (PHQ-8), Generalized Anxiety Disorder Screener 7 (GAD-7), Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF) und Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ). Die statistischen Analysen wurden mit SPSS und R (packages bootnet, qgraph) durchgeführt. In der Netzwerk-Struktur der Gesamtstichprobe zeigte sich, dass eine erhöhte emotionale Reaktivität stärker mit Angstsymptomen, insbesondere der schnellen Verärgerung oder Gereiztheit, zusammenhing, während ein geringeres Planungsverhalten stärker mit Depressionssymptomen, insbesondere Konzentrationsproblemen und dem Freud- und Interesseverlust an Tätigkeiten, assoziiert war. Die maladaptive Emotionsregulationsstrategie Selbstbeschuldigung bildete mit dem Depressionssymptom beeinträchtigter Selbstwert ein Cluster, während Rumination und positive Refokussierung kaum Assoziationen mit Symptomen zeigten. Die Ergebnisse dieser Studie verbessern das Verständnis der differenziellen Zusammenhänge zwischen internalisierenden Symptomen und Facetten der Selbstregulation im Sinne des Spektrummodells und können Präventions- sowie Interventionsmaßnahmen informieren.

332. Psychological, Physiological, and Behavioral Stress Reactivity and Recovery in Dyads: Introducing a Novel Dyadic Trier Social Stress Test Paradigm
Regina F. Schmid | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Regina F. Schmid | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Katrin Rentzsch | Catholic University Eichstätt-Ingolstadt

Social interactions fundamentally shape humans’ psycho-physio-behavioral responses during acute stress and subsequent recovery. However, contemporary stress and recovery research has primarily focused on an individual perspective involving only a single person and relying on highly standardized protocols that neglect the complexities of social dynamics. In addition, multimodal research on interpersonal stress reactivity and recovery processes remains limited. This study addresses these gaps by introducing a novel dyadic version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST). Here, both dyad members are actively and alternately involved in stress induction tasks while witnessing each other’s performances and behavior without the traditional artificial committee. This is followed by a free interaction during the recovery phase. In the present pre-registered study, we explore the utility of this protocol for inducing stress and subsequent recovery across psychological (perceived stress, negative affect), physiological (heart rate, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity), and behavioral (voice pitch) dimensions. We will test 100 dyads (N = 200) at zero acquaintance and collect psycho-physio-behavioral measures at three time points (baseline, stress induction, recovery) from both interaction partners. We hypothesize elevated perceived stress, negative affect, heart rate, electrodermal activity, and voice pitch and reduced heart rate variability during stress induction, followed by a return to baseline levels during recovery. Results will be discussed regarding the paradigm’s potential as an ecologically valid tool for investigating naturalistic interpersonal dynamics in stress reactivity and recovery and its practical implications for dyadic stress coping.

333. Oops!… I did it again (thinking about work): Reattachment-Facetten als Mechanismus von Challenge-Stressor Effekten
Elisabeth Gerhards | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Elisabeth Gerhards | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research | Germany
Prof. Dr. Thomas Rigotti | Leibniz Institut für Resilienzforschung, Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz
Miriam Schilbach | Maastricht University
Hadar Nesher Shoshan | Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz

Obwohl Challenge-Stressoren u.a. Arbeitsengagement fördern können, zeigen sie gleichzeitig auch positive Effekte auf Erschöpfung. Forschung zu den zugrunde liegenden Mechanismen ist bislang begrenzt. Einige Studien zeigen, dass Stressoren mit unterschiedlichen Kognitionen bezüglich der Arbeit einhergehen. Bezugnehmend auf die Conservation of Resources-Theorie sowie das Systematic Self Reflection Model of Resilience Strenghtening untersuchen wir psychologisches Reattachment, also das Nachdenken über die Arbeit vor Beginn des Arbeitstages nach einer arbeitsfreien Zeit, als Mechanismus in einer explorativen Analyse. Hierbei untersuchen wir erstmals drei Facetten des Reattachments: neutral, positiv und negativ. Außerdem explorieren wir, ob die Neigung zur Selbstreflektion beeinflusst, inwiefern Beschäftigte in Folge erlebter Challenge-Stressoren unterschiedliches Reattachment am nächsten Morgen zeigen. Datenbasis ist eine zweiwöchige Tagebuchstudie, die im September 2025 begonnen hat und aktuell noch andauert. In einem zweistufigen Mehrebenenmodell mit Random Slopes (N = 666; 133 Cluster) wurde untersucht, ob Arbeitskomplexität über negatives, neutrales und positives Reattachment mit Work Engagement bzw. negativem Affekt zusammenhängt und ob Neigung zur Selbstreflexion die a-Pfade moderiert. Vorläufige Ergebnisse zeigten auf Within-Ebene positives und negatives Reattachment mit höherem Work Engagement assoziiert, während negatives Reattachment auch mit mehr negativem Affekt einherging; neutrale Reattachment-Prozesse zeigten keine bedeutsamen Zusammenhänge zu den Outcomes. Selbstreflexion moderierte keinen der Zusammenhang zwischen Arbeitskomplexität und Reattachment, und die (moderierten) indirekten Effekte über Reattachment fielen insgesamt nicht signifikant aus. Ergebnisse auf Basis der finalen Daten werden auf der Konferenz präsentiert.

334. Wenn positive Denkmuster zur Belastung werden – Dysfunktionale Positivität aus psychologischer Perspektive
Dr. Cosma F. A. Hoffmann | Universitätsmedizin Greifswald | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Cosma F. A. Hoffmann | Universitätsmedizin Greifswald | Germany
Nathalie Graw | Universität Greifswald, Institut für Psychologie
Prof. Dr. Corinna Bergelt | Universitätsmedizin Greifswald

Positivität, verstanden als positives Denken, eine optimistische Grundhaltung oder die Betonung positiver Emotionen, gilt in vielen Lebensbereichen als erstrebenswert. Gleichzeitig weisen empirische Befunde darauf hin, dass ein übermäßiges Streben nach Glück und eine einseitige Fokussierung auf positive Emotionen mit depressiven Symptomen und erhöhter psychischer Belastung in Zusammenhang stehen können. Vor diesem Hintergrund hat das Konzept der „toxischen Positivität“ an Aufmerksamkeit gewonnen.

Wir untersuchen das Phänomen aus psychologischer Perspektive und verwenden ergänzend den Begriff der „dysfunktionalen Positivität“, um ihn vom populärwissenschaftlich geprägten Terminus „toxische Positivität“ abzugrenzen. Grundlage ist ein präregistriertes Critical Review mit strukturierter und transparenter Literatursuche in einschlägigen Datenbanken (u. a. PsycInfo, PubMed, Web of Science). Zunächst werden Arbeiten ausgewertet, die den Begriff „toxic positivity” explizit verwenden. Erfasst und qualitativ synthetisiert werden Definitionen, theoretische Modelle, angenommene Wirkmechanismen, Operationalisierungen sowie Anwendungskontexte. Darüber hinaus werden etablierte angrenzende psychologische Konstrukte systematisch analysiert, um zu prüfen, inwieweit sich toxische bzw. dysfunktionale Positivität von bestehenden Konzepten abgrenzen lässt oder durch diese hinreichend beschrieben werden kann. Ziel ist die Entwicklung eines integrativen Rahmenmodells und die Bewertung der konzeptuellen Eigenständigkeit des Begriffs.

Ergänzend führen wir auf Grundlage des erarbeiteten Rashmenmodells qualitative Interviews mit Krebspatientinnen durch, um zu untersuchen, ob und wie dysfunktionale Positivität erlebt wird und die Krankheitsverarbeitung beeinflusst. Erste Ergebnisse werden vorgestellt.

Das Poster präsentiert das Ergebnis des Reviews, das konzeptuelle Modell und den Stand der empirischen Untersuchung.

335. Risks and Resources to Withstand Crises in Organizations: Developing and Testing a Cross-Level Framework of Organizational Resilience
Dr. Josef Heribert Jäger-Gammel | ATOSS Software SE | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Josef Heribert Jäger-Gammel | ATOSS Software SE | Germany
Leonard Scheffelt | ATOSS Software SE | Germany
Isabelle Haunschild | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Bernhard Leipold | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

Organizational resilience – the ability of an organization and its members to maintain functioning and recover from adversity – has gained increasing attention in the past decade. As organizations are continuously exposed to disruptive change and crises, it is important to develop theory-driven insights and empirically examine how risk factors and resources located at the individual (I), group (G), and organizational (O) level are associated with individual and collective outcomes. In a first step, we conducted a focus workshop with leaders and experts from various industries (N = 11) as well as additional expert interviews (N = 8) to identify resilience-related phenomena based on experiences from real-world organizations. Identified risk factors and resources were structured based on established stress and resilience models while differentiating individual, group, and organizational domains. The resulting framework illustrates how organizations and their members can sustain functioning despite risks (e.g., individual workload (I), lack of leadership (G), cyberattacks (O)). In a subsequent cross-sectional survey of employees, we test theory-driven moderation hypotheses, examining whether resources at the individual, group, and organizational level, as perceived by employees, buffer the relationship between individual stressors and both individual and collective outcomes. All constructs were assessed via individual employee reports, allowing us to test cross-level hypotheses derived from the framework using moderation analyses. The findings provide initial empirical support for the protective function of resources across organizational domains and offer practical implications for resilience-enhancing interventions in organizations.

Jana Meier | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research | Germany

Prof. Dr. Michael M. Plichta | University Hospital Frankfurt, Goethe University Frankfurt
Prof. Dr. Michèle Wessa | German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) | Germany

Psychological resilience refers to the maintenance or quick recovery of mental health after adverse events (Kalisch et al., 2015). Improving resilience in the general population may help prevent mental disorders and reduce personal suffering as well as healthcare costs. One factor that significantly influences the response to stressors is the (perceived) controllability of the stress-inducing event (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). Greater controllability of unpleasant events is associated with fewer symptoms of depression (Fasset-Carman et al., 2020). However, there is a plethora of measures related to control beliefs, and it remains unclear which ones best predict resilience. Moreover, acceptance of uncontrollability to a certain extend could contribute to an overall higher sense of control and thus, measures of acceptance-related constructs may complement measures of controllability.
Using data of the longitudinal resilience assessment (LORA; Chmitorz et al., 2021) study, Ahrens et al. (2024) found five different resilience trajectories following life events when controlling for stressor exposure. In the LORA dataset (N=707), we aim to investigate if these trajectories can be predicted by different controllability- and acceptance-related constructs and subscales. We will use regularized regression to determine the best predictors by accounting for collinearity. In exploratory analyses, we will try to identify potential common latent factors underlying the predictors. We expect constructs related to higher internal control and acceptance to be related to more resilient trajectories of stressor reactivity. Analyses are pending and the results will be presented at the conference.

337. Day-to-Day Links Between Loneliness and Coping Strategy Use: A 14-Day Diary Study
Peter Mohr | Ruhr University Bochum (RUB) ² German Center for Mental Health (DZPG), partner site Bochum-Marburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Peter Mohr | Ruhr University Bochum (RUB) ² German Center for Mental Health (DZPG), partner site Bochum-Marburg | Germany
Özge Ugurlu | University of California, Berkeley
Bernd Schäfer | Ruhr University Bochum (RUB)
Debora Brickau | Ruhr University Bochum (RUB)
Maike Luhmann | Ruhr University Bochum (RUB) ² German Center for Mental Health (DZPG), partner site Bochum-Marburg

Loneliness fluctuates in everyday life, yet little is known about how people cope with it day to day and how the use of coping strategies and loneliness shape each other from one day to the next. To examine these dynamics, working adults completed baseline measures of general loneliness and trait coping strategy use. Over the following 14 days, participants provided evening reports and, on days with at least moderate loneliness, also reported loneliness-specific coping strategy use, including approach coping, avoidance coping, distraction, and rumination.
First we used multilevel models to estimate (a) within-day associations between coping strategy use and same-day loneliness intensity and (b) bidirectional day-to-day spillover across consecutive days (coping strategy use predicting next-day loneliness and loneliness predicting next-day coping strategy use). Second, because people rarely use coping strategies in isolation, we identified empirically observed bundles of coping strategies and tested their links to same-day loneliness intensity and next-day loneliness persistence. Finally, we compared workdays with non-workdays to examine whether daily context shapes the bundles of coping strategies participants use.
By examining loneliness and coping strategy use across consecutive days, we capture how working adults cope with loneliness as it naturally unfolds. Our findings reveal short-term dynamics between loneliness and coping strategy use and inform the timing and targets of interventions to reduce loneliness among working adults.

338. Religious and Spiritual Struggles: An Issue that Can be Addressed in Therapeutic Settings?
Nina Philippa Burau | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nina Philippa Burau | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Friedemann Trutzenberg | Freie Universität Berlin
Prof. Michela Schröder-Abé | Universität Potsdam | Germany

Religious and Spiritual (RS) Struggles, typically measured as a trait, have been found as a relevant predictor for mental health variables, even for recovery processes in psychotherapy. Therefore, if individuals hold RS struggles, there should be a welcoming space in therapeutic settings to disclose and professionally discuss these topics.

We will present results of preregistered secondary data analysis of an online study (N = 584) in which religious participants (53.18 % highly religious) in Germany were asked about their RS struggles and recent experiences in psychotherapy and counselling.

Preliminary analyses show that patients who experience RS struggles address RS issues more frequently. In contrast and unexpectedly, RS struggles are unrelated to how often therapists address religious issues. Building on these results, we will investigate which variables (e.g., patient-therapist match in religious attitudes) moderate the association between RS struggles and addressing RS issues in therapy. In a longitudinal subsample (n = 278), we further investigate whether religious microaggressions (RMCS-G) committed by the therapist (RS-related malpractice) or general therapeutic malpractice predict patients RS struggles in the context of psychotherapy.

The relevance of the way RS struggles are dealt with in therapy settings will be discussed.

339. Cognitive control of acute pain – comparison of different pain modulation strategies in young and older healthy adults
Dr. Angelika Dierolf | Universität Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Angelika Dierolf | Universität Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Marian van der Meulen | Universität Luxemburg | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Miltner | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena, Germany

Cognitive modulation of pain comprises mental factors altering the perception of pain through top-down neural mechanisms, often accompanied by the release of endogenous opioids. Prominent examples are placebo analgesia, hypnotic analgesia and distraction from pain (via cognitive modulation), reducing perceived pain intensity und unpleasant via expectation and/or attention.
The present study sought to compare the analgesic effect of the pain modulation strategies: placebo analgesia, cognitive distraction from pain, hypnotic analgesia and verbal distraction from pain in healthy younger and older adults. In addition, the influence of chronic stress, physical activity and sleep quality were investigated.
Healthy young (18-30 yrs) and older participants (60 yrs +) underwent either a cognitive pain distraction task (working memory task), a placebo analgesia realized with a sham TENS intervention, a hypnotic analgesia intervention or a verbal pain distraction intervention, while receiving moderately painful, individually adjusted transdermal electrical pulse trains to the back of the left hand. Each task was completed by a corresponding control condition and/or control stimuli. Pain ratings and pain-related evoked potentials via 64-channel EEG were recorded.
While data collection is still in progress, first analysis on the currently still small sample suggests a difference in rated pain reduction between the four strategies as well as an impact of age and lifestyle factors. Our results will contribute to a deeper understanding of the efficacy of cognitive pain modulation and its underlying mechanisms in healthy younger and older adults, helping to optimize pain treatments in this population.

340. MENTAL HEALTH LITERACY AMONG YOUTHS AS A STRATEGIC INTERVENTION FOR SUSTAINABLE NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
Prof. Veronica Makinde | Bamidele Olumilua University of Education, Science and Technology Ikere Ekiti | Nigeria

The youth generation is marked by emotional development and identity formation, and in the quest to understand self and be independent from higher authorities they engage in diverse activities that may leave a landmark outcome on their emotional and mental well-being. This paper therefore explores mental health literacy among youths as a strategic intervention for sustainable national development, with the focus on determining the influence of mental health knowledge on their emotional well-being. It will further examine how their attitudes towards mental health literacy relate to their help-seeking behaviour and how the help-seeking behaviour would predict youth sustainable outcomes in terms of academic involvement and social responsibility. A convenient sample of 500 students drawn from an emerging community would be used for the study, while data would be collected through semi structured questionnaire using mixed method approach. Data would be analysed using inferential statistics. It is assumed that limited access to mental health education, government policies and inadequate school-based counselling interventions may have significant influence on the outcome of the findings towards sustainable development. Based on the findings, appropriate suggestions and recommendations would be proffer.
Keyword: Youth, Mental Health Literacy, Emerging Community, Counselling intervention

341. AI-Powered Assessment of Psychological First Aid Competencies: A Novel Simulation-Based Evaluation Approach
Erik Zimdahl | Technische Universitaet Dresden | Germany
Show details
Author:
Erik Zimdahl | Technische Universitaet Dresden | Germany

Psychological First Aid (PFA) consists of a systematic set of helping actions aimed at
reducing initial post-trauma distress and supporting short- and long-term adaptive
functioning (Ruzek et al., 2007). This study evaluates a PFA workshop where 25
participants from diverse backgrounds (psychology students, interdisciplinary students,
and professionals) completed training meeting DGUV standards through instruction in the
SAFER model (Everly, G. S., Jr. 1996). Traditional evaluation methods for such competencybased training rely primarily on self-report measures and knowledge tests, making
assessment of applied skills challenging, particularly when expert observers are unavailable
(Miller, 1990). To address this limitation, the present study introduces an innovative AI-powered simulation approach within a mixed-methods framework based on Kirkpatrick's
model (Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2016). The evaluation combined traditional measures
such as questionnaires and knowledge tests with a novel chatflow-based simulation system
that presented participants with realistic crisis scenarios requiring PFA intervention.
Simulation responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis (Mayring, 2015),
employing a holistic assessment framework that evaluated appropriateness of
interventions, communication quality, and adherence to the SAFER model. This simulation based approach offers significant advantages: scalability without expert observers,
standardized scenario presentation, and rich qualitative data capturing nuanced
competency profiles. Pre-post comparisons revealed substantial improvements in applied
competencies: participants demonstrated more helpful and appropriate responses, higher quality empathic communication, and stronger adherence to the SAFER intervention model.
The simulation successfully captured competency development, enabling scalable
assessment.

342. Psychopathologie und Persönlichkeit: Eine systematische Untersuchung integrativer dimensionaler Modelle
Gesine Zimmer | Ulm Universität | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Gesine Zimmer | Ulm Universität | Germany
Dr. Elisa Altgassen | Ulm Universität
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Ulm Universität

Im Bereich der mentalen Gesundheit gibt es viele Modelle. Zur Beschreibung der Psychopathologie werden klassischerweise kategoriale Systeme (DSM-5, ICD-11) verwendet, welche allerdings Komorbidität und kontinuierliche Symptomverteilungen schlecht abbilden. Das Modell der Hierarchischen Taxonomie der Psychopathologie (HiTOP) bietet einen empirisch fundierten, dimensionalen Ansatz. Aufbauend auf dem Alternativen Modell der Persönlichkeitsstörungen (AMPD) erwarten wir, dass psychopathologische Symptome extreme Ausprägungen von Persönlichkeitsdimensionen darstellen und strukturell in Persönlichkeitsmodelle integrierbar sind.

Unsere explorative Studie untersucht iterativ Zusammenhänge zwischen Persönlichkeits- und HiTOP-Merkmalen, um die theoretische Anschlussfähigkeit an Big Five und HEXACO zu prüfen. Eine nicht-klinische Online-Stichprobe (Panelstudie, N = 1050) bearbeitete einen Itempool aus deutschem HiTOP-Fragebogen, TSDI (Big Five, Honesty-Humility) und PID (Psychopathie).

Mittels explorativer Extension-Faktoranalysen wurde zunächst eine persönlichkeitsbasierte 7-Faktoren-Lösung fixiert und HiTOP-Merkmale über deren Kreuzkorrelationsmatrix projiziert. Anschließend erfolgte eine HiTOP-basierte 10-Faktoren-Lösung mit Projektion der Persönlichkeitsmerkmale. Aufgrund ausgeprägter Bodeneffekte wurden ergänzend Tobit-Regressionen zur Modellierung linkszensierter Symptomverteilungen berechnet, um Verzerrungen linearer Schätzverfahren zu prüfen. Aufbauend darauf sollen hierarchische und korrelierte Integrationsmodelle spezifiziert und hinsichtlich Passung und Robustheit gegenüber Nicht-Normalität und Zensierung mit unterschiedlichen Schätzverfahren systematisch verglichen werden.

Die 7-Faktoren-Lösung zeigte übergeordnete Dimensionen entsprechend der HiTOP-Spektren Internalizing, Externalizing, Disinhibition, Compulsivity und Antagonism, wobei einzelne Merkmale keine signifikanten Ladungen aufwiesen. Die 10-Faktoren-Lösung ergab substanzielle Ladungen auf vier Faktoren. Die linkssteile Datenverteilung verzerrt herkömmliche Auswertungsmethoden, sodass verschiedene Modelle empirisch untersucht und abgewogen werden müssen. Hierbei sind Zensierung, Null-Inflation, Nicht-Normalverteilung und Robustheit der Schätzverfahren zu beachten.

Ziel sind systematische Analyse und Vergleich integrativer Modelle hinsichtlich Passung und Robustheit, um einen Beitrag zur Optimierung der klinischen Diagnostik zu leisten.

343. Antecedents of Self-Endangering Work Behavior and Mental Health Among Professional Employees
Severin Hornung | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Severin Hornung | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Thomas Höge | Universität Innsbruck | Austria
Christine Unterrainer | Universität Innsbruck | Austria

Self-endangering work behavior is a mental health hazard reflecting new forms of occupational stress. Distinguished are extensification (working harder, longer hours, neglecting recovery) and avoidance strategies (faking accomplishments, lowering quality) for dealing with overtaxing job demands and excessive workload. This study explores a model of multi-level antecedents, including societal norms, management practices, and individual vulnerability, and mental health implications of self-endangering work behavior. An online survey targeted professional employees (N = 207) with academic degrees in different fields, such as medicine, counseling, architecture, engineering, and education. Self-endangering work behavior was assessed with a validated comprehensive scale. Neoliberal ideological beliefs questionnaire (subdimensions: individualism, competition, instrumentality) represented performance-oriented societal norms. High-pressure management practices were drawn from an instrument on indirect control (competitive pressure, intensification, job insecurity). Individual overcommitment was assessed with an established scale. Mental health outcomes were the irritation scale and WHO-5 well-being measure. Scale analyses generally supported conceptual factor structures. However, overcommitment was indistinct from cognitive irritation, which was omitted. Path analysis largely confirmed the theoretical model. Both dimensions of self-endangering work behavior related to emotional irritation, which was negatively associated with subjective well-being. Individual overcommitment predicted extensification and avoidance strategies, but also irritation and wellbeing. High-pressure management practices only related significantly to the avoidance dimension. Regarding social norms, only internalized competition was associated with extensification strategies. Results provide insights into differential effects of macro-level societal norms, meso-level management practices, and micro-level vulnerability toward overexerting oneself at work. Implications for targeted interventions to prevent occupational health impairments are discussed.

344. Die Energiewende im Vergleich zwischen Kohlerevier und Land der Autobauer – Akzeptanz, Soziale Norm, Selbstwirksamkeit

Ein zentraler Baustein zum Erreichen der Klimaschutzziele ist die Umstellung des Energiesystems auf Erneuerbare Energien. Während eine Mehrheit sowohl auf nationaler Ebene wie auch lokal den Ausbau Erneuerbarer Energien befürwortet, können Konflikte entstehen, wenn ein Anlagenstandort geplant wird. Wichtig für die Akzeptanz vor Ort ist dabei u.a. die Kommunikation rund um die Planung und die Wahrnehmung der Einstellung anderer (Hübner et al., 2023). Im Projekt PartEEnschaften (Laufzeit 2023 – 2026) wird in fünf Regionen in Sachsen und Baden-Württemberg die Planung für den Ausbau Erneuerbarer Energien in die Hand der Anwohnenden gelegt und dies durch Telefonbefragungen begleitet (n = 960). In Baden-Württemberg wird Windenergie als passender zur Region bewertet als in Sachsen und die Selbstwirksamkeitserwartung und Unterstützungsbereitschaft hinsichtlich der Erneuerbaren Energien fällt höher aus. Darüber hinaus wird gezeigt, inwieweit sich die Regionen hinsichtlich zentraler Akzeptanzfaktoren wie der Sozialen Norm, der Einstellung zur Energiewende, der Einschätzung wirtschaftlicher Auswirkungen oder Auswirkungen auf die Natur unterscheiden.

Das Projekt „PartEEnschaften - Transformative Partizipation für Erneuerbare-Energie-Landschaften – Wertschöpfung, Beteiligung, Akzeptanz“ wird gefördert vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Klimaschutz (FKZ 03EI5256A) aufgrund eines Beschlusses des Deutschen Bundestags.

345. Validation of the Multidimensional Connection with Nature Scale (CN-12) for German speaking Countries
Fabian Alexis Böttcher | Medical Faculty Mannheim, Heidelberg University | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Elena Buck | Medical Faculty Mannheim, Heidelberg University | Germany

Prof. Dr. Gerhard Reese | Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand
Dr. med. Dr. med. univ. Michael Eichinger | Medical Faculty Mannheim, Heidelberg University | Germany

Background:
Connection with nature is a multidimensional construct comprising identity-related, emotional, and experiential dimensions. It is associated with sustainability and health outcomes including pro-environmental behaviours and quality of life and can be parsimoniously assessed with the CN-12. As the CN-12 was only available in English, we (1) translated the scale into German, (2) examined its content validity and (3) will assess its psychometric properties in the general population.

Methods:
We translated the CN-12 into German using a translation/back-translation approach. Following the COSMIN guidelines, we iteratively refined the German CN-12 through three rounds of cognitive interviews with a diverse adult sample (n=15), until content validity was achieved. Psychometric properties will be assessed in April 2026 in a quota-based sample in Germany (n=600). Using an online panel, we will investigate internal consistency, test–retest reliability (subsample of n=100), structural validity and convergent/divergent validity with related constructs including pro-environmental behaviours and health outcomes.

Results:
Cognitive pretesting revealed several wording difficulties (e.g., self-concept) that were resolved. Unsolicited interview content on climate concerns and self-efficacy suggests potential associations between these constructs and connection with nature. The results of the psychometric validation will be presented at the conference.

Conclusion:
Given its content validity, the German CN-12 shows promise as a parsimonious multidimensional measure to assess connection with nature. After concluding the psychometric validation, the CN-12 will contribute to a better understanding of the multifaceted associations between the dimensions of connection with nature, pro-environmental behaviours and health outcomes in German speaking countries.

Leonie Anna Kaun | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leonie Anna Kaun | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany
Vanessa Gabriela Yarza Navarro-Schär | Ludwig Maximilian Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Eric Eller | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt (THI) | Germany

The present study examines the extent to which sustainable product attributes influence the effectiveness of classical price anchors in a consumer context. Theoretically, the study builds on anchoring heuristics, according to which numerical reference values can systematically bias judgments and decisions, as well as on research into sustainable consumption, which identifies sustainability as an increasingly relevant decision criterion. Since sustainable products are often associated with higher prices and price judgments play a central role in the purchasing process, it is particularly important to analyze whether sustainability alters or overrides the effect of price anchors. To empirically test these assumptions, a 2 × 2 factorial online experiment (𝘕 = 235) was conducted in which the independent variables price anchor (absent vs. present) and sustainability (non-sustainable vs. sustainable) were manipulated. Participants evaluated three product scenarios from different product categories with regard to perceived price fairness, perceived product quality, purchase intention, and perceived price perception. The results of the anova reveal significant main effects of sustainability across all dependent variables, while the price anchor exhibited only limited effects. No statistically significant interaction between the two factors was observed, although descriptive trends in group means suggest a potential tendency. The findings highlight the relevance of sustainable product attributes for positive consumer evaluations and increased purchase likelihood. Initial indications of potential interactions between sustainability and price anchoring provide avenues for further research and practical implications for the strategic design of sustainability communication and pricing strategies in marketing.

347. The Roles of People Pleasing, Conflict Avoidance, and Moral Impression Concerns in Sustainable Food Choices across Social Contexts
Dr. Johanna Werner | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Johanna Werner | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Dr. Christian Blötner | FernUniversität in Hagen

Meat and dairy production contribute considerably to the greenhouse effect, rendering the promotion of sustainable eating an important factor in climate mitigation. Since many eating decisions occur within social settings, it is crucial to understand how individual dispositions, goals, and preferences interact with the demands of social contexts when it comes to sustainable food choices. This study will examine how the desire to reduce meat and dairy, a fear of social conflict, people-pleasing tendencies, and concerns about appearing morally superior affect sustainable eating choices across social situations. In an online vignette experiment, flexitarian participants (Ntarget = 500, to be completed by July 2026) will be presented with various dining scenarios (e.g., eating at a restaurant with friends) and asked to indicate their propensity to choose a sustainable option when the rest of their group selects meat-based dishes. We will explore how social identity, perceived social norms, and people-pleasing tendencies relate to participants’ food choices. We expect individuals high in people‑pleasing tendencies to adjust their choices to match the group, even at the expense of their own preferences and desire to eat sustainably. We further hypothesize that this effect is mediated by fear of interpersonal conflict and apprehension about appearing morally superior. We will also explore whether shared versus non‑shared group identity plays a role. The findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the social and psychological drivers of food choices and support the development of interventions that help people maintain sustainable eating habits even in challenging social environments.

Helene Fidorra | RWTH Aachen University

In light of the current climate crisis, new ways to communicate the urgency of environmental protection and to promote pro-environmental behavior (PEB) are needed. PEB can be increased through moral emotions such as eco-guilt and eco-pride, which the current study aimed to elicit with an environmental serious game. Using an experience-sampling approach, the current study investigates the effect of playing an environmental serious game (vs. a control game) on eco-guilt, eco-pride, environmental attitude, and PEB. After playing either an environmental serious game or a control game, participants reported daily on their eco-guilt, eco-pride and PEB for two weeks. Environmental attitude was measured before playing the game, immediately after playing and two weeks later. Substantively, results on the effects of playing a serious game (vs. a control game) on the dependent variables (eco-guilt, eco-pride, environmental attitude, PEB) and their changes over time will be presented. Methodologically, the study contributes to the understanding of whether and how an experience-sampling approach can be used to explore the effectiveness of environmental serious games on emotions, environmental attitudes and self-reported environmental behavior in daily life beyond the laboratory.

349. About the willingness to participate in community-level sustainable dietary behavior measures: Correlates and group differences
Prof. Dr. Marit Kristine List | Leuphana Universitaet Lueneburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Marit Kristine List | Leuphana Universitaet Lueneburg | Germany

Sustainable dietary behavior (SDB) is among the most effective pro-environmental behaviors for individuals to help reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Numerous measures to foster SDB are already being used or may easily be implemented at local levels, e.g. providing brochures with tips on sustainable food choices, specific events regarding food and diet (e.g. cooking classes), but also local initiatives such as Community Supported Agriculture.
In a sample of adults in Germany (N = 1,264), this study examines the willingness to participate in diet-related activities that may be offered by local governmental or non-governmental organizations [NGOs], and analyzes its associations with dietary behavior and sociodemographic characteristics. Latent class analyses were used to calculate participation profiles based on willingness to participate.
Three different participation profiles emerged: Individuals with generally low interest (22 % of the sample), high interest (37 %), and individuals with high interest in measures regarding seasonal and organic food consumption. These groups differ in sociodemographic characteristics (place of residence, age, gender, lifestyle, SES) and diet-related habits (cooking habits, vegan diet, health-conscious diet). Overall, all measures related to local and seasonal food were the most popular, while measures specifically related to vegan diet met with little interest. Interestingly, interest was greater when the name of the measure referred to "plant-based" rather than "vegan", e.g. cooking class on plant-based (rather than vegan) meals. Results of this study may contribute to the understanding of how communities and local NGOs can interest different groups of people in SDB.

351. Fostering Innovation: A Qualitative Investigation of Innovation Perceptions and Practices in Bangladesh's RMG Sector
Luise Penseler | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden)
Show details
Authors:
Luise Penseler | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden)
Theresa Falter | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden)
Prof. Dr. Dominika Wach | Macromedia University - Leipzig
Prof. Dr. Jürgen Wegge | Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden)

Innovation is widely recognized as a driver of economic development and sustainable growth (Chen et al., 2018; Fagerberg et al., 2013). Beyond technological advancement, it depends on organizational cultures that foster participation, experimentation and learning (Hurley & Hult, 1998). Despite its economic centrality, innovation in Bangladesh’s readymade garment (RMG) sector remains underexamined. The few existing studies rely largely on quantitative and level-specific approaches, leaving qualitative, multi-level understandings of how innovation is conceptualized and practiced largely unexplored. Cultural contexts shape how innovation is understood, legitimized and enacted, making it essential to investigate innovation processes beyond predominantly Western settings. Our study, therefore, enables the development of contextually grounded approaches for a sustainable promotion of innovation. Drawing on 13 semi-structured in person interviews (individual and group interviews) conducted with top and middle managers in February 2023, the study applies a multi-level framework distinguishing innovation types (product, process), forms (technological, administrative, social) and levels of analysis (individual, team, organizational, societal). Findings indicate that innovation is primarily perceived as technological and economically driven. At the individual level, it was found to be associated with employee behavior and knowledge; at team and organizational levels, to knowledge sharing, training and innovation teams. From a societal perspective, the RMG sector is a key economic actor shaped by shared values and global market integration. By integrating administrative and social dimensions, our study advances a broader understanding of innovation and highlights its relevance to the Sustainable Development Goal 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth (United Nations, 2025).

353. Psychological experiments designed by GenAI? Evidence from a scientific creativity task
Prof. Dr. Daniela Czernochowski | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Daniela Czernochowski | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany
Prof. Dr. Thomas Lachmann | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau
Dr. Vera Eymann | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau

Scientific creativity (i.e., the ability to generate novel and meaningful scientific ideas) is a crucial driver of progress across all scientific disciplines. Innovative thinking and creative minds are required especially when facing major global challenges of our time such as climate change, socioeconomic inequality, and misinformation. At the same time, recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (genAI) raise fundamental questions about the future role of human scientists. While artistic creative domains have already been disrupted by AI-generated content, it remains unclear whether similar developments may emerge in science. In the present study, we investigate whether ChatGPT-4 is capable of designing a psychological experiment, thereby demonstrating scientific creativity. Using a newly developed scientific creativity task, we compared AI-generated research proposals with those produced by graduate students enrolled in a research-focused master’s program. Both ChatGPT and students were asked to formulate hypotheses, design an experiment, and justify methodological decisions within a fictitious scenario from experimental psychology. Two independent experts evaluated all proposals using a structured peer-review rating to assess scientific creativity, especially originality, and meaningfulness of ideas. Results revealed that ChatGPT-4 generated ideas were rated significantly higher across all scientific creativity dimensions. In particular, AI-generated proposals were judged as more original and conceptually meaningful. Beyond quantitative comparisons, a qualitative assessment highlighted subtle differences in reasoning strategies and methodological framing between human and AI-generated responses. These findings underline both the potential and the challenges of AI-driven scientific creativity, and reveal implications for psychological research, scientific training, and human–AI collaboration in science.

356. Exploring Mental Model, Trust, and Privacy Issues of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) Application Users
Fransisca Hapsari | TU Darmstadt, Fachbereich Humanwissenschaften | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Fransisca Hapsari | TU Darmstadt, Fachbereich Humanwissenschaften | Germany
Dr. Mark Warner | University College London | United Kingdom

Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) applications are popular worldwide. Speaking practice, a feature in many, relies on speech recognition and natural language processing (NLP) technologies. It is essential to investigate whether privacy concerns—or other factors such as perceived fallibility — affect users’ trust in and usage of the novel feature. To capture this, we conducted semi-structured interviews with Germans (n = 11), Indonesian (n = 10), and UK participants (n = 12). Analysis is ongoing with findings shifting as coding develops:
Most people realised the fallibility of speaking practice, which does not much affect their trust and usage. While some participants knew and accepted their voice being recorded during the practice, others were unaware of this practice and expressed worry about it. When asked to diagram data flows, most described basic data collection (e.g., email, demographics) but were uncertain as to how and why audio recordings were processed.
The privacy paradox was identified: most participants were aware of data-leak risks but unaware of opt-out data-collection settings (e.g., for speech data), likely because MALL apps are perceived as less risky than other apps.
Attitudes toward what data is acceptable to share varied, with Germans most cautious, Indonesians most lenient, and UK participants conditionally tolerant, provided justification was offered.
Although we found high trust in well-known MALL platforms, we underscore the need for transparent communication about common voice recording practices. By clarifying that audio data is stored solely to improve app performance—and that third-party access is tightly controlled—developers can mitigate trust erosion.

358. Overtrust und Undertrust in Fahrassistenzsystemen: Eine experimentelle Untersuchung zur Vertrauenskalibrierung
Timo Voß | Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Fakultät für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Timo Voß | Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Fakultät für Psychologie | Germany
Melissa Hollstein
Dr. Lisa Thomaschewski
Prof. Dr. Annette Kluge

Mit dem Einsatz moderner Fahrassistenzsysteme in Automobilen werden Fahrfunktionen zunehmend automatisiert. Damit verändert sich die Aufgabenverteilung, da Fahraufgaben mit steigendem Automatisierungsgrad häufiger vom Fahrzeug übernommen werden. Fahrende verbleiben bei einer Teilautomatisierung jedoch weiterhin in der Verantwortung und nehmen eine sicherheitskritische Rolle ein. Sie müssen jederzeit zur Übernahme der Fahrzeugsteuerung bereit sein. In diesem Kontext ist die Kalibrierung des subjektiven Vertrauens in automatisierte Fahrassistenzsysteme entscheidend, da Overtrust (subjektives Vertrauen übersteigt die tatsächliche Systemleistung) sowie Undertrust (subjektives Vertrauen liegt unterhalb der tatsächlichen Systemleistung) zu unangemessenem Gebrauch führen können.
Im Rahmen des drittmittelgeförderten RC-trust Projekts V3ML (Verstehen, Vertrauen und Verifikation von Maschinellem Lernen) der Hochschulallianz Ruhr wird ein grundlegendes Verständnis der Vertrauenskalibrierung in maschinelle Lernsysteme untersucht. In dem hier vorgestellten Teilprojekt werden mithilfe eines realistischen Fahrsimulators konkrete Szenarien mit automatisierten Entscheidungsprozessen auf einem Autobahnteilstück umgesetzt. Das simulierte Fahrassistenzsystemsystem ist vergleichbar mit einem SAE-Level-2-Fahrassistenzsystem und übernimmt die automatisierte Quer- und Längsführung einschließlich Spurwechsel, adaptiver Geschwindigkeitsregelung sowie das automatische Befahren von Abfahrten entlang einer navigationsbasierten Route. Die Versuchsperson verbleibt in der etwa 10-minütigen Simulation in der Fahrerrolle, beobachtet das Umfeld kontinuierlich und agiert bei verkehrsbedingten Unregelmäßigkeiten als Rückfallebene.
In einem 2x2-Between-Subjects-Versuchsdesign werden erklärte und tatsächliche Zuverlässigkeit des Fahrassistenzsystems systematisch variiert. Daraus ergeben sich zwei Experimentalbedingungen zur gezielten Erzeugung von Overtrust und Undertrust. Erfasst werden unter anderem situatives und globales Vertrauen, das Eingriffsverhalten der Versuchsperson, das mentale Modell sowie die Nutzungsintention. Der Beitrag stellt das Studiendesign, den experimentellen Aufbau sowie erste Ergebnisse vor.

359. Digitale Beteiligung neugestalten: Der Einfluss von Rückmeldungen auf die Akzeptanz und Partizipation
Anja Poppe | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Anja Poppe | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Jennifer Klütsch | RWTH Aachen University
Luise Haehn | RWTH Aachen University
Prof. Dr. Sabine J. Schlittmeier | RWTH Aachen University

Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligungen ermöglichen es Bürger*innen sich in die Stadt- und Infrastrukturentwicklung einzubringen. Allerdings ist die Beteiligungsbereitschaft oftmals gering und Bürger*innen berichten von zahlreichen Hürden aktueller Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligung. Dazu zählen beispielsweise fehlende Transparenz, mangelnde Nachvollziehbarkeit sowie das Gefühl, keinen tatsächlichen Einfluss auf die dann getroffenen Entscheidungen zu haben. Die vorliegende experimentelle Vignettenstudie (N = 247) untersucht daher die Auswirkungen von Transparenz und Wertschätzung in Rückmeldungen sowie der räumlichen Nähe zum Bauvorhaben auf die Akzeptanz der Entscheidung, zukünftige Beteiligungsbereitschaft, wahrgenommene prozedurale Fairness und erlebtes Empowerment. Dabei nahmen die Teilnehmenden an einer imaginären Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligung teil, wobei die (i) räumliche Nähe zum Bauvorhaben (niedrig vs. hoch) variiert wurde. Anschließend trafen die Teilnehmenden eine Entscheidung für oder gegen das Bauvorhaben und erhielten eine zu ihrer eigenen Entscheidung konträre Rückmeldung, in welcher sowohl die (ii) Transparenz (niedrig vs. hoch) als auch die (iii) Wertschätzung (niedrig vs. hoch) variiert wurden. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass transparente Rückmeldungen die wahrgenommene prozedurale Fairness erhöhen, und prozedurale Fairness wiederum positiv mit der Akzeptanz korreliert. Zudem gaben die Teilnehmenden in einem Ranking an, dass sowohl transparente als auch regelmäßige Rückmeldungen für sie von höchster Priorität sind. Jedoch zeigen die Ergebnisse keine Hinweise darauf, dass Wertschätzung und Transparenz einen direkten Einfluss auf die Akzeptanz, zukünftige Beteiligung oder erlebtes Empowerment haben. Es werden mögliche Erklärungsansätze diskutiert, wie beispielsweise eine zu geringe Vermittlung von Transparenz. Teilnehmende wünschten sich beispielsweise Statistiken des Mehrheitsvotum als transparente Begründung. Schließlich werden praktische Implikationen für die Gestaltung von Rückmeldungen auf digitalen Beteiligungsplattformen diskutiert.

350. Resilienz in sozio-technischen Teams: Systematisches Literaturreview und Evidence Gap Map
Julia Birke | Universität Trier | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia Birke | Universität Trier | Germany
Prof. Thomas Ellwart

Im Kontext von Industrie 5.0 interagieren Menschen zunehmend mit technischen Akteuren wie Robotern oder KI-Systemen, sodass die erfolgreiche Bewältigung interner und externer Störungen (Resilienz) an Bedeutung gewinnt. Während im Kontext von Teams mit menschlichen Akteuren theoretische und empirische Arbeiten Resilienzfaktoren vor, während und nach einer Störung untersuchen, liegen im Bereich der sozio-technischen Teams bislang keine systematischen Überblicksarbeiten vor.
Die Zielstellung des Beitrags ist die konzeptionelle Sichtung und Aufarbeitung der bisherigen Literatur zu Resilienz in sozio-technischen Teams sowie die visuelle Darstellung der Forschungslücken zur Ableitung von Implikationen für die zukünftige Forschung.
Hierfür wurden interdisziplinäre Beiträge u.a. aus Psychologie, Human Factors, Engineering und Wirtschaftswissenschaften in drei Datenbanken gesichtet. Im Screeningprozess der bisherigen 3.377 Reports des systematischen Literaturreviews wurden entsprechend der PRISMA-Richtlinien konkrete PICOS-Kriterien definiert. Angelehnt an bisherige Resilienzmodelle menschlicher Teams wurden in der Volltextauswertung Variablen der Interaktionsprozesse, Kognitionen, Emotionen und Fähigkeiten identifiziert und als Resilienzfaktoren in zeitlichen Phasen vor, während und nach einer Widrigkeit verortet. Zusätzlich werden die Ebenen Individuum und Team differenziert und die Ergebnisse narrativ sowie grafisch aufbereitet.
Vorläufige Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass Untersuchungen in sozio-technischen Teams vermehrt Resilienzfaktoren auf Individualebene fokussieren. Zugleich sind aufgrund der Kooperation mit technischen Akteuren zusätzliche Variablen relevant (z.B. Level of Autonomy). Des Weiteren wird auf konzeptioneller Ebene deutlich, dass aufgrund der interdisziplinären Heterogenität der Resilienzdefinition ein einheitliches Begriffsverständnis fehlt, aber eine disziplinübergreifende Identifikation relevanter Resilienzfaktoren möglich ist.
Der systematische Überblick zu Resilienz in sozio-technischen Teams zeigt Forschungslücken auf und kann eine gezielte Theoriebildung zur Störungsbewältigung in der Zusammenarbeit von Mensch und Technik unterstützen.

352. Veränderte Anwendungsmöglichkeiten beruflicher Fähigkeiten bei roboterassistierten Operationen: Perspektiven der Karriere- und Human Factors Forschung
Johanna T. Paul | Trier University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Thomas Ellwart
M.Sc. Julia Birke
Johanna T. Paul | Trier University | Germany

Hintergrund. Die Einführung von STARA-Technologien (Smart Technology, Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, and Algorithms) verändert Arbeitsprozesse und damit die Anforderungen und Anwendungsmöglichkeiten beruflicher Fähigkeiten.
Ziele. In der Einzelfallstudie wird untersucht, wie sich unterschiedliche Arten der Aufgabengestaltung bei roboterassistierten Operationen auf die Aufgabenmerkmale (Vielfalt, Monotonieerleben) sowie auf die Anwendungsmöglichkeiten beruflicher Fähigkeiten von OP-Pflegekräften auswirken (Frage 1). Neben dieser Human Factors Perspektive wurden Zusammenhänge der Aufgabenmerkmale mit den individuellen Bewertungen von Karrieremotiven betrachtet (Frage 2a, 2b).
Methode. Aufbauend auf Fokusgruppenbefragungen im Krankenhaus (N = 5) wurde die objektive Aufgabenvielfalt von OP-Pflegekräften (N = 36) nach roboterassistierten Operationen mittels Expertenrating beurteilt. Mittels Fragebögen wurden die wahrgenommene Arbeitsbelastung (Monotonie) sowie die Anwendung der beruflichen Fähigkeiten im OP-Setting erfasst. Zudem wurden als Karrieremotive die wahrgenommene Nachhaltigkeit der Karriere und das Wachstumsbedürfnis erfragt.
Ergebnisse. Eine höhere Aufgabenvielfalt steht im Zusammenhang mit einem höheren Einsatz beruflicher technischer Fähigkeiten (r = .39) sowie nichttechnischer Fähigkeiten (r = .46) während Operationen. Eine höhere Aufgabenvielfalt steht zudem im Zusammenhang mit positiven Bewertungen der langfristigen gesundheitsbezogenen Nachhaltigkeit der Karriere (r = .37). Schließlich unterscheiden sich die subjektiven Bewertungen der Arbeitsbelastungen in Abhängigkeit der Karrieremotive, wobei hohe Wachstumsbedürfnisse mit mehr Monotonie einhergehen.
Schlussfolgerung. Trotz interdisziplinärer Perspektiven auf die Auswirkungen der Arbeitsgestaltung mit OP-Robotik bleibt die Generalisierbarkeit durch die begrenzten Daten der Fallstudie eingeschränkt. Deutlich wurde jedoch im Einzelfall, dass nicht die Technik der OP-Robotik allein die Aufgaben und Karriereperspektiven verändert, sondern die Art und Weise, wie Arbeitsprozesse gestaltet und Karriereentwicklung unterstützt werden.

354. Prompt Design for Reliable LLM-Based Scoring of Open-Ended Answers
Sarah Riegert | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sarah Riegert | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Björn Mattes | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stephanie Pieschl | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany

With Large Language Models (LLMs), teachers and learners alike can generate AI-based feedback for open-ended tasks such as homework or take-home assessments without requiring technical expertise. In this context, automated scoring (grading) can reduce teachers’ workload and support self-regulated learning processes. However, the reliability and validity of LLM-generated ratings critically depend on their alignment with human-intended evaluative standards.
We investigated whether GPT-4.1 can approximate expert human ratings of 852 open-ended answers to explanatory knowledge questions, and how specific prompt components influence alignment between human and LLM ratings. Using a within-answer 2 × 2 design, each response was scored ten times under each of the four prompting conditions varying the provision of (a) a scoring rubric used for human rater training, and (b) calibration examples spanning all score levels. Rating quality was operationalised as correspondence with ratings produced by human raters applying the rubric as a gold standard. Alignment was assessed using a bias score capturing systematic over- or underestimation. Both rubric-based prompting (bias = 0.213) and calibration examples (bias = -0.144) improved alignment relative to minimal prompting (bias = 0.677). The combined rubric-plus-examples condition yielded the most accurate alignment and the greatest reduction in systematic overestimation (bias = 0.058), all with p < .001.
These findings indicate that providing rubric-based grading instructions and content-specific calibration examples substantially improves the alignment of LLM-based scoring with expert ratings, reducing systematic overestimation. Accordingly, the educational applicability of LLM-based assessment depends on explicitly aligning LLM-procedures with the evaluative standards they are intended to approximate.

Read-aloud tools are becoming increasingly popular and are used, for example, with children or young people with reading difficulties to facilitate access to written information (Wood et al., 2017). In addition to reading aloud, newer tools also use “dynamic highlighting,” in which the passages being read aloud are visually highlighted. While research has begun to investigate the effect of such tools on children with dyslexia (Keelor et al., 2023), there is a lack of studies on children without reading difficulties, as well as on children whose reading difficulties are based on attention problems.For the latter group, however, there is initial empirical evidence that read-aloud tools may be beneficial (Grunér et al., 2018), since they often suffer from reading problems (Parks et al., 2022).
We therefore conducted an initial pilot study on the use of read-aloud tools combined with dynamic highlighting with fifth and sixth grade students with different attention and reading levels (N = 15). The study compared reading comprehension when reading on their own vs. reading with visual and auditive support in a within-subject design. In addition, decoding performance, concentration ability, and variables related to the reception of the texts and tools used were assessed. The preliminary results of this study suggest that while children with low reading scores certainly benefit from being read to, some average readers also tend to perform better when they are not reading themselves. The results are less clear for children who performed low on the concentration test and those who were good readers.

Assessing socio-communicative skills in medical selection procedures is associated with high economic cost, and as a result not all applicants can be tested. AI-based qualitative content analysis (Fischer, 2025) has the potential to significantly reduce human workload in the rating process of interaction-based assessments of socio-communicative skills. However, the accuracy and validity of such an approach is not yet confirmed in the context of medical selection procedures. In an experimental approach, we therefore test the performance of common proprietary (e.g., gemini-2.5-pro) as well as open-source Large Language Models (LLM; e.g., Gemma-3, mistral-small) against a human benchmark rating of socio-communicative criteria based on the Calgary-Cambridge guide commonly employed for assessments of human communication performance in the medical interview (Observation Scheme-12; Iversen et al., 2020). We additionally introduce state-of-the-art Theory of Mind-benchmarks (ToM; e.g., Xiao et al., 2025) as controls for all LLMs to assess whether ToM capability covaries with LLM performance in identifying socio-communicative skills in medical interactions. In addition to providing evidence for the suitability of an AI-based qualitative content analysis approach to aid in assessments of socio-communicative skills, results may provide tentative answers to the question which aspects of ToM, if any, may be relevant for AI healthcare applications that require socio-communicative skills, including AI-based assessments of multiple mini interview-based medical application procedures, or AI-based psychotherapy.

Laura Reichenbach | University of Freiburg | Germany

Journal writing is a beneficial medium for self-regulated learning by promoting cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies (Nückles et al., 2020). While feedback on strategy use can enhance learning, evidence on the quality and effectiveness of AI-generated feedback remains mixed. Drawing on situated learning theory, we conceptualize ChatGPT – following Vygotsky – as a cognitive tool that may learners enable to learn and to solve problems on a higher level as they would be able to realize independently, that is, without the support by ChatGPT. However, the effectiveness of the cognitive tool use depends on the quality by which learners engage with the feedback provided by ChatGPT. Study 1 examined whether ChatGPT feedback improves learning success and strategy use in journal writing more than teacher feedback. In a field experiment (N=169), feedback increased strategy use but did not enhance learning success compared to no feedback, and ChatGPT feedback was not superior to teacher feedback. A mediation analysis indicated that elaboration strategies partially explained feedback effects. Study 2 (ongoing, current N=45, targeted N=120) investigates whether structuring the feedback as interactive human-AI dialogue improves learning. Preliminary results suggest that the quality of the interaction with ChatGPT strongly predicts learning success. Together, the findings indicate that feedback effectiveness depends less on merely receiving feedback as a static product and more on learner engagement with ChatGPT as cognitive tool. Structuring feedback as an interactive process may better support self-regulated learning, highlighting the importance of pedagogically structured human-AI interaction in educational contexts.

361. Prompting for Prompts, Promptly. A Paper Identification Workflow for Fields with Ambiguous or Inconsistent Terminology
Dr. André Bittermann | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany

Dr. Jasmin Breitwieser | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Dr. Tim Lauer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Dr. Maria Theobald | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Garvin Brod | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany

In educational psychology, prompting refers to time‑efficient instructional support that guides students’ thinking and behavior. Unfortunately, identifying relevant research on prompting as an instructional method is challenging because studies often differ in the terminology used to characterize prompts. Furthermore, the term prompting is used across diverse fields. Specifically through the developments in artificial intelligence (AI), prompting has taken on a new dominant meaning, denoting user inputs for generative AI. As a result, keyword-based literature searches with additional filters frequently lead to false positives or missed papers.
Here, we introduce a paper identification workflow that is particularly useful when traditional search strategies are insufficient. The modular pipeline combines sentence embeddings, machine learning, and large language models (LLM). Using digital prompting in education as an illustrative case, we demonstrate each step of the process. The goal of the empirical study was to identify and conceptually map the various labels used in the educational literature to describe prompts.
Starting with 1,058 papers as training data and 44,639 candidate publications, a random forest classifier reliably excluded 42,616 irrelevant studies (negative predictive value, NPV = 1). To refine the remaining results, we prompted the open LLM Mixtral‑8x7B‑Instruct, which yielded an additional 747 exclusions (NPV = .97). The remaining set of 1,276 papers was then manually screened for eligibility.
We share our R and Python code, describe the prompt‑engineering strategies used, show how the workflow can be adapted to other research domains, and discuss advantages compared to existing automated screening tools.
