Isabelle Haunschild | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Isabelle Haunschild | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Bernhard Leipold | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

In recent years - and particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic - online meetings have become increasingly relevant across multiple life domains. The present study investigated the conditions under which online group meetings may serve as contexts for changes in social perception, specifically interpersonal trust and sensitivity to injustice. We focused on the role of perceived group satisfaction, discussion content (harmful intentions of others versus emotionally neutral tasks), and individual differences in personal characteristics (digital media use, technology commitment, and the Big Five personality traits).
In this intervention study employing a pre–post design over approximately two weeks, 201 participants were randomly assigned to one of three digital conditions that differed in task content. Compared to baseline assessments, interpersonal trust increased and sensitivity to injustice decreased following the interventions. Increases in interpersonal trust were observed particularly in the condition without harmful intentions and when perceived group satisfaction was high. Sensitivity to injustice decreased as a function of neuroticism and was lower in the condition without harmful intentions. Additionally, the results were moderated by gender.

363. Comparing Temporal and Retrospective Cognitive Load in Immersive Virtual Field Trips
Carina Galler | Universität der Bundeswehr München, Neubiberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Carina Galler | Universität der Bundeswehr München, Neubiberg | Germany
Maximilian C. Fink | Universität der Bundeswehr München, Neubiberg
Bernhard Ertl | Universität der Bundeswehr München, Neubiberg

Immersive virtual field trips (IVFTs) are increasingly used in digitally transformed STEM classrooms, yet their cognitive demands remain difficult to assess. Cognitive load (CL) in virtual reality (VR) is typically measured retrospectively. This may overestimate CL peak demands while obscuring temporal dynamics. This study examined the convergence between repeated in headset ratings and a post-test measure of CL.
The paper reports data from N=54 tenth grade students from two German grammar schools who completed a 35-minute IVFT on wastewater treatment in a 2×2 design manipulating annotations and quizzes. The IVFT consisted of 10 stations and CL was assessed inside the headset after each station with one item (Range 1..9); immediately afterwards students completed the CL scale in the post-test.
CL was moderate across stations, M=3.65, SD=1.37, and increased from station six onwards, coinciding with the more complex content (chemical purification phase) of the IVFT. The mean of in-headset load correlated with post-test ICL, r(52)=.316, p=.020, but not with ECL r(52)=.257, p=.061, or GCL. No significant condition differences emerged, although descriptively highest values of CL occurred in the control group and lowest in the combined condition. Female students reported higher in headset load than male students, t(51)=2.26, p=.028, d=.63.
Findings show that in headset ratings aligned mainly with post-test ICL, suggesting that temporally embedded single-item measures primarily capture perceived task complexity rather than instructional demands or learning related effort. This underscores the need to differentiate load facets when designing and validating cognitive ergonomics in IVFTs.

364. Der richtige Umgang mit Smartphones: Sei achtsam und nutze Deine Zeit sinnvoll
Prof. Dr. Christian Bosau | Rheinische Hochschule Köln gGmbH | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Christian Bosau | Rheinische Hochschule Köln gGmbH | Germany
Sarah Klein | Rheinische Hochschule Köln gGmbH

Die Medienlandschaft ist voll von Forderungen nach der Einschränkung von Smartphones – insbesondere bei jüngeren Menschen. Obwohl oftmals bereits die negativen Effekte von Smartphones beleuchtet wurden, fehlt bisherigen Studien häufig der Einbezug positiver Ressourcen der Nutzer – wie z.B. Achtsamkeit/Dankbarkeit – sowie der Frage, ob das Gefühl nichtvergehender Zeit die Smartphone-Nutzung befeuert, die dann wiederum zu Zeitdruck anderswo führen kann.

Die vorliegende Studie (N=67, Alter: Median=22) untersuchte daher in einer Querschnittsbefragung, welche Rolle der bewusste Umgang mit dem Leben - gemessen mit Achtsamkeit (MAAS – Brown & Ryan; 2003) und Dankbarkeit (GQ-6 – McCullough et al.; 2002) - sowie das subjektive Zeitempfinden (STQ – Wittmann & Lehnhoff; 2005) im Kontext einer überbordenden Smartphone-Nutzung spielt - gemessen mit Fear-of-Missing-Out (FoMO – Spitzer; 2015) und Problematic Use of Mobile Phone (PUMP – Graben et al.; 2020).

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass fehlende Achtsamkeit ein sehr bedeutender Einflussfaktor auf FoMO (r=-.48***) und PUMP (r=-.63***) ist. Ebenso führt das Gefühl einer nicht vergehenden Zeit zu mehr FoMO (r=.28**) und PUMP (r=.41***). Als Folge der problematische Smartphone-Nutzung zeigt sich dann erhöhter Zeitdruck (r=.43***) als auch eine geringere Dankbarkeit (r=-.27**). In gleicher Weise hängt FoMO mit erhöhtem Zeitdruck (r=.40***) und geringerer Dankbarkeit (r=-.40***) zusammen.

Diese Studie unterstreicht somit die große Bedeutung eines bewussteren Umgangs mit der eigenen Zeit und dem eigenen Leben. Zukünftige Maßnahmen sollten sich nicht nur auf das Smartphone selbst beziehen (z.B. Verbote/Altersbeschränkungen), sondern viel stärker den Nutzer und seine psychischen Einflussmöglichkeiten in Form von Achtsamkeit und angemessenem Umgang mit seinem Zeitempfinden betonen.

365. Bridging Lab and Real-World: Uncertainty Visualizations in Digital Practice
Stephan Reiche | Leibniz Institut für die Pädagogik der Naturwissenschaften und Mathematik | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Stephan Reiche | Leibniz Institut für die Pädagogik der Naturwissenschaften und Mathematik | Germany
Björn Döge | Muthesius Kunsthochschule Kiel
Prof. Dr. Melanie Keller | Leibniz Institut für die Pädagogik der Naturwissenschaften und Mathematik | Germany

From bus times to medical risk, distributional uncertainty — variation in possible outcomes — is everywhere in daily life and is often visualized with boxplots. Boxplots, however, are frequently misunderstood by both laypeople and experts (Belia et al., 2005; Hofman et al., 2020). Experimental studies suggest that newer uncertainty visualizations like Quantile Dot Plots (QDPs) and Hypothetical Outcome Plots (HOPs) can improve understanding and engagement (Kay et al., 2016; Hullman et al., 2015). We test their ecological validity by providing field evidence on communicating distributional uncertainty in real-world digital information environments with diverse audiences and limited attention.
We conducted a randomized field experiment (n = 2254) on a science journalism website (spektrum.de). In a scrollytelling article on sleep across the lifespan, readers saw one of five visualizations of sleep-duration distributions: boxplots, percentile lines, QDPs, HOPs, and traced HOPs. We assessed understanding with embedded questions and engagement with log data (e.g. time on page). Understanding was comparable across all five visualizations. However, readers spent significantly more time in the QDP condition than in the HOP condition.
Two follow-up studies are underway to explain these patterns and test generalizability, both using more sensitive outcome measures: (1) a survey experiment in February 2026 (target n = 1850) that also tests moderators (graph literacy, numeracy, education, user experience), and (2) a replication field experiment using a similar scrollytelling format on a different topic (data collection ending in March 2026). Overall, lab advantages may not transfer, while some formats increase dwell time relative to others.

366. Does context matter? Trust in Human vs. AI-Based Coaching Across Health Domains
Noelle Steffens | Albert-Ludwigs Universität Freiburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Dr. Marie Luise Ohlms | Albert-Ludwigs Universität Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Markus Langer | Albert-Ludwigs Universität Freiburg

The increasing demand for AI-based coaching has intensified the need for research on their application contexts and users’ trust in these technologies. The present research examined differences in the development of trust in AI-based compared to human coaching and how the coaching contexts affects trust.
Two studies were conducted to address these questions. Study 1 employed a 2 (coach type: human vs. AI-based) × 2 (coaching context: mental vs. physical health) between-subjects design. Participants (N = 300) were instructed to imagine receiving coaching targeting either their mental or physical health from either a human or an AI-based coach. Participants rated the coach in terms of trust, perceived trustworthiness (ability, benevolence, and integrity) and trusting behavior. Study 2 employed a between-subjects design focusing on coaching context (mental vs. physical health) within AI-based coaching and involved real interactions with a text-based AI-coach. Participants (N = 280) interacted with the chatbot for a minimum of five minutes before completing the same measures as in Study 1.
In Study 1, coach type significantly affected perceived trustworthiness, trust, and trusting behavior, with human coaches consistently receiving higher ratings than AI-based coaches. In contrast, the coaching context (mental vs. physical health) did not significantly affect trust, trustworthiness, or trusting behavior. Moreover, no interaction between coach type and coaching context on trust-related outcomes was found. Study 2 replicated these findings, showing no significant differences in trust, perceived trustworthiness or trusting behavior between physical and mental health coaching contexts within AI-based coaching. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

367. The Less You Know, The More You Trust: Metacognitive Miscalibration in AI Literacy
Antonia Rosada | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Antonia Rosada | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security | Germany
Nur Cetinkaya | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security
Dr. Carina Newen | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security
Anna Neumann | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security
Maria Thurow | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security
Simon Lutz | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security
Prof. Nicole Krämer | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security

AI literacy has emerged as a critical driver of individuals' engagement with artificial intelligence. While often promoted as essential for responsible AI use, research predominantly relies on self-report measures, leaving unclear whether perceived competence (self-assessed knowledge) aligns with factual competence (objective performance). This study investigates (1) the extent to which perceived and factual AI literacy diverge, and (2) their independent effects on trust, acceptance, usage intentions, and experience with AI systems.
Data were collected from N=642 participants who completed a perceived AI literacy scale and a factual AI literacy test. Participants were categorized based on self-assessment accuracy (over-estimators, realistic, under-estimators). Multiple regression models examined effects on trust in AI as primary outcome, with additional analyses for acceptance, usage intentions, and prior experience.
Perceived and factual AI literacy correlated weakly (r=.14, p < .001), with only 29% demonstrating accurate self-assessment. Over-estimators (37%) exhibited lowest factual knowledge yet highest trust, whereas under-estimators (34%) were most knowledgeable but more skeptical. Regression analyses revealed that perceived AI literacy strongly predicted trust (β=.67, R²=.45, p < .001), while factual AI literacy showed a suppression effect - negligible bivariate correlation but significant negative regression coefficient (β=-.12, p < .01). Similar effects emerged for acceptance, usage intentions, and prior experience.
These findings reveal a critical pattern: perceived competence, not factual AI literacy, drives trust and AI adoption. This creates a concerning vulnerability: the least knowledgeable exhibit greatest trust. Educational interventions must enhance factual AI literacy to calibrate self-assessment and promote informed, critical engagement with AI systems.

368. Test Centaur: Can LLM reshape cognitive experimental steps?
Yujia Yang | Germany
Show details
Author:
Yujia Yang | Germany

Behavioral experiments vary widely in design and reporting, limiting comparability and slowing cumulative theory building. Mapping the full space of task variables through large coordinated projects is informative but costly and difficult to scale. We therefore explore a complementary strategy: using a foundation model of human decisions as a domain-general cognitive simulator to study behavioral patterns in silico before collecting new data. If such a model generalizes beyond its training data, it can simulate behavior across broad combinations of environmental variables and help identify which paradigms produce meaningful differences before resource-intensive studies. To assess this possibility, we evaluate Centaur, a Llama 3.1–70B model with low-rank adapters fine-tuned on the Psych-101 behavioral dataset, together with two reference models, the base Llama model and a random-choice model. We focus on decision-from-experience tasks. Psych-101 serves as an in-sample benchmark. Out-of-sample tests use the large Decision-from-Experience database, a public resource developed by our team containing 3.8 million individual choices across 168 studies. It is divided into DfE-in, which shares feature structures with the training data, and DfE-out, which includes novel feature combinations. All tasks are converted into standardized prompts, and models generate trial-by-trial choices. We assess predictive accuracy and log-likelihood at the study level. Performance is expected to decline from training data to familiar and then novel paradigms, indicating generalization limits. Task-level differences will show where simulation remains reliable or breaks down, clarifying how LLM-based cognitive simulators can prioritize conditions, refine theories, and allocate empirical resources more efficiently.

The increasing use of screen-based Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in early childhood education has raised concerns on their effects on children’s mental and exploratory behavior. Although AI tools provide engaging opportunities and active learning, excessive screen exposure can compromise emotional well-being and exploratory behavior. Conversely, play-based learning is crucial to the development of curiosity, emotional well-being, healthy psychological growth, exploration, and sustained interest in learning. This study aims to examine the balance between screen-based AI tools use, play-based learning engagement, and mental health among children aged 3-8, with a focus on the underlying psychological mechanisms and observable exploratory behavior. An explanatory sequential mixed-method design will be adopted. In the quantitative phase, cross-sectional survey data will be collected from early childhood teachers and parents as proxy respondents using standardized instruments on mental health, emotional regulation and play engagement of the children. Children will also participate directly through structured observations using validated rubrics to determine exploratory behavior during AI interaction and play activities. Quantitative data will be analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test direct, indirect and moderating effects. Observational and interview data will be used in the qualitative phase to give the contextual explanation of the qualitative data. Study’s findings will contribute to understanding how developmentally appropriate balancing of AI tools and play can promote children’s mental health and exploratory behavior. It will offer evidence-based implications for early childhood teachers, parents, policymakers, and designers of AI learning technologies encouraging sustainable and child-centered digital transformation in education.

Laura N. Peters | Osnabrück University | Germany

Hannah Maaß | Osnabrück University
Prof. Dr. Rosa M. Puca | Osnabrück University | Germany

Text-generative AI-Chatbots based on large language models (genAI) are increasingly used by higher education students. The current study focusses on the explicit achievement motive in relation to perceived advantages and disadvantages as well as the likelihood of using genAI for learning in a hypothetical higher education study scenario. Hypotheses were formulated for students with high hope for success (HS) and students high in fear of failure (FF). It was assumed that as compared to students low in FF students high in FF both rely more on genAI and are more sceptic due to the mistakes genAI systems produce. The sample consisted of 341 students; the achievement motive was measured with the German short version of the Achievement Motives Scale (Engeser, 2005). Reconsidering Marczuk et al.’s (2025) findings, two scales for genAI advantages and disadvantages were developed. The data was analysed using RM-ANOVA. Results revealed that overall students agreed more with disadvantages than with advantages of genAI for studying, irrespective of their achievement motive. As predicted students high in FF significantly agreed more with advantages as well as disadvantages of using genAI than students low in FF. Additionally, they were also scoring higher in the likelihood of using genAI for studying. Although effect sizes were small, the results highlight the need to further explore how motivational dispositions shape students’ attitudes towards genAI. Implications and directions for future research questions will be discussed.

371. Digital Health Literacy as a Predictor of Mental Well-Being in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital health platforms offers both prospects and threats to mental health of university students. Although easy access to health resources can be maximized with AI-driven tools, it also allows users to become exposed to misleading or overwhelming content, potentially upsetting psychological health, leading to confusion, stress, or anxiety among users. Most students rely on digital resources as a major source of health information which may result in mental health disorders including anxiety, depression, sleep, trauma, eating disorders, and stress-related disorders. University students are also stakeholders who may be at risk of being psychologically affected by the AI-generated content because they do not necessarily have the expertise to critically analyze and apply it effectively. This study aims to examine Digital Health Literacy (DHL); the ability to seek, evaluate, engage and make informed decisions with digital health information on mental well-being among university students. A cross-sectional survey design will be used for data collection among university students by employing validated scales on mental health and DHL. To determine predictive relationships and possible moderating factors of exposure to AI-generated health contents, Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) will be used. Results will be used to make related interventions that would facilitate sustainable mental health practices, and integration of AI-mediated health literacy education in tertiary education. This study will help bridge the gaps in promoting evidence-based approaches advancing to mental well-being in AI era by facilitating the digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and psychological resilience.

372. Detecting Stressor Exposure in Digital Behavioral Data Using Large Language Models
Dr. Jan Broll | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research (LIR) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jan Broll | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research (LIR) | Germany
Lea Schaubruch | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research (LIR) | Germany
Dr. Dennis Assenmacher | GESIS — Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences | Germany
Prof. Dr. Claudia Wagner | GESIS — Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Stier | GESIS — Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences | Germany

Prof. Dr. Sarah K. Schäfer | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research (LIR) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Klaus Lieb | Leibniz Institute for Resilience Research (LIR) | Germany

Resilience research relies heavily on self-report data to assess exposure to macro stressors (e.g., serious health events, job loss) and micro stressors (e.g., daily hassles). A key limitation is the timing between stressor occurrence and survey participation, which introduces systematic recall bias. Digital behavioral data (DBD) offer a promising complement by enabling temporally precise detection of stressor signals prior to survey administration.

This talk presents first results from the AI-RESIL project, which develops an AI-powered survey infrastructure combining panel surveys with web tracking data. We focus specifically on the automated detection of stressor exposure in participants' digital behavioral data using Large Language Models (LLMs).

Our approach integrates deductive (top-down) and inductive (bottom-up) knowledge discovery methods. Theory-driven keyword lists derived from established stressor scales (e.g., the Mainz Inventory of Microstressors) are expanded inductively using word embeddings and LLMs. Stressor signals are extracted from search queries, visited URLs, and chatbot conversations. We have developed an LLM-based classifier that identifies which specific macro and micro stressors a person has recently experienced based solely on their digital trace data. Classifier performance is evaluated against self-reported stressor exposure collected in repeated survey waves with approximately 6,000 participants over 12 months.

We present empirical evidence on the predictive accuracy of the classifier, discuss temporal dynamics between digital stressor traces and survey participation, and reflect on methodological implications for resilience research. Results suggest that web tracking data can meaningfully extend the temporal resolution of stressor measurement beyond what traditional survey designs allow.

373. Changes in how far psychological research is looking back: An analysis of how the distribution of age of citations in journal articles develops across decades
Prof. Dr. Robert Gaschler | FernUniversität in Hagen
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Robert Gaschler | FernUniversität in Hagen
Katja Beyfuß | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Helen Landmann | Universität Klagenfurt

Analysis of reference lists of journal articles allows to track changes across decades in how far psychological research is looking back. Work on theory and practice of science suggests an increase in the proportion that recent publications obtain in reference lists of journal articles over the last decades. Recent publications (i.e., covering the last five years) might often represent more directly the research that new work is based on, while older references might often provide additional background. The last decades have changed production and access to psychological literature such that researchers can learn more quickly about new publications they can base their own work on. The amount of publications has increased and researchers have been provided with means to access new literature more quickly. Also, electronic communication allows to more quickly inform other researchers about new publications. Spanning several decades for four general psychology journals, the current work analyzes changes in age distribution of references in Memory & Cognition (N = 184.107), Attention, Perception & Psychophysics (N = 311.616), Motivation & Emotion (N = 79.979) and Psychological Research (N = 129.481). Different from the predictions, the proportion of young references has been consistently decreasing over the last decades. There is no indication that the main focus of current research has become more temporally restricted. Instead, as psychology is accumulating research publications, older work seems to profit from changes in access as well.

374. Clarifying your future career path: How an AI-enabled intervention can enhance career development
Theresa Heinkelmann-Wild | TUM School of Management | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Theresa Heinkelmann-Wild | TUM School of Management | Germany
Dr. Martin P. Fladerer | TUM School of Management
Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus | TUM School of Management

In today’s rapidly evolving world of work, careers are no longer linear or predictable, and the responsibility for professional development is increasingly shifting to employees themselves. As a result, the need for effective career self-management has never been greater, yet access to career counseling and coaching remains limited for many. This study investigates whether established career counseling methods can be effectively adapted into an accessible, AI-driven intervention to promote proactive career behavior among young professionals. Drawing on Savickas’ Career Construction Theory, the intervention utilizes the Career Construction Interview (CCI) as a narrative-reflective tool, delivered via a chatbot-based platform that combines structured reflection prompts, written self-exploration, and individualized feedback.
Through a randomized online experiment, participants engage with the chatbot-based CCI, and their proactive career behaviors (exploration and planning) are tracked over time. Data collection is ongoing, and results will be presented at the conference. By providing empirical evidence of the effectiveness of an AI-supported career counseling intervention, this research advances the field beyond theoretical discussions of AI’s potential. The findings are expected to offer valuable insights into whether a scalable, AI-enabled career counseling can democratize access to professional development resources and support personal career development in an increasingly complex professional landscape.

375. "I prefer AI—depending on the situation": Older Adults’ Preferences for AI Agents Before and After Direct Interaction
Dr. Tingting Huang | University of Nottingham Ningbo | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Tingting Huang | University of Nottingham Ningbo | Germany

Objective: Conversational AI agents have the potential to provide socio-emotional support to the elderly in nursing homes. However, concerns remain about social substitution and the potential for unwanted psychosocial consequences. This qualitative study examined the preferences of interaction with AI versus human among Chinese older adults in nursing homes.

Methods: We conducted two rounds of in-depth interviews with 37 residents aged 68–92. The first round focused on their social lives and initial attitudes toward AI. Several months later, they were introduced to a conversational AI system and were invited to interact with it freely. Follow-up interviews covered their experiences and intentions regarding continued use. The interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis.

Results: Two themes emerged: (1) social isolation and anticipatory preferences for AI versus human support, and (2) context-dependent preferences following direct interaction. The elderly experienced both active and passive social isolation, with active isolation motivating their initial preference for AI agents. After direct interaction, however, they developed more differentiated views and expressed situational preferences; for example, expressing negative emotions to AI agents while sharing positive emotions with human.

Discussion: Older adults' preference for AI is closely tied to their active social isolation. Direct interaction with AI helped them better understand its possibilities and limits compared to human support. These findings underscore the importance of supervised, real-world engagement with AI as part of digital literacy initiatives in long-term care settings.

376. Psychological Dilemmas in Remote and Hybrid Work Settings: Insights from an Agile Organization
Alexandra Anna Halmos | Budapest University of Technology and Economics; Budapest Corvinus University | Hungary
Show details
Authors:
Alexandra Anna Halmos | Budapest University of Technology and Economics; Budapest Corvinus University | Hungary
Prof. Dr. Zsolt Péter Szabó | Budapest Corvinus University; Eötvös Loránd Science University
Dr. Miklós Antal

This study examines how work from home (WFH) and hybrid arrangements reconfigure
work in a large Agile Software Development (ASD) organization following the COVID19 pandemic. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative dataset comprising interviews and
focus groups with 169 employees and managers, we explore how the transition away
from default co-location reshaped psychological and organizational processes.Using
reflexive thematic analysis, we identified five interrelated dilemmas of remote work
concerning information flows, relational structures, leadership and coordination,
contextual stimuli, and learning and knowledge transfer. We further identify six
recurrent questions that organizations confront when institutionalizing hybrid work,
including expectations around office presence, temporal alignment, task-based co-location, exceptions, governance, and the evolving role of office space.Rather than
treating remote or hybrid work as uniformly beneficial or harmful, our findings show that
their consequences emerge through counterbalancing mechanisms that help explain
the paradoxical and inconsistent effects reported in prior research. We demonstrate
how task type, team maturity, and specialization patterns condition when distributed
work supports or undermines performance and coordination. We also show that
leadership is fundamentally reconfigured under these conditions, with increased
demands for facilitation, interpretive work, and identity construction in the absence of
shared physical context.By integrating socio-technical and psychosocial perspectives,
this study advances contingency-based theorizing of remote and hybrid work and
offers practical guidance for designing sustainable hybrid arrangements that balance
autonomy, coordination, and cohesion.

377. Avoid, Neutralize, or Engage? How Teachers Respond to Controversial and Sensitive Issues
Esra Nur Bellikli-Özcam | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Esra Nur Bellikli-Özcam | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Mayweg | Humboldt Universität Berlin

Controversial and socially sensitive issues that can emerge in classroom discussions increasingly confront teachers with complex professional challenges. In times of socio-political polarisation, growing scepticism towards democratic institutions, and an increase in hate speech, disinformation, and science denial, the constructive handling of controversy has gained importance as a core dimension of democratic education. At the same time, it needs additional evidence on how teachers respond to controversy and how ready they feel to navigate controversial topics inside the classroom. This contribution presents an experimentally designed study that will be conducted in Summer 2026 and will use a vignette approach to examine how pre-service teachers, including student teachers and teacher trainees in Germany respond to sensitive and controversial classroom situations. In a 2×2 between-subjects design, the study varies both the level of topic controversy (low vs. high; determined via a pilot testing) and the instructional context (teacher-initiated vs. spontaneously emerging controversy). Thematic vignettes address an everyday topic (family concepts) and a highly controversial, current socio-political issue (Israel–Palestine). Participants’ anticipated instructional decisions are assessed as the primary outcome. The study focuses on relationships between perceived controversy, professional dispositions, affective responses, and instructional intentions. Initial findings are expected to help identify factors that foster reflective and deliberative approaches to addressing controversy inside the classroom and to identify key areas of professional learning and development. Overall, the contribution provides insights into how teachers navigate democratic challenges in emotionally and socially complex classroom situations.

378. Surveying sensitive topics: Video instructions can improve the validity of prevalence estimates obtained in randomized response surveys
Dr. Julia Meisters | Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Julia Meisters | Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf | Germany
Dr. Adrian Hoffmann | Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Prof. Dr. Jochen Musch | Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf

Indirect questioning techniques, such as the Extended Crosswise Model (ECWM; Heck et al., 2018), are designed to mitigate the validity-threatening effects of social desirability bias on self-reports by enhancing the confidentiality of individual responses. However, recent studies have questioned the validity of the ECWM because of its rather complex instructions, which may limit its applicability to higher-educated samples. This study examined whether estimation validity can be improved through video instructions and optimizing answer options, especially among lower-educated participants. To this end, we experimentally compared four ECWM implementations combining text versus video instructions with aggregated versus detailed answer options. For comparison, we employed a direct questioning control condition. The validity of the obtained estimates was evaluated using a strong individual-level validation criterion based on classification accuracy. Across both educational groups, video instructions combined with detailed answer options produced the most valid results. This implementation showed an adequate model fit, prevalence estimates close to the known true value, a substantially reduced rate of false negatives compared to direct questioning, and comparatively low false-positive rates. Overall, classification accuracy was comparable to direct questioning and slightly higher in the higher-educated subgroup. Importantly, when video instructions and detailed answer options were used, the differences between lower- and higher-educated participants disappeared in all validation measures. Therefore, this implementation appears promising in terms of preventing the systematic disadvantage of lower-educated participants observed in previous ECWM studies, thereby extending the applicability of the ECWM to samples from all educational backgrounds.

379. Effects of requiring fast rather than slow responses to lineups on culprit-presence detection and guessing-based selection
Dr. Carolin Mayer | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Carolin Mayer | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf | Germany
Prof. Dr. Raoul Bell | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Dr. Nicola Marie Menne | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Ulla Lichtenhagen | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Dr. Amelie Therre | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Dr. Ana Philippsen | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf
Prof. Dr. Axel Buchner | Institute of Experimental Psychology, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf

Building on the previously reported correlative relationship between response latency and the likelihood that an identification from a lineup is correct, we tested whether requiring eyewitnesses to respond fast rather than slowly improves the detection of the presence of the culprit in police lineups. To this end, we conducted a large-scale online experiment in which all participants were shown a staged-crime video and subsequently responded to four simultaneous lineups. Participants in a fast-response condition were instructed to respond spontaneously after having viewed the lineups for three seconds. Participants in a slow-response condition were instructed to respond deliberately after having viewed the lineups for 20 seconds. In both conditions, the lineups remained visible until participants had responded. To measure the effects of fast and slow responding on the processes underlying eyewitness responses to lineups, the well-validated two-high threshold eyewitness identification model was used. The probability of culprit-presence detection was equivalent in the fast-response condition and in the slow-response condition. In contrast, the probability of guessing-based selection was higher when participants were required to respond fast than when they were required to respond slowly. Thus, the present results suggest that eyewitnesses should not be instructed to respond spontaneously rather than deliberatively because doing so may increase guessing-based selection without improving culprit-presence detection.

380. Perception of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination among young adults (18-26 years) in Germany
Anne-Sophie Tänzer | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Anne-Sophie Tänzer | Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg | Germany
Sarah Eitze
Dorothee Heinemeier

HPV are among the most common sexually transmitted infections and can cause cancer. Although an effective and safe vaccine against HPV is available, vaccination in Germany is primarily recommended up to the age of 18. For young adults aged 18–26 years, vaccination remains possible; however, cost coverage is regulated inconsistently, and data on vaccine uptake and psychological determinants of vaccination decisions are limited. This study examined perceptions of the HPV-vaccine among young adults in Germany and identified predictors of vaccination intention based on the 5C (Betsch et al., 2018) and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB, Ajzen, 1991), supplemented by additional sociodemographic, knowledge-related, and structural predictors. A cross-sectional, pre-registered online survey (N = 481 unvaccinated participants; 54.7% female; M = 22.85 years, SD = 2.46) assessed awareness, knowledge, attitudes, and predictors of vaccination intention. The main analyses were conducted using hierarchical regression analyses. Approximately half of the sample was aware of HPV and the vaccine. Knowledge was rather low, while attitudes toward the HPV vaccine were generally positive. Vaccination intention was moderate (M = 3.1, SD = 1.0). Four predictors contributed significantly (all p < .001) to the explanation of variance in HPV vaccination intention: constraints (β = .17), collective responsibility (β = .25), subjective norms (β = .23), and perceived behavioural control (β = .35). The combined 5C and TPB model explained 43% of the variance in vaccination intention (R² = .43, p < .001). Vaccination intention is shaped by psychological predictors that can be addressed through targeted communication.

381. Effects of yoga exercises on emotional and social competencies in preschool children
Sara Studte | Oldenburg University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sara Studte | Oldenburg University | Germany
Ingo Roden | Oldenburg University

The development of emotional and social competencies in preschool children is a pivotal factor in their future health and well-being. The present study aims to investigate the effects of a children's yoga intervention compared to standardised social-emotional training programmes on the emotional skills of preschool children. In a pre-post design, 46 preschool children (aged 3 to 6 years; 28 male) were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a) yoga (n = 11), b) social-emotional training (n = 21) or c) control group (n = 14). All children underwent screening to assess their emotional skills. The duration of each intervention was four weeks, with each intervention conducted twice a week for a duration of 60 minutes. The dependent variables encompassed primary and secondary emotions, prosocial behaviour, empathy, and delayed reward. It was hypothesised that children in both intervention groups would achieve higher scores on socio-emotional outcomes than their control group. The results of the study will be presented at the forthcoming conference. Furthermore, the discussion will address the question of whether physical interventions have the potential to promote the development of emotional and social skills in preschool children.

382. Welchen Alternativaktivitäten gehen Studierende während des Prokrastinierens nach? Zusammenhänge mit Alter, Geschlecht und Gewissenhaftigkeit
Dr. Lorena Fleischmann | Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lorena Fleischmann | Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg | Germany
Sophia Maria Huber | Universität Mannheim
Prof. Dr. Rannveig Grøm Sæle | Universität Tromsø – Norwegens Arktische Universität
Prof. Dr. Birgit Spinath | Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg

Prokrastination ist ein häufiges Problem unter Studierenden und mit geringeren akademischen Leistungen verbunden (z.B. Steel, 2007). Zahlreiche Studien zeigen, dass Prokrastination häufiger bei jüngeren, männlichen und weniger gewissenhaften Studierenden auftritt (Lu et al., 2022; Steel, 2007). Bisher ist allerdings weitgehend unklar, welchen Alternativaktivitäten Studierende während des Prokrastinierens nachgehen und ob deren Häufigkeit ebenfalls mit Alter, Geschlecht und Gewissenhaftigkeit zusammenhängt.

Wir befragten insgesamt 283 Studierende (227 weiblich und 56 männlich) im Alter von 18 bis 32 Jahren, wie häufig sie Alternativaktivitäten wie „Smartphone“, „Serien/Filme“ oder „Putzen/Aufräumen“ während des Prokrastinierens nachgehen. Die Auswahl der Alternativaktivitäten orientierte sich an früheren Studien (Pychyl et al., 2000; Kaftan & Freund, 2019). Die Gewissenhaftigkeit der Studierenden wurde mit dem BFI-K (Rammstedt & John, 2005) erfasst.

Die Ergebnisse zeigten, dass die Nutzung von Smartphone und Social Media die häufigsten Alternativaktivitäten während des Prokrastinierens waren. Das Alter der Studierenden war nicht signifikant mit der Häufigkeit der Alternativaktivitäten assoziiert. Geschlechtsunterschiede traten selektiv auf: Männliche Studierende spielten häufiger Video-/Computerspiele (η²p = .07), während weibliche Studierende häufiger ihr Smartphone bzw. Social Media nutzten und Serien/Filme schauten (η²p zwischen .05 und .08). Die Gewissenhaftigkeit der Studierenden hing negativ mit der Häufigkeit mehrerer Alternativaktivitäten zusammen (η²p zwischen .02 und .08 ).

Der Beitrag verdeutlicht, dass die Smartphone- und Social Media-Nutzung bei Studierenden während des Prokrastinierens eine zentrale Rolle spielt und dass die Zusammenhänge mit Geschlecht und Gewissenhaftigkeit je nach Art der Alternativaktivität variieren. Maßnahmen zur Reduktion von Prokrastination sollten daher individuelle Unterschiede berücksichtigen und den Umgang mit Smartphone und Social Media gezielt adressieren.

383. Simulating the Shift: Identifying Key Variables to Promote Preference for Larger Later Rewards in Delay Discounting.
Annemarie Hartung | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annemarie Hartung | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Frank Eggert | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie

Individuals frequently face trade-offs between rewards occurring at different points in time. While choices are straightforward when reward magnitudes are identical, conflict arises when both the amount and the delay differ. In decisions between a smaller-sooner reward (SSR) and a larger-later reward (LLR), individuals often prefer the immediate option, despite the superior long-term utility of the LLR. This phenomenon is known as delay discounting. It describes the decrease in a reward's subjective value as the delay to its receipt increases. The selection of the larger reward is frequently associated with self-control, whereas a systematic preference for smaller rewards is interpreted as choice impulsivity. Consequently, steep discounting rates have been identified as a marker for a range of maladaptive behaviors, including overeating, substance use disorders, and risky sexual activity.
Delay discounting is most commonly characterized by a hyperbolic decay function: V = A / (1+kD). Here V represents the discounted subjective value, A the objective reward amount, D the length of the delay, and k the discount rate.
The aim of this simulation study is to identify which systematic manipulations of these parameters are most effective in shifting preferences toward the larger-later reward. By modeling variations in magnitude, delay intervals, and discounting rates, this research identifies the key levers for promoting “patient” decision-making and enhancing self-control in intertemporal choice.

384. Overwhelmed by Helping? Language and Sociocultural Adaptation Hassles in Adolescent Cultural Brokering
Leonie Dreißigacker | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leonie Dreißigacker | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Dr. Kristin Schotte | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Aileen Edele | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Peter F. Titzmann | Leibniz Universität Hannover | Germany

Adolescents in immigrant-origin families often acquire the host-country language more rapidly than their parents and consequently engage in cultural brokering for their families (i.e., they informally translate and help navigate institutional and everyday contexts). However, its psychosocial consequences remain inconclusive, with evidence of both risk and adaptive outcomes. This heterogeneity may be the result of variable-oriented approaches that assume a one-size-fits-all mechanism, although various subgroups with partly different mechanisms may exist. In particular, the heterogeneity may reflect differences in adolescents’ (mis)matches between contextual brokering demands and personal resources in terms of perceived challenges in linguistic and sociocultural domains.

Drawing on Cultural Stress Theory (Meca & Schwartz, 2024), the present study (a) adopts a person-oriented approach to examine whether subgroups exist that differ in their patterns of perceived language and sociocultural adaptation hassles and culture brokering behavior and (b) whether these subgroups differ in relation to psychosocial adaptation in family and peer domains, including family cohesion, social support from friends, bullying perpetration, and victimization. We expect to identify profiles reflecting different demand–resource (mis)matches and predict that adolescents characterized by frequent brokering combined with elevated adaptation hassles will show poorer psychosocial adjustment than those who broker frequently but report fewer adaptation hassles.

We analyze data from approximately 3,000 immigrant-origin adolescents from the "Niedersachsensurvey", a representative survey of ninth-grade students in Lower Saxony, Germany, using latent profile analysis and multivariate analysis of variance. The study is currently being preregistered, and results will be available at the time of the conference.

385. Milestones in the Wild: Mapping Early Gross Motor Development with the Pebbles App
Flavia J. Pfister | University of Zurich | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lisa Wagner | University of Zurich
Flavia J. Pfister | University of Zurich | Switzerland
Miriam T. Loeffler | University of Zurich
Salome Wenk
Prof. Dr. Moritz M. Daum | University of Zurich

Understanding infant development requires methods that capture behaviour as it occurs in everyday life, in addition to controlled laboratory settings. Mobile technologies, such as the Pebbles App (Daum et al., 2022), enable large-scale ecologically valid observations contributed by caregivers. The Pebbles App allows caregivers to document children’s emerging skills as they unfold. It includes over 600 items assessing development across different domains from birth to 6 years of age. The present study focuses on gross motor development from birth to 24 months. We aim to estimate age-of-attainment distributions for N = 65 key milestones (e.g., sitting unsupported, pulling to stand) and to characterise sequences and alternative orders of motor milestone attainment, identifying both common trajectories and individual variation. To meet these aims, we apply survival analysis, which accommodates left- and right-censoring that is often observed in app-based data. For the present study, we will analyse caregiver reports on the attainment of gross motor milestones provided on N > 6000 children, representing one of the largest naturalistic datasets of early motor development to date. We will report (a) milestone-specific median ages and variability; (b) concordance with WHO reference windows; and (c) data-driven sequences and branching points (e.g., alternative pathways into cruising and independent walking). Beyond providing normative and variability estimates in a real-world sample, this work will demonstrate a scalable analytic framework for leveraging app-based observations to study developmental trajectories across domains.

386. Kriteriengeleitete Beurteilung von Kindesmisshandlung und -vernachlässigung
Sven Fath | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sven Fath | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christel Salewski | FernUniversität in Hagen

Hintergrund: In gerichtlichen Verfahren bei fraglicher Kindeswohlgefährdung werden Sachverständige beauftragt, das Risiko von Misshandlung oder Vernachlässigung auf Grundlage psychologischer Expertise detailliert zu beurteilen. Psychologische Sachverständige nutzen für ihre Einschätzung bisher fast ausschließlich eine idiographische Herangehensweise, obwohl eine Überlegenheit der Kombination aus idiographischem und nomothetischem Ansatz anzunehmen ist.
Ziel: Um die psychologische Begutachtung im Familienrecht um eine nomothetische Bestimmung des Ausgangsrisikos zu ergänzen, soll ein Instrument entwickelt werden, das eine kriteriengeleitete Beurteilung von Kindesmisshandlung und -vernachlässigung auf Grundlage der Informationen der Verfahrensakte ermöglicht.
Methode: Es erfolgte eine systematische Literaturrecherche zur Identifizierung relevanter Risikofaktoren. Anschließend wurden diese nach statistischen, inhaltlichen und praktischen Überlegungen selektiert. Dabei wurde eine Unterteilung in elternbezogene Kriterien (z. B. psychopathologische Auffälligkeiten), kindbezogene Kriterien (z. B. frühkindliche Erkrankungen), familienbezogene Kriterien (z. B. Partnerschaftsgewalt) und soziale Kriterien (z. B. fehlende soziale Unterstützung) vorgenommen.
Ergebnisse: Vorgestellt wird ein detailliertes Kodiermanual, welches als Grundlage für die Einschätzung der einzelnen Risikofaktoren (gegeben vs. nicht gegeben) dient und eine einheitliche Anwendung sicherstellt. Die Risikofaktoren werden anhand inhaltlicher Beschreibungen (z. B., wann von prekären Wohnverhältnissen auszugehen ist) und zeitlicher Aspekte (z. B., ob ein Kriterium innerhalb der letzten sechs Monate vorgelegen hat) konkretisiert. Berücksichtigt wird auch die Art der Informationsquelle (z.B. Selbstauskunft vs. Bericht einer Fachperson) und deren anzunehmende Objektivität. Aus der Anzahl der gegebenen Risikofaktoren ergibt sich ein Risikowert.
Schlussfolgerungen: Das Kodiermanual schafft die Grundlage, um das Vorliegen von Risikofaktoren übereinstimmend einzuschätzen. Nach erfolgter Validierung kann das Verfahren perspektivisch zur Güte von Risikoeinschätzungen bezüglich Kindesmisshandlung und -vernachlässigung beitragen und die Qualität gutachterlicher Empfehlungen verbessern.

387. Freundschaften als Ressource zur Bewältigung übergangsspezifischer Anforderungen im Emerging Adulthood
Iris Enengl | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Iris Enengl | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria
Jana Badami | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria
Caroline Vavrik | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria

Hintergrund
Der Übergang zwischen Jugend- und Erwachsenenalter ist von Unsicherheiten und Veränderungen in sozialen, emotionalen, kognitiven und physischen Bereichen geprägt. Eine unzureichende Bewältigung dieser übergangsspezifischen Anforderungen kann mit einem erhöhten Risiko für psychische Belastungen einhergehen, während Freundschaften als soziale Ressource unterstützend wirken können. Vor diesem Hintergrund werden folgernd (1) wahrgenommene Veränderungen in Freundschaften sowie (2) das Unterstützungspotenzial durch Freundschaften im Übergang untersucht.

Methode
Die Stichprobe umfasste N=194 Personen im Alter von 18-29 Jahren (M= 22.32,SD=2.58). Mittels eines Onlinefragebogens wurden Angaben zu (1) wahrgenommenen Veränderungen von Freundschaften sowie (2) Unterstützungsformen durch Freundschaften in dieser Übergangsphase offen erhoben und inhaltsanalytisch ausgewertet. Ergänzend wurden zusätzliche Bereiche der wahrgenommenen Unterstützung durch Freundschaften in emotionalen Belangen sowie identitätsbezogenen Aspekten mittels spezifischer, theoriegestützter Items geschlossen erfasst (1=trifft gar nicht zu–4=trifft voll zu).

Ergebnisse
(1)Die Befragten beschrieben umfassende Veränderungen von Freundschaften, die sowohl strukturelle und lebenspraktische Aspekte als auch die Qualität und Intensität der Beziehungen betrafen.
(2)Gleichzeitig werden Freundschaften in dieser Übergangsphase als Ressource emotionaler Unterstützung und durch regelmäßigen Austausch erlebt. Sie helfen, positive Aspekte an Herausforderungen wahrzunehmen und zu akzeptieren, Probleme zu lösen und Emotionen offen zu besprechen. Zudem schrieben die Befragten Freundschaften eine hohe Unterstützung bei identitätsbezogenen Aspekten zu, hinsichtlich der Wertschätzung der eigenen Person (M=3.71,SD=.51), moralischen Überzeugungen (M=3.33,SD=.74), dem Erkennen eigener Stärken und Schwächen (M=3.18,SD=.71), dem Ausdruck der Geschlechtsidentität (M=3.07,SD=1.07), einem positiven Körperbild (M= 3.05,SD=.77) sowie einem differenzierteren Emotionsverständnis (M=3.03,SD=.85).

Konklusion
Auf Basis der Zusammenschau der Ergebnisse wird konkludierend die Bedeutung von Freundschaften als Unterstützung zur Bewältigung der übergangsspezifischen Herausforderungen und Identitätsentwicklung diskutiert.

388. Assessment der subjektiv wahrgenommenen Einflussstärke unterschiedlicher Entwicklungsbedingungen auf die individuelle Entwicklung
Caroline Vavrik | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Caroline Vavrik | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria
Iris Enengl | Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität Wien | Austria

Hintergrund:

Entwicklungsbedingungen und die Bewusstheit über deren Einfluss für das eigene entwicklungsbezogene Handeln sind insbesondere im jungen Erwachsenenalter von zentraler Bedeutung, da in dieser Lebensphase richtungsweisende Entscheidungen für den weiteren Lebensverlauf getroffen werden. Während etablierte Konstrukte wie Kontrollüberzeugung, Selbstwirksamkeit oder Attribution primär wahrgenommene Kontrolle oder ereignisbezogene Ursachenzuschreibungen erfassen, wurde bisher kaum untersucht, wie Personen den Einfluss verschiedener Entwicklungsbedingungen auf ihre Entwicklung einschätzen.

Der Operationalisierungsansatz stützt sich auf eine zweidimensionale Systematik, welche Entwicklungsbedingungen danach differenziert, (1) ob die Ursache in der Person oder in der Umwelt verortet wird (intern vs. extern) und (2) wie die Entwicklungsdynamik erlebt wird (gesteuert vs. kontingent).

Aus dem sich ergebenen Vier-Felder-Schema werden vier Entwicklungsbedingungen abgeleitet: autonomes (intern/gesteuert) und aleatorisches (intern/kontingent) Geschehen sowie Konditionierung (extern/kontingent) und Ressourcenallokation (extern/gesteuert).

Methode:

Die Untersuchung basiert auf einer Online-Befragung von N=105 Studierenden (18–29 Jahre). Zur Erfassung der zugeschriebenen entwicklungsbezogenen Einflussstärke durch unterschiedliche Entwicklungsbedingungen wurde ein eigens entwickeltes Instrument eingesetzt und mittels explorativer Faktorenanalyse (Hauptkomponentenanalyse mit Varimax-Rotation) sowie anschließender Reliabilitätsanalyse überprüft. Die identifizierten Faktoren repräsentieren jeweils eine Entwicklungsbedingung und deren zugeschriebene Einflussstärke.

Ergebnisse:

Im Rahmen der explorativen Faktorenanalyse konnten vier Faktoren (erklärte Gesamtvarianz=59,21%) extrahiert werden, welche jeweils eine Entwicklungsbedingung mit zugeschriebener Einflussstärke widerspiegeln: Autonomes Geschehen (14.52%,λ=.62-.82;α=.71,rtt=.44-.45), Aleatorisches Geschehen (17.32%,λ=.75-.85;α=.82,rtt=.59-.73), Konditionierung (14.89%,λ=.66-.76;α=.73,rtt=.49-.60) sowie Ressourcenallokation (12.4%,λ=.59-.75;α=.65,rtt=.36-.50).

Konklusion:

Die faktoren- sowie reliabilitätsanalytischen Ergebnisse stützen die inhaltliche Plausibilität der Faktoren empirisch. Die Faktorladungen sowie Itemtrennschärfen weisen durchwegs zufriedenstellende Werte auf. Die internen Konsistenzen sprechen anhand der überwiegend akzeptablen Cronbach-Alpha-Werte für die Reliabilität der Faktoren. Lediglich die moderate interne Konsistenz des Faktors „Ressourcenallokation“ verweist auf Anpassungsbedarf.

389. Is Everyone Above Average? A Meta-Analytical Investigation of Leniency Effects in Self- and Supervisory Performance Ratings
Nikou Ghorbani Vafa | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nikou Ghorbani Vafa | Germany
Prof. Dr. Klaus Moser
Katharina Ebner
Dragos Iliescu

Leniency effects are widely documented in school grades, university exams, employment certificates, and organizational performance ratings. While previous meta-analyses have demonstrated greater leniency in self-ratings compared to supervisory ratings, it remains unclear how frequently both rating sources exceed the scale midpoint. The present meta-analysis examines whether the above-average effect in organizations extends beyond self-ratings to supervisory evaluations.

We analyzed 187 independent samples published between 1974 and 2025 from studies conducted worldwide. To assess leniency across rating sources, performance ratings were transformed into Percent of Maximum Possible (POMP) scores and examined in relation to the theoretical scale midpoint. We further investigated potential moderators, including performance dimension (task vs. contextual), supervisory status, and characteristics of the performance scales.

Across all samples, both self- and supervisory ratings demonstrated leniency, with 100% of mean ratings exceeding the midpoint (POMP > 50). Self-ratings were significantly more lenient than supervisory ratings (Meanself = 71.9, SD = .78; Meansup = 68.7, SD = .91; t(208) = 5.19, p < .001). Leadership position and the number of scale items were associated with increased leniency, indicating that individuals in leadership roles provide more lenient self-ratings and that longer scales elicit higher ratings across sources.

These findings challenge the assumption that leniency is primarily a self-rating bias and suggest that above-average evaluations may represent a broader social norm in organizational contexts, with implications for performance measurement and appraisal systems.

390. Die Quellen der Selbstwirksamkeit - eine profilanalytische Betrachtung
Viktoria Sophie Egele | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Viktoria Sophie Egele | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Prof. Dr. Robin Stark | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany

Obwohl bekannt ist, dass Selbstwirksamkeitsüberzeugungen ein wichtiger Prädiktor für verschiedene Verhaltensweisen, darunter auch die physische Aktivität, sind, ist die Entstehung dieser Überzeugungen noch relativ unklar. Insbesondere fehlt eine ganzheitliche Betrachtung der verschiedenen Quellen der Selbstwirksamkeit, um festzustellen, inwiefern sich interindividuelle Unterschiede in den Konfigurationen dieser Quellen zeigen. Anhand von Daten von 324 Personen im Alter von 18–69 Jahren wurde mittels latenter Profilanalyse untersucht, inwiefern sich die Konfigurationen der Quellen der Selbstwirksamkeit unterscheiden. Die Analyse deutet auf fünf verschiedene Profile hin, die sich sowohl in ihrer Selbstwirksamkeit als auch in ihrer physischen Aktivität maßgeblich voneinander unterscheiden. Die Ergebnisse der Studie legen nahe, dass mehrere Profile von Selbstwirksamkeitsquellen mit positiven Ausprägungen von Selbstwirksamkeit und physischer Aktivität assoziiert sein können, während negative affektive Zustände sich besonders nachteilig auf die Selbstwirksamkeit und physische Aktivität auswirken. Die Befunde deuten darauf hin, dass ein personenzentrierter Interventionsansatz, der die Profile der Quellen der Selbstwirksamkeit einbezieht, zur Förderung der Selbstwirksamkeit vielversprechend sein könnte. Dabei bleibt jedoch zu klären, unter welchen Bedingungen ein ressourcenorientierter oder kompensatorischer Ansatz vorteilhafter wirkt.

391. Diversity in Job Advertisements: A Comprehensive Systematic Review of Quantitative Research
Wiebke Sebering | Universität Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Wiebke Sebering | Universität Kassel | Germany
Dr. Sven Kachel | Universität Kassel | Germany

Job advertisements are often the first contact between applicants and organizations and signal organizational values. Diversity-related cues shape applicants’ perceptions and evaluations. Research is extensive and requires integration. This review synthesizes quantitative research on the representation of diversity in job advertisements and its effects on applicants. Overall, 63 published and unpublished studies (Nparticipants = 814,555) were included. Across studies, various diversity dimensions, predominantly gender, and different types of cues, most frequently explicit structural statements, were investigated. Using reflexive thematic analysis, four clusters, each capturing different operationalizations of diversity cues were identified. Overall, diversity communication in job advertisements was associated with more favorable applicant outcomes, such as higher attraction and application intentions, but remains conceptually and empirically fragmented. Based on available evidence, this review provides recommendations for future research and practical implications for understanding the impact of diversity during recruitment.

Word count abstract: 139/150

392. Linking dream content to personality using natural language processing
Luca Alexander Naudszus | ETH Zürich  | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Luca Alexander Naudszus | ETH Zürich  | Switzerland
Dr. Tobias Altmann | Universität Duisburg-Essen
Prof. Dr. Marcus Roth | Universität Duisburg-Essen

Research has linked interindividual differences in dream content to personality traits for decades, but the analysis of dream content is typically constrained by the expensive and a priori specified nature of manual scoring. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for the analysis of dream reports at scale while improving reproducibility and comparability across studies. However, their use in the examination of personality remains largely unexplored.
In this project, we investigate whether NLP-based analyses of dream diaries can capture meaningful variation between and within individuals. 293 participants completed dream diaries, providing about 3,000 dream reports, as well as several personality questionnaires, including measures of the Big Five and narcissism. A subsample further completed ambulatory assessments of self-esteem and daily social experience. NLP methods, including LLMs, are used to extract continuous, interpretable features of dream content which are then related to traits and day-to-day fluctuations using multilevel modelling, allowing for separation of between- and within-person effects.
We describe which features of dream content are vary between and within individuals and report which personality traits and day-to-day fluctuations in self-esteem and social experiences can explain parts of this variation. The results are interpreted with respect to theories of dream content. Additionally, we evaluate the validity and limitations of NLP-based analyses in this domain by comparison to traditional content coding. If successful, the approach opens new avenues for studying interindividual differences in a central but methodologically challenging state of human consciousness.

393. Identity, Cognitive Sophistication, and Motivated Reasoning in Political Contexts
Lara Grohmann | University of Würzburg
Show details
Authors:
Lara Grohmann | University of Würzburg
PD Dr. Fabian Hutmacher | University of Würzburg
PD Dr. Regina Reichardt | University of Regensburg
Dr. Christoph Mengelkamp | University of Würzburg

Individuals’ reasoning is assumed to be often driven by the motivational goal to maintain a positive social identity and to protect the beliefs of one’s social group against challenging information. However, previous research results remain inconclusive as to how cognitive sophistication (often measured using the Cognitive Reflection Test) influences such motivated reasoning. The current research examines whether the effects of cognitive sophistication on the degree of motivated reasoning might be contingent on contexts in which identity protective cognitions are induced. In a first study, salience of identity was enhanced in a sample of US-Americans (N = 492) by randomly assigning them to either reflect on their political identity (experimental group) or on their group membership as a smartphone (non)user (control group) before judging pro and contra arguments concerning climate change threat. Results of multi-level analyses suggest that participants engaged in motivated reasoning. However, enhanced salience of individuals’ political identity neither influenced the degree of motivated reasoning nor the use participants made of their cognitive sophistication. To increase the strength of the manipulation, in a second study (planned sample N = 1000), identity will not merely be rendered salient but threatened by informing US participants that their personality and moral values profile shows low congruence with either their political ingroup (experimental group) or with other smartphone (non)users (control group) before they evaluate pro and contra arguments on illegal immigration. The complete results and the theoretical implications of the two preregistered studies will be presented and discussed.

395. Same Same But Different? Sustainability Implications of Compressed and Reduced-Hour Four-Day Workweek Models - A Comparative Analysis Based on a Narrative Systematic Literature Review
Virgilia Jansen-Preilowski | Leuphana Lüneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Virgilia Jansen-Preilowski | Leuphana Lüneburg | Germany
Islena Ferreira de Arauja | Leuphana Lüneburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Laura Venz | Leuphana Lüneburg | Germany

Despite increasing empirical attention to four-day workweek (4DWW) arrangements, the absence of a shared conceptual framework has resulted in fragmented evidence. Moreover, by examining outcomes in isolation rather than jointly, prior research has largely neglected trade-offs across outcomes domains, limiting conclusions about the broader implications of 4DWWs. To address these gaps, we conducted a systematic literature review comparing two distinct forms of 4DWWs - the compressed and the reduced-hours model - across social, economic, and environmental sustainability outcomes. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we integrate the findings to explain convergent effects and trade-offs across domains. Our review includes 27 peer-reviewed studies published between 1973 and 2025. The findings suggest that reduced-hours 4DWWs improve work-life balance and employee well-being, indicating gains in social sustainability, although some studies report higher work intensity. Compressed 4DWWs produce positive short-term effects but are more frequently related to higher fatigue and work-family conflict over time, particularly for employees with caregiving responsibilities; outcomes improve when participation is voluntary. Regarding economic sustainability, both reduced-hours and compressed 4DWWs yield largely comparable results, with stable or increased productivity. Environmental effects are mixed: reduced-hours 4DWWs link to increased travel and leisure activity, whereas compressed 4DWWs associate with reduction in mileage. Future research should examine under which conditions and for which employee groups reduced-hours and compressed 4DWWs yield positive versus negative effects, and should further investigate environmental outcomes. It should also adopt integrative designs that assess social, economic, and environmental outcomes jointly to capture potential trade-offs and long-term effects across stakeholders.

396. Gendered Evaluations of Leaders’ Relational Mistakes – Evidence from an Event Recall Experiment
Dr. Stefanie Krauth | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Stefanie Krauth | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Dr. Martin P. Fladerer | Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Management
Dr. Melissa M. Hehnen | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU)

In previous experimental research, we showed that female leaders are evaluated stricter than male leaders for identical relational mistakes. Theory suggests this arises from gendered expectations: Female leaders are expected to behave both agentic and communal, while male leaders are mainly expected to be agentic and may even benefit from behaving communal. Relational mistakes violate communal expectations, making gendered evaluations particularly likely.

Consistent with this reasoning, in two previous complementary experiments, we found stricter evaluations of female leaders for relational mistakes on all outcome measures assessed (i.e., willingness to follow, trust(worthiness), warmth, competence, leadership effectiveness). Building on these findings, we extend this line of research to a more ecologically valid ‘in vivo’ context. We hypothesize that female leaders will again be evaluated more strictly than male leaders for relational mistakes.

Using an event recall experiment, we will invite participants who experienced a leader mistake in the past two weeks. Participants will describe the incident, including their thoughts and feelings, and respond to outcomes (willingness to follow, trustworthiness and leadership effectiveness). Additional measures include perceived warmth and competence, willingness to go the extra mile, and internal vs. external attributions. Leader mistakes will later be coded as relational or task-oriented.

By translating our previous experimental findings into a real-world context, this study further advances the understanding of gender bias in leadership evaluations. This provides important insights for theory and informs organizational efforts to promote more equitable organizational practices.

398. Wie regulieren Kinder ihre Motivation? Validierung eines Fragebogens zur Motivationsregulation bei Viert- und Fünftklässler*innen
Annika Paulus | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annika Paulus | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Nena Kohl | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Dr. Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Prof. Dr. Franziska Perels | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Prof. Dr. Gisa Aschersleben | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany

Selbstreguliertes Lernen (SRL) gilt als fächerübergreifende Kompetenz (Wirth & Leutner, 2008) und zeigt positive Zusammenhänge mit Leistung und Wohlbefinden (Dent & Koenka, 2016; García-Ros et al., 2023). Ein bislang in der Kindheit wenig erforschter Teilbereich des SRL ist die Motivationsregulation (Trautner et al., 2025), also die bewusste Aufrechterhaltung der eigenen Lernmotivation (Schwinger et al., 2007; Wolters, 2003). Aufgrund eines häufig beobachteten Absinkens der Motivation bei schulischen Übergängen (Dörrenbächer-Ulrich et al., 2023) kommt der Fähigkeit zur Motivationsregulation eine besondere Bedeutung zu. Der Beitrag untersucht die psychometrischen Eigenschaften eines für Viert- und Fünftklässler*innen adaptierten Selbstberichtsinstruments zur Erfassung von Motivationsregulationsstrategien (MRS), das im Original für Studierende vorliegt (Schwinger et al., 2007). An N = 490 Kindern am Übergang von der Primar- zur Sekundarstufe wurden Reliabilität, Faktorstruktur, Messinvarianz, Konstrukt- und Kriteriumsvalidität untersucht. Sieben der acht Subskalen zeigten eine akzeptable bis gute interne Konsistenz (McDonald's Omega = .74-.90). Nach Entfernung der Skala “Steigerung der persönlichen Bedeutsamkeit” bestätigte eine konfirmatorische Faktorenanalyse eine 7-Faktor-Struktur. Skalare Messinvarianz wurde für Geschlecht und Klassenstufe nachgewiesen. Erwartungskonforme Korrelationsmuster mit akademischer Selbstwirksamkeit, selbstbestimmter Motivation, akademischem Belohnungsaufschub, Prokrastination sowie Schulnoten stützen die konvergente Konstrukt- und Kriteriumsvalidität. Die Skala “vermeidungszielorientierte Selbstinstruktion” hob sich als einzige maladaptive Strategie vorhersagekonform von den übrigen Skalen ab (Schwinger et al., 2009). Testangst zeigte erwartungsgemäße Korrelationsmuster und stützte die diskriminante Konstruktvalidität. Physisches Selbstkonzept als bereichsfremdes Konstrukt korrelierte jedoch höher mit MRS als erwartet. Die Ergebnisse sprechen für die Eignung des adaptierten Instruments bei Viert- und Fünftklässler*innen und liefern damit das erste validierte deutschsprachige MRS-Instrument für diese Altersgruppe.

394. From Ratings to Comparisons: Forced-Choice Approaches to Measuring Achievement Goals
Constantin Freiherr von Luttitz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Constantin Freiherr von Luttitz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Martin Daumiller | Universität Freiburg
Prof. Dr. Moritz Heene | LMU - Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich

Likert scales are the dominant tool for assessing psychological constructs such as achievement goals, but they have limitations, including susceptibility to response biases. Likert data are often treated as interval-level data, although in many—if not most—cases they are more appropriately considered ordinal. Without claiming that Likert scales are flawed per se, this work emphasizes the importance of developing and empirically evaluating alternative approaches and proposes forced-choice formats as a valuable addition to the measurement of achievement motivation and related cognitive processes.
Across two cross-sectional online surveys, we examined (a) whether forced-choice measures and Likert scales assess the same underlying latent variables and (b) the benefits and limitations of two forced-choice formats (pairwise comparisons vs. rankings). Study 1 (N = 152) measured achievement goals using the 12-item Achievement Goal Questionnaire (AGQ) Likert scale, a 4-item forced-choice ranking measure, and a 4-item forced-choice pairwise-comparison measure. The correlation between ranking and pairwise comparisons was small (r = .11), but should be interpreted cautiously because the forced-choice measures contained too few items to fit a Thurstonian IRT model. Study 2 (N = 130) administered the 12-item AGQ Likert scale and a forced-choice pairwise-comparison format comprising 16 items that yield 24 comparison pairs. Correlations between the Likert and forced-choice formats ranged from r = .38 to r = .68, suggesting partial overlap and potentially format-specific cognitive processes. We discuss methodological refinements strengthening forced-choice measures, argue for the pairwise-comparison over ranking format and outline research questions for which forced-choice formats may offer particular advantages.

397. Validierung einer Testbatterie zur Erfassung exekutiver Funktionen bei deutschsprachigen Kindergartenkindern
Dr. Bianca Ulitzka | Helmut-Schmidt Universität/Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg | Germany

Authors:
Dr. Bianca Ulitzka | Helmut-Schmidt Universität/Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg | Germany
Monika Daseking | Helmut-Schmidt Universität/Universität der Bundeswehr Hamburg
Susanne Enke | Universität Leipzig
