Prof. Dr. Petra Kemter-Hofmann | Germany
Dr. Tina Karabinski
Oscar Oregel-Mendoza

Women are underrepresented in the fields of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), particularly in executive positions. The FioKo project aims to identify factors influencing women’s career progression and to develop evidence-based strategies for achieving gender equity. The study focuses on optimizing support mechanisms to foster sustainable systemic change.
Methodologically, we employed a mixed-methods approach, comprising two quantitative online surveys (conducted from December 2024 to January 2025) and qualitative interviews (conducted from March to December 2024). These targeted STEM students at TU Dresden and professionally active women in STEM. Data collection assessed dispositional traits, including Core Self-Evaluations, professional self-efficacy, and leadership motivation (both “striving for” and “avoidance of” leadership). The analysis seeks to elucidate the development of leadership motivation and the factors influencing career decision-making across academic and professional contexts.
The poster will present and compare the results of qualitative interviews with STEM executives (n = 12) and executives in public service (n = 12). The findings are expected to reveal both differences and similarities in the obstacles and drivers encountered in these two sectors. These insights will be integrated into the design of targeted interventions, such as mentoring and coaching programs, tailored to distinct academic and professional phases.
In conclusion, the findings aim to establish best-practice models for promoting women in STEM, informing personnel development strategies that address their unique needs. The project thus contributes to structural gender equality and the advancement of sustainable career pathways for women in STEM.

429. Rater Meets Item: Applying Explanatory Item Response Theory for Polytomous Rater Data
Robin Bosse | Universität Hildesheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Robin Bosse | Universität Hildesheim | Germany
Prof. Paul Silvia | University of North Carolina at Greensboro | United States
Prof. Selina Weiss | Universität Hildesheim | Germany

Who gets the joke—and who laughs at what? Various areas of psychological research rely on human ratings of objects, phrases, or utterances, which has spurred substantial methodological work on how to model and evaluate rater-related biases and inconsistencies. Recent approaches embrace the use of rater-centric item response theory (IRT) to model the relationship between raters and items, which enables us to characterize rater behaviour using typical IRT parameters, such as leniency of raters. Yet, both rater attributes (e.g. personality traits) and item characteristics (e.g. semantic properties) can systematically influence ratings. Moreover, an interaction between rater characteristics and item characteristics is also plausible. Building on this, the current project aims to extend the rater-centric IRT approach by applying an explanatory IRT model to polytomous rater data, which includes person and item characteristics. We apply this analytical approach to an existing dataset in which N = 621 raters evaluated the funniness of 501 jokes. We included rater-level demographics, and item-level characteristics as explanatory variables according to a previous exploratory analysis. For rater-level variables we included parenthood, level of education, and importance of religion. Analysed item-level characteristics were whether the punchline was a question, concreteness of the joke, and similarity between joke setup and punchline. A significant interaction between level of education and concreteness, and between level of education and similarity on rating levels was found. Results illustrate the practical advantages of the applied methodology for analysing rater data and demonstrate how rater-item interactions can affect ratings.

430. Linking Immediate and Delayed Judgments of Learning to Latent Storage and Retrieval Processes
Franziska M. Leipold | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Franziska M. Leipold | Germany
Arndt Bröder
Jeffrey N. Rouder

Judgments of learning (JOLs) are a central tool in metamemory research and reflect individuals’ assessments of their future memory performance. A robust finding in this field is the delayed-JOL effect: JOLs provided after a short delay are substantially more accurate than those provided immediately after study. A prominent explanation for this effect is that delayed JOLs are more strongly based on information about target retrievability, whereas immediate JOLs rely more heavily on encoding-related cues. Despite its theoretical importance, empirical support for this account has largely been indirect and relies on associations between JOLs and observed recall performance or on differential sensitivity to experimental manipulations. The present study directly examines the latent memory processes underlying immediate and delayed JOLs using a model-based approach. Participants study cue–target word pairs and provide either immediate or delayed JOLs, followed first by a free and then cued recall test. Recall performance is analyzed using a multinomial processing tree (MPT) model that decomposes test performance into latent parameters reflecting associative storage and retrieval processes. Trial-level JOLs are linked to these latent parameters via probit regression, yielding participant-specific estimates of the extent to which JOLs covary with associative storage and retrieval. This approach allows a direct comparison of latent process associations of immediate and delayed JOLs, providing a stringent test of the hypothesis that delayed JOLs more strongly reflect retrieval-related processes. More broadly, the study illustrates how combining metamemory judgments with latent-variable modeling can advance theoretical understanding of the cognitive processes that enhance metamemory accuracy.

431. Zusammen im Klassenzimmer: Chancen und Hürden bei der Integration aus der Ukraine geflüchteter Kinder und Jugendlicher
Dr. Udo Käser | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Stella Wiechmann | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany
Leonie Senf | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany
Dr. Udo Käser | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany

Der Krieg in der Ukraine führte dazu, dass den geflohenen Kindern und Jugendlichen eine angemessene Beschulung ermöglichen musste. Für Polen untersuchten Pyżalski et al. (2022), wie Integration gelingen kann. Für Deutschland haben Boll et al. (2023) sowie Gambaro et al. (2025) analysiert, welche Strukturen und Angebote zur Integration vorliegen, welche Erfahrungen Geflüchtete gemacht haben und wie die Lebenssituation geflüchteter Kinder und Jugendlicher aussieht.

Vor diesem Hintergrund wurde für NRW eine teils quantitative, teils qualitative Untersuchung realisiert: In einer Fragebogenstudie wurden 188 Lehrkräfte (147 weiblich, 21 männlich, 1 divers, 19 o. A.) im Alter zwischen 23 und 69 Jahren (M = 47.0, SD = 9.8) befragt. 51.3% der Teilnehmer unterrichten an Grundschulen, 24.1% an Gymnasien, 12.8% an Gesamtschulen. Daten liegen für alle fünf Regierungsbezirke vor. Ergänzend wurden Interviews mit 12 Lehrkräften durchgeführt und inhaltsanalytisch ausgewertet.

Im Fragebogen wurden Erfahrungen mit behördlichen Regelungen, der Situation der ukrainischen und der deutschen Kinder sowie ihrer Eltern und den spezifischen Herausforderungen / Möglichkeiten für die pädagogische Arbeit im schulischen Alltag mittels 15 Skalen erfasst ( > .6, ri(t-i) > .3). In den Interviews fokussierten Leitfragen auf die Motivation für die Arbeit mit Flüchtlingskindern. Des Weiteren wurde die Wahrnehmung der neuen Situation durch die deutschen bzw. ukrainischen Kinder und Eltern aus Sicht der Lehrkräfte problematisiert sowie Maßnahmen zur Bewältigung der pädagogischen Aufgaben thematisiert.

Die Bewertungen unterscheiden sich in hohem Maße. Dabei spielen individuelle Vorerfahrungen wie die Teilnahme an Schulungen oder Sprachkenntnisse, aber auch Strukturmerkmale der Schulen eine große Rolle für die Einschätzungen der Lehrkräfte.

432. Priming a (financial) scarcity mindset impacts university students’ agentic decision-making
Jessica Schulz | Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jessica Schulz | Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Matthias Nückles | Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg

In this study, we examined whether priming a (financial) scarcity mindset, as opposed to an abundance mindset, influences argumentation patterns concerning possible courses of action in educational decisions.
Financial security allows individuals to think beyond money, while scarcity constrains perspectives in various domains, of which education is no exception. Although, the impact of financial barriers on academic success is well documented (Heine, 2012; Heublein et al., 2017; Lörz et al., 2015), the psychological consequences of financial scarcity are less understood.
Applying an interdisciplinary perspective, we examined key cognitive mechanisms proposed by behavioral economic scarcity theory. Specifically, we tested the heightened focus on scarce resources and immediate needs and the neglect of other relevant information (Mullainathan & Shafir, 2013), such as future academic outcomes in educational decision-making.
A total of 120 students from the University of Freiburg were randomly assigned to one of three comic-based priming conditions: financial scarcity, financial abundance, or a neutral control condition. Subsequently, they were asked to give peer advice in four educational decision-making scenarios.
Planned contrast analysis showed that students primed with a scarcity mindset “tunneled” on financial information, showing significantly more financial arguments and fewer interest/academic future arguments. In contrast, an abundance mindset led to more interest/academic future arguments. However, the control group displayed the highest use of such arguments.
Findings suggest significant psychological consequences of a scarcity mindset on academic decision-making, narrowing students' focus to financial needs and reducing attention to personal interests and future academic outcomes.

433. Improving Outcomes for Families in High-Conflict Separation: Evaluation of a Novel Counseling Approach in Hamburg, Germany
Dr. Annette Clüver | Medical School Hamburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Annette Clüver | Medical School Hamburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sonja Bröning | Medical School Hamburg | Germany

High-conflict (HC) separation and divorce is detrimental to children’s emotional and overall development. While most parents reach amicable child-centered custody and co-parenting arrangements over time, parental conflict becomes chronic in about 5-10% of separations. In Germany, as in many countries, this substantially impacts social and judicial resources, accounting for approximately 80% of the workload of youth welfare authorities, counseling services, and family courts. To date, interventions and counseling approaches for families in HC separation and divorce are not well-researched.
The current study evaluates a novel, highly directive and child-centered counseling approach for HC parents in separation in Hamburg, Germany (Pfister-Wiederkehr, 2021). Parents are court-ordered to participate in a series of up to 10 bi-weekly counseling sessions, guided by a tandem of counselors. Within a highly structured counseling framework, conflict is actively interrupted, contentious issues are addressed from a child-focused perspective, and parents are closely guided towards jointly developing pragmatic, child-appropriate solutions.
We evaluated parents’, counselors’ and family court-judges’ experiences throughout the course of counseling via questionnaires and semi-structured one-on-one interviews. Preliminary results indicate that parents and counselors appreciate the highly structured nature and child-centered focus of the approach. Results are mixed regarding conflict-resolution and parental cooperation: parents, counselors and judges report modest, if any progress. Small changes in parental communication and improvements in children’s everyday life appear attainable, substantial conflict-resolution remains rare. Key factors associated with the effectiveness of the approach are discussed.

Pfister-Wiederkehr, D. (2021). Hochstrittige Eltern: praxisbewährte Lösungsansätze radikal kindorientiert. BoD–Books on Demand.

434. Gender stereotypes in praise: When a child's gender affects the type of praise they receive
Dr. Anjulie Gleich | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Anjulie Gleich | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Rosa Maria Puca | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie

Children receive praise every day, but personal praise (“You're smart.”) can have negative effects on motivation and self-concept compared to process-related praise (“Your effort paid off.”).
Previous research shows that characteristics of the child, such as self-esteem, influence the type of praise received (Brummelman et al., 2014; Graf-König & Puca, 2024). However, findings on gender differences are inconsistent (Graf-König & Puca, 2024; Gunderson et al., 2013).
This study examines whether gender stereotypes held by the person giving praise moderate the influence of the child's gender on the type of praise given. Based on stereotypical attributions (girls: linguistic; boys: mathematical), it is expected that people with strong gender stereotypes will give boys more person praise and less process praise in mathematics than girls, while the opposite effect applies to German.
In an online vignette study, participants (convenience sample) praised fictional 10- to 13-year-old children with a good performance in German and math. Participants' gender stereotypes were then assessed using six items that reflect traditional ideas about differences in performance and ability between boys and girls in the areas of mathematics and language (Schuster et al., 2021). The gender of the children was varied between participants. Praise statements were coded using a coding scheme.
The results provide insight into the extent to which gender stereotypes differentially influence the provision of praise and give rise to stereotypical patterns of praise. They contribute to the understanding of social stereotype effects in educational interactions and offer avenues for more reflective praise practices.

435. How Validity Cues in Study Designs Shape Researchers’ Beliefs about Effects and Judgments of Design Adequacy
Patrick Smela | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Patrick Smela | Germany
Marc Jekel

Researchers do not always agree on the meaning of scientific findings and differ in their explanations why the validity of findings might be threatened. While public discussion has often emphasized the influence of statistical validity—such as sample size or statistical modelling—on the reliability of findings, other types of validity have received comparatively less attention in the research community. Beyond differences in the emphasis placed on validity types, a less well understood issue concerns how researchers use validity-related cues when interpreting findings. We adopted an experimental approach to examine which types of information in an article researchers use to draw conclusions from research findings. To that end, we invited psychological researchers to read a fictional but realistic study and its replication and to rate how well the research design was suited to investigate the target effects, as well as their belief in the effects before and after reading each study. In a between-subjects design, we manipulated the study designs to vary their quality across the four types of validity (statistical, internal, construct, and external) while keeping the reported results constant across all versions. Our results provide insight into which aspects of research design increase confidence in studies and their findings, and how researchers interpret results.

436. How Deep Do Brief Contact Interventions Reach? Effects of Extended and Imagined Contact in Middle Childhood
Dr. Hinna Wolf | University of Education Freiburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Hinna Wolf | University of Education Freiburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Josef Nerb | University of Education Freiburg | Germany

Intergroup contact robustly reduces prejudice (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006). Beyond direct interaction, indirect forms such as extended and even imagined contact have been shown to improve intergroup attitudes, with meta-analytic evidence indicating small to moderate effects for imagined contact (Miles & Crisp, 2014) and converging review evidence for other indirect forms (Vezzali et al., 2014). Recent reviews emphasize open questions regarding the psychological depth, generalizability, and contextual robustness of indirect contact effects under naturalistic school conditions (Tropp et al., 2022). Developmental research highlights that middle childhood is characterized by both heightened category salience and emerging moral reasoning, resulting in a dynamic phase in the development of intergroup attitudes (Raabe & Beelmann, 2011).
The present field study examined short extended and imagined contact interventions implemented in primary and lower secondary classrooms (N = 165). Students were assigned to extended contact (story-based), imagined contact (story plus guided reflection or postcard task), or control conditions. Outcomes assessed intergroup emotions, cognitive evaluations, self-efficacy, and behavioral intentions. Effects were limited in scope and not uniformly aligned with theoretical expectations. Unexpectedly, a small trend emerged indicating less positive behavioral intentions in the intervention groups relative to the control group. This finding suggests that brief indirect contact may not translate into behavioral readiness and could reflect increased salience or ambivalence rather than straightforward attitude improvement. Additional analyses examined underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions of the intervention effects.
The study contributes to ongoing discussions about the scope and limits of scalable contact interventions under ecologically valid school conditions.

437. Simulationsanalysen zu Extraktionsverfahren bei der explorativen Faktorenanalyse
Benedict Jung | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Benedict Jung | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Katrin Patrzek | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Aziz Omar | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany
Dr. Jörg Heine | Universität der Bundeswehr München (UniBW M) | Germany

Die explorative Faktorenanalyse (EFA) ist ein etabliertes Verfahren zur Bestimmung latenter Strukturen in psychologischen Daten. Fehlentscheidungen bei der Bestimmung der Faktorenzahl beeinträchtigen jedoch die Interpretierbarkeit und Replizierbarkeit von Ergebnissen. Trotz umfangreicher methodischer Forschung be- steht weiterhin kein Konsens darüber, welche Extraktionskriterien unter welchen Bedingungen verlässliche Entscheidungen ermöglichen (z.B. Iacobucci, Ruvio, Roman, Moon & Herr, 2022). Insbesondere einfache Heuristiken wie das das Kaiser-Guttman- Kriterium (K1; Kaiser, 1970) und der Scree-Test werden in der Praxis weiterhin häufig eingesetzt, während theoretisch fundiertere Verfahren wie die Parallelanalyse (PA; Glorfeld, 1995; Horn, 1965) oder der Tracy-Widom-Test (TWT; Tracy & Widom, 1996) seltener Anwendung finden. In der vorliegenden Simulationsstudie wird die Leistungsfähigkeit verschiedener Methoden zur Bestimmung von Extraktionskriterien (K1, Scree-Plot, PA, TWT) systematisch untersucht. Hierzu werden Korrelationsmatrizen auf Basis obliquer Faktormodelle generiert. Variiert werden die Anzahl der Variablen (p), die Anzahl wahrer Faktoren (k), der Stichprobenumfang (n) sowie die Stärke von Nebenladungen (l). Die Extraktionskriterien werden hinsichtlich ihrer Fähigkeit verglichen, die zugrunde liegende Faktorstruktur korrekt zu identifizieren. Erste Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass K1, PA und der Scree-Plot unter vielen Bedingungen eher zu einer ¨Überschätzung der Anzahl der Faktoren tendieren. Der Tracy-Widom-Test weist dagegen die höchste Übereinstimmung mit der wahren Dimensionalität auf. Dieser Befund lässt sich durch dessen theoretisch gute Fundierung in der Random-Matrix-Theory und dem Johnstone Theorem erklären, wonach die Eigenwertverteilung von Zufallskovarianzmatrizen approximativ der Tracy–Widom- Verteilung folgen (vgl. Johnstone, 2001). Insgesamt liefern die Befunde differenzierte Hinweise zur Auswahl geeigneter Extraktionsverfahren und leisten einen Beitrag zur methodischen Präzisierung der Faktorbestimmung in der EFA.

438. Forum4MICA - Online Discussion Forum on Research Data
Dr. Martina Baumann | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Martina Baumann | Germany

The constantly growing supply of reusable data sets in the social, behavioral, educational and economic sciences opens up a wide range of potential for empirical research. This expansion is also accompanied by an increasing need for information on the part of data users. A sound understanding of the highly complex data sets forms the basis for high-quality research. Accordingly, support and exchange with the scientific community is of central importance. The quality of advice plays a key role here, as do transparency, openness to discourse and reusability. The applicability of such a forum is not limited to the described sciences, but also suitable for other scientific disciplines, naturally adapted to the specific characteristics of each subject. Open exchange and findability of information are universal components of science.

Forum4MICA (https://forum.lifbi.de/) is a general information and discussion platform for questions relating to reusable data offerings and the handling of this data including the NEPS data. The implementation of a modern forum solution opens up new opportunities for exchange and networking that go beyond bilateral question-and-answer interactions. Simultaneously, the forum functions as a continuously growing knowledge archive in which contributions and discussion threads are openly and sustainably available. Forum4MICA is a low-threshold, well-structured service that supports the introduction to the use of data and the exchange of relevant expert knowledge. Since its launch in February 2023, 18 institutions have already agreed to actively participate in the forum and over 560 registered users have already registered and over 1200 posts have been made.

439. Associations between Momentary Working Memory Performance and Sleep Latency, Duration and Quality Among Older Couples
Beyza Sönmez-Orhan | University of Bonn | Germany
Show details
Author:
Beyza Sönmez-Orhan | University of Bonn | Germany

Higher sleep latency and lower sleep duration and quality can have short- and long-term consequences. While long-term consequences of sleep deprivation, problems in falling asleep and lower sleep quality, short-term consequences of these problems in daily life are still underexplored. The goal of the present study is to understand associations between sleep latency, duration and quality of the previous night and momentary working memory performance in the subsequent day on the within- and between-person level and across partners.
We used data from an experience sampling study (Socio-Economic Panel – Couple Dynamics Study) with 165 opposite-sex couples (Mage = 71.9 years; age range: 56 – 88 years). Participants reported their sleep latency, duration and quality every morning and performed a numerical working memory updating task six times a day for seven consecutive days. Daily positive and negative affect was also part of the daily questionnaires.
Our results showed no evidence for within-/between-person associations between previous nights’ sleep latency, duration and quality and momentary working memory performance in the next day. Sleep indicators of one partner do not seem to be related to momentary working memory performance of the other partner.
Contrary to our expectations, nightly sleep latency, duration and quality were neither related to momentary working memory performance the next day on the within- and between-person level, nor across partners. These findings suggest that day-to-day variations in sleep have less pronounced consequences on short-term fluctuations in cognitive functioning.

440. Why repeating information about the scientific consensus on climate change is not the same as believing it
Dr. Simone Sebben | Universität Zürich | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Simone Sebben | Universität Zürich | Switzerland
Dr. Luisa Liekefett | Universität Osnabrück
Prof. Dr. Johannes Ullrich | Universität Zürich
Prof. Dr. Jörg Gross | Universität Zürich

We show why an experimental procedure used in an influential line of psychological research on scientific consensus communication produces replicable results with large but ambiguous effects. In this procedure, participants are first informed about the scientific consensus on, for example, climate change (e.g., “97% of climate scientists agree that human-caused climate change is happening.”). Later, they are asked about the number they were just given (e.g., “What percentage of climate scientists agree that human-caused climate change is happening?”). The responses to this question then typically serve as a key outcome and are interpreted as revised beliefs or corrected misperceptions. However, from the perspective of a participant, this question can reasonably be interpreted as a prompt to repeat the information they just received, be it as an explicit test of attention or memory or as an implicit demand from the experimenter. Indeed, re-analyses of data based on this procedure revealed that many participants repeated the exact information they were given. We explain how the ambiguity in this procedure has likely led to substantially inflated effect size estimates and overly optimistic conclusions about scalable interventions designed to correct misperceptions about climate change, reduce climate denial, or motivate people to engage in climate action. We also present new data from an experiment (N = 2,414) that substantiates our central claim: repeating information is not the same as believing it.

441. Recovery from career shocks: Employment disruptions, economic stressors and the role of posttraumatic growth for employee well-being
Dr. Katharina Klug | Bremen University, Germany | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katharina Klug | Bremen University, Germany | Germany
Josephine Debus | Bremen University, Germany | Germany
Prof. Dr. Vera Hagemann | Bremen University, Germany

Employees who experience career shocks in the form of employment disruptions often experience heightened economic stress (i.e., job insecurity, financial stress) even long after the disruption, with negative consequences for their well-being. The mechanisms behind such “scarring effects” are yet unclear. We argue that effects of past experiences on current stress depend not only on what employees experience, but how successfully they cope with disruption. Drawing on stress theories and life course perspectives, we investigate relationships between past employment disruptions, current economic stressors and well-being. We test posttraumatic growth, reflecting a result of successful coping, as a moderator in these relationships. We analyze a diverse sample of 290 employees from different sectors, using five measurements about six weeks apart. Respondents retrospectively report employment disruptions during the pandemic, posttraumatic growth at the beginning of the survey (spring 2025), and job insecurity, financial stress and well-being at each time point. Multilevel models will be calculated to test our hypotheses that 1) past employment disruptions relate to current economic stress, 2) economic stress relates to lower well-being, in terms of differences between persons and changes within persons. We expect posttraumatic growth to buffer effects of employment disruptions on economic stress, and effects of economic stress on well-being. The study will contribute to the understanding of scarring effects of employment disruptions, as well as economic stress in the context of the life course. It will also highlight individual differences in how people cope with critical life events such employment disruptions.

442. Put your money where your merch is? Disadvantaged group members’ evaluations of symbolic vs. financial corporate allyship
Dr. Lea Hartwich | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lea Hartwich | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julia C. Becker | Universität Osnabrück, Institut für Psychologie

As it has become increasingly common for companies to declare themselves in solidarity with social movements and marginalized groups, backlash against instances of such corporate allyship that are judged to be hypocritical or performative has also been on the rise. Across three experimental studies in the contexts of Pride Month, Black History Month, and International Women’s Day (total N = 867), we investigate how members of marginalized groups evaluate corporate allyship campaigns. We find that when support is not merely symbolic but includes material contributions in the form of donations to community organizations, members of those communities view it more favorably. While there were some differences across samples, an internal meta-analysis shows significant effects on perceived motive, legitimacy, and effectiveness. If a corporation makes a financial contribution, it is seen to be less motivated by self-interest and more motivated by moral concerns and a genuine interest in social change. It is also considered a more legitimate ally, and its actions are judged more likely to actually contribute to change. We discuss these results in relation to the broader literature on allyship and its heterogenous motivations and impacts, as well as in light of the current political climate where companies are abandoning DEI initiatives and similar efforts under more hostile governments.

443. Flanker Interference: Evidence of differential impact for Letters and Pseudo-letters
Nikta Goudarzi | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nikta Goudarzi | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany
Laís Muntini | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau / Universidad Nebrija, Madrid | Germany
Dr. Omar Jubran | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany
Prof. Cees van Leeuwen | KU Leuven, Belgium | Belgium
Prof. Dr. Thomas Lachmann | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau | Germany

The processing of letters and pseudo-letters stimuli are key to the understanding of how visual context impacts attentional processes. By comparing these two stimulus types, the role of specialization in feature integration can be revealed as letters as highly specialized stimuli. The current study investigated the effect of surrounding flankers on reaction time (RT) and accuracy during a visual discrimination task using letters and pseudo-letters as targets stimuli.
By pressing keys in the keyboard, participants discriminated between targets (two letters and two pseudo-letters under three conditions: no flankers, congruent flankers, and incongruent flankers. The data collected was analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA.
The results showed a significant main effect of flankers for RT and an effect of congruency for accuracy. The presence of flankers increased RT compared to the no-flanker condition and decreased accuracy for pseudo-letters compared to the congruent flanker condition. Letters showed minimal slowing and no accuracy cost, while the flanker and congruency interference were stronger for pseudo-letters.
Our findings indicate that surrounding contextual information has a significant impact on letter and pseudo-letters processing under contextual interference and that this effect operates differently depending on stimulus type. The findings also support literature that emphasize the distinct processing of letters, expanding evidence on competitive interactions between relevant and irrelevant visual information.

444. MAGIE: Embedding Citizen Science in a Randomized Developmental Trial of Adapted Fairy Tales
Dr. Robin Klaus Segerer | University Library Zurich | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Robin Klaus Segerer | University Library Zurich | Switzerland
Dr. Leila Schächinger Tenés | University of Zurich,
Alice Spinnler | Schweizerische Märchengesellschaft
Dr. Meret Fehlmann | University of Zurich,

Fairy tales scaffold children’s language, social cognition, and emotional development. Yet a growing mismatch between traditional narrative scripts and contemporary developmental goals may limit their relevance. Classical tales often rely on rigid gender roles and violent conflict resolution, and robust randomized evidence on adapted versions is scarce. At the same time, Citizen Science—despite its potential to enhance ecological validity—has rarely been integrated into controlled developmental trials.

MAGIE (Magic Tales as Anchors for Growth in Children) addresses this gap through a three-level framework: (1) Narrative Input, comparing classical tales with culturally sensitive, gender-reflective, non-violent adaptations; (2) Psychological Processing, testing dialogic parent–child storytelling quality as a mediator of language growth and Theory of Mind; and (3) Contextual Framing, embedding structured Citizen Science workshops in which parents, educators, and librarians co-design stimuli and document implementation as co-investigators.

In a randomized waitlist-control design (target N = 90 families; children aged 4–8 years; data collection ongoing), families are assigned to adapted, classical, or waitlist conditions. Primary outcomes include adaptive standardized language and socio-cognitive measures, complemented by socio-emotional tasks and observational coding of storytelling interactions. Linear mixed-effects and mediation models test whether narrative condition influences developmental change via storytelling quality.

Preliminary workshop data indicate high acceptance and increased narrative elaboration in adapted conditions. Ongoing analyses examine whether these process differences translate into measurable gains. MAGIE demonstrates that Citizen Science can be embedded within a rigorous developmental trial to enhance ecological validity without sacrificing causal inference.

445. The Impact of Incidental Emotions on Hiring Recommendations in Job Interviews
Fabian Jendroska | Germany
Show details
Author:
Fabian Jendroska | Germany

Candidate evaluations in personnel selection are intended to be objective. Accordingly, many organizations provide recruiter training and education. Despite these efforts, some biases remain difficult to control because they operate outside conscious awareness. Incidental emotions shape decisions through carryover processes from unrelated prior circumstances. Following the Appraisal Tendency Framework (ATF) the impact of specific emotions derives from cognitive and motivational processes, influencing the content and depth of thought.
Based on the ATF, this study examines whether specific incidental emotions affect hiring recommendations within job interviews. ATF suggests that emotions associated with the appraisal of certainty (e.g., happiness, anger) foster more heuristic processing, increasing the likelihood that emotion, acting as information, will be included in candidate evaluation. Consistent with prior research, the incidental emotion of happiness is hypothesized to lead to higher hiring recommendations than anger. Sadness, in contrast, is linked to uncertainty and more systematic processing. Accordingly, sadness is also hypothesized to lead to higher hiring recommendations than anger, although both emotions originate from negative valence.
Conducted on an online survey platform, the study induces emotions through a memory-recall writing task and verifies them with a state-affect measure. Participants then watch the same job interview video. Outcomes include hiring recommendations, attitudes toward the candidate, perceived employability, and control variables.
This study aims to provide initial data on the presence of incidental emotions in the process of job interviews. Results could potentially increase awareness of subconscious biases and inform future research.

446. A Decade of Multiverse Analyses in Industrial and Organizational Psychology? A Systematic Review
Jens Mazei | TU Dortmund | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jens Mazei | TU Dortmund | Germany
Joachim Hüffmeier | TU Dortmund

A multiverse analysis is a method to examine, systematically, how findings are shaped by the selection of alternatives for collecting, preparing, and analyzing data. As such, multiverse analyses give crucial insight into the reproducibility (and, to a lesser extent, replicability) of findings. Although Steegen et al. introduced psychologists to the method already in 2016, it seems underappreciated in Industrial and Organizational Psychology (IOP). This is problematic, as this field is not exempt from failed reproducibility or replicability attempts. Hence, we examined to what extent researchers from IOP make use of multiverse analysis, for what purposes they use this method, and what the existing multiverse analyses reveal about this field’s findings. By conducting a forward search in the Web of Science based on seminal articles introducing the method, as of today, we were able to identify only 27 articles from the field of IOP that included a multiverse analysis. The first one appeared no sooner than in 2021. Moreover, researchers typically did not plan their studies with the aim of conducting a multiverse analysis. Rather, researchers typically used multiverse analysis as a brief robustness check, and it played only a minor role in the corresponding articles. As such, researchers in IOP clearly do not reap the full potential of multiverse analysis. And as a consequence, the field knows only little about how its findings are shaped by the selection of alternatives for collecting, preparing, and analyzing data.

The power of political speech: From persuasion to action ( Keynote Stephen Lewandowsky)
Room: Plenary 1
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

Democracy is in retreat around the world. Even countries that were long considered exemplary democracies are not immune against autocratization. Here we apply the lens of large-scale computational linguistic analysis to illustrate and understand those trends. Language is crucial to democracy: it permits negotiation of power relations; it is used to compete on the “marketplace of ideas” to inform government policy. But language is also the tool of demagogues and autocrats to control the populace and suppress dissent. How does discourse in a democracy differ from the rhetoric of autocrats? Can we anticipate the decline of a democracy by analyzing its political discourse? We present several strands of research that illustrate how language mirrors the health of a democracy and how it can also be used to subvert democracy. We first show that the tacit conceptions of truth and honesty that are embodied in political speech are strong predictors of political performance and societal welfare. An analysis of U.S. Congressional speeches reveals that since the mid-1970s, rhetoric has shifted from being evidence-based to being intuition-based –that is, instead of appealing to data and facts, politicians have increasingly appealed to feelings and hunches when making political arguments. This shift has been accompanied by increasing societal inequality, decreased congressional productivity, and increased polarization. We next show that political speech can be linked to violence in several ways. For example, we show that the language of political manifestos can be used to predict whether a particular manifesto gave rise to political violence, and we show that a model trained on reddit comments that have been identified as being manipulative can also predict real-world violence arising from manifestos.

Cultural-Clinical Psychology: From “Mental Disorders” to Looping Disorders? (Keynote Andrew Ryder)
Room: Room C
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

Over the past half-century, research has revealed striking cultural variation in how mental disorders are experienced and expressed. Cultural-clinical psychology offers a way to explain this variation rather than simply treating it as added complexity. I will argue that culturally shared models and expectations can become woven into feedback loops linking experience with social responses and bodily processes, thereby helping to shape symptoms themselves. Drawing on my own research and related programmes across psychology, I will trace this argument from cross-cultural studies of somatization through recent work measuring cultural consensus, before turning to experimental research on symptom generation and placebo/nocebo effects. Together, these literatures suggest that cultural variation is complex but potentially tractable at the level of mechanism. I will conclude by considering how such loops might be identified in individual patients and redirected in treatment, and by outlining a research agenda for cultural-clinical psychology.

The Psychology of Outliers: Can Exceptional Data Tell the Most Interesting Stories? (Keynote Christophe Ley)
Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

Outliers occupy a unique position in psychological research. They are often viewed as inconvenient observations to be removed, yet they can also reveal measurement errors, unexpected mechanisms, or genuinely exceptional individuals whose experiences challenge established theories. The key question is therefore not whether outliers exist, but what they are trying to tell us.
In this keynote, we revisit the challenge of detecting outliers through the lens of modern statistical methodology. We discuss the principles behind robust outlier detection, introduce a new method for identifying atypical observations, and argue that detecting outliers is only the beginning. The ultimate goal is to distinguish between error, random, and genuinely interesting outliers, enabling researchers to make more informed decisions about the exceptional observations in their data.

Zwischen Krieg und Frieden: Die Rolle der Psychologie in einer Welt im Umbruch. Paneldiskussion mit Impulsvorträgen zu Kriegsgefahr, Resilienz und gesellschaftlichem Zusammenhalt
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Eva-Lotta Brakemeier (Universität Greifswald)
Co-chair(s) Sarah Stapel (Universität Greifswald)
Chair(s) Major Janina Klima (Bundeswehr)
Prof. Dr. Karl-Heinz Renner (University of the Bundeswehr Munich, Germany)
Dr. Malte Petersen (Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung)
Dr. Matthias F.J. Sperl (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs))
Room: Plenary 1
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Krieg ist nach Europa zurückgekehrt, geopolitische Spannungen und militärische Bedrohungen nehmen zu. Zugleich verändern hybride Kriegsführung, Cyberangriffe und gezielte Desinformation die Grenzen zwischen Krieg und Frieden. Diese Entwicklungen wirken weit über unmittelbar betroffene Regionen hinaus: Sie erzeugen Unsicherheit und Bedrohungserleben, stellen Gesellschaften vor neue Anforderungen und können Vertrauen, demokratischen Zusammenhalt und psychische Gesundheit beeinträchtigen. Welche Rolle kann und sollte die Psychologie angesichts dieser neuen sicherheitspolitischen Realität übernehmen?
Zwei Impulsvorträge eröffnen unterschiedliche Perspektiven auf die psychologische Dimension von Krieg und Kriegsgefahr: von den psychischen Folgen von Bedrohung, Krieg und Gewalt über individuelle und gesellschaftliche Resilienz bis zu den besonderen psychologischen Anforderungen militärischer und sicherheitsrelevanter Arbeitsfelder. Dabei geht es auch um die Frage, wie sich hybride Bedrohungen und Informationskriegsführung auf Wahrnehmung, Vertrauen, Entscheidungsverhalten und gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt auswirken.
Im Mittelpunkt der anschließenden Diskussion steht die Frage, was Psychologie und Politik gemeinsam zu einer Gesellschaft beitragen können, die mit wachsender Kriegsgefahr umgehen und zugleich ihre psychische Widerstandskraft, ihren gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt und ihre demokratischen Werte bewahren muss. Welche psychologischen Erkenntnisse können politische Entscheidungen und gesellschaftliche Vorbereitung unterstützen? Was braucht Politik von der psychologischen Wissenschaft, um unter Bedingungen von Unsicherheit und Bedrohung verantwortungsvoll handeln zu können? Wie können Menschen und Institutionen gestärkt werden, ohne gesellschaftliche Resilienz auf individuelle Anpassungsfähigkeit zu reduzieren? Und welche Verantwortung, aber auch welche Grenzen hat die Psychologie in diesem Kontext?
Eine besondere Rolle spielt dabei die Perspektive der jungen Generation: Wie erleben junge Menschen eine Gegenwart, in der Krieg und militärische Bedrohung in Europa wieder Teil ihrer Lebensrealität und Zukunftsplanung geworden sind? Was bedeuten diese Entwicklungen für ihr Sicherheitsgefühl, ihre Zuversicht und ihr Vertrauen in demokratische Institutionen? Und welche Erwartungen richten junge Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler an Psychologie und Politik, wenn es darum geht, Frieden, Resilienz und gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt langfristig zu stärken?

Die Erstellung von psychologischen Gutachten stellt einen wichtigen Bestandteil unseres Berufsfeldes dar und ist in Form der Forensischen Psychologie eines der ältesten Anwendungsfächer der akademischen Psychologie. Psychologische Gutachten haben eine ausgesprochen hohe Bedeutung, sowohl für die zu begutachtenden Personen wie auch für die damit im Zusammenhang stehenden gesellschaftspolitischen Diskurse. Fragen des Kindeswohls, der strafrechtlichen Schuldfähigkeit und Kriminalprognose oder der Glaubhaftigkeit von Aussagen sind für die unmittelbar betroffenen Personen von essenziellem Gewicht, da die daraus resultierenden Konsequenzen entscheidend die aktuellen und zukünftigen Lebensperspektiven und -weisen prägen können. In dieser Paneldiskussion möchten wir mit ausgewählten Expertinnen und Experten die aktuellen Herausforderungen und Perspektiven dieses wichtigen psychologischen Aufgabengebiets reflektieren und diskutieren. Neben aktuellen methodischen Diskussionen (z. B. wie viel Standardisierung benötigt die psychologische Begutachtungstätigkeit und wie lassen sich Freiheitsgrade reduzieren) möchten wir uns mit Maßnahmen der Qualitätssicherung und -entwicklung (z. B. hinsichtlich der vor einigen Jahren kritisierten mangelnden Qualität familienrechtspsychologischer Gutachten) sowie den berufspolitischen und ausbildungsbezogenen Fragen (z. B. wie viel forensisch relevantes Wissen benötigt die universitäre Psychologieausbildung und wie ist der aktuelle Stand und die Perspektiven der postgradualen föderativen Weiterbildung zur Fachpsychologin bzw. zum Fachpsychologen für Rechtspsychologie [DGPs/BDP]) beschäftigen. Die Ziele dieser Paneldiskussion bestehen zum einen darin, offene Forschungsfragen und methodische Kontroversen zu benennen, und zum anderen die Perspektiven dieses herausfordernden wie spannenden Berufsfeldes für interessierte Nachwuchswissenschaftlerinnen und -wissenschaftler zu beschreiben. Die Moderation der Paneldiskussion erfolgt durch den Sprecher und die stellv. Sprecherin der Fachgruppe Rechtspsychologie (FG RP): Prof. Dr. Martin Rettenberger (Kriminologische Zentralstelle [KrimZ], Wiesbaden, und Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz [JGU]) und Prof. Dr. Judith Iffland (Medical School Hamburg [MSH)].

Constructively handling power in academia is challenging, yet—like other management skills—learnable. In recent years, the use and abuse of power, as well as scientific misconduct, have been the subject of intense and controversial debate at various levels of higher education policy. Initial changes are becoming visible both within academic institutions and in legislation. In our analysis (Bössel et al., 2023), we examined a range of causes underlying power abuse. These causes are quite complex, and effective prevention and intervention strategies must be equally multidimensional to achieve sustainable change.Our current focus is on exploring to what extent a lack of training and expertise among academics in their roles as teachers, supervisors, or administrators contributes to abusive behaviour—and how this gap might also serve as a potential leverage point for improvement. While academic qualification pathways naturally emphasize scientific excellence, systematic training in the complementary skills required for becoming a professor is often missing. Such training is sometimes considered unnecessary or even a waste of time. However, we are convinced that it can play an important role in driving systemic improvement. Following a brief introduction to general workshop concepts designed for various target groups—such as early career researchers, professors, and individuals in functional roles (e.g., appointment committees, deans, rectors)—the panel discussion will address the following questions: Do we need systematic leadership training? What should it look like? And if made obligatory, could it be effective—or would it merely add to existing burdens?

Reading research increasingly requires large-scale, high-quality data to test and refine models of visual word recognition. However, progress in the field has been constrained by lab- and language-specific methodological choices and resources, thus resulting in limited comparability across studies. We argue that addressing these challenges requires consensus-driven standards and coordinated data collection efforts that extend beyond individual laboratories. The TRUST network aims to provide a transparent, transferable, and sustainable foundation for psycholinguistic reading studies in German by developing consensus-based guidelines for best practices in lexical decision experiments. To operationalize these guidelines, the German Lexicon Project (GLP) was initiated to coordinate large-scale, multi-lab data collection across more than twenty research sites across the German-speaking regions of Europe. As of this submission, one-third of the data collection has been finalized. When complete, the resulting open dataset will contain behavioral data from over a thousand participants, providing a robust resource to address fundamental questions about lexical, orthographic, phonological, and semantic processing in German. In this position paper, we present the TRUST guidelines, report initial findings from the GLP, and demonstrate how these shared resources can be useful both for researchers focusing on German word processing and for those who are simply using German words as experimental stimuli. Beyond introducing two valuable empirical resources, we argue that the TRUST guidelines and the GLP exemplify how consensus-based, collaborative infrastructures can enhance reproducibility, comparability, and transparency in psychological research and serve as a model for future large-scale initiatives in the field.

If we conceived of the constructs and concepts studied in psychology as a map, we would find that it is fragmentary and directions are hard to come by. Fragmentation has worsened, not decreased, as our field has grown. Partly, this happens because we have too many reverse Columbuses, who, in search of prestige, set out to find a new continent, but just end up renaming India. But partly, we face a real, solvable search problem when trying to connect our fuzzy constructs and flexible measures. Amidst tens of thousands of measures and hundreds of thousands of items, it can be harder to find prior work than to create a new construct. Semantic similarity and, more recently, large language models can help us put the fragments together by connecting measures and constructs by predicting empirical correlations in psychometric space. What will a defragmented map of psychological constructs reveal? Though this map is far from completion, I will argue that, based on genome-wide association studies of personality, we should not expect a simple structure of individual differences, but myriad dimensions. Faced with this complexity, coordination tools and precise communication become even more essential. We should aspire to common standards, fewer jingle-jangle fallacies, and a more cumulative psychological science.

Though results suggest an influence of public value on flow rather than the reverse, causality should not be overly inferred due to the study's correlational design. On a practical level, the results suggest that organizations in the administrative sector should actively emphasize their contribution to the common good in order to promote the commitment, self-efficacy and flow experience of their employees. On a theoretical level, the study contributes to bridging the gap between macro (at the level of societies and organizations) and micro (at the level of the individual) perspectives in research on the public value contribution of organizations and well-being in the work context and opens up approaches to investigate further outcomes and mediating processes.

Prior research on networking has predominantly focused on dispositional antecedents, such as personality, leaving situational determinants understudied. One important situational determinant may be individuals’ position in the organizational hierarchy and, therefore, power. Power is a defining feature of interpersonal relationships at work and shapes individuals’ control over resources and freedom from constraints. Although one might expect low-power individuals to engage more strongly in networking to compensate for resource deficits, we draw upon Situated Focus Theory of Power to suggest the opposite: Power promotes selective attention to goal-relevant information, and, therefore, a more instrumental focus on networking. Accordingly, we predicted that individuals with high (vs. low) power would engage in more goal-directed, instrumental networking. We tested this prediction in an experimental study (N = 206) using a simulated job fair. Social power was manipulated via an established role-based procedure. Participants then chose between networking opportunities that varied in their relevance for achieving professional goals. Results showed that participants assigned to high-power roles engaged in more goal-directed networking than those assigned to low-power roles. Specifically, high-power participants were more likely to select networking contacts that directly supported their professional aims. By providing causal evidence that social power facilitates instrumental networking, this study highlights power as a key situational predictor of how professional relationships are formed.

However, research so far has largely focused either on traditional networking or on PNS, and therefore, the question of how they compare remains unanswered.
We adopt a resource-based framework to delve deeper into the effectiveness of traditional versus PNS networking channels. Building on Hobfoll et al.’s (2018 ) principle that people must invest resources to gain resources, we hypothesize that self-efficacy, as a key resource, predicts investments in networking channels that, in turn, result in the acquisition of networking benefits. Building on theories of resource classifications (Foa & Foa, 1977 ), we also predict that benefit availability may differ between channels. In a two-wave survey of N = 1060 employed individuals, we use structural equation modeling to test our hypotheses. Findings show that investments in PNS are more effective for market-based or universalistic resources, such as job search or business assistance, whereas traditional networking is more effective for particularistic resources, such as social support. Our study emphasizes a strategic element in choosing networking channels and allows us to derive recommendations on when and whether people should invest in PNS or “traditional” channels to reap networking benefits.

Besides these potentially negative ethical effects harming others (e.g., clients), we argue, based on COR-Theory and research linking Machiavellianism with heightened job strain, that Machiavellianism will also foster emotional exhaustion. Furthermore, we suggest that explicit power motive tendencies amplify the positive relationship between perceived neoliberalism and Machiavellianism, as power-oriented employees might be particularly sensitive to social cues embedded in neoliberal environments (i.e., competition, individual success). To test our hypotheses, data was acquired via a longitudinal study in the UK (N = 392). Based on Latent Moderated Structural Equation Modelling we found support for our hypotheses: perceived neoliberalism predicted Machiavellianism and this effect was amplified as a function of power motive. Additionally, Machiavellianism mediated the effect of perceived neoliberalism on both outcomes. Notably, the indirect effect of perceived neoliberalism was nonsignificant at low levels of the power motive, but significant at medium and high levels. Thus, our study provides initial insights that perceived neoliberal beliefs foster Machiavellian tendencies, particularly among individuals with a stronger power motive. Content analysis of open responses identified five types of perceived restrictions, most commonly lack of funding and organizational barriers. Restrictions on research conduct and communication were often experienced as intertwined. Many participants directly linked such restrictions with demotivating effects, but a few also described motivational reappraisal or adaptive coping. Taken together, findings highlight perceived academic freedom as a meaningful psychological construct—with direct implications for researchers’ epistemic agency, motivation, and well-being.

Multiple ecological crises present significant health threats to humans and require behaviour change that offers co-benefits for human health and environmental sustainability. Such a behaviour is the consumption of whole grain products, which has significant health benefits and relieves the food industry’s strain on the environment. Providing information on benefits of a behaviour has shown to be effective in promoting behaviour change in both the health and environmental context, but research on the mechanisms and effectiveness is inconclusive. Specifically, it is unclear whether framing information (health vs. environmental benefits) differs in its effectiveness and whether this depends on individual cognitive or affective differences. To gain a better understanding of the effectiveness of information framing and its underlying mechanisms in the context of increasing whole grain consumption, we conducted a RCT with a convenience sample of 125 individuals. Two intervention groups received an information framing (health or environmental benefits), an active control group received neutral facts on whole grain products. In a three-week EMA study, we assessed daily intention and behaviour as well as self-efficacy and risk perceptions. After a one-week baseline phase, participants received daily messages (health vs. environmental benefits vs. neutral facts). The analyses showed that intentions and self-efficacy increased in the health information group only, while no change in behaviours was observed. Moreover, health risk perceptions increased in all groups, whereas environmental risk perceptions only increased in the environmental information group. These findings contribute to the growing research on behaviour change interventions addressing co-benefits for health and sustainability.

In this context, the perception of time plays an important role. All constructs were measured with established scales. Support for sufficiency policies is measured with informative policy descriptions covering the areas of energy, housing, and mobility. Based on determination of sample size with power analysis, N = 123 participants answered an online survey. Regression and correlational analyses were employed to examine the hypotheses. Future orientation showed a positive effect on sufficiency behavior, support for sufficiency policies, and political sustainability engagement, but decreased well-being. This study seeks to provide insights into temporal structures that are beneficial to both individual well-being and the environment. While interventions aimed at enhancing individuals' perceptions of time wealth, could improve well-being, promoting future orientation holds strong potential to foster sustainability efforts.

Maxim Trenkenschuh | Universität Zürich | Switzerland
Show details
Author:
Maxim Trenkenschuh | Universität Zürich | Switzerland

Meat consumption has wide-ranging consequences for environmental sustainability, individual health, and social justice. Growing awareness of negative consequences of eating meat frequently clashes with motivations to consume it, yet the motivational roots of meat-related ambivalence remain poorly understood.

We used Response Surface Models to examine how simultaneously endorsing different motivations for and against eating animals predicts meat-related ambivalence in two samples (Switzerland: N₁ = 4,447; UK: N₂ = 1,028).

Ambivalence peaked when individuals strongly endorsed conflicting motivations, with especially pronounced effects among omnivores. For omnivores, motivations favoring vegetarian diets were primary drivers of conflict, whereas for vegetarians and vegans, motivations supporting meat consumption predicted ambivalence. Distinct motivational pairings—such as valuing taste while worrying about environmental harm—were associated with specific forms of ambivalence. We developed an interactive tool to visualize motivational conflict patterns.

Ambivalence about eating animals is widespread and shaped by identifiable, conflicting motivations. These findings suggest that most people are ambivalent about eating meat, particularly omnivores, and points to the potential to leverage ambivalence for meat reduction.

Human Cognition and Emotion in the Face of Digital and Robotic Interfaces: A Lifespan Perspective
Dr. Thorsten Kolling | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Thorsten Kolling | Germany

Digital interfaces and robotic systems fundamentally change cognitive and emotional processes across the lifespan. From early childhood interactions with a variety of touchscreen devices to the use of digital assistive health technologies in ageing (e.g., exergames, smart home technologies, assistive and emotional robots), technology increasingly mediates individual cognitions, emotions and social interactions.

Hence, this paper adopts a lifespan perspective to analyze the dynamic interplay of cognition and emotion and technologically mediated environments. Against the background of major lifespan theories of development (e.g., ecological gerontology, selective optimization with compensation, socioemotional selectivity) the paper synthesizes research in developmental psychology, cognitive science and human-computer interaction research.

It thereby explores how digital interfaces, artificial intelligence and robotic interfaces influence memory, problem-solving and social cognition at different developmental stages. Additionally, effects of technologically mediated environments on human-technology attachment, empathy towards artificial agents, trust in automated systems, overreliance and emotional displacement are discussed.

In view of these general effects of technology in cognition and emotion, an individual differences approach on person-technology fit is presented in that influences of major individual predictors of technology acceptance and use (e.g., technology affinity, technology anxiety) are summarized. Finally, ethical challenges are discussed.

The paper ends with a proposal on how lifespan psychological theories and findings feed into technology design considerations developing age-sensitive, inclusive and sustainable digital and robotic environments.

Prof. Dr. Markus Appel
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Markus Appel

Generative artificial intelligence is widely used to create texts and pictures of different kinds, including fiction. At the same time, virtual reality is more popular than ever, and advanced virtual reality technology can create the illusion of body ownership (i.e., the illusion that a virtual body belongs to the user). In this talk I will outline how these two technological developments may change how recipients experience fiction with implications beyond narrative psychology.
Our own research showed that recipients experience less narrative transportation when they are made to believe that a short fictional story was written by AI (as compared to a human author), an effect that was smaller for science fiction stories than for stories set in the here and now. Likewise, the aesthetic appreciation of visual art was lower when these were ascribed to AI artists (as compared to human artists). When comparing fictional short stories generated by AI to stories created by non-professional authors (i.e., students), we found that readers of AI stories experienced less narrative transportation which we attributed statistically to AI stories containing fewer personal pronouns.
A second technological development with potentially important implications to the experience of stories is virtual reality. More specifically, high-end virtual reality technology may lead to the illusion that the body of the avatar moved in first person in a virtual world is actually one’s own body (body ownership). In an ongoing project we examine body ownership and downstream effects on attitudes and inter-group contact in narrative virtual worlds.

Scham in der Supervision
Matthias Heitmann | Clementine Kinderhospital
Show details
Authors:
Matthias Heitmann | Clementine Kinderhospital
Erik Grützner | DIPF I Leibniz-Institut für Bildungsforschung und Bildungsinformation

Die Scham ist eine der herausforderndsten Emotionen, die im psychotherapeutischen Prozess auftreten kann. Aufgrund ihres ansteckenden Charakters ist es häufig zu beobachten, dass sich der
Schamaffekt von der Therapiesitzung in die Supervision überträgt und hier in der Beziehung zwischen Supervisor*in und Supervisand*in spürbar wird. Diese Spürbarkeit sowie der interpersonelle Charakter der Schamals möglicher Schnittstellenaffekt bieten allerdings auch die Möglichkeit der Bearbeitung in der Supervision.

Ausgehend von dem Verständnis, dass Supervision der psychotherapeutischen und persönlichen Entwicklung der Supervisand*innen dient und die Arbeit insbesondere an Übertragungsphänomenen geschieht, wird dabei eine supervisorische Haltung zugrunde gelegt, die entgegen klassischen hierarchischen Vorstellungen nicht als statische Position, sondern als dynamischer Aushandlungsprozess verstanden wird. Dieser erfordert ein kontinuierliches Abwägen von Nähe und Distanz, Unter- und Überlegenheit sowie unterschiedlichen Haltungsformen und verdichtet sich im Affekt der Scham in besonderer Weise.

Vor dem Hintergrund der bislang begrenzten Forschungslage zur supervisorischen Haltung diskutiert der Vortrag die Frage, welche Einflüsse und Auswirkungen Scham und Beschämtwerden in der Supervision haben und wie mit ihnen umgegangen werden kann. Hierzu wird Scham ausgehend von etablierten Schamtheorien als psychodynamisches Konstrukt definiert, nach ihren verschiedenen Formen und Inhalten unterschieden und ihre Funktion sowie die Abwehr des Schamaffekts diskutiert. Abschließend werden die Konsequenzen für den Supervisionsprozess sowie Möglichkeiten der Schambearbeitung elaboriert. Dies geschieht anhand von Fallvignetten, die sowohl erfolgreiche als auch gescheiterte Schambearbeitungen in der Supervision darstellen und zentrale Fallstricke sowie mögliche Bearbeitungsansätze veranschaulichen.

Two key facets are attention to emotion, the degree to which individuals attend to their emotional experiences, and emotional clarity, the ability to identify and label one’s emotions. Prior research suggests that emotion intensity is dynamically linked to both facets of emotional awareness, with potential non-linear associations. However, evidence from daily life is limited. This ambulatory assessment study examined the interplay between emotion intensity, momentary attention to emotion, momentary emotional clarity, and emotion regulation effort in everyday life, focusing on negative emotions. We conducted a 3-week ambulatory assessment with four prompts per day (N = 467 participants from the general population; 5,643 measurement occasions). Multilevel models revealed J-shaped associations between negative emotion intensity and both momentary clarity of negative emotions and attention to negative emotion. Unexpectedly, momentary attention to negative emotion and momentary clarity of negative emotions were not linearly related, but showed a U-shaped association, with lowest clarity at medium levels of attention. Further analyses showed no association between momentary clarity of negative emotions and subsequent changes in attention to negative emotion, and no moderation by negative emotion intensity. Momentary clarity of negative emotions was also unrelated to emotion regulation effort, but was positively associated with perceived emotion regulation effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of considering non-linear associations between emotion-related constructs in daily life.

Hintergrund: Viele Studierende stehen vor der Herausforderung Studium, Erwerbstätigkeit und Privatleben miteinander zu vereinbaren – ein Aspekt mit zunehmender Relevanz angesichts wachsender Flexibilisierung von Studienformen und Arbeitsmodellen, welches im Rahmen der Forschung zur Study-Work-Life Balance (SWLB) näher untersucht wird. Die vorliegende Studie erweitert die Forschung zur SWLB, indem sie Zusammenhänge mit Lebenszufriedenheit und Stress analysiert sowie Selbstwirksamkeit, Zeitmanagementfähigkeiten und soziale Unterstützung als Moderatoren dieses Zusammenhangs untersucht.
Methode: In einer querschnittlichen online-Befragung wurden Daten von 264 berufstätigen Studierenden erhoben (Alter: M = 32.14, 79% weiblich). Eingesetzt wurden Fragebögen zur SWLB (TKS-WLB), Lebenszufriedenheit (SWLS), Stress (PSQ-20), Selbstwirksamkeit (ASKU), Zeitmanagementfähigkeiten (TMQ) und sozialer Unterstützung (F-SozU K-14). Es wurde weiterhin nach Studienmerkmalen (Präsenz- oder Fernstudium, Vollzeit- oder Teilzeitstudium, durchschnittliche Arbeits- und Studienzeit) gefragt. Ergebnisse: Die Ergebnisse linearer Regressionsmodelle ergaben, dass eine ausgewogene SWLB mit mehr Lebenszufriedenheit (b = 3.20, R2 = .27) und weniger Stress (b = -13.11, R2 = .50) einhergingen. Selbstwirksamkeit moderierte den Zusammenhang zwischen SWLB und Lebenszufriedenheit (b = -1.19, ΔR2 = .01). Zusätzliche Analysen unter Berücksichtigung der Studienlage zeigten, dass Fernstudierende über mehr Zeitmanagementfähigkeiten verfügten als Präsenzstudierende. Teilzeitstudierende zeigten ein höheres Maß an Zeitmanagementfähigkeiten und Selbstwirksamkeit als Vollzeitstudierende. Letztere wiesen höher Stresswerte auf als Teilzeitstudierende.
Diskussion: Die Ergebnisse bestätigen Selbstwirksamkeit als relevanten Faktor für die SWLB. Die explorativen Analysen ergeben wichtige Ansatzpunkte für Forschung zu Gruppenunterschieden im Kontext von Arbeit und Studium, auch in Bezug auf Ergebnisse der 22. Sozialerhebung (Kroher et al., 2023). Sie unterstreichen die Notwendigkeit zielgruppenspezifischer Unterstützungsangebote im Hochschulkontext, um das Wohlbefinden berufstätiger Studierender nachhaltig zu fördern.

Insgesamt nahmen 1.117 Gymnasiast:innen (56% weiblich, 43% männlich) im Alter zwischen 12 und 18 Jahren (M = 14.56, SD = 1.06) aus den Jahrgängen 8, 9 und 10 im Winter 2019/20 an der Fragebogenstudie teil.

Zukunftssorgen wurden mittels der Subskala „Zukunft“ des Problem Questionnaire (PQ; Seiffge-Krenke, 1995) erfasst. Als Prädiktoren wurden persönliche Variablen (z.B. Zielorientierungsprofil) sowie umweltbezogene Faktoren (u.a. Klassenklimavariablen, Bildungsgrad der Eltern) berücksichtigt. Als Kovariaten dienten das Alter und Geschlecht der Jugendlichen.

Die Ergebnisse multipler Regressionsanalysen zeigen, dass insbesondere das Geschlecht (höhere Werte für Mädchen), das Zielorientierungsprofil (höchste Werte für ambivalent Zielorientierte) sowie Aspekte des Klassenklimas (hoher wahrgenommener Leistungs- und Unterrichtsdruck) signifikant mit dem Ausmaß der Zukunftssorgen assoziiert sind.

Die Befunde verdeutlichen die Relevanz individueller und schulischer Kontextfaktoren für die Zukunftssorgen Jugendlicher und liefern empirische Ansatzpunkte für präventive Maßnahmen im schulischen Setting.

Hintergrund: Körperunzufriedenheit ist weltweit verbreitet und mit vielfältigen psychischen (z.B. negativer Affekt, Angst und Depressivität) und behavioralen Folgen (z.B. dysfunktionales Essverhalten) assoziiert. Aus Perspektive der Conservation of Resources Theory kann Körperunzufriedenheit als Stressor verstanden werden, der psychologische Ressourcen bedroht.
Ziel: Untersuchung von Psychologischem Kapital (PsyCap; Hoffnung, Optimismus, Resilienz, Selbstwirksamkeit) als potenziell protektiver Ressource und vermittelndem Mechanismus im Zusammenhang zwischen Körperunzufriedenheit und affektiven, essbezogenen sowie sozialen Outcomes.
Methode: Querschnittliche Online-Fragebogenstudie mit einer Convenience-Stichprobe (N=490; 69.4% weiblich; Alter 18–86 Jahre, M=44.05). Erfasst wurden Körperunzufriedenheit (EDE-Q), PsyCap (HERO), negativer Affekt (PANAS), emotionales Essverhalten (IES-2 Subskala), Zufriedenheit mit Freundschaften (FNSS) und Angst vor negativer sozialer Bewertung (FNE-K); Reliabilitäten lagen zwischen α= .86 und .94.
Ergebnisse: PsyCap korrelierte negativ mit Körperunzufriedenheit; eine Regression zeigte einen mittleren Effekt (b=−0.94, 95%-Bootstrap-CI [−1.17; −0.72], β=−.36). Körperunzufriedenheit sagte höheren negativen Affekt, mehr emotionales Essverhalten, geringere Freundschaftszufriedenheit und höhere Bewertungsangst vorher (kleine bis mittlere Effekte). PROCESS-Mediationsanalysen (kontrolliert für Alter und Geschlecht) ergaben signifikante indirekte Effekte über PsyCap; die Mediation war für negativen Affekt (ab=0.078), emotionales Essverhalten (ab=0.045) und Bewertungsangst (ab=0.086) partiell, für Freundschaftszufriedenheit (ab=−0.074) vollständig.
Diskussion: Die Befunde sprechen gegen eine Sicht von PsyCap als stets abrufbarer Schutzressource. Vielmehr ist PsyCap eng mit Erleben und Verhalten verknüpft, entfaltet seine günstigen Effekte jedoch nicht automatisch unter beeinträchtigenden Bedingungen. Körperunzufriedenheit kann in dieser Untersuchung als anhaltende Ressourcenbedrohung interpretiert werden, die mit geringerem PsyCap einhergeht und negative affektive, essbezogene und soziale Outcomes begünstigt. Für belastbare Aussagen zur Wirkrichtung sind prospektive Längsschnitt- und Interventionsstudien erforderlich.

Lara Schießl (Psychology)
Room: GR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Across the lifespan, social bonds are formed and maintained through interpersonal exchange processes that yield affective, relational, and motivational outcomes. This symposium brings together empirical studies that trace such interpersonal processes and their outcomes in various age groups.
The first presentation examines affective outcomes of in-person versus video-mediated intergenerational family conversations, focusing on positive affect and interaction enjoyment among younger and older adults. The second talk investigates how communication modality shapes daily social sharing and perceived closeness in non-heterosexual romantic couples, comparing in-person contact with calls, voice messages, and text-based communication. Drawing on the same daily-diary dataset, the third contribution examines how the fit between desired and received partner responsiveness during social sharing predicts daily relationship closeness. The fourth presentation investigates empathic accuracy as an interpersonal process by examining its association with heart-rate synchrony during naturalistic dyadic conversations in younger and older adults. The fifth talk examines how relational approach and avoidance goals shape romantic partners’ perceived success in emotion regulation during conflictual and comforting conversations, using cross-sectional dyadic data from laboratory and online studies. The final presentation extends the focus beyond close relationships by examining whether and under which conditions mentoring socially disadvantaged children fosters critical reflection on social inequality and social justice motivation among young adults.
Together, these talks illustrate how individual and relational outcomes across the lifespan are shaped by interpersonal competencies and exchange processes.

Maintaining close social ties is critical for adjustment, health, and longevity in later life. Intergenerational family interactions constitute a central source of social and emotional exchange for older adults. Due to geographical dispersion and mobility limitations, digitally mediated communication has become increasingly prevalent for intergenerational family interactions. However, it remains an open empirical question to what extent video-mediated interactions can fulfill socioemotional needs to the same degree as in-person interactions, particularly for older adults. Accordingly, a more nuanced understanding of how communication modality shapes socioemotional experiences in intergenerational family interactions is needed. The present study seeks to contribute to this understanding by focusing on interlocutors’ affective experiences and enjoyment following in-person versus video-mediated family conversations. Drawing on theories of media naturalness and social presence, as well as lifespan perspectives such as socioemotional selectivity theory, we hypothesize that in-person interactions are associated with more positive affect and higher enjoyment than video-mediated interactions. We test this hypothesis in an ongoing within-subjects experiment. Two family members from different generations (one under 65 and one 65 or older) engage in two naturalistic conversations about their past week, once in person and once via video call. Participants report their affective state before and after each conversation, with pre-conversation affect serving as a baseline for post-conversation affect, and rate their interaction enjoyment afterward. Planned analyses include linear mixed-effects models accounting for repeated measures within individuals and dyads. We discuss implications of our findings for intergenerational contact in an increasingly digitalized world.

There were no age-related differences in the association between messaging and sharing emotions.
