These processes have been linked to distinct physiological patterns and forms of interpersonal synchronization. However, little is known about how physiological synchronization between interaction partners relates to EA. This study investigates the association between heart rate (HR) synchrony during naturalistic conversations and EA. Ninety-six younger (24–36 years) and older (74–84 years) women were paired into dyads and alternated between sharing affectively relevant personal experiences and listening to their partner. At eight time points during the conversation, they repeatedly rated their own and their partner’s feelings on nine affective items each. EA was operationalized as the Pearson correlation between targets’ self-reported feelings and empathizers’ ratings. HR synchrony was quantified by cross-correlating partners’ HR time series with a maximum lag of three seconds. Dual intercept models revealed a quadratic association between HR synchrony and EA. EA was highest at weak asynchrony and lowest at high levels of synchrony. These findings suggest that the relationship between HR synchrony and empathic outcomes is multifaceted. We speculate that excessive sharing of others’ emotional experience may impair the accuracy of empathic judgments and discuss implications for future research.

True intraindividual change models are used to compare changes in critical reflection and motivation between the experimental and control group over time (RQ1). Preliminary analyses based on a subsample indicate group differences in critical reflection favoring the mentors (i.e., experimental group). Changes within the mentor group are further predicted by individual characteristics (RQ2) and program-specific factors (RQ3). The results are discussed in terms of their theoretical and practical implications.

Social media use (SMU) can negatively impact mental health. It contributes to addictive tendencies and depressive symptoms, and less happiness. The present intervention study investigated the effects of a conscious and controlled reduction of SMU time and/or an increase of physical activity by 30 minutes daily over 14 days on participants’ mental health (life satisfaction, subjective happiness, addictive tendencies, depressive symptom) and lifestyle (nicotine consume). The study had a randomized controlled trial design with four groups: intervention group 1 (N=162) reduced its SMU time, intervention group 2 (N=161) enhanced its physical activity time, intervention group 3 (N=159) performed both interventions, and a control group (N=160) kept its usual behavior. Data were collected at six measurement time points via online surveys (day 0; day 7; day 15; one month, three months, and six months after day 15). Repeated measures analyses of variance revealed significant group differences. All experimental conditions reduced addictive SMU and depressive symptoms significantly. And they increased life satisfaction and happiness significantly. Effects were stronger and remained more stable over time in the combination group than in single intervention groups. Furthermore, in the SMU reduction group only, nicotine consume decreased significantly. The current findings demonstrate that less time on SMU and more physical activity contribute to more well-being and a healthier lifestyle. Thus, programs that aim to reduce addictive tendencies, to protect well-being and to foster a healthier lifestyle should focus on a conscious and controlled reduction of online time, while time spent on physical activity should be increased.

Based on prior research, we derive four core stress competencies that are assumed to support effective stress management. To examine the validity of the Stress Competence Model, we developed a questionnaire and conducted seven studies. In Studies 1 (N = 130) and 2 (N = 430), we investigated the ability of stress awareness, Studies 3 (N = 95) and 4 (N = 449) focused on stress understanding, and in Studies 5 (N = 101) and 6 (N = 308), we examined the abilities of resource awareness and stress reduction. Finally, Study 7 (N = 410) examined the complete model simultaneously. Across studies, the results indicate that the Stress Competence Model provides a reliable and valid framework for assessing different stress competencies. Our findings suggest that practitioners can use the model to assess current levels of stress competence and to design targeted training or coaching interventions aimed at strengthening specific stress competencies. The empirically-informed insights derived by TSSEM can highlight which mediators are of greater or lesser importance for therapeutic change, and may contribute to increase the effectiveness of psychotherapeutic interventions.

This symposium explores the diverse factors and mechanisms that contribute to the effectiveness of workplace coaching. We discuss how various coaching strategies, formats, situational contexts and technologies impact coaches, clients and coaching outcomes. Workplace coaching refers to customized activities built on a collaborative, reflective, and goal-oriented relationship between a professional coach—who does not hold formal supervisory authority—and one or more coachee to facilitate a range of positive work outcomes.
Meta-analyses in the field have consistently demonstrated that workplace coaching can help individuals achieve coaching goals and improve work performance. However, there is an ongoing need for robust theoretical frameworks and rigorous research designs to better understand which factors affect coaching efficacy and the processes by which coaching leads to positive results. The studies presented in this symposium aim to address these gaps in research and understanding.
Tatar and colleagues compare the mechanisms and effects of problem-focused and/or solution-focused coaching interventions by analyzing the verbal interactions of coaching dyads. Eva Jonas and colleagues examine in multiple studies the extent to which coaching strengthens self-management competencies of coachees that promote the achievement of coaching goals. They compare individual and group coaching, AI-based coaching, and self-coaching formats. Tatar and Antoni investigate general and differential mediation effects of occupational self-efficacy in two coaching formats, coaching by coaches and self-coaching, using a moderated longitudinal multi-level mediation analysis. Gil Bozer and Silja Kotte analyze in their qualitative study how coaches react to the implementation of AI-coaching in their coaching company and how they adopt their professional roles and identities to make sense of their practice in a human-AI environment. Beng and colleagues examine the factors which influence the selection of coaches on digital platforms focusing on how clients tend to rely on heuristic cues such as social proof and electronic word of mouth in their decisions.
At the end of the symposium we will discuss implications for future coaching research and practice based on the findings of these studies.

Coaching serves as an effective intervention within human resource management, yielding positive outcomes such as enhanced well-being, goal attainment, and performance. Central to these results are the interventions employed by coaches. While research indicates that both problem-focused and solution-focused approaches facilitate goal attainment, a debate persists regarding which is more efficient for overall coaching success.
Current literature suggests that solution-focused interventions may have a more significant impact on goal attainment. However, existing studies often fail to align these interventions with the nature of the coaching goals themselves, which can also be categorized as either solution- or problem-focused. Furthermore, comparative research frequently relies on self-reports or manipulated instructions, potentially limiting the validity of the findings.
Since coaching behavior represents the observable dimension of success factors, it is essential to analyze the precise mechanisms that constitute effective interventions. The present study compares a problem-focused intervention (Clarification of Meaning), a solution-focused intervention (Coping/Mastery), and a combination of both to determine their respective effects on goal attainment.
Given that coaching is a goal-directed process, this comparison is examined in relation to specific individual goals: clarification-goals and mastery-goals. We analyzed 30 dyads, each consisting of approximately eight sessions, resulting in a dataset of roughly 240 voice recordings. These recordings were transcribed using noScribe and are currently being coded with the adapted act4consulting 2.0 category system. Additionally, we conducted exploratory tests to examine the applicability of common linear process models, which typically posit that problem clarification precedes mastery. The theoretical and practical implications of these findings are discussed.

In an increasingly challenging environment, individuals are continuously confronted with changing demands. To cope with these changes, many turn to coaching as a form of professional and personal support. Coaching is commonly conceptualized as a collaborative relationship between coach and coachee aimed at facilitating goal attainment. While such relational support is essential, successfully adapting to change requires more than a strong relationship and the pursuit of goals. Rather, it requires a development of the self, characterized by the strengthening of self-management competencies (SMCs), i.e., regulating thoughts, emotions, and actions to achieve goals despite obstacles or setbacks. SMCs include self-regulation (acting in accordance with one’s true self), self-access (reconnecting with one’s self under threat), self-control (translating plans into actions despite conflicting impulses), and volitional facilitation (implementing difficult intentions under high workload). From this perspective, coaching is effective not mainly because of the supportive relationship itself, but because it builds individuals’ capacity to manage themselves in dynamic and uncertain contexts. We examined the extent to which coaching strengthens coachees’ SMCs in both employee and student samples across multiple studies. These studies investigated one-on-one coachings (with one, three, or five sessions), group coaching, AI-based coaching, and self-coaching formats. Across all studies, coaching increased SMCs from pre- to post-coaching, although the extent of the increase differed across samples and coaching formats. Overall, the findings indicate that coaching particularly fosters self-regulation and self-access. These competencies appear to represent central mechanisms of coaching success, as reflected, for example, in goal attainment.

Occupational self-efficacy partially mediates the intervention's impact on stress and well-being in coaching, but not in self-coaching. These results indicate self-coaching could supplement rather than substitute coaching. Theoretical and practical implications for choosing appropriate coaching formats are discussed, highlighting the potential for self-coaching to augment, but not substitute, traditional coaching methods in promoting occupational self-efficacy, reducing stress, and improving well-being.

The integration of AI into workplace coaching represents a disruptive factor that is reshaping the coaching market, along with the roles and identities of coaches. However, empirical research on the real-world implementation of AI-coaching (AIC) remains scarce, creating a critical gap in understanding how professional coaches actually adapt to this technological shift. We investigated how human coaches respond to the organizational adoption of AIC and how they navigate their professional roles and identities to make sense of their practice in a human-AI environment.
Drawing on the automation-augmentation paradox, occupational role identity, and role ambiguity theories, we conducted and analyzed 15 semi-structured interviews with 12 professional coaches employed by an Asian coaching firm, contextualized by pre- and post-interviews with the company CEO and the AI provider.
Findings reveal that top-down AIC implementation triggered significant ambivalence, leading to the clarification of role boundaries and catalyzing both protective and expansive identity work. Coaches protected their identity by anchoring their value in uniquely human skills (e.g., empathy), while simultaneously experimenting with AIC, expansively using it for their own professional development (skill modelling, supervision and feedback) as well as for delivering coaching to clients. This adaptive process enabled the emergence of new human–AI coaching models (collaboration, service division), where coaches redefined their practice by assigning tasks to either human or AI coaches. Our findings culminate in a conceptual framework that demonstrates how the organizational context, through triggering role ambiguity and identity work, catalyzed professional renewal and vocational adaptation.

Results showed a strong main effect of qualification, with higher credentials yielding higher ratings. Social proof and eWOM did not exert significant main effects; but low-qualified coaches (study one) as well as medium-qualified coaches (study two) received higher ratings when accompanied by reviews, particularly when both reviews and star ratings were presented. These findings suggest that peripheral cues only matter when objective information is ambiguous, supporting heuristic-processing theories and underscoring risks of misinformed decision-making in digital coaching markets.

Matthias Roth | GESIS - Leibniz-Institut für Sozialwissenschaften | Germany

This study systematically investigated how links between personality traits and cognitive ability vary across key sociodemographic strata. Numerous studies have supported a robust but modest association between cognitive ability and certain personality traits, notably Big Five Openness and Neuroticism. Recent meta-analyses have also indicated that the personality–cognitive ability link is moderated by sociodemographic factors. However, previous research has often been limited by selective samples and has thus lacked systematic consideration of sociodemographic moderators. Drawing on a large, population-representative sample (N = 117,621) from 27 countries in the OECD’s PIAAC 2023 data set, our analyses filled this research gap by examining associations between the Big Five personality domains and facets and cognitive ability by gender, age, and educational attainment. Results indicate remarkable cross-gender stability of the personality–cognitive ability link. By contrast, substantial differences emerged for age and especially for educational attainment. Personality–cognitive ability correlations were stronger among older and less-educated respondents. Effect sizes for Openness and Neuroticism/Negative Emotionality were up to three times larger in respondents without compared with those with higher education. Furthermore, Conscientiousness was negatively related to cognitive ability among respondents with but not among those without higher education. Robustness checks confirmed the consistency of these patterns across different cognitive domains, Big Five measures, and response tendencies. These findings thus highlight the importance of considering age and particularly educational attainment when interpreting personality–cognitive ability associations, and they support theories proposing personality-driven investment in intellectual growth, particularly among individuals with fewer formal educational opportunities.

Prof. Dr. Kirsten Hilger | Vinzenz Pallotti University | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Human intelligence is essential to understand complex ideas, to engage in various forms of reasoning, to learn from experience, and to adapt to new situations by taking thought. The P300 event-related brain potential has been related to intelligence scores and thus evolves as a promising biomarker of general cognitive ability. However, empirical results are characterized by enormous heterogeneity, and a quantitative assessment of this literature is lacking. This preregistered meta-analysis provides the first systematic overview of neuroscientific studies that have examined associations between general cognitive ability and the P300 in healthy adult participants. Out of 5641 articles screened, 49 studies with up to 381 effects were eligible for PRISMA-based meta-analytic comparison. Study quality was evaluated using a novel Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device, which we developed particularly for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID) and provide together with our analysis code as free online resources to support future meta-analyses. Confirming our hypotheses, a small but significant positive across-study association was observed for general cognitive ability and P300 amplitudes (r = .12; 95%-CI [.06, .18]), while a significant negative across-study association was revealed for P300 latencies (r = -.18; 95%-CI [-.24, -.12]). Study heterogeneity was substantial, and sub-analyses highlighted potential moderators such as type of the task during EEG recording. In my talk, I will present our methodology, results and discuss limitations to ultimately provide concrete guidelines for future research on the neurobiological underpinnings of individual differences in cognitive ability.

Effects of Age and Age Simulation on Dual-Task Performance in Tennis

Show details
Authors:
Anna Lina Heggenberger | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Lucie Berger
Sabine Schaefer | Germany

Aging is associated with declines in cognitive and sensorimotor abilities that can impair sport performance, particularly under cognitive-motor dual-task demands. Dual-tasking requires allocation of limited attentional resources, which is reduced with age. To isolate the contribution of peripheral sensorimotor constraints to age-related performance deficits without directly altering cognitive processing, age-simulation suits have been used to impose age-typical physical limitations in younger adults. The present study extends this approach to a sport-specific context. Experienced tennis players performed a tennis-specific motor task (returning balls to a target field) and a cognitive task (3-back) under single-task and dual-task conditions. Younger adults (n = 18) completed the tasks with and without an age-simulation suit (within-subjects), whereas older adults (n = 18) completed the tasks without the suit. In the cognitive task, younger adults performed better than older adults, and performance did not differ between younger adults with versus without the suit. Across all groups, cognitive performance declined under dual-task conditions. In the motor task, younger adults without the suit performed significantly better than younger adults with the suit and older adults, whose performances were comparable, indicating that peripheral constraints reduced younger adults’ tennis performance to an older-adult-like level. Only younger adults without the suit showed a decline from single- to dual-task performance. This pattern may reflect reduced movement flexibility under peripheral constraints, promoting a constrained strategy already in single-task performance. Overall, peripheral constraints impaired sport-specific motor performance, whereas older adults additionally showed reduced cognitive performance, likely reflecting age-related declines in central processing resources.

Die Auswahl von Vergleichsgruppen als ethische Herausforderung für interventionelle Forschung – wie hält es psychologische Forschung mit der Deklaration von Helsinki?
Prof. Dr. Dirk Lehr | Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lüneburg, Germany | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Dirk Lehr | Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lüneburg, Germany | Germany
Hanna Brückner | Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lüneburg, Germany
Hannah Heimes | Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lüneburg, Germany | Germany
Prof. Dr. Claudia Buntrock | Otto-von-Guericke Universität
Dr. Christin Hempeler | Ruhr Uni Bochum
Prof. Dr. Dr. Kai Spiegelhalder | University of Freiburg
Dr. Lorenz Grolig | Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lüneburg, Germany | Germany

Die Deklaration von Helsinki (DoH) gehört zu den wichtigsten ethischen Leitlinien zur Forschung am Menschen. Basierend auf ihrer Grundforderung zum Schutz von Personen, die an Forschung teilnehmen “The health and well-being of my patient will be my first consideration” sowie dem Anliegen, immer wirksamere Interventionen zu identifizieren, vertritt die DoH die Position, dass eine neue Intervention mit der besten vorhandenen Intervention, dem Goldstandard, verglichen werden muss. (Psychologische) Placebos als Vergleichsgruppen werden nur in Ausnahmefällen als ethisch akzeptabel angesehen.
Am Beispiel der Insomnie untersucht diese systematische Übersicht, ob die klinische Forschung zu einem neuen Interventionsansatz – internetbasierte kognitive Verhaltenstherapie der Insomnie (iKVT-I) – in Übereinstimmung mit der DoH durchgeführt wurde. Dazu wurde eine systematische Literaturrecherche nach entsprechenden randomisiert-kontrollierten Studien (RCTs) durchgeführt, gemäß Preferred-Reporting-Items-for-Systematic-Reviews-and-Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Um den Goldstandard zu ermitteln, wurden die nationalen Leitlinien aller Länder analysiert, in denen Studien durchgeführt wurden.
Es konnten 32 RCTs sowie sieben Leitlinien für 12 Länder in die Analysen einbezogen. Fast alle Leitlinien empfehlen die persönliche KVT-I als Goldstandard, aber nur vier Studien (12,5 %) verwendeten den Goldstandard als Vergleichsbedingung. Keine der anderen Studien erklärte, warum sie den Richtlinien der DoH nicht folgten.
Es ist bemerkenswert, dass die große Mehrheit der Studien eine zentrale forschungsethische Forderung nicht beachtet und dies nicht reflektiert. Diese Situation hat u.a. Folgen für die Versorgungsqualität, da sie Patient:innen, Therapeut:innen und gesundheits-politische Entscheidungsträger:innen im Unklaren über die Wirksamkeit von therapeutischen Alternativen lässt. Es bleibt die Frage zu diskutieren, ob die Psychologie mit diesem Zustand einverstanden ist oder Veränderungen anstreben will.

VAST: a visual tool for organizing ideas (e.g., theories) comprehensively
Prof. Dr. Daniel Leising | TU Dresden | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Daniel Leising | TU Dresden | Germany
Oliver Grenke | Germany
Dr. Marcos Cramer

The Visual Argument Structure Tool (VAST) is a generic tool for jointly visualizing the semantic, conceptual, empirical and reasoning relationships that constitute arguments. Its primary purpose is to promote exactness, completeness and parsimony in systematic thinking about complex matters. The system is more comprehensive than existing approaches in that it expressly captures the difference between mental concepts and the words (“names”) used to designate them, as well as several important ways in which concepts may be related to one another (causation, conceptual implication, prediction, transformation, reasoning). All of this is distinguished from beliefs as to whether something IS the case and/or OUGHT to be the case. The system also accounts for differences in WHO thinks that something is or should (not) be the case, and for the difference between ideas that do have empirical reference points (data) and those that do not. Furthermore, any combination of basic system elements may be grouped together and thus form a new element. This feature enables analyses at different levels of resolution. VAST may be used to improve theorizing in the social sciences, in terms of specificity. It may also be used as a data collection tool, (e.g., when assessing the belief systems of individual research participants, or the narrative structure of written materials).

Psychology faces a variety of challenges posed by digital progress - particularly the use of artificial intelligence, social changes brought about by right-wing populism and social media as well as the open-science movement with its demands for transparent research. The solutions and approaches to these challenges must be as diverse as the challenges themselves. A trustworthy information base built on high-quality data is a good starting point for meeting these challenges. The Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) operates various databases in which numerous research objects from German-speaking countries are collected, enriched with metadata, and stored for the long term. In order to bring these diverse research objects together in one central location, an open-knowledge graph was developed that maps the ZPID databases in a structured semantic network. This allows a representation of relationships between publications, authors, research data, analysis code, preprints, preregistrations, psychometric instruments, and much more, in human- and machine-readable form. The PsychPorta search portal was developed to make this knowledge graph searchable for users. The search portal is open access and offers an intuitive interface. Relevant open-science information of the research objects is highlighted, increasing transparency and reuse of research output. Attractive use cases for analyzing the rich metadata provided may arise, particularly for researchers in the field of metascience. This talk will introduce the functions of PsychPorta and illustrate uses. It will also provide an outlook on planned new features.

Klinische Qualifikationen und Tätigkeitsfelder in psychologischen Stellenanzeigen: Eine KI-gestützte Analyse des Arbeitsmarkts
Johanna Binnewitt | Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung (BIBB) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Johanna Binnewitt | Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung (BIBB) | Germany
Stefan Winnige | Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung (BIBB) | Germany

Durch die Reform des Psychotherapeutengesetzes im Jahr 2020 können Universitäten seit dem Wintersemester 2020/21 den Master „Klinische Psychologie/Psychotherapie“ anbieten, der nach erfolgreicher Approbationsprüfung den Zugang zur psychotherapeutischen Weiterbildung ermöglicht.
Diese Reform wirft die Frage auf, wie sich die neuen Qualifikationswege auf die geforderten Qualifikationen am Arbeitsmarkt auswirken und welche alternativen beruflichen Wege es für Studierende ohne Approbation im psychologischen Arbeitsmarkt gibt.

Als Datengrundlage nutzen wir ca. 20.000 Stellenanzeigen der Karriere-Website von der Hogrefe-Verlagsgruppe aus den Jahren 2015-2025. Mithilfe von manuell kodierten Anzeigen aus dem Jahr 2017 trainieren wir Machine Learning-Modelle, die jeweils die klinische Qualifikation und die Tätigkeitsfelder für die Stellenanzeigen bestimmen. Als Modelle verwenden wir Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), die eine kontext-sensitive Modellierung der Stellenanzeigentexte ermöglichen.

Auf Basis der automatisiert klassifizierten Stellenanzeigen beleuchten wir anschließend, welche klinischen Qualifikationen in Berufen aus dem Bereich der Psychologie gefordert werden. Indem wir die klinischen Qualifikationen mit den Tätigkeitsfeldern der Stellen vergleichen, identifizieren wir mögliche Berufsfelder, die für Studierende ohne Approbation in Frage kommen.

Der Vortrag reflektiert den Einsatz von KI-Modellen zur Analyse arbeitsmarktbezogener Daten im Feld der Psychologie und stellt zentrale Ergebnisse zu Qualifikationsanforderungen und Tätigkeitsfeldern vor.

Presenteeism: Investigating the Role of Health, Motivation, and Organizational Factors on Workplace Attendance
Chair(s) Dr. Sasha Cook (University of Amsterdam)
Chair(s) Dr. Alexander Zill (Hochschule Mittweida)
Room: HR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Presenteeism, defined as working despite feeling unwell or ill, has become a central concern in occupational health psychology due to its links with impaired recovery, reduced well-being, and performance costs and reflects a complex decision-making process shaped by organizational, social, and motivational forces. This symposium brings together four complementary presentations that advance a multi-level understanding of why employees work while experiencing symptoms and how workplace contexts shape these behaviors, using new theoretical approaches and diverse methods, including large-scale survey analyses, qualitative thematic analysis, and longitudinal multilevel modeling.
The first talk presents a theoretical model linking organizational error culture (error prevention vs. error management) to presenteeism and absenteeism through health, motivational, and work design pathways. The second presentation draws on a large online survey of employees with chronic conditions to investigate the role of symptom severity and key work-related, social-normative, and identity-based motives as potential drivers of presenteeism. The third contribution deepens this perspective by applying thematic analysis to open-ended survey responses from employees with chronic conditions to examine perceived constraints, fears of negative consequences, and the role of flexibility and supervisor support. Finally, the fourth presentation expands the scope to menstrual pain, examining how stigma-sensitive disclosure processes and organizational pressures (potentially) shape menstrual-related presenteeism across on-site and remote work contexts in a longitudinal design with multilevel and mediation analyses.
Together, these talks highlight both shared mechanisms (pressure, responsibility, social norms, and resource protection) and meaningful heterogeneity across health conditions and workplace environments.

Presenteeism, Absenteeism, and Error Culture: Health and Motivation as Key Factors
Carolin Dietz | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Dr. Alexander Klamar | Hochschule des Bundes für öffentliche Verwaltung | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Carolin Dietz | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Dr. Alexander Klamar | Hochschule des Bundes für öffentliche Verwaltung | Germany

Presenteeism and absenteeism are defined as working and not working while being ill, respectively. At the individual level, several personal and work related factors have been linked to these behaviors. However, factors above the individual level have mostly been overlooked. The present study investigates the associations between an organizational factor, namely an error culture (varying between error prevention and error management), and presenteeism and absenteeism. Building on theories of occupational stress, we propose a theoretical model with three pathways: First, in an error prevention culture, there is pressure to reduce or conceal errors. Therefore, errors cause strain and interfere with recovery, thereby reducing health. This, in turn, makes both presenteeism and absenteeism more likely (health pathway). Second, in the event of errors, employees may try to avoid resource loss, thereby increasing presenteeism propensity (motivational pathway). Third, the organizational error culture influences work design. For example, in an error prevention culture, leaders may be less open for employees’ autonomy and task variety, as these work design strategies bear greater risk of errors. Thus, even in the absence of errors, an error prevention culture may reduce health and work motivation, which, in turn, influences presenteeism and absenteeism (work design pathway). We will test parts of our theoretical model through a vignette study. Our study integrates research on organizational error culture, stress, and health-related outcomes. For practitioners, we deliver a novel approach to reduce presenteeism and absenteeism.

Presenteeism among Employees with Chronic Conditions: Factors Influencing the Decision to Work While Ill

Presenteeism – defined as working while feeling ill – is widespread in the workforce. Hägerbäumer's (2017) integrative model of sickness behavior in the workplace suggests that the general health status plays a significant role in employees’ decisions to attend work while ill. Around one-third of the European working population reports compromised general health due to chronic conditions. Previous research indicates that presenteeism among employees with chronic conditions is not linearly related to symptom severity but is influenced by individual decision-making and coping processes (Fu & Cook, 2025).
Within the AmiChro project, presenteeism among employees with chronic conditions was examined using data from an online survey (N = 1,175). Analyses included descriptive statistics, scatterplots, and Spearman rank correlations.
A significant moderate positive association was found between symptom severity and the number of presenteeism days (ρ = .35). At the same time, substantial interindividual variability indicated that symptom severity explains only a limited proportion of variance. Key work-related approach motives included completing important tasks or appointments (70%) and holding non-delegable responsibilities (50.6%). Socially normative avoidance motives, particularly the desire not to burden colleagues (53.1%), were also prominent. In addition, illness-specific, identity-related, and coping-related motives were highly relevant, such as the desire “not to give up” (51.2%) or “to be stronger than one’s illness” (50.4%).
Overall, the findings suggest that presenteeism among employees with chronic conditions is shaped by a complex interplay of work-related, social, and identity-related factors rather than symptom severity alone. These insights may help organizations promote health-oriented behavior and sustainable work design.

Meta-analytic research shows stronger relationships between presenteeism and its antecedents for employees with a chronic health condition compared with healthier workers. Previous research on the decision-making process of presenteeism also provides first insights for chronically ill people. Employees with a chronic health condition report particularly limited choices and often show presenteeism despite severe symptoms, fearing negative consequences. Their threshold for calling in sick is significantly higher, leading to dysfunctional presenteeism and potential resource loss spirals. Furthermore, a lack of flexibility and insufficient support from supervisors considerably exacerbate these stressful decision-making dynamics. To gain deeper insight into why employees with a chronic health condition work despite experiencing symptoms, we conducted a cross-sectional online survey of employees with different CHCs as part of a larger research project on chronic illness and work. We recruited participants through convenience sampling with the support of the German Federal Association of Company Health Insurance Funds (BKK Dachverband). We combined the data with a sample recruited from Prolific Academic. A total of 625 employees with at least one medically diagnosed CHC participated in the survey, of whom 519 provided information on their reasons for presenteeism. The answers will be analyzed using thematic analysis. Moreover, we will combine the findings with specific characteristics of the sample (e.g., physical or mental illness, and whether a chronic health condition is disclosed). Implications will be discussed.

Menstrual Pain and Work: A Multi-Wave Study on Stigma, Disclosure, and Presenteeism
Theresa Tschauko | University of Klagenfurt | Austria

Presenteeism is associated with reduced well-being, impaired recovery, and productivity loss. While menstrual pain is a widespread health concern among working women, menstrual-related presenteeism remains underexamined within occupational health psychology. Existing research shows that many employees continue working despite menstrual pain, often without disclosing symptoms to supervisors or colleagues due to stigma, credibility concerns, and gendered workplace norms. However, little is known about the conditions under which disclosure occurs, how it shapes presenteeism behavior, or whether these processes differ across work modalities such as on-site versus remote work. The lack of empirical evidence on disclosure-related mechanisms limits theoretical understanding of menstrual-related presenteeism and hinders organizations from developing effective, stigma-sensitive responses to menstrual health challenges at work.

This longitudinal study across three measurement points examines how disclosure of menstrual pain is related to presenteeism and presenteeism propensity, and how individual, relational, and organizational factors predict disclosure (to colleagues and a supervisor) and presenteeism. Multilevel models disentangle within- and between-person effects, and mediation analyses test disclosure as an explanatory mechanism. Data collection has been completed and analyses are currently ongoing; final results will be available by February 2026. By integrating disclosure processes with organizational pressure in a longitudinal design, this study advances theoretical understanding of menstrual-related presenteeism and clarifies how social and organizational conditions shape health-related work behavior across different work contexts.

Integration ideologischer, moralischer und selbstregulativer Dispositionen für Umweltverhalten und Umweltaffekt: Die moderierende Rolle und der indirekte Pfad von Need for Cognition
Kathrin Fucke | TU Chemnitz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kathrin Fucke | TU Chemnitz | Germany
Luise Wollermann | TU Chemnitz
Marie Günther | TU Chemnitz
Gina Vogelsang | TU Chemnitz
Prof. Anja Strobel | TU Chemnitz

Um dem Klimawandel langfristig zu begegnen, sind neben politischen Maßnahmen auch individuelle Verhaltensänderungen erforderlich. Need for Cognition (NFC), die Disposition zu elaborierter Informationsverarbeitung, könnte angesichts der Komplexität des Klimawandels bedeutsam sein. Ziel dieser Studie war es, die moderierende und mediierende Rolle von NFC im Zusammenspiel mit ideologischen, moralischen und selbstregulativen Dispositionen zu untersuchen. Einbezogen wurden der rechte (RWA) und linke Autoritarismus (LWA), die Ungerechtigkeitssensibilität (US) aus vier Perspektiven (Opfer, Beobachter, Täter, Nutznießer) sowie Selbstkontrolle und Impulsivität. Untersucht wurden Zusammenhänge mit individuellem und kollektivem Umweltverhalten (horizontal und vertikal) sowie Umweltaffekt (Klimaangst und Klimazuversicht). In zwei präregistrierten Online-Studien wurden 428 Personen (30.76 ± 13.06 Jahre; 18–77 Jahre; 71.03 % weiblich) befragt. NFC, LWA und die fremdbezogenen US-Perspektiven zeigten positive Zusammenhänge mit Umweltverhalten, RWA negative. Im Unterschied zu LWA und fremdbezogenen US-Perspektiven war NFC nicht mit Umweltaffekt assoziiert. Selbstregulative Dispositionen zeigten wenig Zusammenhänge. NFC moderierte die Effekte ideologischer und moralischer Dispositionen: Entgegen den Erwartungen verstärkte NFC die negativen Effekte von RWA, erwartungskonform die positiven Effekte der fremdbezogenen US-Perspektiven. Moderationseffekte für Umweltaffekt waren selektiver und weniger konsistent. Zudem zeigte sich ein indirekter Effekt von NFC über die Beobachterperspektive auf Umweltverhalten. Die Ergebnisse erweitern das Verständnis von NFC: Die Freude am Denken fungiert nicht nur als Prädiktor von Umweltverhalten, sondern moderiert die Effekte anderer Dispositionen und könnte als moralische Reifungskapazität Umweltverhalten über erhöhte moralische Sensibilität fördern. Jedoch kann NFC auch negative Effekte auf Umweltverhalten verstärken. Das komplexe Zusammenspiel von NFC mit moralischen und ideologischen Dispositionen legt nahe, auch metakognitives Bewusstsein zu fördern.

Approaching pro-environmental behavior through the lens of cognitive effort
Ruth Krebs | Belgium
Show details
Author:
Ruth Krebs | Belgium

Despite the overwhelming evidence for global warming and recommendations to respond to the climate challenges, the implementation of pro-environmental behavior remains difficult for many individuals. Pro-environmental behavior often involves cognitive effort, which is generally aversive and needs to be compensated by appropriate outcome value. In a series of experimental studies, we probed participants’ willingness to invest cognitive effort for pro-environmental outcomes (financial support of an organization) and how this differs from cognitive effort for self-benefitting outcomes (personal financial gain). Individuals are less motivated to invest cognitive resources for pro-environmental outcomes overall, and display stronger effort discounting (i.e., a reduction of outcome value by expected effort). This inferiority is even more pronounced in the light of direct opportunity costs (i.e., choosing one outcome means foregoing another one). These data illustrate that pro-environmental action in an experimental setting follows common rules of effort-based decision making, and highlight the impact of competing, more tangible goals that can hamper pro-environmental motivation – mirroring rea-life behavior.

Beatrice Beitz | Prosperkolleg e.V. / Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Beatrice Beitz | Prosperkolleg e.V. / Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Wolfgang Irrek | Hochschule Ruhr-West | Germany

Imagining positive collective futures has been shown to increase motivation for social and environmental change by strengthening drivers such as hope, collective efficacy, and shared identity. While experimental studies demonstrate positive effects on intentions to engage in sustainability-related action, evidence from real-world contexts remains scarce. Drawing on social identity theory, this study examines whether participatory visioning stimulates collective engagement in local circular economy initiatives in a real-world community setting and whether this effect is mediated by social identification and collective efficacy. By constructing a shared vision of the future, participatory visioning is expected to strengthen a sense of “we” among community members, thereby enhancing social identification and collective agency. A quasi-experimental field study is conducted within a local community initiative in Bottrop, Germany. Residents participate in one of three conditions: (1) a participatory visioning workshop, (2) an active control condition involving a non-visioning community event, or (3) a passive control group. Participants complete standardised measures of social identification with the community initiative, perceived collective efficacy, and collective action intentions. Participants in the visioning condition are expected to report stronger intentions to actively engage in local circular initiatives. It is anticipated that this effect is mediated by increased social identification and perceived collective efficacy. By examining participatory visioning in a real-world context, the study provides field-based evidence for identity-based pathways to collective engagement in circular urban transformation.

Social isolation and loneliness in the era of climate change
Dr. Samia Akhter-Khan | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB) | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Samia Akhter-Khan | Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg (MHB) | Germany

The role of social well-being in the context of climate change is an emerging area of research, highlighting the profound impacts of extreme weather events on social isolation and loneliness. In this presentation, bidirectional pathways between climate change and social disconnection are introduced, drawing from evidence that extreme events such as floods and heatwaves can isolate individuals from social networks, while loneliness itself exacerbates maladaptive responses to climate risks (Akhter-Khan, Holt-Lunstad & Liu, 2026). Moreover, findings from an ongoing systematic review on the effects of social isolation and loneliness on mortality during climate hazards are presented. Older people are disproportionately affected by these challenges, as they are often more vulnerable to climate-induced disruptions and less likely to migrate due to physical and economic barriers. By framing loneliness as both a climate risk and a lever for climate solutions, we propose novel strategies for integrating social connection into climate adaptation plans. Ultimately, this research underscores the need for interdisciplinary interventions that leverage social well-being to promote both human and planetary health.

References: Akhter-Khan, S. C., Holt-Lunstad, J., & Liu, S. (2026). Social connection and loneliness in the era of extreme weather and climate change. Nature Health. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44360-025-00041-6

Duration: 90 Minutes

Subjective well-being and life satisfaction are at the center of psychological research and are also gaining increasing importance for society and social policy. A better understanding of their stability and malleability, their individual and contextual determinants, and their relevance for policymaking is crucial both for providing targeted support to vulnerable groups and for enabling evidence-based policy design. This symposium addresses these questions and brings together current research on the dynamics, correlates, and intervention potentials of well-being.
First, using longitudinal data, the extent to which health-related and economic anxiety are causally linked to well-being is examined, as well as how socioeconomic status moderates these relationships. Second, large-scale panel data are used to analyze how frequently drastic changes in subjective well-being and personality occur, which predictors they have, and which long-term consequences are associated with them. Third, a review of meta-analyses synthesizes the evidence on correlates of life satisfaction across individual, relational, and contextual domains and highlights the areas in which particularly robust associations exist. Fourth, using longitudinal data from ten countries, an atlas of hedonic adaptation to major life events is presented. Fifth, WELLMOD presents a novel well-being-based microsimulation model that allows policy options to be compared regarding their well-being impact relative to expenses, thereby providing a foundation for evidence-based policymaking.
The symposium offers an integrated perspective on the conditions, dynamics, and socio-political implications of well-being and life satisfaction. It is aimed at researchers in differential, health, and clinical psychology, as well as at those interested in applied fields.

Exploring the Interplay Between Anxiety and Well-Being in Dependence on Perceived SES: Longitudinal Evidence
Dr. Svenja Frenzel
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Svenja Frenzel
Prof. Dr. Ana N. Tibubos
Dr. Lotte Pummerer
Prof. Dr. Sonja Utz
Prof. Dr. Kai Sassenberg

Previous studies provided evidence for a relationship between anxiety and well-being. The present study aims to establish a causal relationship based on temporal order, considering two types of anxiety: health and economic anxiety. Furthermore, we examine the role of perceived socio-economic status (SES) in amplifying the relationship between both types of anxiety and (lower) well-being. Data from NTime1 = 4939 participants were collected during the late COVID-19 pandemic (May 2022 – September 2023) at five consecutive measurement points with a three-month retest interval. The results of a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model showed that, on an interpersonal level, health and economic anxiety were negatively related to well-being. On an intrapersonal level, only health but not economic anxiety predicted lower well-being across time, and this relationship was not bidirectional. Thus, individuals who experienced more health anxiety than usual reported lower well-being in the next wave. Multilevel analysis further indicated that higher perceived SES weakened the negative relationship between health anxiety and well-being. Accordingly, these results reveal that health anxiety is the more dominant predictor of well-being, at least in our research period, and that people with lower perceived SES are particularly vulnerable to deterioration of their well-being. Our findings highlight the need for social policies that also reach socially and economically disadvantaged individuals to enhance their well-being during times of crises.

Frequency, Predictors, and Consequences of Drastic Changes in Subjective Well-Being and Personality Traits
Bernd Schäfer
Show details
Authors:
Bernd Schäfer
Peter Haehner
Michael D. Krämer
Amanda J. Wright
Wiebke Bleidorn
Christopher J. Hopwood
Maike Luhmann

Subjective well-being and personality traits change significantly across the lifespan, with diverging trajectories across individuals. While some people experience drastic changes in their well-being and personality traits from one year to the next, others show only small, gradual changes over time. Theoretical accounts suggest that there are qualitative differences between gradual and drastic changes in these traits, with drastic changes indicating a failure of homeostatic and regulatory processes. However, empirical research has yet to identify when, why, and to whom such drastic changes in subjective well-being and personality traits occur. To close this gap, we introduce a novel approach to investigate the frequency, predictors, and consequences of drastic trait changes using data from the LISS panel. First, we test and compare different metrics to identify drastic changes. Second, we use machine learning algorithms to examine predictors of those changes. Third, we investigate long-term consequences of these drastic changes with multilevel models. Our results will provide novel insights into theories of subjective well-being and personality development. Furthermore, findings may facilitate identifying individuals at need for interventions designed to prevent undesired shifts in these traits.

Variables Associated with Life Satisfaction in the General Population: A Second-Order Meta-Analytical Review
Dr. Bianca Simonsmeier
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Bianca Simonsmeier
Laura Müller
Joanna Schirra
Prof. Dr. Susanne Bücker

Life satisfaction is among the most central aspirations in human life and constitutes a key outcome not only at the individual level but also in societal and political discourse. Understanding the conditions under which people experience a satisfying life therefore requires an integrative synthesis of the diverse correlates that have been examined across disciplines. The present second-order meta-analysis provides a systematic and integrative summary of the current evidence on correlates of life satisfaction. A standardized search (PsycINFO, ERIC, Medline) yielded 10.265 hits without duplicates. After abstracts screening with ASReview, a total of 366 full texts were further screened for inclusion by three independent coders using predefined coding rules. Of these potentially relevant full texts, 85 meta-analyses reporting 215 associations between life satisfaction and another variable met the inclusion criteria and were included in the current review. These associations were ranked in descending order and synthesized in a second-order meta-analysis after determining and reducing overlap of included studies in the primary meta-analyses, whenever necessary. The synthesized associations ranged from strong negative relations (e.g., life satisfaction and neuroticism, r = −.56) to strong positive relations (e.g., life satisfaction between romantic partners, r = .75). Grouping associations into broad conceptual domains further revealed systematic differences across individual, relational, and contextual correlates. Overall, the findings highlight life satisfaction as a robustly embedded outcome that is consistently linked to a wide spectrum of psychological, social, and contextual factors, providing a comprehensive empirical foundation for future research initiatives.

WELLMOD: A Well-Being-Based Micro-Simulation Model
Dr Karan Singhal | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr Karan Singhal | University of Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Yannick Klein
Prof. Anna Kornadt
Dr. Christian Krekel
Conchita D’Ambrosio
Andrew Clark
Anna Gromada

There is growing recognition that people’s well-being should be placed at the centre of public policy design. Governments have begun to integrate well-being considerations into policy appraisal. However, policymakers lack practical tools to systematically compare policy options regarding their well-being impact relative to expenses.
We address this gap by developing a novel well-being-based micro-simulation model (WELLMOD) to support people-centred policy decision-making. The model simulates the dynamic impacts of various policies (regarding income, employment, health, education, housing, and social relations) on both individual well-being (defined as subjective, self-reported mental states such as life satisfaction) and the public purse. Across four European countries, WELLMOD links policy-induced changes in objective life conditions to changes in well-being, while simultaneously accounting for implementation costs, using integration with EUROMOD, a widely used tax–benefit microsimulation model in European policy analysis.
For each policy option, the model quantifies (i) changes in objective conditions relevant to well-being, (ii) resulting changes in subjective well-being, (iii) net public costs or savings, and (iv) shifts in well-being inequality across the population. First applications of WELLMOD show considerable variation across policy options in both their well-being returns and costs, yielding well-being-based cost-effectiveness metrics, expressed as well-being gains per unit of public expenditure.
To our knowledge, WELLMOD is the first model to integrate micro-level well-being dynamics with fiscal simulation in a unified framework. By operationalising well-being as a core criterion of policy appraisal, WELLMOD has the potential to transform how public policies are evaluated, and, ultimately, to improve lives.

Adaptation Across the World
Loris Piccotti
Show details
Authors:
Andrew Clark
Anthony Lepinteur
Loris Piccotti

Set-point theory posits that individuals adapt to major life changes in their lives and return to their baseline happiness level. In this case, the well-being changes due to these life events are only temporary in nature. The existing empirical evidence on the degree of adaptation is fragmentary in terms of both the countries taken into consideration and the life events that are analysed, and in particular we do not know whether adaptation is universal or on the contrary country- or event-specific. This paper represents the first attempt to construct a comprehensive atlas of hedonic adaptation to major events.
We analyse longitudinal data from 10 countries: Australia, Chile, France, Germany, Indonesia, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. We estimate panel regressions that trace out the within-individual changes in life satisfaction in the years leading up to an event and then the years following it. We examine ten major events, and consider a window from five years before the event to five years afterwards.
Adaptation is not universal. Individuals exhibit complete adaptation to marriage, childbirth and divorce, with life satisfaction returning to its baseline level within two or three years. On the contrary, the life satisfaction changes following unemployment, widowhood, poverty, retirement, and starting a relationship are persistent, with little to no adaptation even after five years. These patterns are remarkably consistent across all ten countries, despite their notable differences in terms of cultural norms and economic development.
This cross-country consistency shows that adaptation is determined by the type of event rather than the country context. More generally, our results are not consistent with the hypothesis of a universal hedonic treadmill.

The Cost of Looking “Too Technological” in Eldercare: Wearing an Exoskeleton Penalizes Social Evaluations of Female (But Not Male) Caregivers
Lara Bauer | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Lara Bauer | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria
Prof. Dr. Martina Mara | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria
Dr.in Sandra Maria Siedl | Johannes Kepler Universitaet Linz | Austria

Care work is embedded in gendered norms that frame it as a feminine field emphasizing warmth, making caregivers particularly subject to evaluation by colleagues, patients, and their relatives. A lack of alignment with these norms can elicit social penalties and foster mechanistic dehumanization, that is, perceptions of reduced humanness and increased object- or machine-likeness. The growing use of assistive wearable technologies such as exoskeletons in caregiving may intensify these dynamics, as visible technological augmentation can conflict with normative images of “human” care. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and theories of mechanistic dehumanization, this study examined whether exoskeleton use differentially affects the social evaluation of female and male caregivers.

In a video-based online experiment (N = 223), participants viewed one of four scenarios depicting a female or male caregiver during an eldercare interaction, either wearing or not wearing an exoskeleton. Participants rated the caregiver’s perceived warmth, competence, and machine-likeness.
Results showed no overall effect of exoskeleton use on caregiver evaluations. Instead, gender affected the impact of technology use. Without an exoskeleton, the female caregiver was perceived as warmer, less machine-like, and better suited to caregiving than the male caregiver, reflecting gendered role expectations. When wearing an exoskeleton, this difference disappeared: the female caregiver was perceived as less warm and more machine-like, whereas evaluations of the male caregiver remained largely unchanged.

These findings suggest that assistive wearable technologies do not inherently dehumanize caregivers but interact with gendered norms, selectively reshaping social evaluations in care contexts.

When research on polarization re-enters the polarized discourse: A case study on online virality and science misinterpretation
Dr. adrian lüders | University of Hohenheim, Stuttgart, Germany | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. adrian lüders | University of Hohenheim, Stuttgart, Germany | Germany
Dr. Dino Carpentras | ETH Zurich
Prof. Mike Quayle | University of Limerick | Ireland

Exchanging attitudes is an important form of interpersonal communication. Expressing attitudes allows individuals to reveal aspects of their identity, while observing others’ attitudes supports social categorization and evaluation. In 2023, we published a dataset in a leading social psychological outlet that explored these mechanisms in the context of highly charged political topics within the polarized U.S. electorate. Using belief-network analysis, we were also able to unfold systematic differences in the attitude-structures that define US-Democrats and US-Republicans. In 2025, our research was taken up and reframed by an influential X user (25 Mio views), sparking debate about the meaning and rigor of our findings. Because our results indicated a more compact belief system among Democrats, the claim of an “intolerant political left” went viral across conservative and right-wing networks. Attempts from our side to clarify the interpretation gained little traction, though several newspapers (including The New York Times) offered more balanced coverage. Tracing the trajectories of our data’s unexpected virality, this talk addresses an important dilemma: while disseminating research beyond academia is an important yet rarely achieved goal, researchers have little control over the dynamics that unfold once their findings become politicized objects within polarized debates. By reflecting on these possibilities, this talk aims to spark discussion about the opportunities and challenges of research dissemination as well as about the role of researchers as observers and co-creators of social knowledge.

From Experts to Citizens: Psychosocial Responses to Green Hydrogen in Luxembourg
Dr. Mariangela Vespa | IZES gGmbH | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Mariangela Vespa | IZES gGmbH | Germany
Jan Hildebrand | IZES gGmbH | Germany

The development of a sustainable hydrogen economy is an important building block for energy system transformation. Luxembourg is an emerging case for examining green hydrogen, characterized by early-stage deployment, high institutional trust, and dense governance structures, making it a particularly informative setting for studying acceptance dynamics. Additionally, cross-border hydrogen initiatives in the Grand Region increase the social visibility and perceived relevance of hydrogen technologies. In this context, Luxembourg and the Greater Region provide regional case studies to capture how emerging technologies are socially evaluated across production, transport, and usage structures.
This contribution provides early empirical evidence on the social acceptance of green hydrogen in Luxembourg, using a mixed empirical database. We combine qualitative interviews with expert stakeholders in the hydrogen sector (N=10), a systematic local stakeholder analysis, and a national survey (N=1027). This design links expert perspectives with population-level psychosocial responses to an emerging energy technology.
This contribution offers a context-sensitive national case analysis of acceptance dynamics. Results show how interacting cognitive–emotional, normative, and institutional processes influence social evaluation of an emerging energy technology. By mapping these mechanisms across different application domains of green hydrogen (mobility vs. industry vs. heating), the study offers empirical insights into the psychosocial pathways through which knowledge, trust, risk perception, and social and personal norms shape acceptance. In doing so, the findings advance models of sustainable technology acceptance by specifying how psychosocial variables interact across application domains, and how these interactions translate into differentiated patterns of support and acceptance toward green hydrogen in Luxembourg.

Units First or Tens first: How Home Language Affects Two-digit Auditory-visual Number Matching in Multilinguals
Dr. Angélique Volfart | Université du Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Angélique Volfart | Université du Luxembourg | Luxembourg
Dr. Rémy Lachelin | UniDistance Suisse | Switzerland
Prof. Christine Schiltz | Université du Luxembourg | Luxembourg

Previous literature suggests that speaking multiple languages greatly affects performance at numerical tasks. However, it remains unclear how the home language (HL) interacts with numerical performance in the two languages of mathematical instruction in Luxembourg (LM1 German switching to LM2 French).
In this online study, adult multilinguals speaking either Luxembourgish, German, French, Portuguese or a South Slavic language at home (n=140) were presented with an auditory German (LM1) or French (LM2) two-digit number word and asked to match it with its corresponding Arabic digit form. Presentation format varied such that the Arabic digits either appeared simultaneously on the screen, or with a delay between the decade digit and the unit digit (either decade then unit, or unit then decade).
Our results show a significant interaction between HL group and the task language: while Luxembourgish HL participants displayed a typical advantage of LM1 German over LM2 French in both error rates and response times, those with French HL showed the reversed pattern (LM2 > LM1). In addition, Portuguese HL participants made significantly more errors in German than in French while the opposite pattern was observed in those speaking a South Slavic language at home. No significant difference was observed in participants speaking German at home. A significant interaction effect between the task language and presentation format was also observed.
Taken together these results highlight the crucial role of HL and its linguistic structure, in addition to languages of mathematical instruction, on numerical performance.

Validation of a Process-Oriented Assessment of Listening Component Skills in Elementary School Children
Patrick Dahdah | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Patrick Dahdah | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany
Prof. Dr. Johannes Naumann | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany
Dr. Julia Schindler | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany
Dr. Maj-Britt Haffmans | Universität Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tobias Richter | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg | Germany

Listening comprehension is a foundational skill for learning and successful education, yet its assessment has traditionally focused on product-oriented outcomes at the text level, providing limited insight into the efficiency of processes underlying successful listening. The present study introduces ProDi-H (Prozessbasierte Diagnostik von Hörfähigkeiten bei Grundschulkindern), a computer-based, process-oriented test battery assessing the efficiency of listening component skills in elementary school children. The aim was to test the structural validity of ProDi-H as well as its cross-modal relations with parallel reading tasks.

ProDi-H was administered to a sample of 1,269 children in Grades 1–4 and included tasks measuring six word- and sentence-level processes: phonetic-phonological analysis, word recognition, retrieval of word meanings, syntactic parsing, semantic integration, and local coherence building. All subtests were presented auditorily, were binary decision tasks (correct–incorrect), and assessed both response accuracy and response latency as indicators of processing efficiency.

Confirmatory factor analyses conducted separately for accuracy (CFI=.967, RMSEA=.028) and latency (CFI=.977, RMSEA=.035) supported a six-factor model with distinct but correlated processes, outperforming models with one factor (general listening factor) or two factors (word and sentence factors). Additional models including parallel reading tasks from the corresponding written assessment (ProDi-L) found generally stronger correlations between factors within the same modality than across modalities. However, correlations between analogous listening and reading processes were not consistently stronger than correlations between non-analogous processes across modalities.

Thus, whereas cross-modal effects only partly met expectations, the findings provide clear evidence for the structural validity of ProDi-H as a measure of efficiency in listening processes.

Multilingual students often perform below their monolingual peers in the German school system (Henschel et al, 2022). While teaching approaches incorporating individual multilingualism in lessons and activities are considered particularly beneficial for this student group (Veermann et al., 2025), there is a lack of empirical evidence on potential compensatory effects. Therefore, we investigated the effects of multilingual teaching when implementing a language-supportive curriculum on education for sustainable development in German all-day schools. While all participating teachers and education professionals were trained to implement language scaffolding techniques, one group additionally worked on multilingual teaching approaches. Using multiple regression models, we predicted the posttest scores of 762 students (Grades 3 and 4) in domain-specific and general academic vocabulary, comparing the effects of language background (monolingual vs. multilingual), group (language-support training vs. additional multilingual teaching training) and moderation of language background effects. Relevant covariates (pretest scores, age, gender, cultural capital, basic cognitive abilities) were included in the models. As expected, we found that monolingual students reached higher posttest scores in the domain-specific vocabulary test than their multilingual peers in both groups (b=1.46, p=.008, rp=.10). By trend, the difference between monolingual and multilingual students was smaller when teachers were additionally trained for multilingual teaching (b=-0.99, p=.132, rp=-.05). For general academic vocabulary, no effects of language background emerged after controlling for the pretest covariates. To gain a deeper understanding of the differential effects of the two language support approaches, the results are discussed with consideration of implementation fidelity as well as class composition.

Does the Voice of Virtual Characters Matter? Comparing Expressive and Monotone Voices of Pedagogical Agents

Pedagogical agents — virtual characters designed to facilitate learner motivation and learning outcomes — are increasingly implemented into multimedia learning environments. This trend is accelerated by the availability of AI-based tools that can easily create visually and vocally realistic virtual characters. In contrast to visual aspects, voice characteristics of pedagogical agents have rarely been studied yet. This study investigates how the expressiveness of a pedagogical agent’s voice influences learner perception, motivation, and learning outcomes. Recognizing the prevalence of English instructional videos, we presented university students with an English-language instructional video and randomly assigned them to one of two conditions: expressive vs. monotone agent voice. We measured learners' perception of the pedagogical agent (API-R, Schroeder et al., 2017), their motivation (Isen & Reeve, 2005), and learning outcomes (retention, transfer). We hypothesized that the expressive voice would be perceived as more credible, human-like and engaging, and would further facilitate motivation and learning. To test for an influence of language proficiency, we collected a German non-native speaker sample (n=122) as well as an American native speaker sample (ongoing data collection). Preliminary results from the German sample suggest an interaction between voice expressiveness and language proficiency on learning outcomes: only more proficient non-native speakers benefit more from an expressive voice, while learners with lower language proficiency benefit more from a monotone voice. Data analysis is ongoing. The final results, along with discussion of theoretical and practical implications for designing effective pedagogical agents and virtual characters, will be presented.

Coordinated Growth, Not Attrition: Domain-Specific Slowing and Positive Coupling in Early Dual Language Learning
Dr. Robin Klaus Segerer | University Library Zurich | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Robin Klaus Segerer | University Library Zurich | Switzerland
Dr. Leila Schächinger Tenés | University of Zurich, Switzerland
Dr. Jessica Carolyn Weiner | University of Basel
Dr. Alexander Grob

Background. Early bilingual development is often framed as subtractive attrition driven by cross-language competition. Yet much of the evidence relies on non-equivalent assessments that limit valid within-child comparisons. We examined whether early dominance shifts reflect global heritage-language decline or domain-specific reorganization in a longitudinal cohort of dual language learners in Switzerland and Germany.
Design. The study followed 254 Turkish- and Italian-speaking dual language learners between ages 3;0 and 6;5 across up to three waves spanning the transition into compulsory early schooling. Using parallel-constructed, measurement-invariant instruments, we assessed productive vocabulary, receptive vocabulary, and sentence comprehension in both languages. Multilevel growth models estimated age-related schooling-sensitive effects and cross-language coupling.
Results. Broad attrition was not observed. Growth trajectories were positive across domains. Significant age-related deceleration emerged exclusively in heritage-language productive vocabulary (β = −.018, p = .012), indicating localized slowing during intensified majority-language schooling. Crucially, the main age effect remained positive, demonstrating reduced growth velocity rather than decline. Negative cross-language associations were restricted to productive vocabulary. In contrast, sentence comprehension showed robust positive within-child coupling (β = .027, p < .001), consistent with coordinated bilingual growth and potential transfer.
Conclusions. Early dominance shifts reflect schooling-sensitive, domain-specific reorganization embedded within a resilient and interconnected bilingual system. These findings challenge subtractive trade-off accounts and support a dynamic model of positively coupled early bilingual development.

Carry-over effects of competitive behaviors in cooperative situations: a trust-based reinterpretation of the cutthroat cooperation effect
Lea Lempert | Technische Universitaet Darmstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lea Lempert | Technische Universitaet Darmstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Nina Keith

The cutthroat cooperation effect describes how individuals who experience competition prior to cooperation carry over competitive behaviors (e.g., reduced knowledge sharing, inaccuracy) into subsequent cooperative interactions. Previous explanations attribute this effect to difficulties in transitioning from a chaotic competitive state to a more ordered cooperative state. We propose an alternative explanation based on trust dynamics: prior cooperation may foster trust, whereas prior competition may erode it, thereby shaping later behavior. In a 2 × 2 mixed-design laboratory experiment, 69 participants played a logic-based game with a confederate across two phases. The first phase was cooperative or competitive (between-subjects factor), followed by a cooperative phase for all participants (critical round). Behavioral outcomes included knowledge sharing and inaccuracy. In each phase, we assessed behavioral trust using a decision task and cognitive trust via self-report. In the first phase, cooperation led to higher cognitive and behavioral trust than competition. During the final cooperation phase, participants with a cooperative history reported higher cognitive trust than those with a competitive history, while behavioral trust did not differ. During the first phase, cooperation increased knowledge sharing and reduced inaccuracy. However, this difference did not carry over to the last, critical cooperative round. Mediation analyses still revealed the expected indirect effect of prior interaction type on knowledge sharing and inaccuracy via cognitive trust in the critical round. These partially supportive findings highlight cognitive trust as a potential mechanism shaping subsequent behavior and offer a trust-based reinterpretation of the cutthroat cooperation effect.

Asset or Liability? How and Why Ghost Negotiators Impact Opponent’s Psychological Perceptions and Distributive Negotiation Behaviors
Annik Strauch | Leuphana Universitaet Lueneburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Hiring consultants who advise during negotiations without being present at the bargaining table—so-called ghost negotiators—is common practice. Promising to increase negotiation success, ghost negotiation is a multi-million business. While ghost negotiators may offer important strategic benefits to their clients, opponents may dislike their involvement (e.g., due to fairness considerations). This mixed-methods paper combines qualitative, bottom-up data with sequential quantitative data to examine the effect of ghost negotiator involvement on opponents’ emotions, perceptions, and distributive behaviors. Contrasting social identity and social comparison theory with power and dominance complementarity theory, we explore beneficial and detrimental effects (i.e., decreased vs. increased competitiveness) and the underlying mechanisms. In Study 1 (N = 69), we categorized 962 open responses into 85 emotional, perceptual, and behavioral reaction clusters using large-language-model and thematic analysis, revealing predominantly negative reactions. In Study 2 (N = 435), a sequential quantitative experiment examining the most prevalent 25 emotional and perceptual clusters and distributive negotiation behaviors (e.g., first-offer behavior) corroborated these findings, also illuminating the underlying psychological mechanisms via exploratory factor and mediation analyses. Overall, opponents appear to become more competitive (e.g., less willing to make concessions, more assertive with their first offers) when facing ghost negotiator involvement. This effect was mainly driven by decreased trust and by perceiving the negotiation as more of a challenge, ultimately risking more impasses. Our findings suggest that the decision to hire a ghost negotiator consultant requires carefully weighing strategic benefits against opponent-related detriments. We discuss implications for theory, practice, and future research.

Jane Martha Momme | IPN - Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education | Germany
Show details

Trust in science is an important prerequisite for the societal acceptance of scientific knowledge. Participatory approaches in science communication, such as involving non-scientists in the co-design of science communication materials, are often proposed as a way to strengthen trust. However, the psychological mechanisms through which participation shapes trust-related judgements remain insufficiently understood.
The present work examines psychological distance to science (PSYDISC; Većkalov et al., 2024) as a potential mechanism linking participation and trust. Based on Construal Level Theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010), we propose that participatory formats foster trust by reducing perceived distance between publics and science, thereby shifting evaluations from abstract to more concrete construals.
In study 1 (N = 1,442), we tested the causal influence of social and hypothetical distance on trustworthiness perceptions and trust in scientists using a 2×2 vignette design. Reduced hypothetical distance (operationalized as the perceived applicability of scientific findings) significantly increased perceived expertise (d = 0.16), and multiple behavioural trust indicators, including willingness to be vulnerable (d = 0.26), influence granting (d = 0.19), and funding support (d = 0.14). In contrast, effects of social distance were nonsignificant.
Building on these results, study 2 adopts a pre-post experimental design to test the full causal chain: whether participation in the design of science communication materials (vs. no participation) reduces distance to science, and this, in turn, enhances trust. Together, these preregistered studies contribute to a more precise understanding of how participatory science communication can foster trust in science by targeting specific dimensions of psychological distance.
